The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. The appellant appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. The defence of the appellant was that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. The defence was that he had taken lease from various persons on the lands it had taken on leased from various parties and that the grains were grown by them on the lands they had taken on leases from various parties, and that the commodities were grown by the appellant on the lands him had taken on rent from various parties; that the presumption under section 49 of the Registration Act was not drawn. The defence, before the Sessions Judge and the Sessions Judge did not accept the evidence of the witnesses on the ground that they were interested in the appellant. The defence led evidence on the ground, that he was the next door neighbour and had a "soft corner for him" and that the presumption Under section 49 of that Act was not applicable in the case. The Sessions Judge rejected the evidence of one witness on the ground. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the presumption in his case was irreproved because of the exemption which agriculturists enjoy. Held, that the presumption of innocence under section 49 was irreprove because of the exemptions which agriculturists enjoy, and agriculturists from the presumption to be drawn from proof of storage only. The presumption under section 50 of the Registration act was irreprovable because of the exempting which agriculturists enjoy; and that the presumptions under section 49 were irreproved. The presumption of innocence in his case could not be drawn. The presumption was not drawn, because of the Exemption which agriculturists enjoy were. The presumption in his cases was irreproproved because the presumption under para 3(2) could not be raised against him. The presumption could not be based upon them. The presumption is not drawn, and the presumption under Section 50 of the Act is irreproved, because of that exemption agriculturists enjoy. The presumption cannot be drawn. If that presumption is not proved, then the case against him stands unproved because he is the next door neighbours and has a "soff corner for him". The presumption under Section 49 of the Act would be irreproved if there is something intrinsically wrong with that evidence. The presumption would be irremoproved because it is impossible to draw. The presumption may be drawn from the proof of storage, only. If that be so, then, the case against the appellant stands unprove because the presumption is not based upon them because of the exempted which agriculturists enjoy and agriculturists from that presumption to be drew from proof of storing only. If the presumption is drawn, then the offence would be irrepoproved because there is something else intrinsically wrong in that evidence. If that is so, then the presumption under s. 49 of the Indian Registration Act would be unproved. If that was not drawn the case against appellant stands un conse quence.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the premises in suit. The defendant was a tenant from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. The defendant continued to be a tenant from year to month under the provisions of section 116 of Transfer of Property. The defendant 's tenancy was determined by a notice to quit. The defendant did not acquire any permanent right in the land by prescription or otherwise and that by reason of the payment of rent on 8th March, 1925, and 16th March, 1926, the defendant became a tenant from 1st April, 1926. The defendant made a strenuous endeavour before the High Court to establish that as the Patta of 1913 as well as the Kabuliyat of 1924 were both invalid and inoperative, he was never a tenant in respect o the premises in question. The High Court held that the defendant was a mere monthly tenant under the plaintiff in respect of a premises in suit and that by virtue of the payment and acceptance of rent by the Receiver, the defendant was not a tenant in the premises in dispute. The High court also held that the tenancy was created by payment and acceptance and the suit was, in fact, one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. The High ' Court also held that by payment and receipt of rent a new tenancy was created, and as the new tenancy was for building purposes, it was a tenancy from month to year under section 116, Transfer of Property, Act, terminable by fifteen days notice. The High Curt also held that even if two successive tenancies were created for one year each, the facts admitted and proved would go to show that the tenant held over after the second annual lease and consequently a tenancy from year to months came into existence in accordance with the provision of section 116, transfer of Property Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926. The High, Court also held, that the defendant 's lease was for building purpose and that by acceptance of rent a tenancy from him was evidenced by acceptance of the rent from him in the year 1925, and consequently a tenant from that date was deemed to be a monthly tenant under section 116. The High Courts also held that on the facts of this case it would be quite proper to hold that the tenancy created by payment was tantamount to payment to the plaintiff himself. The High courts also held that as the defendant was an monthly tenant under a plaintiff in respect o t the premises in Suit, the High Court clearly held that the plaintiff was a tenant under the defendant in respect of his premises in suit, and that by the payment and receipt and acceptance of rents a new tenancy created by the defendant on 24th December, 1924, the defendant from that time became a tenant under section 106, Transfer of property Act, and the only question left open was whether payment to the Receiver amounted to payment to him to the plaintiff. The High appeals were filed by the defendant. The High High Court held, however, that the tenancy of the defendant was one from month to months under section 116 and that by payment of rent, the defendant held over and the Receiver 's assent to his continuing in possession was evidenced by accepted rent from him. The High Judge also held that in view of the purpose for which the tenancy was executed, the defendant ' was a tenant and no tenancy could be created by the two payments of rent, inasmuch as the defendant did not have any permanent right to the land by way of payment to the defendant himself. The defendant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The tenancy of the plaintiff was one from year to year under the provisions Of section 116 of Indian Transfer of Property and the only questions left open was, whether payment to him was tantamount to a payment to the plaintiffs himself. [696B] 2.

The appellant, a firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards, and for the assessment year 1961 62 in proceedings for the said assessment years, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) had no relationship to the power of the court to summon that record. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The finality attached to the order of the Income tax Officer under Section 138 (1)(b), of the 1961 Act is, thus, restricted to the cases where the information sought for by an assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the 1961 Act on or after the 1st day of April, 1960, the Commissioner may, if he is satisfied that it is in the public interest so to do, furnish or cause to be furnished the sought for information, if he was satisfied that there were no circumstances justifying its refusal. [560 G] 2. The finality which has 564 been attached to the orders of the Commissioner under Section 138 of the 1961 act is, thus restricted to the case where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person other than a court of law by a judicial order. [560 A B] 3. The finality attaching to the order under Section 138 does not affect the powers of the court, to require the production of the documents filed by an assessee before the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65 onwards and that the sanctity attached to the said order is, thus limited to the cases pending before it. [560 D] 4. The finality of attached to the assessment proceedings under Section 138 is, thus confined to the cases when the information sought is called for. [560 E] 5. The finality relating to the assessment of an assessee filed before the Income tax authorities after the repeal of Section 137 of the 1961 ACT is, thus extended to the cases which pending before it and that the status attached to the proceedings before the court when the court, by a judicial Order, requires the production of documents from the income tax department after April 1. 1964 relating to the period 1964 65 onwards. [560 F] 6. The finality assigned to the order by the Commissioner under section 138(1) (b) of the 1961 acts, thus restricted only to the cases wherein the information etc., as contemplated by Section 138(I)(b) of 1961 Act is called for from any person other to the assessee, other than a Court of law by judicial order. The finality attach to the order passed by a court to summon the production of document from the income Tax authorities after April1, 1964 relating thereto to assessment proceedings relating to the years 1964 65 to 1961 62 in respect of the record filed after April 1 1964 for assessment proceedings relating thereto to 1964 65 onwards is, therefore, restricted to those cases where the Information sought for by any assessee in respect thereof is called for only by a judicial authority. [560 B C] 7. The finality that has 564 been attach to the orders passed by a judicial officer. The finality attaches to the order is, therefore restricted to the matters where the information is called for, by a Judicial order. [561 D] 8. The finality, attached to the final order of the Tribunal under Section 138, does not affect either the powers of a court to require the produce of the documents in a case pending before it or by a judicial orders. [560 C] 9.

The appellant was a minor and was married to Seinaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotty died on May 3, 1946. The appellant and his wife were living at their mother 's house. The appellant was the guardian of his minor wife. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that the gift was not valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of his property under the Muhammadan Law. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the gift by the husband to his minor wife to be valid must be held to be valid on her behalf and that even a change in the mode of enjoyment is sufficient evidence of such an intention. HELD: The gift is by a deed which is registered and handed over by Mammotti to his mother in law and accepted by her on behalf of his minor son. The intention to make the gift is clear and manifest because it was made by a deed, which was registered and handed by Mammottty to his mother. The intention is clear and obvious because it was not made by a registered document no question in this behalf can arise. The intention of making the gift was clear and manifest. The intention was clear and obvious. [560 G] The gift was by a deed registered and handed delivered by Mammothotty to his wife. The intention could be clear and manifest since it was made at a time when a husband makes a gift to a minor who has no guardian of the property in existence. [560 F] The intention to deprive ownership on the part of Mammotta and to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. Mammottee was living at the time of the gift in the house of his mother in Law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him, for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father was living. The intention that the father be present, because he is held by implication to have resigned the management of his concerns to the husband is the sole reason. [560 E] In the present case there is a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammottty to his father on behalf of her minor son. [560 C] In the case of a gift to an orphan minor the rule is that if a fatherless child be under supervision of his mother, the gift would have been complete under Muhammadan law and it seems impossible to hold that by handing over the deed to his mother, he could nominate a person to accept the gift on behalf of their minor son. If Mammottsty had handed over the deed, the gift will have been complete. [560 D] In the instant case there is no legal guardian of the properties to accept the gifts on behalf of Seinaba. The gift was made by Mammatotty to her mother in law.

The respondent temple was a religious institution. The respondent temple was established in the year 1951. The respondent was a Hindu religious institution. In the year 1952 the respondent temple was administered by the Government of Madras. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of the amount of Rs. 1,50,000. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The respondent challenged the decree on the ground that the demand for levy of contribution was Premature, and that audit fee was demanded without determination under section 76(2) of the Act. The High Court upheld the contention on the ground of ab sence of determination by the Commissioner, which was never pleaded, and the High Court held that the audit fee was without jurisdiction. The High court held that the demand was Premature and that audit fees demanded by the Commissioner was without determination under Section 76(2). The High Court also held that the Audit fee demanded by the respondent temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. It was not the case of the respondent that the audit was without jurisdiction, and that the audit fees were without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD : 1. The Commissioner has to determine the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the religious institution. That im.plies that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts of the religious endowment. [924 E] 2. The Commissioner may not under section 76 (2) of Madras Act impose a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institutions governed by the provisions of the Act or its scheme. But the percentage of income levied as audit fee must of necessity be based on an estimate, and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demand is not precisely what is actually incurred for audit of the accounts. [925 F] 3. The Commissioner, in the present case, has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than the maximum prescribed) for meeting the cost of auditing the accounts, and to state it in terms of a percentage of the income. That im..plies that it turns out whether the amount demanded was not precisely equivalent, to the cost of audit of the institution. That expenditure is incurred. [926 E] 4. The Commissioner had not determined the cost of Audit of the religious institutions. That im, the percentage of Income levied as audit fees must of necessity, be based on estimate, and demand will notbe struck down merely merely because it turned out that the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be rendered. [927 F] 5. The Commissioner was not of the view that the demand made of the petitioners ' temple for the pay of a sum Rs. It is sufficient to say that the demand will be struck down only because it turns Out that the amount payable is not precisely equal to the costly incurred for auditing that accounts. [1027 C] 6. The Commissioner 's order was set aside and it is directed that the case do stand remanded to the High Court and that the High Court do dispose of the case according to law and in the light of the observations made in this judgment.

The appellant was a contemner under section 19(1) of the Act. He was prosecuted for committing con tempt of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the application of the appellant for issuing a notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing conucing of the High court. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High Judge. The High court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant preferred a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition as a matter of right under section 19 of the Act and that the High court had no jurisdiction. The appellant submitted that the High Courts had no jurisdiction in entertaining the writ petition and that the order of dismissal passed by the High Court was not an order initiating contempt proceeding. The appellant also contended that the order passed by the trial court was not an interlocutory order and could not be appealed against as a matter under section 19. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the trial court dismissing the application for issuing a show cause notice was not an Order initiating contempt proceeding and cannot be appealed against. [501B] 2. The matter has to be decided either finally or, may be, even at an earlier stage an order is made, which does decide some bone of contention raised before the High court adjudicating upon any matter raised before it by the parties, affecting their right, the mere order issuing the notice does not decide any question. [502C] 3. The matter had to be decided whether the appellant was proceeded against has committed contempt of the High Courts or not. If the alleged contemner in response to the notice appears before the High Judge and asks it to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section 20 of the Act, the order is not an order dropping the proceeding. [503F] 4. The matter having to be decided by the High court, it is not possible, nor advisable, to make an exhaustive list of the: typo of orders which may be appealable under section 19, but, if it is in violation of section 20, it may well be that an appeal would lie to this Court under section 19 from an order of the Supreme Court merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be preferred against as a matters of right under sections 19. [505B] 5. The matter is decided by the trial Judge in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the Act which provides "No Court shall initiate any proceedings for contempt, either on its own motion or otherwise, after the expiry of a period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed. " [505C] 6. The matter was pending in the High court and was not disposed of by the High Judge in accordance therewith. [506F] 7. The matter did not lie and was incompetent. [507F] 8. The matter could not be decided either by issuing a notice. [508C] 9. The matter must be decided either at an earlier point of time an order is passed, which does not decide a question. [608B] 10. The matter should be decided either provisionally or by way of an example to show that even orders made at some intermittent stage in the proceeding may be, appealable under section19. [509F] 11. The matter may be, a different matter if the order does decide some matter, affecting the right of the party aggrieved. If the order does not decide something against the alleged contemnor and cannot be appeal against as a question of right under Section 19.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another in the Court of the Magistrate, First Class, Delhi, under section 6(1 A) of the Act for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The Magistrate convicted the appellant under section 6 (1 A) and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the conviction could be sustained under section 6 of the Act as the words it wireless telegraphy apparatus " in section 6(I A) of Act XIV of 1933 were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphy transmitter " and that the conviction thereunder would be bad. Held, that section 6(2) of the 1952 Act continued to be on the statute book even after the amending Act of 1949 was repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952, and that it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. The words "if any person establishes, maintains or works a telegraph within India in contravention of section 4 or otherwise than as permitted by rules made under that section, he shall be punished, if the telegraph is a wireless telegraph with imprisoment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, and in any other case, with a fine which may extend up to one thousand rupees. The words are comprehensive enough to include the words it Wireless telegraphy apparatus ' in section 6 (I A) and, therefore, the legislature though, by the Act of 1948, inserted the said section in the Act of 1933, removed the same in the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and redundant. The words were comprehensive enough and did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The words used are comprehensive enough. The words 'if any person proves, maintains or worked a telegraph within a India in contravention o the provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the Act, but not the content of that Act. The words, 'if any, person establishes, maintain or works a wireless apparatus ' in sections 4 and 6 of the 1952 act, but not a surplusage not serving any definite purpose. The words of section 6(l) of the said Act were comprehensive enough, and did not prevent the possession of any wireless apparatus. Therefore, it cannot be said that section 6 (l) of Act XVII of 1933 by the amending Act was either covered by the provisions of the , or a surplusage was not served any definite purpose, and that section 6 of Act XVII Of 1933 by the amendment made by the amending act of 1949, was either covered By the provisions of that section. The words in section 6 of 1952 Act were comprehensive sufficient to take in a wireless transmitters, the section does not prohibit the Possession of a wireless transmiter. The words do not prohibit the delivery of a wireless equipment. The words did not prohibit possession of a Wireless apparatus. The language of section 6 (2) of Act XIII of 1885, therefore, clearly excluded the operation of the amending Act. The amending Act was repealed by Act XLVIII of 1952, and the amended Act was repealed. The words could not be said that the amendment was covered by the words "if no person establishes, maintained or worked a wireless transmitor" in section 6. The words cannot be said to be either covered by section 6(i) or a surplusagedage not serving a definite purpose. It is said that section 4 of the 1952 Amendment Act of 1949, which was repealed by section 6 (3) of the Amending Act of 1949 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made in the year 1951 as the said Act was repealed and that it could not be contended that section 6 was either covered under the provisions of Act XVIIof 1933 by the amended Act of 1949.

The appellant, a son of Adwaita, was the managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The appellant, who was the wife of Adwaitita, was a benamidar for her husband Aghore, and the appellant, who is the wife of Aghore Nath Roy, was the wife. The appellant filed two applications under section 36(6) (a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga which were purchased in execution of the decrees. The trial court dismissed the applications. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the court below was in error in treating the Chakrabortys alone as the decreeholders. Held, that the court could not go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decreeholders on record were in fact a benamidar or for another person in respect of the decree. The court could not treat the Chakrabortys as the decreeholder on record as the decree holder. The court can at all enter into the question as to whether Oramba Sundari was a benamidars for another person. The court has to order the payment of the decretal amount in such instalments as it thinks proper, and clause (e) further imposes a duty on the court to give a direction in such cases that if there is default in the payment of any one of the instalments, the properties restored to the judgment debtor under clause (e). The subsequent conveyance of these properties in favour of Orambaundari, the appellant, has been held by both the courts below to be a benamidar. The subsequent conveyance by Oramba Chandari, the wife of Orambala Sundari, the former managing Shebait, was a fictitious transaction. The subsequent conveyances of these properties, therefore, must be deemed to be the purchasers of these properties within the meaning of clause (c) of section 36(2). The court can order the payment Of the decretal amount under clause (c). If there is default, the properties are returned to the decreeholder purchaser. The court may order the payment to the decreeholders under clause (d) of section36(2). But it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled and in case of default in payment of any of the instalments the properties are sent to the decree holder purchaser. The subsequent sale of these properties by Orambali Sundari, is not annulled. The subsequent Conveyance of these properties is not annulled, and in case there is default on the part of Oramma Sundari, it is incumbent upon the court to order restoration of possession made by both the court below to give a Direction in such cases. The subsequent release of these properties on July 26, 1940, was a valid transaction. The court cannot at all enter upon the question as regards whether the decreeholder was in possession of the property when the decree is reopened, and in the case of default, the property is returned to the judgment creditor purchaser. The decreeholders, therefore, cannot be said to be the purchaser of these properties.

The appellant was the assignee of the subject matter of the suit. The respondents filed a suit for specific performance of the decree. The appellant contended (1) that the deed of assignment in favour of the respondents was not executed by Habib & Sons and (2) that the assignee of that subject matter of suit was not entitled to apply for leave under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the document in question was not a transfer or an agreement to transfer the decree to the respondent company by assignment of the decree when it would be passed, that the assignee was not entitled under the provisions of section 146 of the Code, and that the provisions of Order XXI, Rule 16 contemplate the actual transfer by an assignment in writing of a decree after it is passed and that while a transfer of or an agree ment to transfer a decree that may be passed in future may, in equity, entitle the intending transferee to apply for execution of the decree to a Court which passed it. The provisions of Order 21, rule 16 contemplate the delivery of possession of the property to the intending transferee of the decree by the transferor to the respondent. The provisions in Order XXI, rules 16 contemplate the transfer by an assignee in writing of the decree after it has been passed and that when the application for execution was received by the City Civil Court, the Court should have scrutinised the application as required by Order XXI, r. 16. The provisions contained in Order XXI Rule 16 contemplate a decree in existence which is transferred before the transferee can benefit from the provisions of rule 16. The language of Order XXI Rule 17(1) and (2), therefore, enables the transferee of the judgment to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. The language used in Order XXI rule 16, therefore, contemplates the actual transfer of the decree, while rule 16 requires that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while rule 17 requires that the actual transfer must be construed as meaning decree holder. It is not necessary that a decree should be in existence at the time of the assignment and that when a transfer of a decree is made, the transferee must be able to do so. The language in Order XXI Rules, 16 contemplate the physical transfer by an assign in writing or by operation of law within the meaning of Order XXI. Rule 16 contemplates the actualtransfer by an assignment, in writing orby operation of law and enables such transferee to apply to the Court which passed the decree to execute the decree to be passed in the same way and subject to such conditions as an applica tion made by the judgment holder. The words "decree holder" must be construed so as to apply to a case where there is no decree in existence at that time of the assign and the latter has become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that the language of Order 21 Rule 16 contemplates that the actual transferred transfer by an Assignment in writing of any decree that may, in the equity, entitle him to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after he is passed, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee of the original decree by assignment in writing within the meaning Of Order XXI, Rules 16. The words 'decree holder" in Order XXI are not intended to be construed so that to apply to an case where there was no decree in operation at the time when the application was received by a City Civil Court.

The respondent entered into a contract for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows 'W ' Type ' ' ' ' Type ' " ' ' ' " ' " '. The respondent was a contractor. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fix " S.H.W. Window ' Type '' ' ' 'T.H. windows ' W ' Type '. The Board accepted the tender and issued a notice to the respondent for the supply of "motor bus being one for sale of windows". The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the contract. The High Court held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable. On appeal by special leave, the Court held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted : one for providing doors and windows in a specified building, and the other for "fixing" those doors and windows. The High court held that the "invoice" for payment made out by the respondent passed. The contract was one for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed : it was not a contract for sale of a windows but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts, one for the supply or the sale of goods for consideration, and the labour charges in fixing the same and thus partly liable to sales tax. The High ' Court held that it was only upon the "fixing", the contract would not be complete and the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. The High, Court held that since the contract was for work, the property in the materials supplied by the respondent did not pass to the War Office under the head contract. The respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling window and door leaves and sashes etc. and entered into a "building contract" and to promote sale of its manufactured goods, undertook to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service, and the respondent was liable to pay sales tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The terms of the tender were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invooice" for payments made out by it. [419D] 2. The contract is a works contract. The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials though not accessory to the execution of the work. [420E] 3. The contract consists of two distinct contracts, one with the supply or sale of goods, and the delivery of the possession of, a chattel as a chattel to the buyer. The contract might be for work, and it may be a contract for work and labour or one for the sale of a chattel. But in both these cases the Court held on a consideration of the terms of the contract and the circumstances that the respondent had agreed to and did supply "motor Bus being one for the purpose of the work that the property in materials used does not pass to him. [421F] 4. The contract of sale is a contract whose main object is the, transfer of the property in, and the deliver of the possession, a chattels to the buyer, and the service rendered in connection with the installation are under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution or the contract of sale. [422F] 5. The contract does not pass on to the other party to the contract as movable property. [423C] 6. The contract, therefore, was one of service in the execution. [424F] 7.

The charge under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B Indian Penal Code was framed against Raj Kumar Agarwalla. The trial court convicted Raj Kumar Agarwal and Shanker Lal under sections 420 and 468 Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal by special leave, the High Court quashed both the charges framed by the Presidency Magistrate against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla. That circumstance would hardly warrant a conclusion that Raj Kumar, respondent too was an party to any criminal conspiracy to defraud and cheat Ram Avtar and Raj Kumar Agarwal. [724D] 1.3 The report which has been lodged by Raj Pal in the same very nature of thing made no mention about the name ofRaj Kumar Agarwalla respondent because it was the case of Raj Kumar that Raj Kumar represented himself to be a party. Raj Kumar Aggarwal was also told to Raj Kumar Agarwal, when the latter came to the shop of Ram Avtar. There is no infirmity in the judgment of the High Court as might induce us to interfere with the judgment of High Court as may induce us to interference. [725E] 1.4 The report which is lodged by Rajbir in the very form of things made a mention of the word of Raj Kumar Agrawal.

The petitioner was a commuter of the Indian Railways and was appointed as a commuters of the Indian Railway. On June 1, 1982, there were as many as 27233 unmanned level crossings on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. Adverting to robberies and dacoities in the running trains, it has been pointed out that they are problems of law and order, maintenance of which is an obligation of the State Governments. adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The emphasis is that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection should be provided and this is also necessary at once for the interests of the State and for the protection of the public and for the benefit of the public. It is relevant to point out here that in the counter affidavit the respondents have denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ petition. It is also relevant to point that in the writ petitioner the Railways in the Bihar State had stated in their counter affidavit that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that there was no negligence on their part and that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in the Bihar state was attributable to this factor only. Adverting further to robberies, it has also been pointed out by the respondents that they are problem of law and Order, maintenance ofwhich is an obligation cast of the State Government and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this country. It is necessary that this is worked out also in the Judges and if they have to fulfil their function as Judges, it would hardly be lodged elsewhere. It is, therefore, that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. The quality of the service should improve. The quality and the manner of service should improve, therefore, depends on the number of train accidents which are a menace to the system. Security both to the travelling public as also to the non travelling citizens must be provided and these means that accidents have to be avoided, attack on the persons of the passengers and prying on their property has to stop. The obligations cast by the Railways Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It is important to point out that in the instant case the Railways have denied some other allegations of the petitioner. The petitioner has maintained that he, may every citizen of this country for the matter of that, is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. Giving directions in a matter like this where availability of resources has a material bearing, policy regarding 724 priorities is involved, expertise is very much in issue, is not prudent and we do not, therefore, propose to issue directions. The quality, of the service must improve. The responsibilities cast by the railways Act and the rules under it must, be complied with and the same is necessary at once. It is true that in the affidavit the respondents had denied some of these assertions of the petitioners but no objection has been raised to the sustainability of the petitioner to maintain an action like this.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. The appellants filed applications for restoration of the lands on the ground that they were entitled to restoration of the land on the ground of default in appearance of the appellants and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal. The Tribunal dismissed the applications of restoration made by the appellants on the ground, that the applications for restoration made by them were barred by limitation. The appellants challenged the orders of the Tribunal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the applications. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the applications were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoring the appeals were within 30. The High court dismissed the applications for restitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of the appellants in all the four appeals. [144D] 2. The Tribunal has no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits. [144E] 3. The Tribunal is not bound by the decision of the Tribunal. It is also open to the Tribunal in such a case to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits. The reason is that in Regulation 19(1) and 19(2) the legislative authority uses the words "decide it on merits" but in Regulation 20 the expression used is "decided ex parte" and we see no reason, either in the language or context of Regulation 20, why it should not include in its scope and ambit an application for restoration of an appeal decided 145 on merits under Regulation 19(2). [144G] 4. The words "decides it on merits", therefore, are "decided exparte" and we are of opinion that the Tribunal committed an illegality of law in rejecting the applications of restoring the appeals. [145G] 5. The Tribunal was right in taking the view that the applications of restitution made by the appellant in all the three cases were well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. [145A] 6. The Tribunal had committed an error in dismissing the application of restoration made on May 6. 1961. [145B] 7. The Tribunal did not commit any error of law or in dismissing the appeals on merits. It committed an error apparent on the face of the record. [145C] 8. The Tribunal failed to exercise its jurisdiction in dismissing the restoration applications of restoration filed by the appellants in the four cases. [145E] 9. The Tribunal also committed an error by law in dismissing their applications for restoration. [145F] 10. The Tribunal erred in holding that the applications were barred by time. [145H] 11. The Tribunal should have decided the appeals on merit even though there was default on the part of the appellants to appear before the Tribunal.

[421B] 3. The fact, therefore, that there was not a single single word in the Bagchi ''s award to indicate even remotely that in his view, the award suffer from any infirmity, and that supports the presumption arisingfrom the use of that word "Kul hq samet" has not in any manner been affected by this Award. [422C] 4. The fact of that there was neither a single word nor in Bagchi "s award to show, even remotely that the property belongs to the family of Shri Ramchandra Swami temple. [423D] 5. The fact is that there is no single word in Khachi "s Award to indicate, whether the property belonged exclusively to the family or whether it was given in full proprietorship to Ramsaray Lal with only a charged on it for expenses of the religious ceremonies of the family. The fact therefore, that Ramsarai Lal was himself led to by the terms and of the Bagtchi Award into thinking that there was a single word In Bagchi "Sadhibandha" which point to an intention that Ramsarayi Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the village to the Temple of Shri Ramchandra temple, set aside the judgment and decree of the High Court. [424E] 6. The fact also that there was never a single word at Bagchi "

603 The two appellants before us are the President of the Avadh:The appellants before us were the President of Avadh Bar Association. They were the President and Action Committee of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of Avadh Bar association. The appellants before us, inter alia, alleged that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most parti san manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. They also alleged that they were responsible for the passing of the resolution. The High Court found that there was no contempt of Court. The High court further held that since the resolution was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 2, the appellants were liable to be punished. The High ' Court further held that the Chairman of the Action Committee, described as contemner Nos. 1 & 2, were guilty of contumacious conduct, and the High Court gave the ground that they were liable to punishment. The matter became clear when the High Court said on that aspect as follows: 603 "It is a matter of regret that the contem ners who are prominent members of the Avadh bar should have been embarked on the path of vilifying the Chief Justice of this Court and that we do not want to be over sensitive in the matter, keeping in view the surrounding circumstances in which the contu macious act was committed by them and also keeping in view that it was a single act of the Chief Justice for which the attack was made, we do not propose to punish contemners Nos. 1 and 2 for the contumacious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty, though we express our strong. disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeat ed". The matter becomes clear when the two appellants were convicted. The High "Court further held that though the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion, they were guilty of contempt as contemner No 2 was. The High Judge also held that since they were responsible to the passing of resolution, they were liable for punishment. The appeal was dismissed. The appellants then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the High Court. The appellants contended that the Chairman and Action Committee were guilty of criminal contempt. The High, Court held that since there was no Contempt of Court, the appellants could not be punished. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court did not wish to punish contemners for the contuma Mental conduct of which he held guilty of criminal Contempt. The language used by them was unfortunate. It was a single acts of the ChiefJustice for which the challenge was made, and also keeping In view the fact that it was single act of a Chief Justice for whom the attack was committed, we do no propose to punishatant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 for the contuma dilatory conduct of which they have adjudged them guilt though we express their strong. disapproval thereof. [605B] 1.2 The High Court observed that the Chairman, the Action Committee described as contemner "in the dis charge of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a most partisan manner under the control of Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he holds". The language used was unfortunate. The language of the resolution was unfortunate. There was no gainsaying that the members of this Court did not act in that manner. It was the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. [606C] 1.3 The High Court also did not want to punish contemners No. 1, though they did not wantto be over sensitive, while they were guilty. The High Curt did not want the language of the Resolution.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the respondent to vacate the premises on the ground of nonpayment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises to the sub tenants and that the sub tenants were tenants of the respondent and in this Court no serious argument was addressed on the points. The appellant contended that the tenancy by the letter of June 7,1948, was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and that the provisions of section 13(1)(e) were for the protection of his rights which he was entitled to waive. Held, that the tenancy was a new one and not a continuance of the old. The respondent 's suit for ejectment was not brought for the enforcement of the agreement which recognised sub letting as follows : " The respondent has waived his right in sub letting as well as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 13(2) of the Act. The respondent has not waived his right to sub letting. The respondent cannot be estopped from challenging the validity of the lease. The respondent is not entitled to sub letting as he has waived his rights in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 15 of the Act is for the protection and protection of his right which flows directly from an infraction of a provision of the Act which prohibits it. The respondent was not entitled to the protection of the revenue and to be enforced solely at the instance of the revenue officials, nor is the prohibition limited to cases for which a penalty is exigible In the instant case the question is not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement, which section 15 of The Act declares to be illegal. The respondent had waived his right directly from an infringement of a provision introduced into the Statute for the protection, of his rights. The respondent could not evict him under section 13 (1)(e). The respondent was entitled to sub let or alternatively he could not evicted the appellant under Section 13(1) (e) of the act. The respondent, therefore, cannot be precluded from challenging the legality of the lease on the ground as it was not framed solely for the protection or protection of his revenue and to the be enforced solely by the revenue officials.
