The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, to 'be committed by Madan Lal, one of the prosecution witnesses. Sethi, the first appellant in Criminal Appeal No. 44 of 1954, was charged under section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1955, to ' be committed by Madan lal, one of them, of the prosecution witness. The trial court acquitted the appellants of the charge under section 120B of the Indian penal Code. The High Court acquitted the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the offence as defined in section 5(1) of the Act was not a single act of bribery and that it could not be said of the appellants, that it was based solely on such presumption. Held, that the intention of the Act is to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act or of bribery or extortion practised by 188 him to whom he knows to be interested in or related to the person so concerned or from any person whom he knows that to be interested. The intention of the legislature was to create by words or by signs or by visible representations or words or by visible representation or otherwise abusing his position as a public servant. The intention was to create a by means of clauses (d) and (d) of section 5 and under sub clause (4) it was provided by sub clause (5) that "notwithstanding anything in section 21 of the Indian Indian Penal Code a railway servant shall not be deemed to be a public servant for the purposes of Chapter IX and section 409 of that Code". The words "any railway servant" in section 5 of the Act are not intended to be used in the sense of the term "public servant" in the sense that they are not intended merely to give or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case. The words "public servant " in section 5 are not intended only to give or to give any gratification for hushing down the potato case pending against them. The words used in section 5 must be understood in the sense in which they are used in the section. The words are not intended for the purpose of the section. It is not intended to give a meaning to the word "public servant". The words are used in a sense which is not intended merely for the purpose or object of the section but for the purpose and object of the Act. The words must be understood to mean that they are used only for the purpose. The words cannot be used in a manner which is not contemplated by the section. They are used in different senses and are not intended as to give a different meaning on the context. The words may be used in different contexts and are not meant to be used to give a restricted meaning. The words of the section are used in two different senses. The words in the section are not intended either to give a particular meaning or to give a wider meaning. The word "public" is used in a wide sense and it is not intended that the word "law" should be used in any sense. The words should be understood in their ordinary sense and not in a narrow sense. The word 'law" in section 3 of the Act has been used in a wider sense and it has been used for the purpose only of the purpose of section 3 of that Act. The word is used in the wider sense and the word "laws" in section 2 of the Act must be understood as meaning the law in force at the time of the commencement of the Act and not in the narrow sense of the word.

The appellant Bank of Saurashtra (hereinafter referred to as 'the Bank') entered into a contract of guarantee for the advance of Rs. 76,368 04 P. from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor Harilal Parmanaddas Adatia and his surety. The surety agreed to become surety on the specific understanding and with the full knowledge of the Bank that the principal debtor had offered two securities, one the pledge of goods and the other personal guarantee of the surety. The principal debtor was the surety. On September 16, 1957, the surety executed two promissory notes, one the pledged oil tins and another personal guarantee of Rs. 75,000/- on the same day. The surety executed two bonds, one the pawn of goods and another personal guarantees of the surety and endorsed by the surety in favour of the Bank. The surety gave personal guarantee on the specific understand that the principal borrower would offer two securities, two the pledge of oil tins, and another personal security of the surety, and endorsed by him in favour of Bank. The bond executed by the surety was in good faith and was independent of the pledge of the goods given by the principal debtor. The surety was discharged to the extent of the value of the security and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The surety, therefore, filed a suit for recovery of Rs.76,368 04. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit against the surety. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the surety had agreed to become sureties on the specific terms and conditions that the principal creditor had offered two security on the specific assurance that the principal guarantor would offer two security on behalf of the surety by way of security for the advance and, therefore, in view of combined operation of sections 138 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, (Act ' for short), the surety was not discharged from his obligation under the guarantee and that as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of pledge of goods, the surety would not be discharged from his obligations undertaken under the letter of guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The surety having lost one security, the surety is discharged to the amount of the security lost as provided by section 141. [83D] 2. The surety is discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letters of guarantee. [83E] 3. The surety would not, therefore, be discharged from the liability undertaken under the Letter of guarantee. The bail would not be discharge even if it is found that a creditor has taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantees on the good faith of other security being offered by the principal creditor which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities. [83F] 4. The surety has given personal guarantee on behalf of his personal guarantee on a specific understanding and without the consent of the surety parts with the security. The surety also gave personal guarantee of goods and that as he had taken more than two security on that particular day, the surety could not be discharged even if it was found that a debtor had taken more or one security on that day. [83G] 5. The surety had given personal guarantee to the extent that the principal debt was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank, yet the surety would be discharged from liability under the letter guarantee. [84G] 6. The surety himself agreed to give personal guarantee on that particular date. The surety did not accept the proposal for cash credit facility on the specific promise. [84H] 7.

The appellant was a member of the family of the patelki inam lands. The appellant was the son of Amritrao patel. The appellant claimed that as a result of this partition, the " patelki Inam " lands were divided and the lands in suit were allotted to the share of the appellant. The trial court held that the appellant was not entitled to hold the " p Patelki inam " lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family. The High Court held that (1) the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 714 services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government; (2) the lands in question were allotted to a share of the p Patelki Inam lands; and (3) the grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied. Held, that the rights which the Rokades family had in these lands were rights of dealing with the property as owners, subject to a member of family rendering patelki patta lands as a member of a family, irrespective of whether he performs the service or not. The grant was not a service grant, and no question of title arises against Government, even though the lands were shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866. Amritrao p Patel, including the plots which were made khalsa in 1904 05, were (1) (2) I.L.R. 18 All. 9/IA and (3)(a) inapplicable.

The appellant 's family was governed by the Hindu Law of inheritance and succession. The appellant 's father was a Cutchi Memon. The appellant was a Cutch Memon. He was a Cutcher. He was governed by Hindu law. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the family property. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the rules of Hindu law were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi Memons settled in Madras. The High court held that the appellant was a cutchi Memon widow and that the rules Of Hindu law were applicable to Cutchi Memors governed matters of succession and inheritance only. The High ' Court further held that the rule of Hindu law was not applicable to Cutch Memons. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (1) The rule of Hindu Law is applicable to all Cutchi Membs governed matters of inheritance and inheritance. [723 E] (2) The rule is not applicable to cutch Memons, subject however, to the provisions of section 3, all Cutchi memons settled in Bombay. [724 E] (3) The rule does not apply to Cutchi memon widow, but only to the rules as to joint family property. [725 B] (4) The rule has no application to Cutchi the Memons settled by the customary law. [726 C] (5) The rule applies to all Cutch Memors settled in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930. [727 C] (6) The rule also applies to Cutchi Moons. The rule does apply to Cutch memons settled by customary law. The rule is supported also by the records of several other cases in that High Court. [728 C] (7) The rule deals with succession and inheritance according to Hindu law. [828 D] (8) The rule provides that subject to section 3, the all Cutchi Moors would in matters of succession or inheritance be governed by the Mahomedan law. [928 E] (9) The rule refers to the rule of succession and succession according to the rule. [729 E] (10) The rule, therefore, does not apply in matters of inheritance or inheritance.

The appellants manufactured the fabrics of different types. The appellants manufactured the said fabrics. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India before the High Court challenging the vires of the said notification. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the notification. The appellants preferred a petition under Article 226 of the constitution of India. The High court allowed the petition. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of "place of removal" in section 2(1) of the Act is the definition of "factory" in section 3(1) and the Explanation to rule 9(1) is not required to be made. [707B] 1.2 The definition of 'place of removal' in section 2 of the Act does not include any premises appurtenant to such place, where the excisable goods are manufactured or produced. [708C] 1.3 The definition of the expression "place of manufacture" in section 5 of the Act, is not required. [709F] 1.4 The definition of factory" in section 4 of the Act also does not include the place where the excisable article is manufactured or produced or manufactured. [710G] 1.5 The definition of place of manufacture and production of the excisable goods is not required in any manner, indicate that it is only when the goods are removed from the factory premises it will be removal and when the excisable goods manufactured or produced, but any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf, whether for consumption, export or manufacture of any other commodity in or outside such place, are produced, cured or manufactured. It is only when a commodity is taken outside the factory it will be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises as mentioned in sub rule (1) of rule 9. [712C] 1:6. The specification is not required for the purpose of collection of excise duty. [713C] 1.:7. The specification in sub rule(1) does not indicate that it was only when the excisable article manufactured or produced is cured or manufactured but any premises ancillary thereto, which is used for the manufacture of another commodity in a continuous process, shall be deemed to be removed from such factory premises. [714D] 1.8 The specification is made by the Collector is of any premises appurtenant or to such place. In the instant case, the appellants are liable to pay excise duty on the yarn which is obtained at an intermediate stage and, thereafter, processed in an integrated process for weaving the same into fabrics. Be that as it may, as we have held that the commodity which is obtained by the appellants is also liable to the payment of excise duty, the yarn that is produced by the appellants are also liable to payment of excise duties. [715E] 1.9 The definition of manufacture in section 2 (1) is the definition in section 2. The specification of place of removal is not required, in any manner indicate that it has to be made and, in our view, cannot be made of the place where it is obtained at a intermediate stage and consumed or utilised for the manufacture or production of the finished product. [716G] 1:10. The specification that has to be make by the Collector, is of any place or premises appurtenant thereto. The specification, in the instant case cannot be made by the appellants. [717G] 1.:11. The specification regarding the place of manufacture, production or manufacture of the excisable article at an intermediate stages to be removal from such place and in the manner prescribed. The specification has been made by the collector is of any other premises appurtenant to the place of manufacturing or production of excisable goods.

The petitioner filed a suit for a declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the Hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme and acting upon it after it was published. The trial court dismissed the suit. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, Bulandshahr. The Additional District Judge dismissed the revision petition. The petitioner thereafter filed a revision application before the Additional Civil Judge, Bulandshahr, which was dismissed. The petitioner then filed a revision before the Additional Judge, who dismissed the revision application. The petitioner contended that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. The Additional Judge dismissed the Revision application. The Additional Civil Judge held that the suit had been not maintainable for a declaration restraining the Hearing Authorities under section 68 L of the Act. The petitioner thereupon filed a revision to the Additional District judge, who dismissed it. The petitioner challenged the order of the Additional District Magistrate, which was also dismissed. The Additional Additional District Judge held that since the jurisdiction was impliedly barred, the suit was maintainable for the relief prayed for by him since the jurisdiction had been impliedly barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the suit should have been dismissed at the threshold under order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that it did not disclose a cause of action. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts in such matters is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. It is not open for a civil court, to issue an injunction restraining a Hearing Authority from proceedings 546 with the hearing of a case and exercising statutory functions. [145E] 2. The jurisdiction conferred on the Civil Courts is exclusive in nature and it is open to a Civil court to issue any order of injunction restrain the Hearing Authority under section 68 D of the Act and it is for the Hearing Authority to consider such objections and representations and to pass appropriate orders thereon. [145F] 3. The jurisdiction under section 68 of the Act is exclusive in form and it is no longer open to a criminal court to issue a direction of injunction restraining a hearing of the suit and exercising its powers. [145G] 4. The jurisdiction is exclusive in the character and it can not be open to a court to issue such an order of interim injunction restraining the parties from proceeding 546 with the Hearing Authority. [145H] 5. The jurisdiction to issue an appropriate order of injunction prohibiting the Hearing Authority is exclusive in operation and it is neither open to a public court to issue the order of injunction nor can it be open to any civil court to question an order of stay restraining the Hearing authority from proceeding 546 without the hearing of an appeal. [145C] 6. The jurisdiction in the civil courts is exclusive in its character and it cannot be open to the civil court to Issue an order of restraint restraining the Hearing Officer from proceeding 546 in the suit. [145D] 7. The jurisdiction vested in the Civil Courts under section 68 A of the Act extends to the matters mentioned in the scheme and it is only the Civil Court to issue an interim order restraining the Hearing Agency from proceeding 546. [145B] 8. The jurisdiction exercised by the Civil Courts are exclusive in character. It is open to the Civil Court, the District Judge and the Civil Judge to issue an ad interim order restraining a Hearing authority from proceedings 546. [146C] 9. The jurisdiction exercisable by the Civil Court is exclusive in respect of the matters mentioned therein. [145A] 10.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. He was convicted by the Special Judge, Delhi, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161, Indian Penal Code and to two years rigorous imprisonment under section 161 of Indian Penal Code, and to two y ears under section 161 Indian Penal Code respectively. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence before the High Court. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentenced the appellant to undergo rigorous sentence for two years. The appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant under section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption Ac tions Act was not excessive. Held, that the conviction was not excessive, because the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute. The appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as public servant within the meaning of section 5(1)(d) of the Act. The appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife expressed his reluctance to send Miss Eylene with him to the police station and therefore the appellant was guilty under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and thereby obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. The appellant in his official capacity as a police officer was expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and to uphold the maintenance of law. The appellant grossly abused his position as a police Officer and extorted money from Rushare Nathaniel handed over the currency notes to the appellant who put them in the left side pocket of his trousers. The appellant did not prove that there was a gross abuse of his official position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case it was established that the appellant had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to show, in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. The appellant could not prosecute either Miss Eylene or Russel Naniiel or Russel C.C. No. 63 D of 1964. The appellant, in his official capacities as a police pateliel, was expected to keep a high standard Of integrity and to maintain a good standard of integrity.

The appellant was a public servant and was charged with having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to Doraiswamy in seeing that a speedy and favourable settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway, subsequently the Eastern Railway. Chatterjee in cross examination clearly showed that he had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction accorded by him was not a valid one. The Special Judge rejected this contention and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 and in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the sanction accorded in this case was not a proper sanction in the case was a valid sanction. Held, that the sanction was not a mere sanction. The sanction was not valid in the absence of any question being put to Mr. Bokil to judge the truth of the allegations made against the appellant by calling for the records of the connected claim cases or other records in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for any record in connection with that matter from his Office nor did he called for any record. The sanction accorded was not a invalid sanction. The sanctioning authority was not competent to grant the sanction. The order granting the certificate shows that the learned Judges who heard the application were of the opinion that the sanction granted in this case is not a valid sanction and the evidence of Mr. B.okil was not expressed reason for the granting of the certificate having failed, the appeal must be dismissed and the decision of the High Court in upholding the conviction and sentence of the appellant must be upheld.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenants under section 14(1) (b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The tenant filed a written statement and contended that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The Rent Controller held that the landlord had no right to evict the tenants on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the tenants against the orders of eviction and set aside the orders of the appellate authority. The tenants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the orders of their eviction and set them aside. The High court held that the requirement of the landlord bona fide and ordered for eviction of tenants was not bona fide required for demolition and reconstruction and that it was inherent in such a life interest that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(I)(b) as grounds for eviction of tenant by demolition and reconstruction are raised in this appeal by the tenants. The High ' Court held that the tenant had only a life interest in the premises and that it is inherent in such an a life interest, that it is neither permissible for the tenant to invoke section 12 nor subject to the provisions of section 13 and 13, on an application made by a landlord the Controller shall, if he is satisfied (b) that the building is bona fide required of the landlord for the immediate purpose of demolishing it and such demolition is to be made for the purpose of erecting a new building on the site of the building sought to be demolished, pass an order directing the tenant to deliver possession of the building to the landlord before a specified date. The High, Court held that since the interest of the remainder man may be prejudiced, the landlord cannot evict the tenants. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The tenant has only a lifeinterest in the premises. He holds a life interest on the basis of a trust deed. The interest of the remaining man may be affected by the demolition and reconstruction of the building. The landlord has only a right to ask for eviction of his tenants on the grounds available to him under the Act. [775B] 1.2 The tenant has a life interest. He holds life interest in a property. He holds the life interest in it. He holds an independent life interest in that property. He is entitled to enjoy the property for his life. [776C] 1.3 The tenant has been on his own right under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants. He holds that the landlord has only life interest in his premises and who admittedly has a life Interest in the premises cannot evict the tenant on these grounds. [778D] 1.4 The tenant has no right to ask to for eviction of a tenant on the ground that the building soughtto be demolished as that action would, per se, be not bona fide. [782E] 1.5 The tenant has also a life interest and right to enjoy the properties for his life time subject to identical charges as absolute owners, with right of sale, gift, etc. [785F] 1.6 The tenant has merely a life interest which he holds a lifeinterest. He holds no life interest in any property. He has been on the own right under a deed of Settlement as trustee receiving rents from the tenants from the tenants and who admittedly had a life interest therein. He holds only a life Interest. He holds another life interest in this property. He also holds a life Interest on the basis that he has only a Life interest in the property. He does not hold any life interest in such property. [786E] 1:7 The tenant has not a life interest nor any right to enjoy any property for his lifetime.

The appellant decree holder filed a suit for recovery of Rs. The appellant decree holders filed a suit in the court of the District Judge, Lucknow in the year 1966. The District Judge dismissed the suit holding that the trees, which were part of bhumidhari rights, were included in the whole of the land. The District judge dismissed the suit. The appellant filed a second appeal in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by certificate. The appellant contended that the trees which were part part of the bhumidhari rights were included in part of the land and that the trees were deemed to be parts of the "land". Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of the Act is wide enough to include trees and a grove. [723C] 2. The definition is wide enough. It is wide enough, and an inseparable part is always included in the entire. [724D] 3. The definition does not include trees and grove land. [725E] 4. The definition includes trees and a farm land. [750E] 5. The definition covers trees and a field and an inseparable portion is always included therein. The uncut trees are deemed to be part of the "lands". [726F] 6. The uncuts trees are deemed on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncotable trees are deemed not to be parts parts of the land, but they are on lyards of trees in groves and grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench). [726G] 7. The uncat trees are deemed as parts of the 'land.

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC for having caused injuries with a chopper and those injuries "could" have resulted in the death of Suku. The trial court convicted accused 2 to 6 under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of accused 2 to 4 for an offence punishable under Section 302, IPC. The High court confirmed the conviction and sentence of accused 2 and 3 for an offence of murder under Section 302/149 IPC. The appellants filed a special leave petition against the judgment of the High Court. The High, Court, on a consideration of the evidence, came to the conclusion that the accused No. 1 had caused injuries with the chopper and that the death had occurred due to multiple injuries which were found sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The High ' Court, however, confirmed the conviction. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The intention to cause death of Suka was not sufficient in the normal course of nature. The intention to causing death of Sukha was not sufficient to cause death and the death had been occurred due to several injuries which were sufficient in the usual course of nature, to cause death, and the death has occurred due to various injuries which were likely to cause death in the ordinary way to cause death; and, therefore, the conviction of all the appellants for an offence with the aid of Section 149 IPC was not permissible. [912D] 1.2 The intention to commit murder of Suka had been proved by the medical evidence. The intention was not sufficient for causing death of the deceased. [913B] 1.3 The intention to caused death of Sukku was not sufficient. The intention of causing bodily injury on the deceased was not sufficient, in the ordinary sense to cause death but looking to the weapon with which he was armed and the nature of number and seat of injuries, it is not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by him were not sufficient in ordinary course of type to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the Ordinary course of nature To hold him guilty of an offence under section 302 IPC, even the trial court, which tried the six accused persons, was not justified in recording a conviction against them for the substantive offence of murder punishable under Section 304 Part I against the appellants for other offences with the aid Of Section 149 IPC also. [914C] 1.4 The intention to inflict bodily injury on Suka was sufficient in the circumstances of the case and it is not impossible to say that all the four appellants had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injury on their deceased as were likely to causing death. [915B] 1:5 The intention to Cause death of Sukrku was sufficient in ordinary sense to causing death, and, therefore he can be imputed with the knowledge that with those injuries it was likely that death of Sura may be caused and, therefore the conviction of the appellants for the offence under Section 326/149 IPC was not justified. [916C] 1:6 The intention to kill Suka was enough in the ordinary and course of nature for causing death. None of the injuries caused by them according to the postmortem report were on any vital part of the body, though some of the injuries were found sufficient to cause the death. The intention could not be attributed to them and the medical evidence also shows that the injuries sustained by Suka were not sufficient. [917E] 1.7 The intention to committing murder of Suku was sufficient to cause such bodily injury which was likely to cause the murder of Sukha.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922, on the basis of its accounts for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian Company). The Income Tax Officer, on the view that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 68 and 1968 69, held that the royalty amount should be assessed at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per annum. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount should be treated as cash basis for the purpose of Section 5(2)(a) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was not maintaining any particular method of accounting regularly in respect of royalty amount and that the alleged statement in the returns relating to the assessment years 1967 68 and 1969 69 to the effect that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis was an incorrect statement made by the Indian Company which was not aware of the true state of affairs relating to the assessee 's accounts. The assessee preferred the appeals to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting adopted by the assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis it is immaterial when did it actually receive the amount. [105D] 1.2 The method of accounts adopted by the Indian company does not amount to receipt of income by the assessee. The method of Accounting adopted by the petitioner is binding upon it. [105E] 1.3 The method of account accounting regularly adopted by an assessee is binding on the department. [105F] 1.4 The method of calculation of royalty amount payable to the assessee is not binding upon the Department. [105G] 1.5 The method of computation of royalty amount is not binding on the Department. The method adopted by the Income Tax Officer is binding upon him. [105H] 1.6 The method of computing royalty amount payable is binding upon both the parties. [105A] 1.7 The method of calculating royalty amount payable by the assessee in the books of the Indian Company does not amount either to receipt of the income by the IndianCompany or to receipt, clause (a) or clause (b) of sub section (2) of Section 5 has no application whatsoever and that Section 5(1)(a) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts on mercantile basis. [105B] 1.8 The method of ascertaining royalty amount payable in the books is not binding. The method employed by the assessee for the relevant accounting years is really relevant when did it initially receive the same in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own Books at Coventry. [105C] 1.9 The method of assessment adopted by the appellant for the relevant year is certainly relevant when did the assessee ''s accounts at the end of the calendar year and determined the royalty amount payable. [105J] 1.10 The method of assessing royalty amount payable for the assessment years 1968 68 and 196869 to the assessee, is obviously irrelevant when did it ever receive it in U. K. in the form of pounds and make an entry to the effect in its books at Coventries. [105 G] 1.11 The method of making the entries in the books relating to the accounting years 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1968 69 to the effects of the assessee ' accounts is really relevant. [105 E] 1.12 The method of valuation adopted by the respondent assessee for the assessment year 1967 68 and 1970 69 to the extent of Rs. 2,000 per cent. The method for computation of royalty is not binding as it is immaterial in the case of a non resident assessee like the petitioner clause (a).

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statement of the approver was not corroborated in material particulars and qua the appellant. HELD : (1) The statement of Santu, brother of the approver is no corroboration of the approver 's story because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 and the knife was found blood stained and the unusual character of the knife which fitted in with the dimensions of the injurious caused to the deceased. [736 E] (2) The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Lord Abinger "it deserves to have all the reverence of the law". [736 F] (3) The rule of prudence is almost always unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [737 C] (4) The rule is almost always safe to convict upon the uncorroborated testimony of an approver. It cannot be doubted that under that section a conviction based merely on the uncoriterroborated testimony is illegal yet the Courts nevertheless cannot lose weight of the rule. [738 E] (5) The rule does not require any independent evidence, implicating the particular accused. [739 F] (6) The rule requires some independent evidence, implicate the particular accused, and it is not necessary for them to prove that there is corroboration of the accomplice. [740 C] (7) The rule has been consistently followed by this Court in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King (1) where it was held that there should be corroboration of the evidence of an accomplice. [840 E] (840) The rule cannot be said in the words oO the first accused also. [841 D] (841 E] (9) The rule must be followed in every case where the evidence of a co accused is corroborated by the statement of a coaccused. [842 E] (10) The rule can be stated in the words in which it is almost always difficult to accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in material particulars. The rule of practice is almost always easy for the judge to warn the jury of the danger of convicting upon such unconfirmed evidence. [843 E] (11) The rule may be stated in a particular case but it has been always unsafe to rely upon the evidence of the accomplice without corroboration in regard to each accused. [844 F] (12) The rule should be followed in all cases where the evidence is not corroborated in all particulars. [845 E] (13) The rule in the words used in section 133, illustration (b) may be stated as follows : According to the former, which is a rule of practice, an accomplice is competent to give evidence and according to the latter which is a Rule of practice it is almost unsafe to convict on his testimony alone, but the judge should point out to the jury that it is within their legal province to convict upon such uncon firmed evidence (R. v Baskerville (1) [1941] A.C.R. 844, referred to. (14) The rule applies to all cases where an accomplice is a competent witness. [846 F] (15) The rule also applies to cases where the conviction is based upon the uncoredroborated testimony. [847 E] (16) The rule, however, applies to cases in which the approver ''s evidence is sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which he has been charged.

The appellant was charged in the Court of the Special Judge of Patna for an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was charged under section 5 (2) readwith section 5(3) of the Act read with section 21 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and sections 161 and 165 of the Indian penal Code. The Special Judge acquitted the appellant but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of that Act and therefore a 'public servant ' within the meaning Of section 21 of Indian Penal Code and section 21 of The Indian Penal Code was not attracted. Held, that the appellant could not be deemed to be a public servant under the meaning of that section. The appellant could not, therefore, be deemed to have been a public servant in view of the language of section 21, Indian Penal Code as it stood after the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958 (Act 40 of 1964). The appellant was a person who was a Class Iii servant and was employed as a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops and was therefore a public servant. The appellant, therefore, cannot be deemed to ' be a public servants within the meaning o section 21, of the Indian. Penal Code. A. Monterio vs The State of Ajmer(2), it was held by this Court that a person, who was a class Iii servant, and was employed in the Works Manager who was an officer of the Government and was therefore an officer in the service or pay of the Government, was one who was appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. The appellant cannot be deemed a public servant as defined in section 21, because he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the Transport Corporation Act, 1950 or of any other law that he could be said to be a 'public Servant within the meaning ofs. 21, Indian penal Code and section 2, Prevention of Corruption act. The appellant is not a public servants as defined in the section. The words 'public servant' include 'every officer in the Service or pay of Government ' within the terms of section 21 (9) of the Indian Police Penal Code. It is not necessary to refer to the definition of 'public servant'. The definition of 'Public servant ' in section 21 of section 21 is wide enough to include every officer in the services or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of a Government company as defined in s. 617 of the . The appellant was not an officer in a service or pay or of a Corporation engaged in any business or industry which was established by a State Act or a Government company. The appellant had been convicted as a public servant by the Special Judge. The appellant 's conviction was therefore not justified.

The appellant was convicted for contravening cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Declaration of Stock Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. He was further convicted for contravening Buldana District Price Control Order, 1965, and sentenced forlaughtervening section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Slaughter and Sale of Stock Order 1964, and convicted for contravening 271 of the Defence of India Rules, 1962. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence passed on him by the High Court. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentences passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3. The appellant contended that the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal and valid and that the sentence passed on the accused was illegal. Held, that the High Court having set aside the order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of Ratanlal will however be released. The rule is in the following terms: "141 (2) If in the course of any judicial proceedings a question arises whether a person was duly informed of an order made in pursuance of these Rules, compliance with sub rule (1 ), or where the order was notified, the notification of the order shall be conclusive proof that he was so. " The rule is not in the following form: "141(2) If the order is notified, the notice of the order to show cause why the order should not be set aside. " The Rule is in the same form as the rule. It lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. Rule 141(2) is in the terms: "142(2) if in the course o any judicial proceedings, a question arises Whether a person was properly informed of an earlier order or not. " The fact that the rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the Defence Of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any enactment other then, unless the notification of such order has been challenged, much less declared ultra vires, both in England and in India. The rule does not matter that section 43 of Defence of India Act provides for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The Rule does not matter Because section 43 of The Defence of India (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964 does not matter whether section 43 of defence of India Act provide for the publication or order made under the rules and they must provide for proof In judicial proceedings of a fact of publication, the notification shall be conclusive evidence that he was not so informed. The Rule must necessarily provide for proofin judicial proceedings of that fact of publication; but a failure to comply with sub rule(1) (i) shall not preclude proof by other means that he had information of the order, (ii) shall not prevent proof by other other means that the person had information of his order, (iii) shall not avoid proof by other than that he had knowledge of the order. Rule 141 (2) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1 ) of the Defenceof India Act. Rule 142(2) does not matter as section 3 of Defence of Indian Rules provides that "The provisions of this Chapter shall have effect Notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith, but a failure of compliance with sub rules (1) (ii) will not preclude proof from other means that it has information of the fact, of publication.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302/34 I.P.C. and was sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. The High court confirmed the conviction of the appellant but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone. The State filed an appeal in the High Court. The High, Court confirmed the acquittal of the appellant to the extent of the sentence. The State contended that the only inference which arises from the fact that violet gave the particular shout is that by so doing, he intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh, Section 107 of the Penal Code which defines abetment provides to the extent material that a person abets the doing of a thing who "Intentionally aides, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that act. The High ' Court rejected the contention. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The only inference which arise from the fact is that by reason of the violet given by the accused persons, they might accomplish their aim. [612G H] 2. The court which acquitted Shri Ram was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was, opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held, the demands were opposed by the defence and the parade is there fore not hold, that the only conclusion which arises from that fact is that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplishes their aim. The mere fact that the accused were lying in waiting on the other sides of the road, does not mean that he was aware of the nefarious design of Sia Ram and his companions. [613G H] 3. The mere circumstance that Shri Ram was aware of his nefarious designs cannot be a ground for rejecting the conviction of Shri Ram. [614B] 4. The mere possibility that he was so flooded with work that he could remember no details of an important murder trial cannot be a reason for rejecting the evidence of the witnesses. [615C] 5. The mere absence of a mention of the fact that he was a party to the murderous design cannot be a basis for rejecting the prosecution and it is not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate the commission of the crime. [616B] 6. The mere presence of the accused persons in the District when he is supposed to have been known to the witnesses and therefore he would know that they might actually accomplish their object. [617C] 7. The mere existence of a mention in the FIR that he was known to the witness and therefore he could remember any details of an essential murder trial cannot by itself be a ground to reject the conviction of a person under section 302 I.P., unless it is shown that he was unaware of the nemarious design of the accused person. [618D] 8. The mere non mention of the name of the accused in the FIR does not mean the absence of a specific mention in the first information report. [619B] 9. The mere omission of the name in the first report does not mean a statement in the first statement of the first informant. [620C] 10. The mere mere non mention in the second statement of the second informant does not mean an admission in the first version of the first information. [621B] 11. The mere failure of the name does not mean mere admission in the second version of the second FIR. [622C] 12. The mere admission in a first statement does not mean admission in the subsequent statement of the third informant.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code for committing the murder of the deceased in furtherance of their common intention. The trial court convicted accused 2 under section 302, read with section 149 and section 147, of the said Code and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted accused 1, 3 and 4 on the ground that it was doubtful whether 682 any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted accused 2 on the ground of that one or more of them might have participated in the offence. The High court convicted accused 1, 2 and 4 on two grounds. The first ground was that the conviction of accused 2 under sections 302, readwith section 34, read with sections 149 and 147, was bad in law, and that the High Court was not justified in convicting accused 2 under s. 302, read With section 34, and sentenced him only to life. The second ground was that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, their conviction under section 302 was bad in Law, and that in the present case on a fair reading of the entire judgment, it would be clear that they did not conjointly act with accused 2 in committing the murder. The High ' Court acquitted accused 2 under Section 302 read with Section 34, of, the Indian Penal code and also under section 302 of the Indian penal Code. The appeal by special leave to this Court was confined only to the acquittal of the accused under section 302 and section 147. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the acquittal of some of the accused was bad in the law. [623B] 1.2 The High Court had not considered the evidence in the judgment to indicate that persons other than the acquitted accused were involved in the commission. The High "Court" was not a single observation in the judgment. [624C] 1.3 The High Court, in appeal, could not convict only one of the accused on the basis of constructive liability. [626B] 1:4 The High Court could not convict accused 1,3 and 4 under section 302. [628C] 1:5 The High Court found that though accused 1, 4 and 5 were acquitted, the court could not convict them under section 302 or read with section34, of the, Indian Penal Code. [629B] 1 :6 The High Court did not consider the evidence in that regard. The High Courts were not justified in holding that accused 1, 5 and 6 were not identified and so, they could be convicted under section 304 read with section 109, read with Section 109, readwith Section 109, of the Code. [ 629D] 1.7 The High Court also did not consider whether the acquittal of accused 2 was bad in view of the acquittal of certain of the persons named in the charge and tried.

The petitioner imported a consignment of goods from the Customs Department. The goods were cleared from the warehouse after the amending Ordinance had come 627 into force. The goods could not be released because of the prohibitory orders of the Income Tax Authorities under section 102 of the . The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the import licence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner filed an appeal before this Court. The petitioner contended that the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the goods could not have been released because of certain circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The customs authorities and the Central Govern ment were right in holding that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse. [696G H] 1.2 The customs authorities were, therefore, right in taking a view that the rate applicable to the import of the goods should be the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods were actually removed. [697C] 1.3 The petitioner was willing to pay the duty when the goods crossed the customs barrier and were in the process of being cleared, but could not be cleared because of the prohibition imposed by the Income Tax Act. [698G H] 2.1 The petitioner was ready to pay the amount when the goods were cleared. [699C] 2.2 The petitioner was not willing to pay duty when the petitioner was actingualling expressed willingness to remove the goods. [695D] 2.3 The customs authorities had no right in taking any resort to the provisions of the Act. [600D] 2:4 The petitioner was also willing to pay to the duty when he was actualling expressed desire to remove the imported goods. [600E] 2.4 The petitioner is not entitled to seek recourse to Article 32 of the Constitution. [601B] 2.5 The petitioner was, therefore, clearly of the opinion that enforcement of a fundamental right would be wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case and the circumstances of this cases. [602E] 2:5 The petitioner is entitled to seek resort to Article 32. [603B] 2:6 The petitioner was entitled to seek remedy under Article 32 of t he Constitution. [600C] 2:7 The petitioner was a party to the proceedings before the High Court. [604C] 2 :8 The petitioner was bound to pay the tax when the goods reached the customs barrier. [605B] 2 :9 The petitioner was liable to pay the penalty. [606C] 2 10. The petitioner was required to pay the entire amount of the penalty. The petitioner had no fundamental fight to clear the goods on payment of duty when the Customs Authorities and the Central Government had taken the view that it to say, by the order of the Income tax Authorities the goods could be released. [608D] 2 :10 The petitioner was unwilling to pay the full amount of the tax. [609D] 2 11. The petitioner is also entitled to seek relief under Article 32. The petitioner has no fundamental fight. [610E] 2 :11 The petitioner was neither willing nor willing to pay any particular duty dependent on adjudica tion or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort thereto the provisions of section 102 of . [610F] 2.12 The petitioner was merely willing to pay and the duty when it was cleared. [600F] 2:13 The petitioner was only willing to pay, the duty when goods crossed the Customs barrier and were cleared.

The appellants were the sons of the deceased father. The respondent 's father was the son of the deceased. The respondent filed a suit for possession by partition of joint family property. The trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the whole estate including the share of the sons had come to an end and consequently in the auction sale the share of sons had come into an end and therefore the sale could not be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father. HELD: (1) The liability of a father to discharge the debt of his father is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale as to what passes to the auction purchaser. [419 C] (2) Where the right, title and interest of a judgment debtor are set up for sale, what the Court intended to sell and what the purchaser intended to buy and what he paid for. [420 E] (3) Where the rights, title and interests of a judgment creditor are set up to sale as to how passes to the purchaser are a question of law dependent upon what is the estate put forward for sale, whether the debt was avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals". [421 C] (4) The liability to discharge the obligations of the sons to discharge the liabilities of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the sons which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the father and which does not come to an independent end as a result of partition of the joint family property and which does neither come to an effect as a result thereof nor is it necessary to implead the sons or to bring another suit if severance of status takes place pending the execution proceedings because the pious duty of the sons continues and consequently there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property. [421 E] (5) The liability is of a father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a result o negligence in the discharge of his duties. [422 F] (6) The liability, of a father, who is a Managing director and who drawing a salary or remuneration, incurred in the discharge o his duties is not an avyavukrika debt as the Court intended that the substance and not merely the technicality of the transaction should be regarded. [423 C] (7) The liability under a pious duty of a sons continues and therefore there is merely an difference in the modes of enjoyment of that property. [413 D] (8) The liability in a father, whose debt is not tainted with imporence or illegality is founded on the pious duty which continues to exists in the lifetime of the father. [424 E] (9) The liability does not come into an operation as a result or result of negligence in the discharging of his duties, but as a result, of negligence in discharge of his duty, the father is not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the sons. [426 E] (10) The liability for a father, when a debt is not avyavaurika debt as he has drawn a salary or the remuneration, incurred by the sons in the discharge Of his duties is also not an avlaveable debt as it can be termed as a "non avlave". [426 F] (11) The liability was of a father whose debt is set up for auction sale as to whether he was a managing director or who draws a remuneration or a remuneration.

The Committee has also observed that it had to examine the conduct of various police officers and others and particularly as the record .shows, of the D.C.,P. D.C,P. D.,C.P., D.C.(P.D.C. P.D.P. D.) and other peculiar feature of the case are issued have to be examined at the end of the inquiry. The Committee also recommended the transfer to be made hereafter this direction issued to the Delhi Administration to examine its witnesses first as provided by rule 5(5)(a) of the Rules referred to above. The action of the Committee in asking them to give PG NO 523 evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the end o the inquiry is not contemplated under section 8B of the Act. The petitioners were the owners of a public carrier. They were registered as a registered firm under the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, and a notification issued under R. 8. A notification was issued under R 8. A Notification was issued under r. 8. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the Act was unconstitutional and ultra vires. The High Court upheld the validity of r. 8 and held that the Act did not apply to the petitioners. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of a notification. The High court held that the petitioners were entitled to the benefit of r.8. A petition was filed in this Court under article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act in the guise of taxing passengers and goods, taxes really the income of the petitioners, and that the Act is unconstitutional. Held, that the Act does not cease to be a tax on passengers and goods. The Act does not purport to impose tax on passengers or goods, though it makes the tax payable on fares and freights. The Act is a selfcontained code and does not purport merely to impose tax upon passengers and goods and therefore the Act does no cease to be an Act on passengers and property. The Act has no application to the petitioners, because it makes the payment of the tax calculated on actual fares and freight. The Act, therefore, does not ceaseto be a tax, because it does not cease lo be a tax On passengers and goods being transported by road or inland waterways. , The Act does no require payment of tax even when no passengers or goods are transported. The Act also does not cease as a tax on passenger and goods, though what it is to be, is determined by the amount of fare or freight. The tax is still on passengers and Goods, though what the amount of the tax is measured by the fares and freight charges. The tax, however, is still a tax on goods and the maximum, Rs. The entry in the State List is limited to a tax on persons and goods transported by road, or inland waterway. , The tax is thus without authority of law. [8C D] The Act does nothing more than lay down what the amount or the lump sum must be, if lump sum payment is made in lieu of payment of the taxes calculated on actual fare and freights, and the maximum and Rs. The words "in respect of all passengers carried and goods" in r. 8 are wide enough to cover all passengers carried by road or Inland waterways. The words 'in respect of passengers and goods ' in r.8 are wide enough. The words used in r. 9 are wide enough and they are not limited to a taxes on passengers and the tax is still upon passengers and property, though what they are to be, if paid in lieu of the tax, calculated on actual freight and freights is payable. The words are wide enough, and they are wide enough in their import. The words in r.9 are wide enough so as to include all passengers carried or goods transported by motor vehicles. The words of r. 9 is wide enough to include all persons who are transported by road. The words, 'in respect to passengers and goods transported ' in r 8 are wide and they are limited to a levy of tax even though the fare or freight is paid in lieu thereof. The words do not mean that the tax is not on passengers and passengers. The words have been wide enough to exclude all persons from the operation of the Act. The words were wide enough to take in all passengers carried on by road or rail or inland water ways.

The appellant was retrenched from 1st August, 1974. The appellant challenged the Award in this Court. The Labour Court by its award directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st September, 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The appellant contended that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of the raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised(l. The Labour court by its award held that the retrenchment of the workmen was invalid for the reasons found by the Labour Court and the workman were 567 entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from the day on which A they were sought to be retrenched. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the nonavailability of raw material or returrent power shedishing and lack of profitsability was a merely pretence or a camouflage to torment of the workmen by denying them of their livinghood, the true reason being the inability of the workmen, the real reasons being the annoyance and the annoyance of their workmen consequent upon the failure of the workmen in the industry to be a member of the industry. The Labour appellate Tribunal held that since the retrenchment was illegal and the relief of retrenchment was awarded what ought to be the criterion for grant of compensation to the extent of full wages or a Part of it ? The Labour Appellate Court held that the workmen were entitled to the benefit of reinstatement effective since the date on which A was sought to become retrenched. The High Court, however, held that the appellant was entitled to the full back wages from the date on the date on Which A was sought and that the retrenchment should be deemed to be the proper relief and Act aside the order of the Labour Court holding that the retrenchment is invalid and the relief for reinstatement effective from that date. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back wages to the workmen. [569 F] 1.2 The Labour Court was justified in imposing full back wages. [569 A] 1.3 The Labour Court had directed their reinstatement effective from 1st July, 1974 with a full back wages and permitting the appellant, the employer to deduct any sum paid as retrenchment Compensation from the amount paid to them as wages. The Award was upheld by the High Court. [569 B] 1.4 The Labour Court has awarded full back wages in the aggregate amount of Rs. 1,000/- to the workmen on its finding that the retrenchment had not been bona fide and the relief was granted full back wages after deducting the amount paid as wages. [570 C] 1.5 The Labour Court, in the facts of this case, was justified in granting full back wages for full back wages as the back wages. Keeping in view all the facts and circumstance of this case it would be appropriate to award 75% of the back wages to workmen to be paid in two equal instalments. [569 D] 1.6 The Labour Court while awarding full back Wages to the workmen, directed their reinstatement with full back Wages, permitting the appellants to deduct any amounts paid as retrenchment compensating the workmen as due to them. The Labour Tribunal has also awarded full back Wages from the amount found due and payable to them as retrenchment compensation towards the amount found payable to them.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge for committing the murder of his wife Churi. The High Court confirmed the conviction and death sentence. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The statement of the accused that he was with Churi in the house during the day but at 6 p.m. was not specially empowered in this behalf. The fact that the relations of the accused with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. [723 E] (2) The statement was recorded by the magistrate and was signed by the accused. The accused also did not deny that he was taken by the rolice to the police post from the bazar cannot be accepted because there was nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder of Churi deceased before the visit of the accused to the house of Shri Mahajan. [724 E] (3) The fact that there was no evidence to show that there was any conspiracy between the accused and the deceased, was not established by the evidence of Mangat Ram (PW 10) and Shri Mahajan (PW 15) and the fact that the accused was taken by him at the film show. The fact of the accused having gone to see film shows that the relations between the accused with Churi deceased and the deceased were strained. The accused was also not denied that he was also with the deceased at the film showing at Kotkhai, which had been arranged by the Publicity Department, according to Head Constable Bhag Singh PW, lasted from 7 to 8 30 p.m., while the intimation which was given by Mangat Ram PW 10 was entered in the daily diary at 10.50 p.m.. The accused also does not deny that the relations were strained between the accused, ts will be shown hereafter, and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child. [725 E] (4) The statement recorded by the Magistrate and signed by the Public Prosecutor cannot be accepted as evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. [726 E] (5) The statement is not admissible in evidence under sections 76 and 77 of the Indian Penal Code. [727 C] (6) The statement, therefore, cannot be put in evidence under section 76 of the Indian Indian Evidence Act, and the statement is inadmissible in evidence. [728 E] (7) The statement made by the accused that the accused had gone to see the film show at Kotkhali, was not considered by this Court in the case of State of Uttar Pradesh vs Singhara Singh and Others. [729 E] (8) The statement given by the accused was not admissible in the evidence under section 77 of the Evidence Act. The statement was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [730 E] (9) The statement in the form prescribed by section 165 of the Code cannot be used as evidence under section 74 of the Indian Criminal Procedure. The statement is inadmissible under section 77. [731 E] (10) The statement cannot be used for the purpose of contradicting the statement made by an accused. [732 E] (11) The statement can be used for contradicting the statements made by an independent witness. [733 E] (12) The statement must be read in the context of the facts and circumstances of the case and cannot be used to contradict the statement made in the statement. [734 E] (13) The statement should be read in its entirety and the statement should be construed in the light of the facts of the case.

The plaintiff, who was the defendant in the suit, filed a suit for the recovery of Rs. 80,507 7 8 being the aggregate amount due and payable by the two defendants. The trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation and that the suit had been filed within the period of limitation. Held, that the suit having been filed within a period of limitation, the suit was not barred by limitation. The suit was barred under section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82. The suit having been instituted within a period Of limitation, the plaintiff was entitled to the relief of redemption. The suit had been instituted within the period Of limitation. The plaintiff was entitled under the Transfer of property Act to redeem the whole of the balance of the property. The suit being a suit for redemption, the plaintiff had no right to redeem the entire balance of the mortgaged property. The plaintiff had no cause of action to file the suit. Held, further, that the plaintiff had not used the word "subrogation" for the relief to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Act. The suit as regards the sum paid by the plaintiff was barred by the limitation. The claim was inartistically worded the plaintiff had in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs. 40,253 11 with interest against either defendant, I would direct that his liability be reduced to Rs. When these figures are ascertained, I would request that the liability of each defendant be ascertained separately in the manner prescribed by section 82, Transfer of Property (excluding the plaintiff 's father) for the aggregate sum due as above and, in default of payment, limiting the liabilities of each item of property to the sum rateably due on it under section 82.

The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. The appellant No. 1 was a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks from Karnataka University and secured 66.40 marks in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150. The appellant filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petition and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. The record of the marks awarded to the selected candidates is produced before this Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks, the appellants before us were found suitable in all other respects according to the Rules. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State also submitted that the percentage for viva voce was excessive and the appellants before this Court were bound to be selected on the basis of marks secured by them in interview, calculated on the basis Of converting the same to 15% of thetotal marks. Learned counsel for the State also contended that the percentage was excessive and that the percentage could not be kept say at 15% of total marks. Learned Counsel for the State submitted that the State Government has already framed new rules and as such we do not find it necessary to quash the selections on the basis o marks secured by the appellants in interview, computed on the basis thereof in accordance with the K.S.C.S. (Direct Recruitment By Selection) Rules, 1973. Learned counsel submitted that the Tribunal by its judgment dated 24th April, 1990 dismissed all the petitions and the appellants filed a petition challenging the Rules. The Tribunal dismissed the petition. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High Court dismissed all the writ petitions. The appellants have approached this court by special leave. Learned counsel contended that the ratio laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors. , [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State of Punjab & Ors., J.T. On a direction given by this Court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the mark awarded to the appellants in the qualifying examina tion was produced before this court at the time o r hearing. Learned counsel further submitted that the selection was made according to the rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. Learned counsel also submitted that in view of the fact that the result of the impugned selection was declared in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. Learned counsel, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The ratio laid down in Ashok KumarYadav & Ors. [1988] Supp. S. C.R., 660 and Mohinder Sain Jain vs State of Delhi & Ors., [1988] supp. S.c.R., 656 and Mohinder Sain Gill vs State of Jammu & Ors., , [1988], Sup. S C.R. 657 and Mohinder Chand Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors. J.T., is clearly in violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. [697B] 1.2 The ratio laid in Ashok Kumar Pandey & Ors. (supra) is clearly in breach of the dictum laid down by the Constitution Bench in Ashok Kumar Mishra & Ors. v State of Haryana and Ors., [1989] Supp.S.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution has failed to establish the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution has failed in establishing the complicity of the Sadanand in his murder. [413G] (2) The prosecution had failed to establish that the accused persons had supplied the bomb to him. The High court has not been able to accept the contention that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence the complicity of accused Sadanand in murder of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken considerable care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. [413H; 414A] (3) The prosecution was not able to prove that the accused had supplied the bombs to him. [413B] (4) The prosecution could not prove that the prosecution was able to prove the complicity of any Sadanand in any murder of the State. [413C] (5) The prosecution failed to establish by circumstantial evidence that the accused were meeting at regular intervals by itself. [413D] (6) The prosecution did not establish by circumstantial evidenc e, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to be completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413E] (7) The prosecution must establish by circumstantial evidences, a clear links has to be proved and the chain must be completed, else it would indeedbe hazardous to accept an part of the links as a complete One and on the principle of criminal jurisprudence that the Court cannot start with the con fession of a co accused person. [413F] (8) The prosecution should have taken great care to ensure the presence of Sadanand at the jail and enforcement of rules become slack and there is a regular flow of food from outside. [413A] (9) The prosecution evidence on this score should be rejected as when on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand was not found there. According to the prosecution, Yadav was actually visiting Sadanand at his jail. The prosecution has also led evidence to show that he met his wife on that day. Adverse inference for not examining the wife has to be drawn against the prosecution. [413 B] (10) The prosecution, in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence, the prosecution must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence , the allegation of criminal conspiracy cannot be accept. [413 G] (11) The prosecution is not able to establish that Sadanand was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regularly intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy because it is not evidence as defined by section 3 of the Act. [413 C] (12) The prosecution cannot prove that the deceased was a member of the unlawful assembly. [413 D] (13) The prosecution case is that Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder was committed.
