The High court held that the tribunal had not properly considered the total effect of the increase it was granting in basic wage and dearness allowance and that the Tribunal should have taken into account the trend in that region and provided wage scales on the same lines so that, so far as manufacturing concerns in the present appeals are concerned, there will be equality in the matter of competition. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the total wage value of the concerns with which the Tribunal had dealt with the matter of Competition. [520 E] 2. The Tribunal had not specifically considered whether the dearness allowance fixed by it as it should has done, for purposes of finding out if there are a large number of concerns in the same region carrying on the same industry. [521 E] 3. The Tribunal was in 375 our opinion right in following the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing the same scales of dearness allowance for factory workmen as for clerical staff and other staff including factory workmen. [522 F] 4. The Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total wage Lists including basic wages, for each category of factory workmen, and then compare it with the total wages packet including basic wages fixed by it in the case of clerical staff and others including factory workmen and the Tribunal must when passing comparisons take account the total wages packets including basic wage, for each class of factory workmen. But in doing so the Tribunal must while making comparisons taking into account the factor in that region can take into account any comparison for factory workmen in the same line of business for the purpose for fixing wage scales and dearness allowance, and then comparison it with the financial loss occasioned by misconduct in case of dismissal for misconduct. [523 E] 5. The Tribunal should when making comparison for factory workmen, take into account all the trend in the region and also take into account its trend in that area, can be successfully challenged so far as retrospective effect and adjustments as also fixation of wages and dearness Allowance with respect to clerical staff are concerned. [524 F] 6. The Tribunal is right in applying the correct principle of the formula which is adopted by it as the basis for fixation of wages. [526 G] 7. The Tribunal, therefore, was in 375 Our opinion is that the Tribunal has not properly considered what the maximum instead of ' 15 months wages would be on the basis of the scales of wages and Dearness allowance fixed by the Tribunal as it should had done, for each categories of factory workmen in comparable concerns which it had made comparison for clerical and subordinate employees in all these concerns and also taking into account that trend in that regions can be successfully assailed so far as clerical staff are connected with the same industry and also arrive at a just figure for basic wage, and thereafter comparison it with total wage packet including basic wage and Dearness allowance and thus arrive at a reasonable figure for basic wages, and then compared it with the net wage packet of comparable concerns and thus arrive a just figure. [527 C] 8. The Tribunal also has not specifically denied what the total wages for these categories in comparable concerns are, though it appears that some exemplars were filed before it.

The plaintiffs 1 and 2, who were the legal representatives of Annappa, filed a suit for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof. The trial Court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that the plaintiffs were agriculturists, that they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High Court having refused to grant leave to appeal to this Court, the mortgagees defendants 1 to 4 applied to and obtained from this Court special leave to appeal against the decision of the Division Bench in so far as it upheld the rejection of their claims to Annappa 's share by the Rajinma. The appellants contended that the Raj inama was a complete relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers, and that as Shiddappa was the manager and karta of the joint family, the Rajinamama executed by him operated upon the entire occupancy and amounted to a relinquishment of the right of both the sisters, and that on take accounts the mortgages were subsisting, that the defendants could not acquire title by adverse possession. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Rajinama was a completed relinquishment of the interest of Annaappa to the mortgagees and, therefore, operated to extinguish the equity of redemption not only of Shiddappa but also of Annappala, for there was sufficient evidence on record that a notice of relinquishment given by the registered occupant must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the 701 registered occupant, or that the registered occupant has the right to give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in the occupancy. [775 E] 1.2 The Rajinma was a complete relinquished of the rights by the defendants to the mortgagees. [776 E] 1:3 The Rajinaka executed by Shudappa did not purport to file, the same on behalf of any occupant other than his 701 registered occupant. [778 E] 1 :4. The contention that the RajInama was a full relinquishment of the estate of Annaiah was not accepted by the trial Court. [782 F] 1.4 The Rajinna was a complete relinquish of the rights and interest of Ananappa to the mortgagees, and, therefore the Rajinaka was binding on his brother Annappa. [785 C] 1.5 The Rajinada executed by Shriddappa did no purport to file a suit for the redemption of the mortgage in favour of Annaayya. [786 E] 1.:5. The Rajinata did not purport either to file, or to make a new case. [787 E] 1.-6 The Rajinsa did not purport, to file, it on behalf of Anna arbitration. [794 F] 1:7. The Raj inama did not purport even to file, and in the absence of any specific pleading and cogent proof, that a notice given by the Registered occupant must necessarily, be a notice upon behalf of all occupant or any particular person, the principal of such persons, must enter into a written agreement to become the registered occupant, and his name shall thereupon thereupon be substituted in the records for that of the previous registered occupant. That does not mean, in the absence absence of any express pleading and cogent evidence, that a Notice of relinquishment given on behalf of an occupant must necessarily mean a notice on his behalf. [795 E] 1 8.

The appellant Mills was a registered Sugar Mills at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the appellant Mills at Amroha at a time when they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Sambhal. The appellant Mills was running only one factory at Amroha. It was alleged that the respondents 1 to 3 were employed by them at a time while they were not partners of the Sugar Mill at Amroha. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager of the appellant Mills ordered the transfer of the respondents 1 and 4 to the new mill at Bulandshahr. On February 6, 1955, a General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents 1, to 4 from service on the ground that 117 920 they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thereby they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. " " " " The appellant Mills filed an appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India against the order of the Labour AppellateTribunal. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the management had no right to transfer the respondents 1. The appellant contended that the respondents had disobeyed the order of transfer, and that the order dismissing them was illegal. Held, that the order of dismissal was illegal. The order dismissing the appellant was illegal. It was not a condition of service of employment of the respondents either express or implied that the employer had the right to transfer them to another concern stared by him subsequent to the date of the employment. The question raised was one of law, namely, whether the appellant had the right, to transfer the employees from one concern to another. The question whether the appellant was the right to be transferred to another concern was essentially to be decided on the facts of each case. The question was one of fact and not mixed question of law and fact. The question of law involved was one of principle governing the right of an employer to transfer his employees from one place to another. It was well within the powers of the Labour Court to entertain the appeal and to entertain the same. The question involved was one which was not of law, viz., whether the appellant should be transferred to any place where the business of the employer in the same line was situated, unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract of employment between the appellant and the respondents. The question that arose was one of general law, namely whether the appellant could transfer the respondents to another concern. The question arose whether the appellant having the right to the transfer of an employee from one concern, to another was implicit in every contract of service between the appellant, and the respondents the duty to join the concerns to which they may be transferred. The question, therefore, was one of jurisdiction.

The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of various types of articles. The appellant company was a registered company under the . The appellant company had been providing medical treatment and attendance to insured persons and the provisions of the . The Employees ' State Insurance Corporation Act, 1948 was enacted in 1948. Chapter V A was headed "Transitory Provisions" and provides for the payment by the principal employer of a special contribution which shall be in lieu of the employer 's contribution payable under Chapter IV in the case of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V are in force. The appellant Company was also providing for the payment of benefits and provision of medical treatment and Attendance to insured persons. The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948, was enacted in 1949. Chapter VA was inserted by section 20 of Act No. 53 of 1951. The provisions of Chapter V A were inserted by section 23 of Act No 53 of 1951 by Act 53 of 1951 and section 24 of , which provided for the payment to the employees under the or other similar payment or benefit under various social welfare legislations. The appellant contended that the contribution payable under the various social welfare legislation must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. The appellant 's contention was that the contribution paid under Chapter V A is a fee and its levy is illegal as the Act does not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The appellant also contended that the payment of special contribution under Chapter VA is a fee, and its levy was illegal as the act did not contemplate the render of any service to the appellant. The appellant further contended that the amount of special contribution was a fee and not a tax and that it had been so laid down in argument that the benefit should not be indirect and remote The reference, therefore, to indirectness and remoteness was not made in connection with any delayed benefit from the point of view of time, but with reference to the very benefit itself and its connection with the levy. The appellant submitted that the contribution was a tax and not a fee in the order to attain credibility or not at any point of view. The appellant relied on the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income Tax vs M/s. M.K. K. K.K. & Co. Ltd. , and contended that the special contribution was not a tax or fee in order that it might be indirect and indirect. The appellant, however, contended that the benefit could not be indirect or remote and the connection with the imposition was not made with reference to any delayed benefit. The appellant urged that the contribution should not be direct and remote and the reference, therefore was not made to indirectness or remoteness. The appellant argued that the contribution made under Chapter V was a fee, but its levy was a tax or an a fee in lieu of that benefit itself and that it was not necessary to retain this Chapter. The appellant referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in Commissioner, Income Tax vs A.K.K. M. K. M. M.M. M. Mehta & Co. (P) Ltd. , wherein it was held that the payment was a fee. The appellant pointed out that the contribution under Chapter IV A was a fee but its levy is a fee. Held, that the contribution to the appellant was a fee which was not a fee and that it did not require the rendering of service or the conferring of any benefit on the appellant company as quid proquo for the payment, and that it has been so laid in argument that it had not been so laid. The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the special contribution as a tax.

The plaintiffs were the appellants before this Court. The trial Court held that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0. r. 12(i) of the Calcutta Money Lenders Act and that the mortgage by the National Agency Co. Ismail was not the full owner of the entire interest in the property and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire property.
