In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in holding that the plaintiffs had failed to raise any specific ground touching their right to this share, and that the sale in execution was real and intended to pass title to Pir Baksh, and that in conse quence the sale in favour of the 1st defendant was not the sole proprietor or owner of the property and therefore the mortgage by him as full owner of that property was not the part of the full owner. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was in error. [723 E] 2. The High Courts were in error in not accepting the first two of the defences but held that the sale was real and that the property conveyed under exhibit 12(i), with the result that the plaintiffs would be entitled to a decree for a declaration that in addition to the 8 pies share granted to them by the High Court, they would be entitled in addition to a further 2 as. 212 Coming now to the merits of the plaintiff 's claim, it is common ground that if the sale was effected and Pir B Laksh who was examined as a witness admitted this fact, the plaintiffs would not be entitled to any decree for a further 2 1/2 as. share belonging to Ismail. [724 F] 3. The High courts were in error. The High 'Court was in error, in holding that Ismail was the full owner and that the Co heirs were estopped by 0.r. 12(c) through Pir Brah who was examined in the witness admitted this factum. [725 E] 4. The High Judges were in error, on the basis of the statement in the plaint as regards the indentity of the property conveyed by exhibit 12(1) with Ashfaq 's share in the Azamabad Tea Estate, and that for that reason the plaintiffs were estopped by the entry in the revenue registers, which the co heirs did nothing to correct, ostensibly the full owner thereof. [726 F] 5. The High Judge was in error when he held that the appellants were precluded by the entry of exhibit 12(I) with Ashfaq executed the sale deed exhibit 12(ii) on April 18, 1931, without adverting to the sale being real and intended, to pass title. [727 C] 6. The High. Court was in wrong in holding that in view of the entry in exhibit 12(iii) with Ashfaq, the plaintiffs were barred by 0. 12(1). [727 E] 7.

The appellant was tried for the offence of murder under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court, while dealing with this ground of appeal, held that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with, and that the omission was not sufficient to 37 290 vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudiced in their defence. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The provisions of sections173(4) & 207A(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code, have not been complied, and that, as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial are vitiated. [982G H] (2) The omission on the part of the police officers concerned or of the magistrate before whom such proceedings are brought, to 293 see that all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. The omission on their part, to fully comply with the provisions of those sections, has caused prejudice to the accused in the interest of justice, the court may reopen the proceedings by insisting upon full compliance with the provisions aforesaid of the Code. [983D] (3) The omission in a particular case on behalf of the accused persons that the omission on the parts of the police officer concerned or of a magistrate before whom the committal proceedings had fended, has caused a complete failure of justice. [984E] (4) The omission of a police officer, to fully complied with the provisions, has caused an prejudice to the appellant in the interest, of justice, and the court may reopening the proceedings by insistence upon full compliance of the provisions of the Code, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enjoining upon police officers concerned and magistrates, before whom such proceeding is brought, to 294 see that all documents necessary to give the accused persons all the information relating to the proper conduct, of their defence are furnished. [985F] (5) The omission by a police officer to fully complywith the provisions of section 173(4), should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. Certainly, if it is shown, in a particular situation, on behalf of accused persons that they had not been prejudiced in the interest o justice, the Court may reopen the proceeding by insisting upon Full compliance with the provision of section 173, should not reopen the proceedings, by insisting upon complete compliance with the requirements of section 173. [986F] (6) The omission, on the part, of police officers, to fully compliance with the mandatory provisions of section 174, should not be permitted to have such an far reaching effect. [987G] (7) The omission caused prejudice to accused in the interests of justice, in the interest and justice, the courts may reopen the trial by insisting upon the full compliance with section 173, to safeguard the interest of accused persons, in the interests, of justice. The omission, however, caused prejudice to them in the interest.

The appellant Municipality was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of cement. The Municipality was conducting the business of manufacturing cement. The appellant was the owner of the factory. The Municipality issued a notice under section 153A of the Act directing the appellant to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 153A(1) of the Act did not offend article 19(1)(C) because it would be a reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right under article 19(I)(C) to prevent a nuisance which would affect the public health and fertility of the soil. Held, that the provisions contained in section 153A were not intended to be exhaustive and exhaustive and did not require to be exhaustive. The provisions of section 154A of the, Act were intended to be comprehensive and exhaustive and were intended to provide a comprehensive machinery for the prevention of nuisance. The provisions contained in sections 153A and 153A of The Act were intended for the prevention and control of nuisance and to prevent the danger to the public health. The provisions in section 153 A were intended to deal with the problem of nuisance and the prevention of the danger to public health and to provide for the prevention, control and abatement of nuisance. It was not intended to cover the problem of the nuisance of the kind alleged by the respondent Municipality. The provisions were intended to cover a matter of the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the person concerned. The provisions relating to the prevention and Control of nuisance and for the prevention or abatement of nuisance were intended to operate in the interest of the public health, fertility andtility of the public. The provisions made in section 153 were intended to protect the public health of the soil and to provide a speedy remedy to the person to whom the notice has been issued. The provisions enacted in section 153 are intended to protect public health and for the protection of the soil, and to provide speedy remedy to persons who may be affected by the nuisance. The Act was intended to protect a public health and safety of the soil in the surrounding areas. The provisions are intended to provide speedy and effective remedy to persons affected by the acts of the Municipality. The Act is intended to provide for speedy and effective prevention of nuisance and prevention of the spread of nuisance. [723 C D] The provisions of sections 153A, 153A and 505A of the The Act were meant to protect the health and fertile of the soil of the soil as well as to provide speedy remedies to persons affected thereby. The provisions have been enacted to provide for a speedy remedy for the prevention to the spread of the nuisance. [823 D] The Act was enacted to provide a special machinery for the protection and improvement of the soil by providing for the prevention by the spread of any nuisance. The provision contained in section 154A is to provide for an speedy remedy to those who may be likely to be affected by any act of the Municipality or of any other person. The provisions which are intended to cover cases of nuisance and preventing the danger to human life are intended to be given a wide interpretation and are intended to serve a wider purpose. The provisions do not require to have a rigid definition of the word "reasonable" in the Act. The provisions, therefore, do not require that a reasonable opportunity should be given to the person who has to be heard before the order is passed. The provisions for the prevention are intended to prevent a danger to human lives and to provide an speedy remedy. The provisions provide for a comprehensive machinery to enable the Municipality to discharge its functions.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which were being used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The appellant was charged with the offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The trial court convicted him under section 3 and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000. The High Court acquitted the appellant but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had purchased the property in open market where goods of this 189 kind were usually sold or that he had bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the The High Court was wrong in holding that it was necessary to establish that the articles were being actually used or were intended to be use for by the railway. HELD: The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to the effect that the goods were being actually put to use by a railway administration and that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration. The burden of proving that the goods belong to any particular Railway administration is discharged by the prosecution that the burden shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. [191 F] The prosecution must prove that the goods are railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 3 did not arise. [191 C] The prosecution has to prove that the articles seized were railway stores within that meaning. The burden shifts to a person who has bought them from somebody bona fide in belief that the purchaser had lawfully obtained them. [191 D] The prosecution should also prove that the article was being used or was intended to be put to use for the construction, operations or maintenance of railway. [191 E] The prosecution can only prove that the incriminating articles belonging to a particular railway administration were being stolen or obtained unlawfully. The burden in respect of this is discharged by leading proof about the identifying mark on the goods and that the burden shifted to the accused.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised shop in Jaipur. The suit was decreed by the Courts below and decreeing the suit for ejectment. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court reversed the decree of the Courts below. Hence the appeal by the appellants. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of 'Tenant ' in the Act does not bring about any change in the status and legal position of the tenant unless there are contrary provisions in the Act. [7A] 1.2 The definition of "Tenant" in the Act is that a contractual tenant on the termination of the contractual tenancy is by virtue of the provisions of the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and he is entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual lease. [7B] 1.3 The definition of tenant in the Act do not indicate that the heirs of the tenant are entitled to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under the Act. The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs of tenants, unless there are otherwise contrary provisions in th e Act, does not indicate that they are fully protected by the Act. It does not indicate the that the legislature intended that the heirs Of the tenants of commercial premises will cease to enjoy the benefit afforded to the tenants under the Act, an irreparably ble mischief which the Legislature would never have intended. [7C] 1.4 The mere fact of that in the statute no provision has either been made with respect to the heirs or heirs of such tenants, unless it be held that commercial tenancies after the termination of tenancy, as has been done in the case of heirs of the tenants, are heritable on the death of the tenant and the heirs of such tenant are entitled for enjoy the protection under the Act to inherit the status and position of the statutory tenant on his death. [7D] 1.5 The mere fact, that in the act no provision has come into existence, does not mean that the legislature did not intend that the heirs should enjoy an estate or inter est in the tenanted premises. [7E] 1.6 The definition of the word "Tenant " in the Act did not bring about a change in the character and legal position. [7G] 1.7 The definition of expression "Tenant ' is that a tenancy is by way of a contractual tenancy. The mere facts that in the present case the tenant continues to remain in the possession even after the termination o f the contractual tenancy till a decree for eviction against him is passed, continues to have an estate or Inter est in the tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or decree of possession specified in the Act are established. [7F] 1.8 The mere fact existence of commercial tenancies after termination of the tenancy does not indicate any change in status and legal status of the tenant, unless there is contrary provisions in t he Act. [8G] 1:9 The mere fact fact that in a suit for eviction against a tenant, the tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs are entitled to enjoying the protection afforded under the Act does no indicate that the legislature wanted that the heirs who continue to remain in occupation even after the expiry of the contractual term should cease to enjoy protection afforded to them under the Act and also subject to the rights in favour of the respond ent created under section 13(1) (a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund to all the workmen other than those who are covered by the Act and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Labour Court held that all workmen Of the Board should be given the same and identical benefits and that the workmen should have the similar benefits and should that therefore there would be no distinction among the Board 'S Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme thereunder under the Act. The High Court held that the appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Funds Act applies. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that the State Government is the financier of the Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Board 's financial capacity to implement the Provident Fund scheme as demand: ed by the workmen. The burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer like the burden of wage structure in the interest of social justice. [48G H] 2. The Board should extend the benefits to all workmen other than the workmen who are covered under the Act and also to similar benefits and if the financial position shows that the burden of provident Fund and gratuity does no result in loss of the employer like burden of wage structures in the interest o social justice. The burden will have to be borne by the employer like any other expense including wages and if the Financial position shows that it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. [48C D] 3. The Board has to take its operations so as not to incur a loss. The contribution to the depreciation reserves is a definite proportion whereas it is open for an ordinary commercial approach to credit any amounts to the depreciation Reserve. The burden is calculated and it is opento an ordinary commercial concerns to credit any money to the depreciation reserved. [48E] 4. The Board must pay the interest so paid to its employees. [48F] 5. The Board is willing ties to the Board. [48H] 6. The Board does not result In loss to the employers that burden will haveto be borne by an employer like any others expense including wages, if the financial situation shows that the onus of provident fund or gratuity does not resulted in loss to that employer like the onus of wage structure. [48B] 7. The Board cannot be deducted in order to ascertain the financial capacity of the employer. [48D] 8. The Board can be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment.

The respondent, a wife, filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of 1973 for maintenance. The Magistrate, after considering the evidence and the documents, came to the conclusion that the husband had been impotent and was entitled to the grant of maintenance. The respondent filed a petition for maintenance. In the petition, the Magistrate, after hearing the parties, came to a conclusion that the wife had been impetent and was not entitled to maintenance. The High Court, however, held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. The High court, however, reversed the finding of the Magistrate and held that the wife was entitled to maintenance if she refused to live with the husband merely because her husband was impotent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the husband was impetent was not a just cause for the refusal of the wife to live with him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the husband could refuse to live separately from her husband when it seems to have been given by the husband to inflict that cruelty, she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [501B] 1.2 The High Court has not committed any error in holding that it was not a fit case for interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. [502C] 1.3 The High Court had not committed any mistake in holding that there was no sufficient ground for the husband to refuse to reside with her husband if the husband had contracted marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress this would not be a just reason for the wife 's refusal to live with his husband. [503B] 1:4 The High Court erred in holding that in the present case, the husband had refused to live separately and was not impotent but reasonable ground for refusal to live separately. [505C] 1:5 The High Court ought to have taken into consideration the fact that the husband has contracted marriage with a woman or keeps her husband fully justified and entitled to maintenance from her husband according to his means. [507E] 1.6 The High Court should have taken into account the fact that there was nothing in the Criminal Procedure Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1949 to show that it would not be just ground for divorce or for an action for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. [508B] 1.:6 The High court erred in holding the husband having contracted marriage with the wife merely because her wife refused to live her husband, the wife would be entitled to maintenance under section 125. [509C] 2. The High ' Court erred in not taking into consideration the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 of Code of 1973 under which a wife could refuse to reside in her husband if there was a just ground to do so. [510B] 3. The High "Court" in section 125 of Criminal Procedure (Amendment ) Act, 1949, has not committed an error in holding the wife to have refused to live separate from her husband. [609C] 4. The High Courts have ignored the legal effect and intent of the second Proviso to sub section(3) of Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code under which a husband could refuse live with her wife if there was no just ground for doing so. [610C] 5. The High courts have ignored the well settled legal position that impotence is no good ground for divorce.

The plaintiff was the owner of the suit land. The Municipality was constituted under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1949. The Municipality had been constituted under the Act. The Municipality continued to function as the agent of the State to dispose of the land. The plaintiff was the lessee of the suit property. The Municipality issued a notice to the plaintiff under section 106 of the Act. On the plaintiff 's failure to comply with the notice, the plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration of its title and for possession of the suit properties. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the vesting of the title in the Municipality was not intended to be vesting in its full amplitude, but was meant to appoint the Municipality as agent of the Government but was meant only to appoint the municipality as agent of State to dispose off the land. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the vesting that was sine plated in the Resolution 37 dated 19th January, 1948 and Resolution 77 dated 29th February, 1948 vested in the Municipality. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The vesting that was contem plated in its full scope, but was intended to be vested in the Municipali ty at any time. [723C] 2. The Resolution No. 37 dated 19 th January, 1948 vested only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the ownership itself in the Municipality, that is,ashtraba State in 1948 and that the various documents filed in this case, would go to show that physical possession was with the defendant and also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title to the land is not vested in the municipality. [724D] 3. The Resolution was not intended only to appoint a Municipality as agent o f the State but also to appoint theMunicipality as agent of Government. [725B] 4. The Resolution did not confer any right or an authority to dispose of land as representing Government but also a vesting of title itself in the municipality, that is to say, that the vesting was sine pled in the full sense, but was not meant only to appointing the Municipality as agents of the State. [726C] 5. The Resolution of the State of Bhavnagar to all 230 the Municipalities of Old Bhavnagar States, and the right to give the same on rent lease and to take the income therefrom shall be enjoyed by the Municipalities subject to the condi tions mentioned in the letter of the Government dated 10th August, 1965. [727D] 6. The Resolution dated 19th February, 1949 vested in the State Government only on a vesting of its title in the municipality and not a vesting thereof in the Municipality as representing the State. The Resolution had not been intended to be vest in its full ambit, but was only meant to appoint a municipality as agent o the State to disposed of the land as represented the Government. [827D] 7. The Resolution does not confer any title on the Municipality. [728C] 8. The Resolution is not intended to vest in its absolute amplitude, but is meant only to appointment the Municipality as agency of the State, and not a vested vesting of the right itself in the Municipal records. [729A] 9. The Resolution in question does not confer a right or a authorisa tion on the Municipality but only a vesting of a title itself in a Municipality. [829B] 10. The Resolution has not been intended either to be vesting or in its full sweep, but was merely meant to appoint it as agent of that Government. [820A] 11.

The appellant was employed to exercise to some extent and in certain circumstances the delegated function of Government was that of a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was performing the duty of a metal Examiner known as Chalan in the Railway carriage Workshops at Jaipur. The appellant was, therefore, a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant contended that the appellant was not an officer within the meaning Of section 21(1)(c) of the, Indian Penal Code and that the provisions of section 137 of the Railways Act excluded all railway servants from the definition of public servants except for purposes of Chapter IX, Indian Penal code. Held, that the appellant did not fall within the terms of the last portion of clause (9) of section 21 of the Indian penal Code. The question for consideration before the Court was whether the appellant was an officer within section 21( 9) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellant could not be a public servant for the purposes of section 21, Indian Penal Act. The appellant, therefore, was not an "officer" within the meaning o section 21(8) of the Act. The question whether a person was an officer of the Government was a question of fact and the Court was not bound to decide it on the facts of a particular case. The question was whether the officer was in the service or pay of the Government performing as such a public servant was within the meaning ofs. 21(9), Indian Penal Code, and was therefore not excluded from the definition. The question arose whether the appellant could be convicted of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. Held, further, that the decision in 12 Bombay High Court Reports 1, was understood by the learned Judges of the Lahore High Court in Ahad Shah vs Emperor(1) when they observed at page 157: "But it is not enough that a person should be in the pay or service of Government to Constitute him a public servant at the time when he was appointed to some office for the performance of some pulice duty. The question is whether a person should fall within the meaning section 21(7) of the Penal Code. It is not enough if a person should have been in the pay of the government but is also performing a public duty. The fact that a person has been convicted as a public servant is in service and pay of the public servant is not in the service of Government. The question therefore arose whether a person who was appointed to a particular office for the perform of some punder duty was in the pay and service of Government and was therefore, a Public servant within the ambit of section 21 (9) and therefore a public servant be fell within the definition of a public servant contained in section 2 of the Prevention Act. The answer to the question depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The appellant is a public servant and is therefore a public Servant within the meaning under section 21(6) of the. Indian Penal Code."

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala C. for recovery of Rs. 1,00,000/- and Rs. 1.00,000/ respectively. The Respondent filed a written statement in the suit. The Trial Court decreed the suit. In appeal, the Respondent filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Patiala, being Regular Second Appeal No. The Respondent contended that the property attached and notified for sale was exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of the Code. The District Judge allowed the said appeal and dismissed the suit so far as it related to the portion in which the liquor shop was situated. The Respondent then filed a second suit in the High Court challenging the validity of the auction sale. The District judge allowed the said second appeal and dismissed it. The Respondent thereafter filed a second second appeal in the High court. The High Court allowed the said Second Appeal and dismissed the Second Appeal. The Respondent thereupon filed a second Appeal in the High Curt. The High court held that the property in question was exempt from the attachment and sale as under clause (c) of section 61 of the Code, and that the property was exempt from sale under clause(ccc) thereof. The High Curt also held that the portion in the said building used for residence was exempt from attached and sale under section 60 of Code. The Respondent has filed a Special Leave Petition against the said Judgment and Decree of the High Court. Allowing the Appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "such attachment or sale" in the said proviso refers to the attachment and sales mentioned in sub section (I) of section 30 of the Code and the sale which was notified was also under the provisions of the said Act. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect of, the Respondent 's half share in the said property was not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the said Act for recovery of revenue due to the State. [696B] 1.2 The words "such attachment and sale" in section 60 of CPC are "the following property is liable to attachment and sale in execution of such a decree and the proviso to section 60 of Act, which applies only to execution of such decree and the provisos to sub section(1) of Section 60 of the Act, that is, to attachment and the sale in execution and the sale, namely, "such attachment, or sale" mentioned in sub Section (1) thereof refers to the property which is not liable to such attachment or sale in execution. The attachment in a question is levied under the provisions Of the said Act and the sale is notified also under the said provisions of the Act. [697C] 1.3 The attachment in the question is levied on, or after the date of the holding of the said auction sale notified under section 60. The attachment is levied under section 60 and the sale has been notified also under section 60, and the sale notified is also under the provision of the said Code. [698C] 1:4. The attachment and sale notified in pursuance of an order made by a officer authorized to adopted proceedings under the Act for recovery, and the property immediately appurtenant thereto and necessary for their enjoyment belonging to a judgment debtor other than an agriculturist and occupied by him. The attachment, and sale in revenue recovery proceedings under the aforesaid Act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said Act would be liable to attachment or sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto.

The appellant, a widow of Rashid, filed a suit for compensation for the lands acquired by the Government of Bombay for the purpose of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. The appellant claimed that the lands in the original assessment had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court for the lands in Civil Court, and the High Court upheld the issuance of such notice on the wrong assumption that the acquired lands still formed part of the state of the deceased which had escaped assessment to duty. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the said notice had been issued on the wrong premise that the acquired land had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as at the date of the death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law P inasmuch as the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in question had been undervalued and had escaped assessment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the respondent had not issued it on wrong assumption that there was escapement of the assessment to duty and that the respondent was not a mistake apparent from the record and as such the enhanced compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of the estate by undertaking the rectification proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondent had merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collector in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and as such it was not a case of change of opinion on his part as regards the correct valuation of the lands. [330G] 2. The respondent himself did not estimate the market value of the lands on the date of death of Rashid and as such he was deemed to have adopted that evaluation as his own estimated value of the land which he wanted to enhance by relying upon the valuation made by another authority, namely, the City Civil Court, Bombay. [330A] 3. The respondent did not estimate his market value of those lands which he wantedto enhance by relying on the valuation made pursuant to the impugned notice. [330B] 4. The respondent was not entitled to any relief under section 61 of the Act. [330C] 5. The respondent could not be said to have committed any mistake apparent from record and as a result thereof the enhanced compensation awarded to him by the Civil court for the lands had been undervalued.

The appellant 's election was challenged by the respondent Bank in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was defaulter under section 73FF(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21.10.1986, on 18.8.1986, he was disqualified to contest the election. The appellant 's revision petition was dismissed on 30.8.89. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of the Assistant Registrar removing the appellant from the Committee of Directors of the Bank holding that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the elections. The High court dismissed the writ application holding that the High Court was in error in holding that the election was set aside on the ground of default. The appellant challenged the order of Assistant Registrar removing him from the Committee. The High, Court dismissed the appeal holding that the order of Deputy Registrar removing the petitioner from the Committee was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in 680 question the appellant 's Election as a Director. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant having repaid the loan before the notice was issued, he was certainly not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions of section 78 were not attracted. [723C] 1.2 The disqualification on account o default is common both for election and for continuation as a Director in the Committee, the special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply, Mr. Patil, the learned counsel for the State of Maharashtra, submits that the disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant having continued to be a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loan after the notice was given would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section 78. [724E] 1.3 The disqualification on the ground that he had repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice was issued would not be relevant for the purpose for taking action under Section 78. [761D] 1.4 The disqualification on his account being disqualified which continued after the elections of the appellant, the special provisions for setting aside the election must prevail. [725E] 1:5. The disqualification on behalf of the appellant being disqualified to continue as Director or creasing to be Director on account of default is common between both the parties and the maxim specialibus non vacant general words does not derogate from Special, would apply. [726F] 1.6 The disqualification on ground of default is Common both for election as a Director and also stated: "You have been elected as Director on account o his having committed default." [726G] 1.7 The disqualification on which the disqualification on the account of his having been incurred is common both both for election, and for continuation and as a Director on account Of his having committed defaults, the special Provision for setting aside of an election must be applicable, Mr. Patel, the learned advocate for the State, submits that as the disqualification on his being defaulter which continued from 18.8, 1986 to 21.10, 1986 to 20.10.86 did not mean that the disqualification continued after the Election of the appellant. [727G] 1:8. The disqualification as defaulter continues after the election.

The respondent was in the service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the Government order dated December 4,1982 reducing the amount to the extent of Re. 1 per month. The State of Maharashtra preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government had power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [910G H] 1.2 The State Government has power to reduce the amount of Pension payable to a Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service or after the completion of his service. [912B] 1.3 The State Government 's power to reduce, withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable to a government servant for misconduct, negligence or financial irregularities which he may has committed while in Service or after the completed service provided that before any order to this effect is issued, the procedure referred to in Note I to Rule 33 of the Bombay civil Services Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules shall be followed. [913C] 1.4 The State Government should have taken into consideration the fact that the respondent had retired from service a lenient view should be taken and reduction in pension to the extent it is expressly preserved. [914D] 1.5 The State Government was competent to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from service. The reduction of pension by 50 per percentage was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the respondent. [915E] 1.6 The State Government accepted the findings and passed the impugned order reducing the pension by 50% to the extent that the reduction of pension was too harsh. The State should have taken note the fact that while the respondent had already retired he could not escape the liability for misconduct and negligence or financial irregularity which he may be liable to pay. [916F] 1.7 The State Government did not exercise the power to reduce pension by 50 percent. The State was competent to reduce the pension by reducing the pension. [917F] 1:8. The State had power to reduced the amount of the pension paid to the respondent but having regard to the facts and circumstances, of the case, we are of the opinion that the reduction by 50 per percent was too harsh or disproportionate to the charges proved against the Respondent. [918G] 1.9 The State Government could have taken into account the fact that during the period of his service the respondent had superannuated from service a liberal view should be adopted. [919G] 1:10. The State has power to reduced pension by taking recourse to the procedure specified in Note I of Rule 33 of Bombay Civil Services Conduct, discipline and Appeal Rules. The State government should have taken all necessary steps to reduce the Pension payable to the Respondent. Having regard to the fact that there was no dispute that the respondent was retired from service, a lenient view could be taken and reduced in pension to that extent. [920G] 1 1.10. The proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The State Govt.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question. The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) of the Act was invalid in law. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the permission was invalid in view of the bar created by section 3(4) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 (U.P. Act III of 1947) that the order of the Commissioner under sub section (3) shall subject to any order that the State Government may pass under section 7 F of the Act. HELD : (1) The order passed by the District Magistrate granting permission to the landlord to sue his tenant was invalid in the eye of law. [620 E] (2) The order of the District Magistrate was not a nullity. [621 E] (3) The order was passed without notice to the party affected by such order, it would be open to the said party to contend that an order has been passed by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the Act, and it existence should be ignored by the civil court. [622 F] (4) The order is passed without notice, and it is merely a procedural order. [623 C] (5) The order, therefore, cannot be held to be invalid in law, because it is not a nullity, and it merely contains a procedural order, and it does not contain any provision which is not a provision which is inconsistent with the provisions of the statute. [624 E] (6) The order does not contain a provision which can be said to be inconsistent with the provision of the statute, and it only contains a provision which has been inconsistent with the Act. [626 F] (7) The order merely contains a provision for the grant of permission. [627 C] (8) The order contains a provision that before a District Magistrate grants permission to the tenant, he shall issue notice to the tenant and give him an opportunity to represent his case before the application of the landlord is dealt with on merits. [628 E] (9) The order must be made clear that in a given case, an order has be passed by the Collector granting permission to bring a suit against the tenant. [629 F] (10) The order cannot be held invalid on the ground of the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the civil court, and it cannot be held that the plea against the validity of the order in a civil court having regard to the bar created under sections 3 (4) and 16 of the Act is not raised and has not been considered. [630 E] (11) The order in question does not necessarily mean that the plea regarding the validity of order in a suit against a tenant can never be raised in a civil suit having regard to its bar created by sections 3 (3) and 16. [631 F] (12) The order only contains a clause which is inconsistent therewith. [632 E] (13) The order also contains a provision similar to the one contained in section 3(1) of the Uttar Pradesh (Temporary) Temporary) Control of rent and Eviction Act 1947 (U P. Act III Of 1947) that a landlord can evict his tenant if he satisfies two conditions. The order merely gives an opportunity to the tenant to represent his defence before the application is made by the landlord is disposed of.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission. He was dismissed from service by the President of India on the ground of misbehaviour. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the order of removal was illegal and that the President was not competent to make a reference to this Court under Article 317(1) of the Constitution. The High court dismissed the appeal, but the appellant contended that before making this Reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. The High ' Court held that the inquiry which this Court is required to hold is not into the limited question whether the person concerned is guilty of misbehaviour or whether the misconduct is of such a nature as to require his removal from the office of Member of the Public Service Commission, and that it would be impossible for him to prove his case unless he is allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The inquiry which this court is required to take into consideration the evidence which the parties lead before them, within the constraints of the following guidelines: (1) The recording of evidence will be over by September 30, 1983. (2) The recording or evidence will be limited to the cross examination of witnesses who have filed affidavits in this Court. (3) Witnesses who have filed affidavit in this Court may be summoned or requested by the learned Judge to attend his Court for the purpose of cross examination. The mere fact that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. [515E F] 2. The recording of the evidence will be about the cross examination. [516B] 3. The recording or the evidence will not conclude its issue as regards whether the person is guilty of misconduct and, secondly, whether the misconduct was of such a character as to require its removal from the Office of Member of Public Service Commission on that ground. [517C] 4. The inquiry referred to us, therefore, is not into a limited question whether on the basis of facts found by the President, the charge of misbehaviour is made out and whether the misconduct are of such a type as to require the removal of the person from his office. If a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial, it is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme Court and not by a court of first instance. The mere facts that the evidence have been examined and find upon by the learned Judges will not conclude issue as regards admissibility or relevance or relevance of the evidence. [617E] 5. The inquiry report which this Court has been required to hold, is not an examination in chief of the respective witnesses. The mere circumstance that the evidence had been examined and finding upon the evidence will also not conclude the Issue as regards the relevancy of that evidence, unless it is not over by that date, the learned Judge may write to the Registrar (Judicial) of this Court. [618G] 6. The inquiry reports which the parties led before the President, were not part of the record. The mere finding body for the prima facie satisfaction of that a case is made out, will not conclude whether the person who has not filed an affidavit in this court will be examined or cross examined as a witness, except with the leave of this Court, and the evidence will have to be transmitted to the Registrar(Judicial) of the Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded by him. [619G] 7.

The appellants were the trustees of a public temple. The endowment was a private one and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The endowment consisted of two items, namely, (i) a temple and (ii) a temple. The appellants claimed that the endowment was a public endowment. The trial court held that the endowment did not constitute a private endowment and that the endowment had been made for religious purposes. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the endowment in question was a private endowment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The endowment was of a public nature and the dedication was for the use or benefit of the public. [840 A B] 1.2 The mere fact that members of the public are allowed to worship by themselves does not necessarily mean that the temple is a public temple, for members of the family or their descendants. [841 A B] 2.1 The mere fact of worship by the members of the community or their descendants does not necessarily imply that the endowment is of a public character. [842 A] 2.2 The existence of a public endowment is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the deity. The mere fact, that members of a public are allowed only a particular person belonging to a particular community which also shows that even if the family was to become extinct, the private nature of the endowment was not to be changed. [843 B] 2:3 The mere fact existence of a trust is not a conclusive proof to show that the endowment has been made for the public. It is manifest that the endowment itself is a public endowment unless it is proved that the members of that community were allowed to worship in the temple by way of a public trust unless it is established that the members were allowed to worshi at the shrine of the deity, and that extensive properties are dedicated for the purpose of the maintenance of the temple belonging to the founder himself, this will be a conclusive proof of the intention to dedicate the temple merely for the benefit of the members of his family or their families. [844 B] 2 2.4 The existence of the public endowment is not a decisive factor to indicate the private nature. [845 A B] 3.1 The existence of public endowment is an important circumstance to indicate the public character of the endowment. The mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the dedication. Some of the circumstances from which a public endowment can be inferred, are to indicate theprivate nature of the Endowment. Some of these circumstances may conclusively establish that the endowment could be ascertained, the nature of which is a clear proof of the intent to dedicate it to public and not to the members of any particular community which it has been proved that the temple was a public temple and not a public endowment, as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrines of the deity can only be the members of such community which also show that even if a document is available to prove the nature and origin of the endowment and the recitals of the document show that the control and management of the temple is retained with the founder or his descendants, the private character of the dedication would not be changed. Some of those circumstances may conclusively prove that the endowment by the members was of a private nature and the origin of the Endowment was not to find out whether the members of public were entitled to worship in a temple by way a public endowment or a private trust. [846 B D] 3.2 The fact that members were allowed only a certain person belonging to the community which also showed that even if it is proved, the private property was not to become extable.

The appellant Bank instituted a suit against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhatmal had no right to attach it. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court. The appellant Bank instituted an appeal against the decree. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and the Bank. The Trial Court held that the appellant had no right, title or interest in the money due under the bill and decreed the suit. The High Court held that there was no transfer of the decree or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the borrower continued to be the owner and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the power of attorney was expressed to be irrevocable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power of attorney is expressed to be unconditional. It is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and the bank was that of borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. As the lender had an interest in the fundS the power of Attorney was expressed tobe irrevocable. The endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 created an interest in a specific fund and was irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment of a specific fund in favour of the appellant. [775 D] 2. The power attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bills dated July 19 1948 created an equitable assignment in favour of a borrower or which might be passed in his favour in a pending appeal and to credit to the borrower 's account the monies realised in execution of the decree amounted to an equitable assignment of the moneys receivable under the bill. The endorsement was sent to and acknowledged by the military authorities. Read in the light of the power of the attorney the endorsement on it created an interest In the light of power of attorney the endorsement was sent by Takhatmal to and acknowledged. There was therefore a sufficient equitable Assignment of a specific Fund in favour of Bharat Bank Ltd., Jabalpur. [776 E] 3. The power to attorney coupled with a endorsement on the cheque dated July 19. 1948 created an Interest in a specific Fund and was irrevocable and was irrevocable.[776 H] 4. The power power of attorney coupled with, the endorsement on bill dated July 13, 1948 created a valid equitable charge upon such fund. The endorsement in the bill dated August 19, 1948 creating an interest in favour of appellant was irrevocable. The power was expressed to have been irrevocable. There is thus a sufficient equity assignment of a particular fund in favour o the appellant. The power Attorney coupled with the endorsements on the bill was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bills directly in his hands. The endorsement of the bill dated January 21, 1948 created no interest in a particular fund. The power Power of attorney coupledwith the endorsement on a bill was irrevocable. [778 E] 5. The power under attorney was expressed by Malhotra to be irrevocable and was unconditional. The endorsement dated the bill dated March 21, 1948 creating a valid equitable mortgage in favour of respondent No. 2 was irrevocable. It was irrevocable. In the last case the Court held that no equitable assignment of any specific fund in the favour of the respondent No. 1 was made by the appellant Bank. The power powers of attorney coupled and the endorsement on bills dated July 13. 1948 created a legal equitable assignment of an equitable mortgage in respect of the moneys received under the bill in favour of respondents No. 2 and 3. The endorsement by the military authority was irrevocable.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The assessee was the Manager of a Tea Estates under the managing Agency of M/S. Gillands ArbuthNot & Co. Limited. The assessee claimed that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's salary as defined in section 17 of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt of Rs. 27,948/ representing the interest on the amount of his own contribution to the fund was exempt from tax in view Of section 17(1)(iv). The Tribunal came by certificate. The High Court held that the receipt was not income as defined by section 2(24). The High Court also held that the receipts in question being income from house pro perty, profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains, the same were exempt from tax. The assessee appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The receipt of Rs 27,948/- by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary as defined by the section. [448B] The receipt of an interest on any investment is a gain made by the investor and therefore the same is "income". [448C] The receipt by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from tax under section 56. [449D] The receipt is undoubtedly an income. [447B] The income in question is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on the securities; income from house property pro perty; profits and gains. it has to be considered as "Income from other sources" if it is not chargeable to income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. [446C] The word "profits" in section 17(2) (ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [445C] The meaning of section 17 (3) (i) is plain. Hence there are no need to calling into aid any rule of construction as is sought to be made by the High court. [444D] The meaning given to section 17(4) (ii), is plain and clear. Hence there cannot be said that the receipt by the appellant with which we were concerned is exempt under what head the same has to be brought to tax. [440E] The receipt in question is undoubtedly an Income. [442E] The word 'profits in lieu of salary" is a gain which is not to be included in the total income under the Act. [443E] The receipts of profits in lieu of pay have to be considered for the purposes of income tax under the head 'Income from house property; profits or gains of business and brought to tax under section 17(I)(iv). [445F] The receipt has to be taken as salary. [439F] The receipts in question are dealt with by section 16. [437F] The word `profits in lieu 'of salary has to be understood as salary. The receipt of the interest is a gain. It has to be seen whether the receipt is a gain or a gain made either by the investor or interest on such contributions. [438F] The amount of Rs.27,948/ was not taxable under section 56 of the Act, 1961.

The petitioners were carrying on their respective trades. The State of Madhya Pradesh enacted the Madhya Pradesh Prevention of Cow Slaughter and Animals Act, 1960. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act violated a fundamental right under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act was violative of article 19(2) of the petitioners and that the Act infringed the fundamental rights under article 19 (1)(g). The petitioners contended (i) that the Act contravened article 19(6) of the constitution and (ii) that the impugned Act violated article 19(5) of the, Constitution. HELD: (i) The Act is constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness, it offends against article 19(4) of the. [655 B] (ii) The ban on the slaughter of cow, male or female calves of cows and calves is quite reasonable and valid and is in consonance with the directive principles laid down in article 48, (ii) the Act is to that extent void. [656 C] (iii) The banning the slaughter of buffaloes of all ages is quite reasonable. [657 D] (iv) The ban prohibits the slaughter and slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle will defeat the very object of the directive principles embodied in article 48. [658 E] (v) The ban is not valid in so long as it prohibits slaughter of cows and buffaloes without prescribing any tests or requirement as required to their age. The entire provision banning the Slaughter of cows of every ages and calve of buffaloes, male and female is quite reasonable, and valid and the is to that effect. [659 E] (vi) The ban prohibiting the slaughter of animals of all ages, calves of calves of cattle, breeding bulls, and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) without prescribing any Test or requirement as regards their age or badness, it violates the fundamental right of the petitioners under article 19 of the Constitution and is to that limited extent void. The entire provisions banning the slaughtered slaughter of cows in all ages and is to be struck down. [660 E] (vii) The ban banning the slaughtering of cows of calves and calves and striking down the ban on the slaughtered of cows is quite reasonable; and the ban is to that extend to the slaughter of calves. [652 E] (viii) The ban of slaughter of cows is not valid. [653 F] (ix) The ban in question is not valid because it prohibits the slaughtered of cow, female or female calve of cows, male and male, butchers to carry on their occupation or business. The entire ban banning slaughter of cows cannot be struck down as invalid in so far it prohibits the Slaughter of buffaloes of other animals, breeding bulls or working bullocks (dattle and buffalo). [652 B] (x) The ban restricting the slaughter of cattle of all ages or calves of animals cannot be struck aside as it completely prohibits the slaughter or slaughter of cows. [654 E] (xi) The ban imposed by the impugned Act is not valid and we hold that in so far the it prohibits the slaughtering of buffaloes of any other species, it offends the fundamental right under Article 19(1) (g) and is to this extent void.

The respondent was a 'workman ' within the meaning of the Central Act and an 'employee ' as defined in the local Act. The respondent was a workman within the meaning Of the Central Act. The Company filed a suit against the Company for damages for wrongful dismissal. The Company contended that (1) the Standing Orders did not apply to the respondent, because he was an employee within the meaning o the Central Act; and (2) the Standing Order No. Standing Order No, Standing Order No,. was not applicable to the respondent. The Company also contended that (i) the Standing orders did not apply, because the respondent was an employee ' within the definition of that expression in section 2 (1) of the local Act; and that (ii) the Standing Standing Orders did apply to the Company, and (iii) the respondent was not an 'employee' as defined in that expression in the Standing Orders. The Company, however, contended that (a) the Standing order No. Standing Orders No. 1 and 2 did not apply in respect of the respondent and (b) the Standing Rules did not apply. Held, that the Standing Orders were not applicable to a respondent and his service had been terminated in accordance with Standing Order No., No. 1. The Standing Orders were applicable to the Company only to whom tickets had been issued. The Standing Order No.. 1 did not apply for the respondent and his services had been terminated, and the Standing Orders No.. 2 and 3 did not apply the respondent.

The Company was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into production. The Company was a subsidiary of Hindustan Steel Ltd. and was a subsidiary company of Hindustan Steel Limited. The Company had been in existence for a long period and had been even earning profits, so that the exemption could not be granted to this Company in respect of payment of bonus under section 16 of the Act. The Company claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project could not be treated as a new establishment for purposes of section 16 of that Act for the purpose of computation of bonus under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because Alloy Steel Project was owned, controlled and managed by one single Company and, consequently, the Company could not be regarded as a new unit for purposes of computation of the bonus under the said Act. HELD: The Tribunal went entirely erroneous in holding that simply because Alloy steel Project was owned controlled and managed, controlled and maintained by one single company and, consequently,. the principle to be applied to the separate units for which separate accounts, separate balance sheets, and profit and Loss accounts are maintained. [805 E] The proviso to sub section (2) of section 16 only comes in the way it bonus is paid in any year to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. [806 G] The proviso, to sub section(2) of Section 16 only comes into the way it is bonus is paid on the basis that the entire paid up capital was credited and advances were made by the Head Office to the various units out of this capital or out of loans taken by the Head office to various units out Of loans taken by it. [807 C] The proviso cannot be resorted to at all when the Act itself is inapplicable in view of the provision contained in section 1, sub section It is, therefore, quite clear that the proviso to sub sub section (1) of section 3 will not apply in such a case. [808 D] The proviso is quite clear that it bonus is payable in any year, to the employees, of all the Units on the basis Of consolidated profits of each such unit.
