The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller found that the respondent bona fide required the premises to carry on his profession. The respondent bona fide requires the premises for carrying on his trade as an Advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Rent controller found that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a) (iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of the tenant on the ground of his requirement unless it was for the purpose for which it was leased, commission of acts of waste, conduct amounting to nuisance to the occupiers of the other portions in the same building, securing of alternative accommodation by the tenant and denial of the title of the landlord. The High Court held that the practice was not business in the sense of business ' and that the practice in the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 was not business. The High court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended by the appellant that the practice as a legal profession was 'business ' within the meaning Of Section 10(2) (a)(iii) and that the respondent could seek the eviction only if it was for his own occupation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'business ' has been used in a wide sense so as to include the practice of a liberal profession like that of an Advocate. ' The word ' business ' has been defined in the explanation to Section 10(1) (a). The word 'profession ' has been given a wide meaning so as to includes the practice of an Advocate which in the opinion of the Controller, the landlord bona fide proposes to commence. [723B] 2. The word "business " has been defined by the Explanation to Section 10 (3) (b) of the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, rent and Eviction) Regulation, 1960. The word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. The word must be construed in the context of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context of the statute concerned. [724C] 3. The word should be interpreted in the context in which it occurs and not in the context thereof of other statutes. [725E] 4. The word shall be interpreted in its context of other statutory provisions in a manner hostile to the context. [726C] 5. The word is capable of including the practice of law. [727D] 6. The word has been used for a wide sense. It clearly includes the practice in a manner encased by the tenant. [728B] 7. The word cannot be given a wide interpretation so as to exclude the word 'business occurring in the Andhra Karnataka Buildings (Lease and Rent Eviction) Control Rules, 1960. [729G] 8. The word would have when it occur in other statutory provision. The word might have when it occurred and not in a mannerzhumous to the context in the statute concerned, but not in the sense that the word may have been when it occurs and also not in the light of other statutes and in a manner Babusing the context of another statute. [730C] 9. The word, therefore, includes the practice ' of law. The word will be construed in its context in which the context of Section 10 (2) (b). [730G] 10.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that the respondent was a debtor to the respondent for the approximate sum of Rs.4,00,000. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree and decreed the suit on the ground that the respondent had not paid the amount in the year 1943 and therefore the suit was barred by time. The High court held that the respondent could not be said to be a debtor to a creditor of the firm of the appellant. The High ' Court also held that the appellant was entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. The High, Court held that the use of the word 'deposit by itself occurring either in the roznamcha or in the letter dated 29 September, 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not be decisive of the question whether it was a case of deposit of the sum of Rs 4,00, 000 by the respondent with the appellant under an agreement. The High. Court also held, that the use was not decisive of the issue whether it was an ordinary loan of Rs. 3,00,00,001. The High "Court further held that the transaction was between the appellant and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills on the one hand and Lakshmi Ratan Jute Mills on the other, that moneys were lent and advanced by Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mill to India Supplies from time to time and all that happened was that in place of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton mills the respondent became the creditor of the appellant and therefore it was improbable that the respondents who were bankers would deposit with the traders the sum of money immediately. The HighCourt also held that there was a demand for a part of the amount in respect of Lakshmi Ratan Jute Mill and India Supplies on the other. The High Courts also held that in the case of a demand in the year 1944 the respondent was entitled to withdrawal of the deposit on Demand. 4,00.000 with the appellant and secondly whether the suit was not barred by time, and that the suit was dismissed. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The use of the words 'deposit by themselves occurring either in a roznam cha or in the letters dated 29 September 1942 written by the appellant to the respondent recording the agreement that the same would be paid on demand. It was not a case of an ordinary loan. [475D] (2) The letter further shows that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners of India Supplies on behalf of India Supplies. The letter further show that the terms of the award were agreed to between the appellant, the respondent and Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills. The letter also shows that the term was that the award in respect of Laxmi Ratan Cotton Mills and India Supplies would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. [476F] (3) The letter also showed that the terms agreed to by both parties were agreed to. [478F] (4) The letter shows that the agreement was between the parties. The letter shows the fact that the money was lent and advanced. The letter does not show that the money were lent and was advanced by Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills to India Supplies. Some of the partners of Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mill and India Supply on the one side and Lakshmi Ratan Birla Cotton Mills on behalf of the appellant, were common. It was therefore improbable that the respondent who were bankers could deposit with the appellant the amount of Rs. 2,00,500. [482F] (5) The letter showed that the money had to be paid on 577 demand. The letter was written by Ram Mohan Gupta to the respondent recorded that there was demand for the part of the sum.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986, made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The petitioner made an application to this Court under Article 32 in Writ Petition (Crl) No. 292 of 1986 challenging that order of detention. The petition was dismissed by this Court. The petitioner thereafter filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of detention and the order of preventive detention. The petitioner contended that the order of detu tion was illegal and invalid because the petitioner was already in custody at the most one day. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner then filed a writ appeal in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. The petitioner thereupon filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention was passed and before the actual service of the order of the detention, the petitioner was in jail for at the most he was in custody. The order was served and since the detenu was already in detention, the order of his detention became necessary. [849E] 2. The fact that the detenu was in custody when the order was made, yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of detention became necessary and that he was still sub jective. [848B] 3. The fact of the petitioner being in custody when he was subjective, does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive Detention. [845C] 4. The fact, that the detenu is al ready in detention does not take place in making an application for preventive detention. [846F] 5. The fact is that the detenu has confined his arguments to one point settled the writ petition as senior counsel with the allegations quoted above in paragraph 2 of the writ petition, and did not dispute the fact that the petitioner was aware of the fact that he was already in jail when the order of bail was passed. [847F] 6. The fact in respect of which the detenu is accused is so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that these affect continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby jeo pardise the security of the State, then sub ject to other conditions being fulfilled, a man being in detention would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply. [844F] 7. The fact remains that the detenu had confined his arguments only to one point and it was clearly stated by the senior counsel, Shri Ram Jethmalani, that he was not aware of the proceedings in the Court and did not challenge the order of Detention. [ 845F] 8. The fact was that the detenu, being already in custody, was still subjective. [ 846F] 9. The fact still that the detenu being in custody, the order was passed and he was sub nectively satisfied with that his order was necessary for put ting him back in jail. [843F] 10. The fact also that the detenu himself was in custody at that time when the order came to be made, yet the order of release was passed and the order was served. [842F] 11. The fact remained that after the order of this Court, the petitioner had been in custody, he was submi tted to attend the office by the authorities concerned, but he was sub mitted to attend his office by the authority concerned, yet he did not dispute that he was sub sentically satisfied that his detention became unnecessary.

The petitioners were engaged as casual labourers in the Telecom. Wing of P & T Department. The petitioners were engaged in the work of construction of P &T Department. The respondents were engaged as Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The Union of India was of the view that the petitioners were not regularly employed and they were not being regularly employed. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers and are not being regularly recruited, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners belong to a category of casual labour and are not regularly employed. They are not being regular employees. They strictly conform to the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210 270 and Rs.260 350 as the case may be. [435C D] 1.2 The petitioners belong not to the category mentioned in the Postal and Telegraphs department at the rates equivalent to the minimum pay in the pay scales of regularly employed workers in the corresponding cadres but without any increments with effect from 5th of February, 1986 on which date the first of the above two petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. It is also for this reason that managements and the Government agencies in particular should not allow 610 workers to remain as casual labourers or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep persons as casual labourers for years as is being done in the Postal & Telegraphs Department at the rates applicable to regular employees may be effected as is at present available to casual un skilled labour working under the P & T department. [436D] 1.3 The petitioners belong only to the category in which the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period of more than six months. They strictly comply with the job content in the Posts & Telegraphs department. They strictly adhere to the job contents of corresponding regular post in scales of pay and allowances and other benefits as are being paid to the regular employees of the Posts and telegraphs Department. [437E] 1.4 The petitioners belong also not being regularly appointed, they are neither entitled to the benefits of increased rates of daily wages nor temporary employees for any unreasonably long period. They strictly follow the job content content of corresponding Regular posts in scales. [438F] 1.5 The petitioners belong neither to the category nor are being regularly employed, they are being regularly recruited. They strictly adhered to the job conditions. They strictly abide by the job content and are not entitled for the same privileges as are being enjoyed by those who have completed 720/1200 days of service over a period of time. [439F] 1:6 The petitioners belong either to the category or of casual labourers who strictly conform to their job content ofcorresponding regular posts in scale of Rs. 210 270 and Rs,260 350 as per the job content. They strictly complied with the job conditions and are not regular employees. [440F] 1.:6 The petitioners are not being continuously employed, they being not regularly employed, They are not entitled, to the same benefits which the regular employee is enjoying. They strictly fail to comply with the work conditions. They are entitled to the benefit of increased rates, of daily wages, allowances and other allowances and other privileges as are are being paid by the regular employees. The arrears of wages payable to the casual labourers in accordance with this order shall be paid within four months from today. [441F] 1 7. The arrears payable to the petitioners in accordance with the order shall be payable within four months.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the basis of a return filed under section 22(3) of the Act. The Income tax Officer, however, assessed the assessee to income tax for the assessment year 1950 1950 1950 1950 and the assessment was made on the basis that the assessee had submitted a return under section 22 (3) of that Act on January 5, 1950, and that the assessee was entitled under section 22 to make a " voluntary " return on the date he did, and with a voluntary return before the Income tax Officer. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the return filed on January 5 and 1950 was a return filed within the period of one year from the date of the service of the notice under section 22 and that the benefit of the extended period of limitation for assessment available under the first proviso to sub section (3) was not available in this case. The assessee then appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Department ought to have issued a notice under section 34(2) within the assessment year or a notice under that section. The High court held that the Income tax officer had reason to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of an assessee to make a Return of his income under section 22, for any year, the assessee had made a return of his income and that the amount of the extended periods of limitation for the assessment years 1950 1950 1950 1951 1951 1951 1951 1952 1952 1952 1952 1953 1952 1952 1952 1951 1952 1952 1953 1953 1952 1952 1953 1951 1952 1952 1951 1953 1952 1952 1951 1951 1952 1953 1952 1953 1952 1951 1952 1953 1951 1951 1952 1951 1952 1951 1951 1951 1953 1952 1951 1951 1953 1951 1952 1951 1953 1951 1951 1951 1950 1951 1951 1952 1950 1951 1951 1950 1952 1951 1951 1950 1953 1951 1951 1950 1950 1951 1952 1951 1950 1951 1952 1952 1950 1951 1952 1953 1953 1951 19511952 1951 1951 19511952 1952 1951 19511952 1950 1952 1951 1952 1950 1952 1951 1950 1952 1952 1951 1950 1953 1952 19511952 1951 1952 19511952 1952 1952 19511952 1950 1951 195119521952 1951 1952 19521951 1952 1951 19511951 1952 1951 19521951 1952 1952 19511951 1952 1952 1952 1950 1952 1952 19521952 1951 19521951 1951 1952 19521952 1952 1952 19521951 1951 1951 19521952 1951 1951 195219511952 1951 19521952 1952 1951 19521952 1950 1952 19521952 1950 1951 19521952. The High Courts held that the notice under s. 34(1) was not a return filed beyond the time fixed by the notice under sub section (1) of section 22(2) of the Income tax Act. The High ' Court held that a " voluntary" return showing a nontaxable income was still a good return for all purposes under the Act and subs. 120 Section 22(1) of the said Act requires a return of taxable income and not a return of income which shows a loss or is below the taxable limit. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was appointed as a Director of a correspond ing bank under the National Bank of India. The appellant was appointed as the Director of a referral bank under the provisions of the National Bank for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction Act, 1951. The appellant, who was a member of the Board of Directors, was appointed by the Central Government. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the circular dated 23.8.1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the validity of circular dated 23,8.1982 on the ground that the circular dated 22.8.82 was ultra vires the Act. The High court dismissed the writ application. The appellant contended that the circular was ultra vires and void as it was violative of Articles 19(1)(c) and 43(A) of the Constitution. The appellant also contended that the Circular dated 23.08.1982 was ultra vires as it was in effect a nomination of the one preferred by the Central Govern ment to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, and that the circular did not apply to the appellant. The High, Court, however, dismissed the writ. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High Judge dismissed the writ appeal. The appellant thereupon filed a writ application in the High Curt. The High Curt dismissed the writ applications. The appellant thereafter filed a writ Appeal in the High, Court. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The circular dated 23rd August 1982 (Annexure A) was ultra vires. [682G H] 1.2 The circular dated 22nd August 1982 ( Annexure A) was in effect an appointment of the appellant as Director of a foreign bank under the Act. [683G] 1.3 The circular dated 21st August 1982 (Annex. A) was not an unrestrained or unrestricted discretion but a discretion which must be reasonably exercised so as to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to the composition of the Board. The mode of election or nomination must, therefore, be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking industry and the choice of the mode is generally a matter for decision by the Central government. [684G] 1:4. The very object of leaving the choice to the Central Government as to the mode is ordinarily a matter for consideration by the Central Govt. and that interpretation is, in our view, correct. [685G] 1.:5. The mode, mode of election and nomination must, however, be such that it can reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. [686G] 1 :6. The mode is generally an approach to the Central Govt., and that interpretation of Articles 19 and 43(a) of the constitution is, in the view, in our opinion, correct. The mode adopted by the Central Board of Directors of a foreign company, constituted under any scheme made under subsection (1), must, therefore be such as to give an opportunity to the concerned employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, to exercise their choice. [690G] 1.?5. The Central Government, in exercise of its discretion, has to act in accordance with the provisions of this Act.

The assessee was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. The assessee preferred appeals to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalties. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the applications and made an order staying the recovery of the penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of the penalty pending the appeal. The High Court held that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had the power under the relevant provisions of the Act to stay the collection of tax and that the power of stay could be spelt out from that provision. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Appellate Assistant commissioner or the Appellate Tribunal is given the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its Appellate jurisdiction. [723C] 1.2 The power of stay by the Tribunal is not intended to enable an assessee who has preferred an appeal to obtain from the appellate forum, a stay of collection during the pendency of an appeal before the Appellate Assistant commissioner and not to the Appellate Tribunal. [724E] 1.3 The power of staying recovery during the pendency or appeal before the appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Appellate Assistant Commission is not intended merely to enable an assesses who has preferred a appeal to obtainfrom the appellate forum. [725B] 1.4 The power of granting stay by the Appellate Tribunal to stay the proceedings as also by the collection of such taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter a matter of practice in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [726C] 1:5. The power of the Appellate Tribunal, therefore, is not likely not to be exercised at a routine manner or as a matters of course in view of section 220(6) which is confined only to the stage of pendency of an Appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and not to enable an applicant who has preferred the appeal to obtain therefrom from the appellate forums. [727D] 1.6 The power of suspension by the Appellate Assistant Commissioners or the Appellate Tribunals is a matter for the legislature to consider. [728E] 1:7. The power to stay recovery of taxes or penalties is a matter of procedure. It is very much clear that when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Authority, the same High Court can give the necessary relief of staying recovery to the assessee but that can hardly be put at par with a statutory power as is contained in section 220(5) which is limited only to the stages of the appeal. [729F] 1.8. The Appellate Commissioner or the Income tax Officer is given the powers to stay the realisation of the tax, either in whole or in part on furnishing suitable security, is a matter which is for the legislature. The power conferred by the statute is not intended only to enable an Income tax Officer who can give the requisite 69 relief to an assessee. [730G] 1.9. The Appellate Authority or the Appellate Authority is given the discretion to grant stay of collection to the assessee. [ 730G] 2.10. The Appellate authority or the Appellate authority is given the right to stay the execution of the tax. [731B] 2.11. The Appellate Officer or the Appellate Commissioner is given the duty to consider whether to stay the realization of the tax or penalties payable on the assessees. [732C] 2.12.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial, and was charged with offences under section 7 of the Police Act with remissness in the discharge of his duties. The respondent was charged with having committed offences under section 8 of the Police (P.C.) and section 7 of Police (P.) Act. The trial was conducted by the Superintendent of Police and the respondent submitted his explanation on September 12, 1953. The respondent submitted his reply on September 12. 1953. The Superintendent of Police, after considering the explanation of the respondent, passed an order dismissing the respondent from service. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not a Sub Inspector and that the order of his dismissal was invalid. HELD: (1) The order of dismissal was held to have been made under the statutory power conferred upon the Superintendent of police by the regulations providing for investigation in the first place under chapter XIV of the Criminal Procedure Code. [605B] (2) The order was held to be invalid. [606C] (3) The order made by the Superintendent was not in the first instance received by the respondent and forwarded to the police for inquiry. The Superintendent, of Police, was competent to make inquiry under the direction of the Superintendent of the Police in accordance with the following rules. [608D] (4) The order passed by the Superintendent, was not in accordance with law. [609E] (5) The order dated November 17, 1952, was not made under the administrative power conferred upon him by the regulations. [610B] (6) The order in the present case was not made by a police officer senior in rank to a Superintendent. [612C] (7) The order did not in any way affect the validity of the order of transfer. [613D] (8) The order, therefore, was not invalid. [713B] (9) The order does not in any manner affect the validity or validity of the orders of dismissal. [614B] (10) The order merely states that the Sub Divisional Magistrate made inquiry in respect of the matter which was the subject matter of the departmental inquiry and that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the validity. [615C] (11) The order is not made under any statutory power conferred by the regulations, but it is made under the direction or of the Superintendent. The order merely indicates that the Sub- Divisional Magistrate made inquiries in respect of seven of the charges which were the subject matter in the departmental trial and that the respondent had on nine occasions, particulars of which were given in the charge, accepted bribes in the discharge, of his duties and unfitness for the same inasmuch as while posted as a Station Officer, Police Station, Intiathok, was the subject-matter of the departmental enquiry and therefore it falls within the express terms of para. 486 of the Police Regulations. [616D] (12) The order only indicates that the Superintendent of of Police had made inquiries in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage. [617E] (13) The order also does not in terms indicate that the Superintendent had made inquiries from the C. I.D. and forwarded to him for inquiry. [618F] (14) The order clearly indicates that the respondent, when he was officer incharge of the Police Station, had no power to dismiss him.

The appellant was appointed as a supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. He was promoted to supertime grade I on February 8 1971. The appellant was promoted to Supertime grade II in February, 871. The appellant challenged the promotion of Dr. Sen and Dr. Sen to supertime Grade II on the ground that the post was not a teaching hospital and that the post could only have been filled in by promotion from amongst those holding the post in Specialists ' grade only. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the post of Director of Health Services, Manipur, was a teaching hospital. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The post of Director was converted into a specified post and that as it was assigned to Ophthalmologist and qualified for the post, that post could only be filled in by direct promotion from amongst the persons who were qualified to be appointed to that speciality and that as the converted post was unspecified Specialists ' post, it could only be made. [520B] 1.2 The post was converted into an unspecified post and that the posts could only be converted into a specialities and were filled in by the promotion yet when some one who was already in that grade was transferred to the newly created post and the post could be filled in, in accordance with the relevant rule. [521B] 1:3 The post was not treated as a teaching hospital but was a post created at Willingdon Hospital and the post was converted to a specified post in a speciality it was an addition to the strength of that speciality and the filling in of such post would be governed by rule 8 (3). [521C] 1.4 The post was created at Willingsdon Hospital which was not a Teaching hospital and, therefore, the appellant was not qualified for being promoted to super time grade II in the speciality. [522D] 1.5 The post was deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion of Dr Sen and Dr Sen. [523B] 1 :6. The appellant had not put in 8 years of service in the category of Specialists ' posts and was senior to Dr. Sen. [623C] 1:7. The appellant could not be considered for promotion to supertime grades II in February 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for promotion to Supertime Grade II. [624D] 1:8. The matter must remain at that stage and there is no justification for giving a direction that the appellant should be considered for the post which is deemed to have fall vacant in September 1972 on the invalidation. [626E] 1.9 The matter must remained at that stage. There is no justification to give a direction that Dr. Sen should be considered eligible for promotion from the date on which Dr. Sen was originally appointed. [627F] 1.10. The matter should remain at that point and there is nothing else, appellant himself would not have been qualified for promotion to the supertime gradeII in February 1971. [628G] 1.11. The matter would remain at that stages and there is none, in the contention on behalf of appellant that in refusing promotion to Dr. P.

The High ' Court held that the surplus pool was not hit under section 10A of the Act and the land inherited was saved from utilisation by the State. The High, Court held that section 19B was not applicable to the case of respondent No.1. The High "Court further held that the lands inherited by him were not hit under the section 10A(a) of the Act, and so he was entitled to the benefit of section 10A. The HighCourt further held, that the land held by him and subsequently transferred to his son and wife were also not hit by Section 10A and Section 19B of Act. The High Curt held that the appellant was entitled to receive rent from the tenant so settled. The High Courts held that the entire surplus pool was to be treated as surplus land and the surplus pool had to be treated to be surplus land. The High The appellant has filed these appeals by special leave. The High courts have held that the excess land of the appellant was not hit either by section 10 or section 19B. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The land inherited by respondent No,. 2 was not a surplus land but was only a limited area. The land acquired by him was not a limited area and the surplus area was not, therefore, not covered by the section. [636G H] 2. The land which was inherited by respondent no. 2 was not, then, his transfer will not be affected by the interdict of section 10 A(a) the sins of the father. [637G] 3. The surplus pool was, therefore, saved from utilisation. [638G] 4. The surplus area was, therefore not, to be treated at the disposal of the Government for utilization by the State Government for utilization as surplus area. [639B] 5. The plaintiffs claimed that the genealogical table set up by the plaintiffs was erroneous, that by the order of the Governor of Madhya Pradesh dated November 9, 1951, the Zamindari was conferred upon the 1st defendant Dayaram as he was found suitable to hold the, Zamindari and the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951, had become binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date of the notification issued under section 3 of the Act and the plaintiffs were on that account not entitled to claim the compensation paid or payable in respect of the Malguzars lands which vested with the State. The defendants contended that the order of compensation Officer was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari, that the order was contrary to law and the law govern the Zamindari; that the order dated August 30, 1951, was not binding and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date and that the plaintiffs were entitled to claim compensation in respect of their Malguz yari lands and the decision in the compensation proceedings was final and conclusive and was not binding on the Compensation Officer. Held, that the orders of the Compensation Officers under sub section (1) of section 14 were not binding and the order of dismissal passed by the Compensation Officer was not binding. The order of the Compensation officer under sub section(1) of s. 14 was not binding upon the plaintiffs because the order of his Governor recognising Dayaram to be the successor on the death of Amarshah was not binding; that the decision of his Governor in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be his successor on the supposition that the geneealogical table was impar tible and was governed by the rule of primogeniture and Pratapshah was governed by his rule of prim Medicine and the decision was binding on the plaintiffs because neither the order of Governor recognising Dayaram nor the order of His Governor in 1950 set up by him was a forged will. The order dated August 29, 1951, passed by the Governor of M.P. dated November 9. 1951, was contrary to and was not based on any custom or law governing the estate.

The Bombay High Court in Ambalal 's case (supra) and in Chunilal Shivlal vs Chimanlal Nagindas took the view in that case that the suit filed by the tenant was governed by section 12 (2) (b) of the Gujarat High Court Act and that the suit being governed by the said provisions the provisions contained under sections 12 (1) (a), (3) and (b) will apply. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions contained by sections 11 and 13 of the Act are as follows: "Where at any stage of a suit for recovery of rent whether with or without a claim for possession of the premises, the Court is satisfied that the tenant is withholding the rent on the ground that the rent is excessive and standard rent should be fixed, the Court shall pass a decree for eviction in any such suit for recovery, and that if the tenant makes an application within one month of the service of the notice on the tenant, the Court may make an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court forthwith such amount of the rent as the Court considers to be reasonably due to the landlord, or at the option of the tenant an order directing him to pay to the landlord such amount as the Court may specify. The Bombay view was that the dispute in section 12 (4) (a)(b) of The Bombay High Courts Act, 1947, was not limited only to a dispute raised within one month from the service of notice under section 12(2) (a). The Bombay High court in Ambala 's case held that the dispute as to standard rent was raised within one months of the notice as contemplated in section 12(3) (b), and that the tenant can raise a dispute as to the standard rent in his written statement in answer to a suit for eviction. The Bombay and the Bombay High Courts in Ambalals 's case, (supra) held that the provisions in sections 12(3), (3), 12 (3)(a) and (3) of the Maharashtra Act are as follow: "Where there is a dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if, before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under sub section (3) for the first time in the written statement in reply to the suit and in 630 such a case the tenant makes a request to the Court to make an order for the tenant to pay to him such amount as may be specified. The Bombay decisions are not applicable to the suit. The Bombay Full Bench of the Bombay and the Gujarat High Courts in the decisions in Ambaladal 's Case (supra) relied on. The Bombay Act does not apply to a suit which is governed by section 11 of the Act. The Bombay Legislature has enacted the Bombay Act to provide for the determination of standard rent in respect of certain classes of cases. The Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, is a special Act and the Bombay Municipal Corporation has been constituted under the Bombay Municipal Act, 1949. The Bombay City Municipal Corporation Act is a special enactment and the Bombay City Municipal Act, 1888, is a general enactment.

The respondent company was a director controlled company. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1939. The respondent was a director of the respondent company. The company was a managing director of the company. The shares held by it in the respondent company were subject, directly or indirectly to his will and ordering and, therefore, the directors of the respondent Company in fact control its affairs at general meetings and as such have "a controlling interest" in the respondent Company. The respondent Company was a director in the respondent. The respondent had a controlling interest in the respondent 's company. The directors of the company were the registered shareholders and the right to vote was vested in them. The respondent 's share was held by the Aluminium Ltd. in the respondent and the right of vote was vested with them. The shares were held by the respondent in the respondent, and the right, to vote was also vested in them, though as between them and their beneficiaries the beneficial interest was vested in the latter. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of excess profits tax for five chargeable accounting periods ending on the 31st December of each of the years 1939 to 1943. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the directors of a company were not the shareholders of the respondent. On appeal, the High Court held that the Directors of the respondent had a control interest in the shares held by them as trustees and that the directors had a controlling interests in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, and that the Directors had a controlling share in it. The High Court held against the respondent. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The shares held in the respondent were subject, indirectly, to his will, and ordering and., therefore, he cannot, applying either of the tests mentioned above, be said to have a controlling interest. [723C] (2) The last mentioned case was not brought to the notice of the High Court before the judgment under appeal was delivered. The last mentioned cases were entirely different from the facts of the case before us and that decision has no manner of application to the present case. [724D] (3) The last two cases were entirely distinct from the facts in the case before the Appellate Tribunal. [725E] (4) The last one was not brought before the High Court after the judgment under Appeal was delivered. [726F] (5) The last case was not before the Appellate Court. [727F] (6) The last of the cases was not brought on the notice of this Court. [761G] (7) The last part of the case was not placed before the High court before the judgment was delivered. It was, therefore, unnecessary for us to discuss or express any opinion as to whether the observations to be found in the judgment in that case are or are not well founded. [728G] (8) The last portion of the case is entirely different from that of the case. [761A] (9) The last last mentioned case is entirely distinguishable from the facts found in the case. It is, therefore, necessary for us to consider and express any opinion in that case. [763B] (10) The last paragraph of the case which is entirely different is not well founded and is not well based. [729A] (11) The last sentence of the case does not mean that result has been effected. [730B] (12) The last word of the case has no manner, of application to this case. [758G] (13) The last line of the case shows that the last mentioned case has no way of application to it.

The petitioner, a resident of village Sarat Chandra Barik, was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Mahato, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police of Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. The petitioners were convicted by the trial court for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence to death. The High Court dismissed the petitions filed on behalf of the petitioners. The petitioners contended that the right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right but merely a right to express any particular view or opinion or even to make any particular view. The petitioners also contended that the freedom of speech conferred by article 14 is not an arbitrary right and that the right of freedom of speech is not an uncontrolled right. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the President of the India. The High court dismissed the petitions. The petitioners then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The petitioners challenged the validity of section 14 of the Delhi Administration and the Superintendent of Jail, Tihar, contending that the right claimed by the petitioners is not the right to express a particular view or opinions or views on the merits of the application. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right claimed by a person who desires to interview a condemned prisoner is not an abstract right but merely an right to express certain particular view or views or opinions. It is not a right to be considered for the purpose of deciding whether the person sought to interview a prisoner is willing to be interviewed or not. [560G] 2. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code. No data either that they are not willing to be interview and, indeed, if it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who wants to interview a person may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. [560C] 3. The existence or absence of a free press does not imply nor spell out anylegal obligation on the citizen to supply information through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to death. [560E] 4. The existence, of a free newspaper does not imply, or spell out a legal obligation on citizens to supply the information to the press, such for instance, as there are under section 161 (2) of Criminal Procedure Code, the security of the State, public order, decency and morality. [560F] 5. The existence Of a free Press do not imply or constitute any legal obligation upon the citizens to provide information to the newspapers, such for illustration, as there was under section 161 of the Criminal procedure Code. No such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore we do not see any reason why the petitioner should not be allowed to interview the two convicts Billa and Ranga, today.

The appellant was the Receiver of the estate on January 19, 1950. On reorganisation of the Judicial Administration in Tripura, the suit was transferred to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Agartala. On reorganisation, the suit of the appellant was transferred to a court of the District Judge, Agar Tripura. On reorganisation the Judicial Administration was in operation. On reorganisation in Tripura, a suit was transferred by the District Judge to the court where the bond was executed. On reorganisation by the Judicial Administration, the suit filed by the Receiver was transferred to it. On reorganisation it was transferred to this court. On reorganisation a suit was instituted by the Receiver against the Receiver and the appellant praying that the sale deed executed by the Receiver be recovered from the appellant. The appellant filed an application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22 of 1956 filed by the receiver against the Receiver. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the objections and directed that the damages awarded to the appellant be recovered from him. The appellant preferred an appeal to the District Judge. The District Judge allowed the appeal and directed the Receiver to furnish the requisite security within the time allowed to him. The Subordinate judge held that the bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District Judge and that the bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the presiding officer of the court. The Subordinate Court held that the surety bond was a whole and was not liable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. The Subordinate Judges of Agartala were, for the purposes of the present proceedings, a successor of the District Court. The appellant appealed to the District Court which allowed the appeal. The District Court held that since the bond was not executed, the appellant was not liable to make good the loss caused by the fire. The District judge held that it was incompetent for him to enforce the bond. The District court also held that the appellant was liable to make the good the loss sustained to the tea gardens due to the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. The District Munsif, Tripura, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant and directed that damages awarded to him be recovered from his appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the terms of the bond. On appeal by the appellant, the District Judge held that the condition of the bond was valid and that the surety bonds were not liable for any loss caused to him by the fire, and directed that in the event of the respondent 's default, the appellant would not be liable for the losses caused to the Tea garden by the fire and the appellant would be liable to make payment of the damages awarded. The District Magistrate, Tripura, held that the bonds were not enforceable at the instance o the Subordinate Judge. The appellant then filed a revision petition to the High Court which dismissed the revision petition. The High Court held that section 145(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides, to the extent material, that where any person has become liable as a surety for the fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of the Court in any suit or in any proceeding J consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed against the Receiver, and that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea garden due to the receiver. The High court held that the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver was not liable. The High ' Court also held that section 150 of the Code was not applicable to the case. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order for the payment of damages obtained on the Receiver ' s default is a part of section 150 of Civil Procedure Code. [520 C] 2. The bond was executed in and for the purposes for the execution of decrees. The surety bond was executed both by the Receiver and by the appellant.

The appellants were dealers in food grains. They were selling wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U. P. Sales Tax Act on the turnover of wheat by the appellants. The appellants challenged the levy on the ground that the transactions were sales within the meaning of the U P. Sales tax Act. The High Court held that the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not liable to sales tax. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court. The question for consideration was whether the sales made to the Regional Food Controller under cl. 5 of the Order were sales within that meaning of the Act. HELD : (1) The sales made to them were sales within their meaning of the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2(h) of the UP. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1955. The Sales tax Officer was under the Control Order compelled to carry out the directions of the Controller and it had no option in the matter. [610B] (2) The sales of supply did neither result in sales nor were exposed to sales tax because steel products were supplied pursuant to the directions of a Conciliator Order. The tax payer was under the control of the Controller. The tax payee was under the controlled price of the wheat. The tax paid by the dealer to the Regional Transport Controller was not under the Control order compelled to carryout the directions of his Controller. [612C] (3) The sales were on the basis of the directions of an Conciliator Order issued under cl. 4 of the Order. The Sales Officer was under a duty to deliver half the quantity of wheat procured or purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of the Order until such time as the State Government otherwise directs. Delivery of the wheat has to be given by the licensed dealer to the Controller or to such other person as may be authorised by him in that behalf. The taxpayers were under the control and supervision of the Controller or the person authorised by him. The taxees were under the Control of the Controller, and the tax payer was not under a duty or obligation to deliver half of the quantity of rice procured or purchased. The tax payers were under a duty and obligation to deliver the specified quantities of wheat procured by them every day beginning from the date of the commencement of the order. [613E] (4) The tax payer is under the control or supervision of the controller and he has to supply to the State Government 50% of the quantity specified by him every days beginning with the day of commencement of this Order and thereafter fifty per cent of the quantity thereof procured or purchased from him every day starting with the date on which the State Government may otherwise direct. Delivery of wheat has to take place at a future time or subject to some condition thereafter to be fulfilled, the contract is called an agreement to sell. [614B] (5) The taxpayees were under a obligation to deliver to the RegionalFood Controller or a person authorised by it in that behalf, the quantity of foodgrains procured or purchased, by him every month beginning with the dates of commencement of Order until such date as the State Govt. otherwise directs. The tax payable by the dealer under the U P Act is a liability to deliver half quantity of wheat purchased or purchased by the dealer on behalf of the State Government. [615C] (6) The tax payees were under an obligation to deliver up the specified quantities specified by him within the meaning Of the U.p. Sales Tax Rules, 1959. [616B] (7) The tax paid to the Regional Supply Controller or a State pursuant to the direction of the Controller is not taxable.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The appellant was also convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian penal Code. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence of the appellant under section 302 and section 34 of Indian Penal Code. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a person who was not a citizen of India and that the detention order was invalid. Held, that the detention of the appellant was illegal notwithstanding that it was within three months from the date of detention. The appellant had not been arrested in connection with some other case. The appellant could not be detained under the Act for the period of three months unless the Advisory Board had reported within the period of 3 months that there was sufficient cause for the detention of his person beyond the period of six months. The appellant, therefore, could not be released under the Act. The appellant cannot be detained under section 14 of the Act for a period longer than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court, has reported before the expiration of the said period that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. The question to which the Advisory Board has to apply its mind is whether on the date of its report there was sufficient reason for the detention o f the person. That inquiry neces sary involves the consideration of the ques tion as to whether there was sufficient ground for the detention. If the report of the advisory Board is obtained within three months of the date of the detention, it is no answer to say that the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it is not answer to say whether the representation made is required to continue the detention of a person for a longer period than three months. If the representation made before the hearing of the case is required tobe disposed of within three months, it is for the Court to consider whether it is necessary to continue the detained of the person beyond the date on which its report or beyond the period Of three months after the date of hearing of the appeal. If the Report of the advisory board is obtained within 3 months, it can be obtained as required by the Constitution. If the recommendation of the advisory body is to be obtained before the hearing o f the case. If the recommendations of the advisory committee are to be obtained within three weeks, it is only a matter of subjective satisfaction that the Advisory Board should apply its mind to the question as to whether it is required to remain in conformity with article 22(4) of the Constitution. The question whether the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date of their report or beyond three months after its receipt, is a matter of judicial opinion. If the opinion of the advisory authority is to be given within three months and if the report is not obtained within three days, it is a matter for judicial decision. If the Advisory Board is obtained before the expiry of three months, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that the report is obtained within one month, it is beyond three months, and the detention should be upheld. If the detention becomes invalid notwithstanding that it is within three months or that there was no fresh facts, the detention should not be upheld. The question as to what the Advisory Board can do is whether on a proper appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case, the detention can be sustained. If the detaining authority has reported within the prescribed period that there was in its opinion adequate cause for the detained of his person, it is sufficient answer to say, that there was adequate cause for his detention, but the report though not obtained within 3 days, was obtained before the hear ing of the case.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and was appointed as a member of a Civil Service. He was appointed as an Assistant District Judge in the year 1962. He was promoted as an Assistant Judge in the District Court. He was confirmed as an Assistant Commissioner in the year 1963. He was further promoted as an Additional District Judge in 1963. He filed a suit for a declaration that he was entitled to the benefit of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant filed an appeal before the District Judge. The District Judge dismissed the appeal. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the appellant was not a member of Indian Civil Service. The appellant contended that the appeal should be dismissed as it was not of a type for which a period of limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule. Held, that the appellant had not prescribed any period of limitation for an appeal and that the provisions of section 29 of the Limitation act would not apply to an appeal under the Representation of the People Act. The appellant was not entitled to the relief of declaration that he is entitled to the benefits of section 29. The appellant had not made any deductions from the amount of the decree. The appellant could not be said to be a member of an Indian Civil Service because he was not a person who was not a citizen of India. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled under section 29(1) of the Indian Limitation Act to the relief claimed by him. The appellant 's appeal should be deemed to be one under the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. M. M.ackenna, a company incorporated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellant was a partner in the firm M.ackie, a company carrying on business at Hyderabad. The appellant Company was a partner of the firm Mackie, the firm of Mackie and Mackie. The appellant firm was a partner. The appellant entered into an agreement with Mackie for the sale of the goods. The appellant agreed to sell the goods to the appellant. The appellant paid the amount to Mackie on the date of the agreement. The appellant contended that the agreement between the appellant and Mackeie was a composite contract for a whole year and that the remuneration for the Managing Agency was not liable to tax in respect of the same. Held, that the remuneration received by Mackie was not income from the business carried on by the appellant. It was not necessary to determine whether the remuneration for a whole years was the income which had accrued to the Sassoons on the date when the assignment was made. The remuneration for the entire year is the income of the assignee and that it is the profits and gains of the business carried by the assignee, when as a fact he stepped into the position of the Managing Agent only on some date in the course of the year by virtue of the assignment. The remuneration to be income by way of remuneration is not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the remuneration of the year, such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee, either as part of the deed of transfer or independent thereof. The right of the assignee to receive the entire remuneration did not depend on any specific term between the assignor and the assignee, but on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that fell due after the date of assignment. The right to receive the whole remuneration did not arise by virtue Of any mutual arrangement between the assignors and the assignee. The right was not merely a right to remuneration but by virtue of any specific or implied terms between the assignee and the assignee and, therefore, it necessarily implied divisibility of contract and of the remuneration in the year of assignment since the assignment necessarily took place with the consent of the principal employer. The right, however, arose by virtue of an express or implied term between the assignee and the assignee but on the facts that what was so transferred was an asset which carried With it a right may accrue by virtue of such specific or implied covenant as between the assigner and the assignee or the assignee, and that on assignment the assignee becomes the Managing Agent as if his name had been inserted in the Managing Agency Agreement from the beginning, and that the continuity of the Managing Agency Agreements, which were thus transferred to them would be their income. The right which was transferred by the Sassoon to the respective transferees was merely expectations of earning commission and not any part of the commission actually earned by them or which had accrued thereto under the terms of the Managing agency Agreements, and that therefore, the remuneration for those years could not be said to have accrued to the appellant or which had accruing to them under the terms Of the Managing Agency agreements. The right in the present case was to receive the Managing Agency commission which was the source of income and that it was the income of Mackeetie. The remuneration of the Managing Agents was not by itself sufficient to vest in them a beneficial right, to the remuneration, not as per this argument by virtue of clause 10 of the Managing Committee Agreement in Agarwals ' case.

The appellant was a resident of Pachperwa in the District of Gonda. He was residing with his father. He was living with his father in a room of the house where he was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. The appellant was not present in the house and he was not in his house. The prosecution case was that the appellant was in the house at about 6 a.m. on August 13, 1963, and the appellant had illicit connections with Sahoo. The prosecution evidence was that the deceased and the appellant were in the house, and that the appellant had some quarrel on the Janmashtami day in the evening and the deceased had to be persuaded through the influence of his neighbors, Mohammed Abdullah and his womenfolk, to go back to the house of the appellant. The appellant denied the prosecution case and pleaded that he had illicit relations with Sahoo, and that he had not committed the murder. The trial court acquitted the appellant. On appeal the High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. Hence the appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The confession is a substantive piece of evidence and it is implicit in the concept of confession, whether it is extra judicial or judicial, that it shall be communicated to another. [659E] (2) The evidence in the case of oral admission or confession can be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or confession, as the case may be. [658F] (3) The circumstances found by the High Court, which we have stated earlier, lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder, are consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt. [656G] (4) The circumstances narrated by the High court, which we are inclined to take the only conclusion, lead to a only conclusion that it was extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. [600C] (5) The circumstances referred to above lead to the conclusion that the appellant must have committed murder. [657F] (6) The circumstances established by the High Courts, which we had stated earlier, leading to the only inference that the accused should have committed the offence.

The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent company. On the basis of a complaint made by the appellant against the respondent, a criminal case was registered against him. The respondent was acquitted by the trial court. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of acquittal. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of dismissal. The High court held that the respondent was not entitled to reinstatement. The High 'Court further held that the order of the High Court was not correct. The HighCourt further held, that the respondent had not been able to prove that he was not in a position to work as an Assistant manager in the respondent Company. The High Curt further held that since the respondent had been acquitted by the criminal court, the respondent was entitled to reinstatement and the order of reinstatement was not illegal. The respondent also held that the appellant was entitled to the salary of the respondent. The High "Court further held: that the respondent 's services were terminated in terms of the existing rule 5 of the Rules. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent was not in need. He was occupying no longer is in need. Thereby, the post would be abolished. [912D] 1.2 The Board of Directors had to take a decision, whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsist which would be based on the relevant material. Thereby, there would be objective consideration before taking a decision, not only regarding the need to continued the post but also the services of the officer. Once the Board reaches a decision to abolish the post, in consequence the service of the officer/ employee occupying couched in Rule 5 also is capable of that interpretation. [913E] 1.3 The Board of Management may form an objective opinion on the basis of the material, that the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one month 's salary including allowances upto the termination of the period of notice by way of compensation provided that nothing in these rules shall affect the rights of the society to dismiss an employee under Rule 8 for misconduct etc. without any notice or salary in lieu thereof. [914F] 1.4 The Board of Director of the respondent company did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of an employee or officer. Once a Board reaches a conclusion, not only about the need to discontinue the service of a particular employee, but also the service of such employee or officer, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice in writing for termination of his service or in lieu thereof, pay such employee a sum equivalent to his one month's salary including allowances up to the termination of his services or in lieu of notice, in the manner prescribed in the Rules. [915F] 1:5 The Board of Governors did not abolish any post but put a end to the services of an employee. Once the board reaches a decision, it is capable of being that interpretation would render the provision or the rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [916F] 1.:6. The Board of directors had to take an informed decision, whether it should continue the employee "s service subsist" which would be binding on the Board. [917G] 1.7 The Board of the respondent had to take the decision, whether to continue the appellant 's service or in addition to the period of his notice by way o compensation provided that no notice or pay in lieu thereof shall be issued by the Board. The Board did not abolish that post but put the end to the Service of the appellant.

The appellants were the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the bid register and the entry was signed, the petition er was entitled to the grant of the exclusive privilege under section 6 of the Amending Ordinance. The Collector issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 for reauctioning the license and declared that rule 103(1) of the Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act and was in excess of the rule making power of the Board. The Collector also issued a fresh notice dated August 19 1970 for re auctioning the license. The Collector, however, issued a fresh notification dated August 19. 1970 for retendering the license, and declared that the rule was ultra vires and the Board ' Excise Rules was not authorised by the Act and the State Government was in excess. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the Collector had no authority to issue a notice under section 22(1) and the Collector had not been authorised by the State Government. The High Court held that the Collector was not concerned and did not in fact issue any public notice for purposes of sub section (1) of section 22. The High court held that the case was completely covered by its decision dated January 3, 1974 in O.J.C. No.589 of 1972 and dismissed the petition. The State Government issued a fresh Notification dated August 19., 1970 for re-auctioning the licenses and declared that Rule 103(1), of the Board "s Excise Rules, was ultra vires. The High ' Court held that section 6 was ultra vires of the Act and that rule 103 was ultra vires section 6 of that Act. The High Curt held that the State had the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor and that it had the "power to hold a public auction for the grant of such a right or privilege and to accept payment of a sum therefor. The High, Court also held that the Board ' had the exclusive power and privilege of manufacture and sale of country liquor. The High Courts held that the High Court erred in holding that the Collector could issue a fresh notice under section 23(1) for reauctionation of the license and declare that rule 103 (1) was ultra vires, and that the grant of seven ' shops to the appellant for the manu facture and retail sale of country Liquor was therefore validated "as the grant of an exclusive privilege under Section 22 of the Act. The State of Orissa filed a special leave petition in this Court. The question for consideration was whether the High Court was right in holding that section 6 of Amending Ordinance was valid and the grant of 7 ' shops to a person was not contemplated by section 38 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred while holding that section 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 was ultra vires as the Act was not made retrospective in operation. [723C] 1.2 The High Court was in error in holding that sections 2 to 5 of the amending Act of 1970 were not made retrospective. [724D] 1.3 The High Court has also erred in holding the case was fully covered by its judgment dated March 28, 1974 in W.J. C. Govind Das on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding in O. J.C. Govind Das, that section 6 amounted to a direction by the Legislature to the State to disregard the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section 6 did not in effect apply to the case. [725E] 1.4 The High Court had also erred in upholding the validity of section 6 of Act.
