The High Court reduced the punishment of accused No. 2 to the substantive offence of murder under section 302 of the Indian. The High court reduced the punishment to the substantive sentence of death. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The conviction of accused No 2 and 3 under section 302 was altered and accused No. 3 was convicted of the offence under section 304 read with section 120B. [615 A B] (2) The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that there was sufficient corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in material particulars and that Dinkar was a reliable witness and it was proved that accused No. 1 and 2 were guilty of the offence, In view of the fact that there was corroboration of the medical evidence as to the skull and the bone is not of importance in view of the death of Narendra, the High Court rightly reduced the punishment. [616 B] (3) The High court rightly came to a conclusion that there is sufficient corroboration of evidence of Dinker in material particulars in regard to the connection of the accused with the crime and in regard to accused No. 4. [617 C] (4) The High ' Court rightly came into the conclusion that accused No 2 was guilty of the offences, In view Of the fact that the relationship of father and son between accused No. 5 and accused No 6 was not to be lost sight of. The High 'Court rightly came to that conclusion. [618 D] (5) The High "Court rightly came into a conclusion that the accused No. 6 was guilty of offence, In the instant case the High Court was right in holding that there was no corroboration of the prosecution evidence. [619 E] (6) The High Courts were right in holding the accused guilty of the charge under section 302. [620 A] (7) The High courts were right in reducing the punishment of death. [621 B] (8) The High Judges were right in interfering with the order of the High Court. [622 C] (9) The HighCourt rightly came on the conclusion that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against accused No. 7. [623 A] (10) The High Judge rightly came to his conclusion that there were sufficient corroboration of prosecution evidence in material particulars.

The appellant was the owner of a plot of land which was acquired by the respondent for the purpose of construction of a town planning scheme. The appellant claimed compensation for the loss of land. The respondent contended that the Act specifies a principle of compensation, and that the amount of compensation payable to an owner for loss of land was not appealable. The respondent also contended that the Town Planning Officer had no power to determine compensation in the appellant 's case. The appellant contended that the High Court was right in holding that the Act does not specify a principle of 'compensation, and that it was not a law relating to compensation. Held, that the Act is not a law dealing with compensation. The Act does not provide for compensation for loss of property or right injuriously affected by the making of a town plan. The Act is not dealing with compensation for loss or damage of property. The Act has not prescribed any principle of compensation. The Town Planning Officer has a duty under section 64 to calculate the increment to accrue in respect of each plot included in the final scheme. The Town planning Officer has a statutory duty under section 69 to calculate the amount to be adjusted, and that is the guiding rule in respect of all lands covered by the scheme. The principle for determining the compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not; compensation is payable on the basis of the market value of the plot at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. In determining the compensation the Town Planning officer has a duty to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner of any property or right which is injuriously affected thereby the making of an town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of section 69. Section 69 states that the amount by which the total value of the plots included in thefinal scheme with all the buildings and works thereon of such person shall be deducted from or added to, as the case may be, the contributions leviable from such person, each of such plots being estimated at its market value at the date on which the declaration of intention was made. The principle of determining the compensation was the same whether a owner of land was given a reconstituted Plot or not; and compensation is payable to him by the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. The principle in determining the compensation has to be the same whether the amount of loss is payable on a basis of the value of the land at the date the declaration of the intention to make the scheme. In the present case it would be the value of each plot which was acquired. The Town Plan Officer has a power under section 64 (1) (f) to calculate the annual value of the original plots at the date when the declaration of intent to make a town planning Scheme was made. In determining compensation the amount to which the total of the values of the original plot included in final scheme, the Town Planning Authority has a duty Under clause (viii) to calculate increment to accrue In respect of each plots included in final Scheme (which we will refer to hereinafter as the final plot for brevity 's sake) in accordance with section 69. Under clause (xiii) the Town Planning Officers are required to estimate the amount to payable to the owner by the local authorities in cash or with such other way, as may be agree upon by the persons benefited or partly from the local authority and partly from such person as may be specified by the parties, determine. The principle that the compensation is to be paid by "the local authority in Cash or in such manner as may be determined by the parties" is the guiding principle in respect of every plot included in a final scheme.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama Iyer who died in 1934. The appellant was the second son of Seethama Iyer who was the third daughter of Seetharam Iyer. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the words " he shall deliver possession of the remaining properties to the two daughters and stress is laid on the words " the legatee to select" and that the words show that it was in the legatees who wanted to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the selection. The High court also held that the gift was altogether void for uncertainty and for the reason that the gift did not amount to an agreement to give the land to the two sons. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words ' he shall deliver the possession of the entire property to the two children and that the gift could not be said to be void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, for it was contended that the gift in the will was altogether void and that the testator intended to give the selection to the daughters and stress was laid on the language of the will and the words " shall give to the female children". Held, that the words in the will show that it is impossible to make it certain. The words show that the testator was giving the right of selection to Seetharama in the legateies making the selection but still intended to give one kani out of one kani and three quarters of land was clear and certain and difficulty only was as to which part of one katta and three quarters should go to the legatee. The words " he will give to the male children" are contrasted with the words "the heirs of the three children will get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The words are contrasted with words used in the will which show that the intention of the testator was to select the property to be handed over to each son. The words indicate that it was Seetharama who was to make the selection and give the devised land to each son, and therefore there was no question of his legatees making selection but still intend to make a gift which could be made certain by selection made by the legatee.

The plaintiff and the defendants were in joint possession of the plots in dispute. The defendants were in possession of the plot in dispute. They were in joint occupation of the plots. The plaintiff and the defendant were in joint ownership of the plots and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The defendants had no concern with the plaintiff and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The plaintiff had lost her title by operation of law. The suit was dismissed by the District Judge. The District Judge, however, found that the plaintiff was not entitled to any share out of the produce and, therefore, the suit was dismissed. The District Court further found that the defendants were co sharers of the plaintiff and the right of the plaintiff was extinguished. The District judge also found that the name of the plaintiff as a co sharer with the defendants was wrongly deleted after 1359 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff 's name was wrongly deleted. The District court further found that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the plaintiff lost her title and continued to remain so until 1359 fasli as would appear on exhibit 2. In the present case, it is obvious that the possession of the defendants, apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of plaintiff. The High Court, however, held that on the admission of the defendants the plaintiff lost his title by operation and, therefore the plaintiff lost the title by operation. The High court, however, reversed the decision of the District Judge and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. The plaintiff 's suit for joint possession was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding that the plaintiff should be deemed to be ousted from possession, was not maintainable in law and the judgment of the High Court cannot be allowed to stand. HELD: 1. The High Courts have committed an error of record because the clear finding of fact that a clear fraud was committed by Mohd. Bashir, and Mohd. Rashid, is to the effect that she was not at all informed about the consolidation proceedings and was assured by the defendants that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. [723C] 2. The High Curt erred in law by holding that the possession was not in law to be the possession of The defendants, apartfrom being co sharers, unless a clear ouster was pleaded or proved the possession of defendant as co sharers would be deemed in law to have been the possession of 'the plaintiff. [724D] 3. The High ' Court erred in holding that there was no evidence to prove that the plaintiff had been prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and land Reforms Act, 1951 or that the defendants assured the plaintiff that they would taken proper care of their share in any proceeding that may be filed. [725E] 4. The High "Court erred in law while holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act. [726F] 5. The High `Court erred in holding the plaintiff to be ousted of possession.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Establishment and was employed in the Indian Railway Administration. He was employed in a railway company as a railway servant. He was a member in the Indian Railways. He was appointed in the Indian railway as a railway employee. He was paid a salary of Rs. 2,500 per month. He was given a notice of demand on the ground that the stoppage of work on the night of the 1st November, 1948, was illegal and that the workers who had participated in the said strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act. The appellant contended that the stoppage was illegal because the interruption 221 caused the stoppage of the work on 1st November 1948, and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strike were not eligible to annual holidays. Held, that the stoppage amounted to a strike so as to amount to a strike and the workers were not entitled for the leave. The word "strike" as given in section 2(q) of the and it was an illegal strike. The word 'strike" in section 2 (q) of The Factories Act has been defined in section 2 of the and the expression 'strike ' as given in the Act. The word has been defined by section 2 of The Act. The definition of 'strike' as given in s. 2 of the Act is wide enough to include a strike which is not a concerted action on the part of the workers. The word is defined in section 3 of the Act. It is not a definition of the word 'stock ' as given under section 2 of that Act. The expression 'stock' as given under the Act is a wide definition and includes a strike which has been caused by the illegal strike and the workmen are entitled to privilege leave and there is no provision in those rules similar to the one that has been made in section 49 B or in the new rules and that the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounts to an illegal strike and consequently an interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 49 B. The word means 'strike'. The word means a strike which causes or is likely to cause a strike. The words 'strike " as given in sections 49 A and 49 B are wide enough to cover a strike which may be caused by the wrongful strike and the employees thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The word includes a strike, which may be effected by the wrongful act of the employees concerned. The word does not include a strike. It is a strike which does not cause any interruption in the service of a workmen for the purpose for which it was given and hope that the workers would also take it in that spirit. The word refers to a strike which occasions a half a day 's leave or which may be made in section 50 B or in any other manner. The word also refers to a casual act which causes or may be caused to a workman for his work. The word cannot be given a wide meaning so as to include a casual act. The word must be given a wider meaning so as not to include a kind of strike which may or may not be caused by an act of the employee concerned. The words "strike " are wide enough and include a strike that may be caused or may be effected without the intervention of the workmen concerned. The expression "strike ' is wide enough and includes a casual act, which may or might not be caused to the workman concerned. The term 'strike is wide enough. It is wide enough in its import and it is not a mere casual act.

The appellant was the proprietor of a theatre known as "A " certificate " issued by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing vexatious or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. The prosecution was launched against the appellant under section 292 I.P.C. The appellant was prosecuted under section 292 read with section 5A of the Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that the film had been given "A " Certificate by the Central board of Film Craft Censors. The High court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the film having been certified by the Central Government under the (for short, the Act), there was no justification for its display thereafter, and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 of the Penal code, the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film, even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence, section 292 I P.C. was attracted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The offence under section 292 IPC is not an offence which is done by any person who is justified by law or who by reason of a mistake of fact, not by reason of any mistake of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law in committing the act, or alternatively, that he entertained a mistake of law, in doing it. [520 E] 1.2 The offence under Section 292 IPC is an offence which, in the absence of such certification, may constitute an offence under section 293 I.P.,C. [521 E] 1:3. The offence under sections 292 and 292 I. P.C., is not an offences which is done either by any person or who by reasons of a mistake or law in good belief believes himself to have been justified by law, or who by virtue of a mistake o fact and not by reason thereof, believes himself so to be justified in committing the acts, or alternatively. [522 F] 1.4 The offence under Sections 292 and 292 IPC is a non bailable offence. The offence of cheating is a non non bailable offence and the offence of cheating under section 292 is a non nonbailable offence. [523 C] 1.5 The offence under the Penal Code is a non- bailable offence. It is an offence under the penal law. The offence is a nonbailable offence. The accused can irrefutably establish that he is actually justified by law. [524 C] 1:6 The offence under s. 292 IPC is non bailable offence, and the offence under section 80 is a non cognizable offence. [525 A] 1.7 The offence under ss. 292 and 292 is non bailable. The offence for cheating is a bailable offence. [500 G] 1.8 The offence under Ss. 292 and 293 IPC is non non bailable. It is a noncognizable offence. The offences under Ss. 293 and 292 are non bailable. [526 C] 1 9.9 The offence under S. 292 is non non non bailable and the offence for cheating under section 293 is a non compoundable offence. [626 E] 1 10.10 The offence under [Section 292] IPC is non cognizable. The offence punishable under section 292 of the Penal Act is non bailable and non bailable. There is no reason to hold that the offence under Section 293 IPC is not non bailable. If the offence is non bailable, then, the offence under s 292 IPC is also non bailable. In the present case, the prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 79 of I.P..C.

The petitioner was a Government Pleader for the Patna District, including lucrative land acquisition litigation, as part of the professional 'estate ' of a Government Pleader. The petitioner was the sole representative of the Government in courts. He was a lawyer for the Patna district, including lucarative land acquisition litigations, as part and parcel of the professional "estate ' of the Government Pleader. He was also a member of the legal profession, in the Patna District. The petitioner 's case was a claim of monopoly of all government cases in the Patna district including lucre loving appetite for law offices, in the absence of a wholesome ceiling on lawyer 's fees, 762 are issues of moment in a developing society controlled by the politics of skill and enjoying a legal monopoly. The appellants held a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India. The Mills exercised the right to apply for the shares of the Mills. The shares were allotted to its nominees. The Mills decided to sell the shares to its nominees and the shares were allotted in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by them in this company. The Mills issued a notice to the appellants to pay the amount due. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court held that the distribution of the right to applied for the shares amounted to a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Income Tax Act. The High court held that the release by the Mills of the shares amounted "dividend" within the meaning Of section 2(06A) of Income Tax Act and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. The High ' Court also held that the sale by the Mills amounted to a sale of the right of the value of the right released in favour of the shareholders though taxable under section 12 of the Act. The appellants contended that the distribution amounted to a distributed of dividend within section 2(7A) of income Tax Act and that the value of that right was indisputably the value of "dividends" within the extended meaning of that expression in section 2(5A) of that Act. Held, that the distribution by the Mills was a distribution of "d metes and bounds" and was taxable under section 2(8A) of Act. The distribution of the rights to apply for and obtain two shares of the Mill amounted to distribution of dividend. The Mills did not distribute any dividend. The shares did not distribute dividend. The Mill did not distribute the right amongst the shareholders as dividend. The shareholders did not distribute dividends. The Mills could not sell the right to the shares of its shareholders as dividend within the extended definition of section 2 (6A) and in answering that question, the High Court was right in holding that the distribution was not dividend within the ordinary meaning of that term in section 2 (7A) and was taxable. The High " Court was right. The High Courts were right in holding, that the distributed right to apply and obtain two share shares of the Banks was indisputably the price of the right. The Tribunal was right in answering the question in the light of its ordinary meaning. The High courts were right in answering that questions. The High appeals must be dismissed.

The appellant was a candidate for election to the post of Sarpanch of the village. The appellant was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was not a candidate for the post of Panch. The High Court rejected the appellant 's prayer for a writ of certiorari quashing the election of appellant. The appellant contended that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to examine the witnesses who were called to produce documents, and that the High Court had erred in refusing to examine the witness. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court had no jurisdiction to refuse to examine the evidence of such witnesses. [696B] 1.2 The High Court was not justified in refusing to exercise its discretion to refuse to call the witness. [697C] 1.3 The High Court has no jurisdiction to decline to examine the person produced by the party and kept present when the evidence of the party is being recorded and is not closed, and the Court has no power to refuse to summon the witness. The only jurisdiction the Court has to decline to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction. [698C] 1:4 The Court has no discretion to refuse the examination of the witness. If the party would be in a position to produce its witnesses without the assistance of the Court, it can do so under Rule 1A of Order XVI. [699B] 1:5 The only jurisdiction of the Court to proceed with the trial of suits is the one set out in proviso to Sec. Save this the Court has jurisdiction to refuse the examine the witness is the one which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a witness on being summoned through the Court. [695C] 1 :6. The only power the Court has under sub rule (1) of Rule 1A is to ensure that the party has sufficient cause for the omission to mention the name of such witness in the list. [694D] 1.6 The Court has the discretion to refuse, for reasons to be recorded in writing, to examine any witness or witnesses if it is of the opinion that the evidence of a witness is not material for the decision of the petition or that the party tendering such witness or witnesses is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. [693E] 1.7 The Court has to refuse to exercise its power to summon the witnesses. [795G] 1.8 The only jurisdiction, the Court has, to satisfy itself that the party had sufficient cause for his omission to mention his name in the list and yet the party is unable to produce him or her on his own under Rule 1 A. [692F] 1.9 The only jurisdiction is the Court to decide the case. If the Court is satisfied that the party is able to keep his witnesses present despite the fact that the name of the witness is not shown in the list, the party would, be entitled to examine them and to produce documents through the witnesses who are called to produce them under Rule 1. [691F] 1:10. The only Jurisdiction the Court has the power to refuse examination the witness is that the party should bring any witness to give evidence or to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1(A) of Order XVI irrespective of the fact whether the name of witness is mentioned in the list or not.

The appellant was appointed as a Principal of the College by the Committee of Management of the College. The appellant was appointed by the Committee. The Committee of Management issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of management had no power to make any appointment and therefore the appointment of the appellant was not valid. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the appointment order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Committee had no power under the regulations to make appointment and that the appointment of appellant was not invalid. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order contained in the radiogram had suspended or withdrawn its power. The order contains an order of appointment. The order containing the radiograms had suspended or withdraw its power. [982G H] 2. The order dated April 7, 1981 clearly shows that on April 7,1981 the order contained in radiogram was communicated to the Manager of the Institution. If the order was valid and power to make appointment was suspended it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make any modification or rescind any regulation as also make any order consistent with the provisions of the Act, the second contention of Mr. (I) confers power on the State Government to make, modify or rescind any regulations as also make such other order consistent with provisions of the act as it deems necessary and in particular, may by such order modify or rescind or make any order inconsistent with the provisions thereof, if such order is necessary. Sanghi vehemently contended that if the appointment of a teacher was not suspended it would be open to it to the Selection committee to make, modification or rescind the regulation or make any other order consistent therewith the provisions of this Act as it deems appropriate and in particular may by such orders modify or rescind, make any regulation in respect of any matter. [983D] 3. The power to make appointments is conferred by the regulations. The power of appointment is conferred by regulation. 16A and the Scheme of Administration envisages the setting up of a Committee of Management and the Committee of the Management has the power to make such modification or rescind or makes any other order inconsistent with any provisions of the law as it deems proper. [984E] 4. The power conferred on the State government to make, amend or rescind any rule as also make an order consistent with any provisions thereof, is not an absolute power. The power is conferred on the Committee of Board of Management to make, alter or rescind any such regulation as also makes any other orders consistent with the provision of the Act. [985F] 5. The power under the Regulations is conferred by regulations. 16A. The regulations confer power on the Committee to make, vary or rescind any Regulation as also make appropriate order consistent with such provisions of the statute as may be necessary. [986F] 6. The power vested in the Committee of Directors to make, revise or rescind any order consistent therewith is not an arbitrary power. [ 986F] 7. The power which the State Government can make, modify, rescind or make an order inconsistent with or rescind any rules as also make provisions in respect of matters. [987F] 8. The power in making appointment is conferred on a Committee of management to make, altering or rescind any Regulations as also make provision for such consequential order as may be appropriate. The power can be exercised by the Committee to modify or rescind the regulations. [988G] 9. The power has been conferred on the committee of Management to give effect to the provisions of any law. The power cannot be exercised by a body not authorised to make the appointment. [994G] 9 A.C.R.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and incidental work. The respondent was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. When the matter was thus pending consideration the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court, Patna. The Government of Bihar transferred the case to Labour Court Dhanbad. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of section 33 B of the (14 of 1947) the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the respondent and without opportunity to 294 the management transferred the case. The Government accordingly acceded to the request of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the reasons given by the Government for transferring the case to the Labour Court, Dhanbad. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant company challenged the legality of reasons given by Government for transferring it to Labour Court Patna. The High court dismissed the writ application. The appellant Company challenged the legality and correctness of the reasons of the Government for transfer. The HighCourt dismissed the writ appeal. The appellant contended that the Government was misled by the representation of the workman. The High Courts were not justified in refusing to interfere with the order of transfer. The appellant has challenged the legality, correctness of the order of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government was misled in the representation of th e workman. The representation of the respondent was not denied by the workman. There is no presumption against the bona fide or the honesty of an assessee and normally the income tax authorities would not be justified in refusing an assessee a reasonable opporunity of representing his views when any order to the prejudice of the normal procedure laid down in section 64(1) and (2) of the Act is sought to be made against him, be it a transfer from one Income Tax Officer within the State to an Income Tax Officer without it, except of course where the very object of the transfer would be frustrated if notice was given to the party affected. [412C D] 2. The Government is misled by the representations of the workman and normally the Income tax authorities would be justified in refuse to an assessee a reasonably oppor tunity of representing their views when any orders to the prejudice o f the normal procedure prescribed in section 64 (1) and 64(1). [412E] 3. The order of transfer in that case was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the prejudice or the honesty or the honesty o f an assessee and ordinarily the income tax Authorities would not be unjustified in refusing to an assessee an reasonable oppor tentunity of representing its views when any such order to the detriment of the normal procedures laid down in Section 64(1), and transfer it for disposal from the stage at which it was so transferred. [413B] 4. The order dated August 8, 1988 by which the Government of Bihar transfer was quashed for non compliance with the provisions of section 64(2) of Act, 1961, was quashed for failure of justice. [415C] 5. The order was quashed for noncompliance with the provisions contained in section 64 of the Act. [417C] 6. The order is quashed for non prosecution. [418E] 7. The order passed by the Government of India transferring the case from the Labour Court to Labour Court was quashed for violation of section 64 of Act, 1922. [419D] 8.

The appellant was a hotel operator. The hotel was closed down on October 7, 1955. The appellant was not allowed to work in the hotel. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of reference. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the reference was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support of it. The High court held that the reference in this form is incompetent. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The reference in this case does not become incompetent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will actually represent the workmen before the tribunal, but mentions the union itself. [283E] (2) The fact that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer and its employees, does not affect the competence of the order of Reference. [283A] (3) The fact remains that the dispute was between the management and its employees which were mentioned as its workmen. The fact that in the order of the reference the words "as represented 36 282 by the Hotel Workers Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " have been added would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent merely because the union itself was not a living person can only be served through some officer, so as to mention the names of particular workmen who might have been responsible for the dispute. [283B] (4) The fact is that the dispute is of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the name of particular workmen whose number is generally large large. [283C] (5) The fact of the dispute is also specified in the terms of reference. It is that officer whose number is ordinarily large large. The officer who will really represent the workmen who might be responsible for the disputes. The nature of the dispute also is specified in the order. [283D] (6) The fact also that the union itself has sufficient knowledge of the nature of the disputes. [283G] (7) The fact remained that the dispute referred for adjudication is between the employer, namely the management of the hotel and its employees. The nature, of the dispute being also specified in, the terms of Reference. It is, therefore, that officer who would actually represent the workman before the tribunal. [283F] (8) The fact, therefore, does not mean that the reference which is otherwise valid does not become competent merely because it was mentioned therein that it relates to retrenchment or reinstatement. [283H] (9) The fact still that the dispute relates to retrenchment and reinstatement does not affect either the competence of a person to whom notice of dismissal had been given and in that connection the names of the workmen concerned were mentioned in the order, of reference. [283L] (10) The fact further that in the application of the appellant the reference was vague, as it did not indicate how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The fact remains, that the dispute has been referred for adjudication by the Tribunal. [283I] (11) The fact was that the dispute between the hotel and the employees which were referred for adjudication were clearly specified in the orders of reference. There was no dispute between the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra and its workmen and it went to this length that the dispute did not mention any officer of the trade union, but mentions that the union was itself specified in the reference.

The appellant imported a consignment of rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by the appellant. The appellant claimed exemption under the Notification. The Notification exempts parts of the engines mentioned in column (2) of the Table annexed to the Notification, which is relevant for our purpose, not only parts of the engine or engines, but also parts thereof. The Notification provides that the articles specified in column (1) of the table annexed to the notification, which are included in Heading No. 84.06, will get the benefit of exemption as provided by the Notification irrespective of the fact that they or any or some of them have already been included under Heading No.8406. The Notification also provides that the parts of the machinery specified in column(2) of that Table shall be all the parts of engines or engines, mentioned under Heading No 84.06. The appellant contended that the parts imported by the appellants are parts of the parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading No, 84.06 and not parts of the diesel engines falling under heading No. 8406. The Collector of Customs rejected the claim. The appellant filed an appeal before the Customs authorities. The Collector rejected the appeal. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification exempts also parts of the machines mentioned under Heading 84.06 of the Notification irrespective Of the fact that the bushes, which have been imported by the Appellant, are parts of such engines. [227G H] 1.2 The Notification exempts only parts of engines mentioned under Heading Nos. 84.05 and 84.06 which are included under Heading 8406. [227C D] 1.3 The Notification exempts specifically parts of the Engine or engines, which must be all the part parts constituting the engine or engine in question and not a few parts thereof. [227F] 1.4 The Notification exempts all parts of the vehicles mentioned under Heading no. 8406, but it does not, therefore, include parts of the components mentioned under Heading nos. 8406 and 8406. In the instant case, there is no material or evidence nor is there any finding of the Appellate Tribunal or the Customs authorities that the bushes imported by them are parts of internal engines falling under Item No. 8405. [227H] 1.5 The Notification exempts further parts of the equipment mentioned under Heading NO. 8406 of the Table. [227B] 1.6 The Notification exempts, inter alia, parts of the motor vehicles mentioned under Item No.(2) of Table annexed to Notification, which are specified in column 2 of the Table appended to the Notification. [227D] 1.7 The Notification exempts the parts of motor vehicles mentioned in column 2, which are parts of motor vehicle, motor vehicle or other motor vehicles, motor vehicle, or other motor vehicle, and motor vehicle, vehicles, motor vehicles, or other vehicles, motor transport vehicles, motor omnibus or motor vehicles, and motor vehicles, vehicles, and other motor vehicles. motor vehicles, Motor vehicles, motor cars, motor vehicles and motor vehicles. Motor vehicles, Motor Vehicles, motor vehicles or other motor Vehicles, motor vehicle and motor vehicles of motor vehicles, other motor vehicles and other motor vehicle vehicles, motor Vehicles, vehicles, vehicles and motor vehicle vehicles. Motor Vehicles, Motor Vehicles and motor vehicles are motor vehicles, omnibus or motor vehicle, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Motor Vehicles Act 1988, does not, however, contain or refer to the parts of those vehicles. [227E F] 1.8 The Notification exempts both parts of the vehicle mentioned under Heading numbers. 8406 as well as the parts of parts thereof.

The plaintiffs claimed through female members of the Dargah and even if they were entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Dargah, the same was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was right in holding that the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by limitation by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathimaee were entitled to the right of Mujawar. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in holding that Fathimaira Bee was a co sharer in the right of management and possession of the Dargah as well as the plaintiffs who had claimed through Fathim Bee. [116B] 1.2 The only question that was raised was whether the High Court could have held that Fathimira Bee was not entitled to any share in the management of the Dargah. [116C] 1.3 The High Court has not gone into the question whether Fathima Hussain was a co- sharer in this right of management or offerings in the offerings. [116D] 1.4 The High Court is right in holding the aforesaid judgment and decree. [116E] 1.5 The High Court had not gone into that question. [116F] 1.6 The High Court ought to have gone into the questions whether Fathimma Bee was a party in that suit or not. [116G] 1.7 The High Court should have gone into that aspect and should have decided the question of ouster against Fathimsa Bee. [117G] 1:8 The High Court erred in holding that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that the right of Fathimida Bee was denied and she was expressly ousted out from the enjoyment of any share in any share in that Dargah. [117H] 1.9 The High Court could not have held that the rights were specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of the defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiffs of Fathiman Bee. [118G] 1.:9 The High court was right in setting aside the decree of trial court. [118H] 1:10 The High Court also erred in holding the plaintiffs who are claiming ouster on the basis of expressed denial of Fathum Bee. [119G] 1 :11 The High Court failed to appreciate that Fathumma Bee was not a party in the suit nor any such question was raised or decided that females were not entitled to claim any right of management nor was there any question of any knowledge to Fathima oyees. [119H] 1.:11 The High court erred in holding in holding that there was no question of any ignorance to Fathimiya Bee or the plaintiffs were claiming ouster on any particular occasion till her death in 1957. [119A] 1.12 The High Court, in the impugned judgment, has erred in holding it to be a case of ouster of Fathyam Bee from the fight or management of the Wakf. [119B] 1:13 The High Court committed a serious error in holding the suit filed by Fathimumma Bee as a matter of fact. [119C] 1:14 The High Court did not go into the question of whether Fathumum Bee was a necessary party in that case. [119D] 1:15 The High Court in the impugned order has erred in reversing the decree of first appellate court.

The appellant was employed as a railway employee in the respondent 's house. He was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled to withhold the house rent allowance. The appellant was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance because he had refused the house rent allowances. The respondent 's claim for house rent allowance was rejected by the Authority. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Authority. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the house rent Allowance claimed by the 1st respondent was "wages" as defined in the Act and that the claim was inadmissible on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent ''s wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allotted railway quarters in a suitable type. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the house Rent allowance claimed by the appellant was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act and the rules framed thereunder and that the appellant was entitled to withhold house rent allowance; that the claim for house Rent allowance was inadmissible on that ground because there had been a violation of the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee; and that the respondent had not been allotted railway quarter of a suitable nature and as such the claim was not admissible on the ground of non est deduction. Held, that the claim of the appellant was admissible on the basis of the definition of "wages" contained in the Act. The definition of " wages" contained in section 2(v) of the the Act does not include "the value of any house accommodation" as defined under section 2(vii) of the , and the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Act are not inconsistent with any of the terms mentioned in the contract between parties. The definition in section 2 (vi) of The Act does not create any absolute right in the employee to the house rent payable to him. The rules do not make the grant in such absolute terms. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases to be entitled to the house Rent Allowance and that allowance thus ceases to be "wages" under the definition in the Act, because it is no more payable under the terms of contract between the employee and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places will cease to be so entitled. The rules which must be included in the terms of their contract are inconsistent with some of the terms contemplated the grant of house rent allowance to every employee of a particular category but the rules do not provide for the grant in the absolute terms. The rules are not inconsistent With some of the clauses of sections 7, 11 and 12 of the Act. [766 H; 766 A B] The definition of 'wages' contained in the definition of ' wages' contained in section 3(i) of the, Act does not make the grants in such absolute term. Once an employer has been offered alternate accommodation and he is refused it, the employee ceases to be so entitle.

On April 4, 1980, these copies were received by the State Govt. under their covering letter, dated March 14,1980. On April 5, 1980, when the detenu received a letter, dated April 3, 1981, from the State Government requesting him to supply the copies of the statement and documents relied on in the grounds. On April 6, 1980, another letter was received from the detenus on March 14, 1981, and was received by them on April 3 1980. On May 3, 1980 copies were supplied. On the direction of the Central Government, the State Government supplied the copies of certain statements and documents to the detenus. In reply to this letter, the detenus made a request to the State Government to refuse the supply of the copies of statements and documents. On May 14, 1981 the State Government communicated to the detenus that the detenus had acquired gems in question from those persons. On April 11, 1980, again copies were supplied by the detenus to the detenus on May 14,1980, but were actually received by them. On April 12, 1980, they were actually received. On April 13, 1980, there was an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of those portions of statements after undue delay on the direction of this Central Government, there was a reference to the earlier statements which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been specifically communicated to the detenu by the detenus. In the copies of these statements, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus, were supplied to him. On April 14, 1980 copies of the basic materials and documents were supplied to detenu with reasonable expedition to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. On April 15, 1980, in reply to this request, the detenus were supplied. The detenus, however, challenged the detention mainly on the ground that the detenus were not supplied with copies of the material relied in the grounds, of detention. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The delay of more about a month in supplying the copies of those statements to the detenus has vitiated the detention.

The appellant was tried by the trial Court for the offence of murder of one person and was acquitted by the trial court. The High Court in its order referred to ss 258, 410, 417 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The Division Bench of the High Court, however, held that the scheme disclosed by these provisions and particularly by sections 419 and 423 of that Code is against the locus standi of a joint appellant. The High court in its order, referred the question to a larger Bench. The High ' Court in its judgment referred to ss 259, 410, 418 and 423 of Code of Criminal Procedure and came to a conclusion that the Scheme of Chapter XXXI is against the law of the land and that the scheme is against the ill will of the accused persons. The High, Court in its very order referred to the Full Bench and came to this conclusion that the Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High Court was wrong in holding that the Full bench decision of the Bombay High Court was not binding on it. The High Curt held that the Full Court decision in Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal(1) was wrong in dismissing the appeal without going into the merits. The High "Court further held that the decision of the High court was wrong in rejecting the appeal without examining the merits. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Full Benches of the High Courts in Beorajan 's case(6) were wrong in holding the joint appeal to be maintainable in law. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1.1 The Full Bench decision in Mahadolal Ranigra vs The AdministratorGeneral of West Bengal (1) was not binding upon it. [620 E] 1.2 The Full Bench of the Gujarat, in Mahadeosal Ranodia v The Administrator General, West Bengal(2) was wrong. [621 E] 1:3. The Full Bench judgment of the Gujarat Court was not a binding precedent on it. [613 A] 1.4 The Full Bench in Mahadeoolal Rania vs The Administrator, General of West Bihar(1) held that the earlier decision was wrong. The Full bench of the Gujarat was wrong in taking the view that the earlier decisions were wrong. [613 B] 1.5 The Full Bench was wrong in reversing the decision of a single Judge of the High 'Court. [613 C] 1.6 The Full Bench has rightly distinguished and explained this decision. [613 D] 1.7 The Full Bench is wrong in holding a joint appeal to the High Court by two common orders. [613 E] 2.8 The Full Bench decisions of the Gujarat and the High Court rightly distinguished and applied the principle that the Appellate Court hearing an appeal cannot admit it only on a question of sentence and that such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merits. [613 F] 3. The Full Benches of two Judges of the same High Court were wrong in taking a contrary view.

The assessee was a firm called O.R.M.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such was not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 Act but only receipt of the income in British India was assessed and it cannot therefore be held that the foreign business of the assessee was charged to tax under the 1918 Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that in the context of these facts the foreign business was not charged under the 1918 act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act because the foreign business had been discontinued in the year of account. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Indian business of the appellant was not charged to tax on the foreign business and that the foreign income was chargeable to tax under section 3(1) of the 1918 act and accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to relief under section 25 (3) of 1922 Act with regard to the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the years of account. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the foreign company was only taxed on remittances received from the profits of the foreign business but only received from the foreign business. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The foreign business of O.R.,M.SP., Firm which was discontinued by virtue of section 3 of The 1918 Act within the meaning of section 25(1) was within the meaning Of section 25(2) of the 1961 Act. [912 E] 2. The assessee was entitled, to relief under sections 25(3), 25(3). [912 F] 3. The exemption under section 24(3) was general. The assessee is entitled to relief in respect of the rental income of the foreign income from the house properties owned of the foreign firm. [913 E] 4. The exemption is general. The exemption was general. [914 F] 5. The exemption in section 25(4) is general. It must therefore be taken that there was an assessment to tax on income of the assessee. [915 B] 6. The exemption of tax in respect of interest on securities as well as income from house property owned by the Foreign firm which was discontinuance in the year was not charged. [916 C] 7. The exemption from liability to pay tax in respect thereof is general. [ 916 E] 8. The exemption cannot be claimed by an assessee but the assessment of the tax is on the basis of various heads of income derived by the assessee one of which is business.

The assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department for the construction of the Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. The assessee entered into an agreement with the Public works Department of the State Government on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and sale of kiln burnt brick bricks to the aforesaid Department for the supply of bricks. The agreement provided that the contractor shall give notice to the Executive Engineer or his Assistant of his intention of making delivery of materials and on the materials being approved, receipt shall be granted to him by the Executive Engineer. The assessee was required to furnish a certificate to that effect, but the delivery was not to be considered to be complete until the contractor was given notice to the contractor. The assessee filed a suit for damages against the Public Works department of the Government. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the transaction was a works contract. The High court held that the contract was a works Contract. The High ' Court held that it was a works contracts. The High, Court held that in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract was not a works contract and the contractor was bound to complete the work and that the decision of the purchaser in that behalf was final and conclusive. The High "Court further held that the agreement was a works agreement. The High. Court also held that the transactions envisaged by the agreement were not a works contracts and the High Court was wrong in holding that the transaction envisaged in the contract was one of works contract. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a works Contract and the High court was wrong in answering the question in favour of the assessee. [723C] 2. The contract is a contract for sale and not works contract. It is a contract which is a works contract, and not a work contract. The property in the bricks was entirely of the assessee and the contractor hereby guarantees that the said articles would continue to conform to the description and quality of materials for the period shown in the Schedule from the data of delivery of the said articles to the purchaser and that notwithstanding that fact that 163 the purchaser may have inspected and approved, the said articles if during the aforesaid period stated in the Schedule and accompaniments hereof and the contractor will pay such materials only as are approved and passed by the Executive engineer or his Assistant, and no materials which is not so approved shall be considered to have been delivered. [724D] 3. The property is a contract where the materials are approved and taken into account by the Executive Officer or his Assistant and no materials, which is not otherwise approved shall be deemed to have been supplied. [725E] 4. The property has to be understood that in quoting his rate for the bricks, the appellant would take into account the free supply of earth for making the bricks. [726A] 5. The property, in the bricks, is entirely of the applicant. The property does not mean that the contract in this particular case is a works Contract, but it is a contract that is a workscontract. The property was entirely of his assessee. The essence of the contract was, therefore, the delivery of the bricks after manufacture. [727B] 6. The property did not mean that in quoting the rate for the brick, the appellant will take into account any free supply of soil for making the brick. [728B] 7. The property of the bricks was wholly of the assessee, and the contractor would pay the same himself, and the applicant would have no claim for any compensation for any loss that may accrue on account of the collection of the materials or engagingments entered into. [729A] 8.

The petitioner was a member of the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir. He was elected as a member of a Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Srinagar. The petitioner was elected as the member of the Assembly of Jammu & Kashmir. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3rd December, 1971. The petitioner contended that the duration of the House of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 (Act 30 of 1976) had no effect and consequently all Acts passed by the House of The People (Extension to Duration) Act 1976 (Act 31 of 1976) were ultra vires the constitutional Constitution. The petitioner also contended that the Proclamation of emergency issued on 3.12.1971 was either ultra vires or had ceased not to be in force on 3rd February, 1972 and since the Proclamation of Proclamation of Emergency had ceased to operate by 26th August, 1975, the House of Parliament (Extension of duration) Act,1976 (Act 30 Of 1976) had not been passed by Parliament, the House had no effect. The petitioner further contended that the period of five years in relation to the present House of the people could have been extended only when the Proclamation of the Emergency issued on the 3rd December 1971 and on the 25th June, 1975 were both in operation. The petitioner submitted that the duration for which the House of President may, under clause (2), of Article 83, continue from the date appointed for its first meeting) in relation to a present House of Parliament and since the three Proclamation of Emergency were in operation by 26th June, 1976, the House could not have validly extended the period of the House for a period not exceeding one year at a time. The petitioner, on the other hand, contended that the two ProClamations of emergency were in operation on 3rd January, 1972 and the Proclamation of Proclamate of Emergency issued by the President of India on 26th June 1975 had ceased to have effect by 26th July, 1975. The petitioner therefore, submitted that the period for which the Proclamation of Temporary Emergency issued on 26th July 1975 had ceased, while the Proclamation of AM was in force, by virtue of the resolutions passed by the Houses of Parliament approving the two Procts of Emergency as required by law and that actually the proclamation of Emergency issued in exercise of the powers conferred by sub clause (b) of clause (4) of Article 352 of the Constitution (as it stood during the relevant time had not been published in the official reports of the two Houses of Parliament and the time when the resolutions were duly adopted by the two Houses had also to be extended for a period of one year at the time when each of them was issued as the resolutions of the Houses of the People (Extension) Act, 1977 had ceased to exist. The petitioner accordingly submitted that the two Proclamation of Emergency dated 3rd December., 1971 and the Proclamation dated 25th June 1975 were ultra vires and that the two proclamations had ceased to function by virtue of their resolutions dated 3rd January 1972 and 25th June 1974 respectively. The petitioner urged that the Proclamation dated 3rd March, 1972 had ceased to remain in operation by virtue of section 2 of the first of these Acts and that therefore the two Proctions of Emergency were ultra vires. Held, that the two Notifications of 1976 and 1977 were ultra vires of the constitutional Constitution and were not ultra vires the Constitutional Constitution. The Proclamation of Emergency were valid and the Proclamation was valid.

Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of the said family and that it was incapable of valuation. [157 G] 1.2 The High Court ought to have held that the subject-matter of dispute in this suit was the public temple. [157 D] 1.3 The High Court has not committed any error in proceeding on the aforesaid assumption. [157 E] 1.4 The High Court is wrong in proceeding on that assumption. [158 G] 1:5 The appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. The appellant did have to pay Court fees as it might in either case require the property. The appellant was therefore entitled to leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b). The appellant 's case was that the property fell within the meaning of Madras Act 19 Of 1951. [157 A] 1.8 The appellant did no have to pay courts fees as it could have in either case no market value. The appellant could not claim that the property had in either case, no market value and therefore was incapable of valued. [157 B] 1.9 The appellant did nothing more than pay court fees and therefore was not entitled to leave. [157 C] 1.10 The appellant did never have to pay any court fees as the judgment and order passed by it did not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question resecting property of the value of Rs. 20,000/ or more and (c) that the appeal did not involve any substantial question of law. [157F] 1.11 The appellant did make a claim or dispute in the first suit on a valued valuation made by it therefor. The suit in the first case was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High Court. The appellant had to pay court fee as it would be in the case. [157G] 1.12 The appellant did so in the form of an application, being O.P. No. That being 157 the dispute between the parties, the High court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondent the property was valuable of alienation. [157H] 1.13 The appellant did in his plaint, and since according the respondents the properties were inalienable and was capable of being valued, the High Courts ought to have valuation the property accordingly although according to the appellant the property was compulsorily acquired. [157E] 1.14 The appellant did file an application for leave to appeal to this Court. [157C] 1.15 The appellant did, in his plaint to the District Court, for directing an inquiry into the value of the property under 0.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the appellant company. The appellant was employed in the appellant Company. The appellant claimed that the practice started by the appellant of re employing retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations. The Tribunal held that the practice was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffin of its employees. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The Tribunal has erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance for tiffin. [635D] The appellant 's grievance against the direction in the award that 572 As. /8/ and As. /6/ per day should be paid respectively to the members of the clerical staff and the substaff on all working days, can be upheld. The fact that the appellant had throughout been making provision for tiffins of its employees and, in fact, when after the award was pronounced in the proceedings of 1956 and this question was taken up for direct negotiations between the parties, the appellant agreed to consider the claim sympathetically and make a suitable provision in that behalf. [636E] The appellant cannot, therefore, be blamed on that account. [637B] The appellant is introducing a wage structure in respect of its reemployment and that clearly cannot be permitted under industrial law. [638B] The fact that in 1956 there was an industrial dispute between the parties coupled with the prevailing practice in the comparable concerns in the comparable concern in the comparable industries in the comparable States, strongly supports the view taken by the Tribunal that in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, a provision for turtin arrangements made by the appellant in re employing the retired personnel was an amenity to which the employees were entitled. [639C] The appellant has throughout been making provisions for tiffining its employees and the correspondence between the parties on this subject shows that the policy adopted by the appellant was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. [640B] The Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the respondent in re employing tiffin to its employees. [642C] The fact of reemployment is certainly inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appellant by the award , and that clearly not cannot be permitted to under industrial law, because the appellant is introducing an amenity to its employees, and generously considered their request for cash allowance in lieu of tiffin, that clearly cannot, therefore be blamed on the ground that the appellant is approaching a wage structure which is certainly inferior. [646B] The question posed by the respondents ' demand must be considered. [647C] The question formulated by the Tribunal is either improper or unjustified. [648B] The facts that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for the turtin arrangement to its employees by way of giving them a cash allowance for each employee by way of give them a cash Allowance for tiff in lieu of the tiff in. [649B] The respondent 's grievance that the practice adopted was not based on humanitarian grounds, cannot be accepted. [652C] The Tribunal had overlooked the fact of re employment of retired persons. [653C] The facts of the case shows that the appellant has throughout was making provision for the supply of certain cash allowance for liffin. The correspondence between the appellant and the respondent on this subject show that the policy followed by the appellant is not based solely upon humanitarian grounds. The fact of the matter introduces a serious infirmity in the appellant's case that though the re employed person had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant sympathetically and generously consider their request for re employment and that clearly can be permitted under Industrial law.

The appellant was employed as a pump manufacturing enterprise, issuing a notice ending the ,employment and offering one month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing orders. The appellant was terminated from service on the ground that information regarding tenders was being passed on by the workman '. The appellant challenged the order of termination before the Labour Appellate Tribunal in Buckingham & Carnatic Co. 2 SCR 822) wherein the view taken by the Labour Appellate tribunal was approved and it was held that the appellant had merit on his side, judged by the social conscience and judicial construction of the law in this branch of discharge simpliciter versus disguised ' dismissal. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the motivation for the termination was the suspicion Which lurked in the mind of the Regional Manager that information regarding tender was being passed On the facts of that case, the Court was satisfied that order of termination was not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1) 496 of dismissal. The Court, in appeal, held that the action was regarded as punitive and that the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. The Labour appellate Tribunal held that even in a case like the present the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination was a colourable exercise of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. The Labour Court further held that the motive for the termination of service was the suspicion which lurked the mind of Regional Manager that the information regarding tenders were being passed on to the workman ' and the ground given was that he was an cantankerous man undesirable to be retain was good. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was a canter and that the termination was not an illegal termination. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1. The appellant had not even filed a counter affidavit and the counsel for the Union agreed that the order of retrenchment was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground that he was not a mere camouflage to coverup what really was a dismissal for misconduct 'as a result of unfair labour practice. [819D] 2. The appellant did not even file a counter affidavit. The form of the order in such a case is not conclusive and the tribunal can go behind the order to find the reasons which led to the order and then consider for itself whether the termination was an unfair labour practice or unfair labour practices. [820F] 3. The form is not conclusive. The form, in such a situation, is not conclusive, and the tribunal cannot go behind the form of the orders to find the reason which led to a conclusion, it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set aside such termination. [821B] 4. The form in such a matter is not conclusive or the evidence, or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence, or was the result of any misreading of the materials evidence, or are the result of unfair Labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside the termination. [ 822C] 5. The form and the order in the present case is not decisive and the tribunal has to go behind the language of the order. [822D] 6. The form has been given in such a way as to look at the substance and set aside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter, if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for offence 'as a colourable exercise Of the power or was a result of harassment or unfair labour Practice. [823F] 7.
