The petitioner No. 1 was the President of the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti. He was elected as President of the said Samiti. The petitioner No. 2 was the President. The petitioner was the President and the petitioner No. 3 was the President respectively of the said Board. The petitioner challenged the legality of the order of the Governor of Assam in the writ petition by contending that the order of Governor of Assam was illegal and void. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Governor of Ass am and the order of his Governor dated 1.10.84. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. The petitioner contended that the order passed under the Ordinance and the Act was ultra vires and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right to form an association, in fact, the Act and the noti fication issued under Section 3 of the Act do not provide for as to how when the temporary measures comes to an end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalika were substituted by Board appointed by the Government and all the functions, properties and affairs of the Samiti were taken over by this Board and all the powers, properties and functions of the Samiti are taken over by the Board and all those properties and affairs were taken over as by this Board. [912D] 1.2 The right to be form an association is necessarily implies that the persons forming the Association have also the right to continue to be associated with only those whom they voluntarily admit in the Association. [913E] 1.3 The right to forms an association, is necessarily implies a implies that the person forming the Association has also the right t o continue to be so associated with only the those whom they voluntary admit in the association. [914F] 1.4 The right to continue, therefore, implies that the rights of the members of the association have also the power to continue to remain associated with only such persons whom they voluntarily admitting in the Association and therefore we are restoring to their elected authorities and office bearers despite the fact that they voluntarily admit them in the Association, but unfortunately it appears that with out considering the question and its constitutional aspects the reply came that the State has no desire to restore it back to its elected authorities and offices bearers despite the facts that they voluntarily admitting the same in the Association but unfortunately it is made clear that the Karyapalika and Byabastha pika Sabha which were in existence in 1984 when initially the action under the emergency provi sions was taken followed by the notification under the Ordinance, and the Act shall be restored back and they will take over the management of the Samiti from the Board imme diately but it is made known that the Karyaprada Sabha which was functioning in 1984 has come to an end though from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. [915F] 1:5 The right to constitute an association, under Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution, necessarily implies that when the temporary measure comes to an d end the elected byabasthap oika Sabha and Databgarh Sabha which were 176 functioning in 1984 have come to an e mployment and they have sufficient time to go on and in this view of the matter the State has not chosen to take any steps to restore the Samiti and therefore we is restoring the writ petition and the writ petition which is the subject matter of challenge in this Writ Petition. [916F] 1.:6 The right to function as an association, according to the pro visions of the Constitution is necessarily implies the right to form a association, in which case the Act and noti ficate issued under Section 2 of the Act.

The appellants and the respondents were married on May 10, 1938, and the deed of gift was executed and registered on March 10, 1940, some two years after the marriage, but the deed of gifts was later confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938, some two year after the marriage. The deed of gift in the present case was made some two years before the marriage and possession of the houses was also given to her. The gift was later confirmed by Nand Lal Sao on the occasion when the Dwirak (Gownb) ceremony was performed on May 10. 1940, some three years after the death of the father and son in law. The deed was executed and unregistered on March 10. 1940. The deed in question was executed and registration was also given on March 10 and 1940, some one year after the death. The deed also recited that Sumitra Devi got an absolute right in the properties given to her as her share on partition. The deed further recited that Sumitra had made a gift of the four houses at Asansol in favour of Kamala Devi 457 on the 10th March, 1940, a gift which she was not competent under the law to make. The deed recited that Sumitra was competent to make a gift to the daughter as her marriage portion created a moral or religious obligation in fulfilment of which it was competent for the father to execute a deed of gift. The deed then recited that Sumitra would be competent to execute any deed of gift, except with regard to a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband at the time of the marriage. It was further recited that the gift was of a reasonable portion and was not essential to make a valid gift at the time when the marriage was performed on the occasion. The deed, however, recited that Sumitra 's wife was competent to execute a gift of a reasonable share of the property of her husband to her daughter. The deed stated that Sumitra Devi was competent to do so. The deed provided that Sumitra Devi would be competent under the Hindu law to make a good gift of a specified portion of the property. The deed did not mention any particular provision in the deed. The deed merely stated that Sumitra ' was competent to give a portion of the joint family property for the benefit of the daughter and the son in law, and the gift was later made some two year later after the marriage may be supported upon the ground that the gift when made fulfils that moral or religious obligations. The deed mentioned that Sumitra Devi had made a "sankalpa" of the gift of four houses at Churamania, which was accepted by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala Devi, and the document was actually executed and registered. The deed thus recited that Sumitra " was competent to create a moral or social obligation in fulfilment o the promise made by her father to the daughter. The gift in the instant case was made at the time the marriage was a religious duty and the promise to make a Gift to the daughter was made by her. The deed therefore was made some one year before the marriage, and the offer to make a declaration to the daughter that she made a gift to her daughter as her daughter was not essential for making a gift at the relevant time. The deed however recited that Sumitra will be competent to make any gift at the date of the marriage but it was not essential that make a gift at a time of the contract but it may be made afterwards in fulfilment of the promise. The deed expressly stated that Sumitra was entitled to the reliefs which she claimed.

The appellant was elected to the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The election of the appellant was challenged by the respondent (Tej Singh) on the ground that he was guilty of corrupt practices, detailed in the petition an(l in the Statement of facts. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices were not established. The High court held that the allegations were not proved. The appellant filed an appeal in this Court against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the allegation of corrupt practices was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [123A] (2) The High court was in error of holding that the charges of corrupt practices had been established. [123B] (3) The High Courts were in error in interfering with the findings of the courts below. [123C] (4) The High courts were in error of law in holding that no corrupt practice was committed by Tej Singh and Ruplal. The High Courts have not committed any error in holding the appellant guilty of corrupt practice. [123D] (5) The High Judges were in error to hold that the allegations made by the appellant were not proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The High courts have not committed an error in holding so. [123E] (6) The High 's judgment is quashed and the election of the first respondent is set aside. [123F] (7) The High "s judgment is set aside and the election petition is restored. [123G] (8) The High Judge is directed to dispose of the election petition within a period of six months from the date of receipt of this order. [123H] (9) The appeal is allowed.

The appellant was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. The appellant was a member of the Council of ministers headed by Shri M.S. Sharma, Chief Minister of the State. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court in a writ petition. In the writ petition, the appellant contended that the High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction under the Act. The High court dismissed the writ Petition. The appellant contended that as no punishment was imposed on the alleged contemnor, the High Court did not exercise its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution. The appellant also contended that the jurisdiction of the High court to punish for contempt was not barred. The High ' Court dismissed the petition. The High, Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the High court. The appellant thereafter filed a writ application in the High courts challenging the order passed by the High Court and the order passed in the writ petition was stayed. The appellant thereupon filed a writ Petition in the High Courts challenging the order. The High Judge dismissed the writ application. The appellant preferred a writ petition before the High court challenging the order and the order of punishment. The High judge dismissed the writ appeal. The High Bench dismissed the writ petitions. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has exercised its jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of it to punish for Contempt is not to be exercised by the High court, it is difficult to say that when the High Court acquits a contemnor after hearing the parties and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the High court does so also in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for disobedience. [793C] 1.2 The High Court does not exercise its power or jurisdiction to punishfor contempt under Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt. [794D] 1.3 The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to punish for the contempt is to be exercised only by punishing for contempt. The jurisdiction of High Court to punish is also to punish for it. [795E] 1.4 The High Court cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or power to punish for contemnor under Article 215. [796F] 1.5 The High Court, in exercise of its power or power conferred on it by Article 215 of Constitution, cannot be said either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him. [797F] 1:6 The High Court can exercise its jurisdiction or the power conferred on the High Court to dismiss for contempt. When no punishment is imposed by the High Courts, it is impossible to say that the High court should act in a particular manner, that is to say, by imposing punishment for contempt under Article 216 of the Constitution, it is not possible to say that such punishment should not be imposed on the contemnor or that no contempt has been committed by the alleged contemnor and acquits him, such decision of the High Courts acquitting the contemnor is made in the exercise exercise of its powers or jurisdiction to punishing for contempt under article 215 of the constitution. [798F] 1.:6 The High court does not exercise jurisdiction or power conferred by Article 215, of the Constitution to punish for execution. [799F] 1 7.1 The appellant in such a case can move this Court under Article 136. [701B] 1.7 The High Court exercising its jurisdiction and power to punishfor Contempt also includes the jurisdiction to decide whether such punishment should be imposed on a contemnor after considering the fact and circumstances of his case, the Court and the contemnor.

The appellant was the tenant of the respondent. The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the respondent had committed a breach of the terms of the rent note. The trial court held that the respondent was entitled to the protection of section 111 (g) of the and that the lease was determined under section 111 (b) of the . The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amendment made in 1929 to section 111(g) of The Act was merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not based on any principle of justice, equity and good conscience and that the principle of equity is applicable in this case and that the principles of equity are not such a variable commodity, that they change and stand altered on a particular date on the mandate of the legislature and that to leases executed prior to 1st April, 1930, the principle of justice is the one contained in sub section (g) as it now stands. Held, that the rule laid down in sub section(g) is not based upon any principle of equity, justice or good conscience and cannot govern leases made prior to 1 st April, 1930. The rule laid down by the Master of Rolls in the present case is not based merely on any principle or law of equity, equity and justice, equity or good conscience. The rule enunciated in sub section 1 of section 111 of the Act prior to its amendment in 1929 and which still governs leases executed between 1930 and 1930 the principle of Equity is the one stated in the sub section as it now stood. The High Court was fully justified in finding that the rule enunciated in section 111(b) of The that in the case of forfeiture by denial of landlord 's title a notice in writing determining the lease by the lessor bad been given. The High court was fully justified by finding that the amendment introduced in 1929 to sections 111(g), 111(g)(g) of . The High court had not interfered with the 1028 discretion of the courts below in refusing to grant relief against forfeiture for non payment of rent under section 111(h) of the. and that the High Court was not justified in finding the amendment made by the legislature as a rule of justice, justice or justice, equity.

The appellant was a tenant of a private forest and was cultivating the nilam at the commencement of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969. The appellant was a lessee of a private forests and was cultivating it for a period of not less than ten years. The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was in possession of the land for not less than two years within a period of twelve years immediately preceding the 11th day of April, 1957. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had not actually transferred possession of the property to the landlord before the commencement of this Act, and that the appellant could not be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land for not more than two years. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not a tenant if the court had delivered a judgment or passed an order before the date of publication of the Kerala Revenue Reforms (Amendment ) Bill, 1968, in the Gazette that the occupation by such person was on the basis of an oral permission or an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. [610B] 1.2 The appellant was in occupation for not less ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding any order of court, and 112 (c) such land had become the property of such other person as a consequence of any judgment, decree or order of court. [611B] 1:3. The appellant could not claim to be a tenants if he or their predecessor in interest had paid amounts for occupation of the land to the landlord after the 11thday of April,1957, and was cultivating such land for a period exceeding ten years immediately preceding such commencement. [612B] 1.:4. The appellant had not been able to establish that he or his predecessors in interest were in occupation of the lands for not less two years to be considered as tenants. [613C] 1.5 The appellant was entitled to be deemed tenant if he had paid amounts towards occupation of the property. [614D] 1.6 The appellant was also entitled to be treated as a tenant if his predecessor in interests was in occupation. [615B] 1.(a) The appellant was, therefore, entitled to be considered to be a "tenant" if he or her predecessor in interest occupied such land for non less than two year immediately preceding the commencement of Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, on the basis that deed, notwithstanding the fact that the lease was granted by a person who had no rights over the land. The appellant is entitled to be regarded as a tenant. [616C] 1:7. The appellant has not been able or able to establish any right over the property. The appellant cannot claim to be deemed to have been a tenant if it had been lawfully leased out to him. [617B] 1(b) The appellant is not entitled to be a deemed tenant if the Court had delivered a decree or passed an Order before the date on which the Act came into force. [618C] 1.(c) The appellant has been able or unable to establish any tenancy. [619D] 1.(d) The appellant could claim to be treated to be a 'tenant if he or he had been in occupation of any land on the 11th April, 1957, on the date of the commencement of that Act, such deed shall be deemed tobe invalid and such person shall be deemed not to be a licensee.

The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(b) (ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000/ , and in default, to three months further rigorous imprisonment. The appellant was also convicted under Section 135 (d) (ii), of the , of the , Act. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the goods were illegally imported into India without an import licence and in contravention of the provisions of the Government of India, Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Import Control order No.17/55 dated 7 12 1955, which was to be deemed to be an order passed under Section 11 of the Act. Held, that the appellant was not in possession of the offending goods though he had admitted the production of keys from his possession and he had also not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The appellant could not have succeeded in explaining satisfactorily how he was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported or smuggled. The mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable the prosecution to apply Section 106 of the Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where the goods came from or when the goods were imported or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them. The mere appearance of the goods and the manner in which they were packed indicated that they were newly manufactured and brought into this country very recently from another country of their assumed origin after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. The appellant had not produced evidence to show how he was a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty. The mere fact that the goods in question were actually smuggled or brought into the country without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory, could not enable him to know where the articles were seized. The mere presence of the goods in unopened boxes was not sufficient to enable the prosecution. The mere production of the key which, according to the prosecution, could not be treated as a breach of the law. The appellant did not admit the possession of the goods at all. The mere circumstance that the goods had been imported or that the duty, if levied, was not P a d on them, could not lead the Court to the conclusion that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of law. The mere absence of evidence to show the existence of the goods, could not by itself lead to the conclusion of the guilt of the accused. The mere admission of the goods by the accused, could not, by itself lead the Court, to hold that the goods could not be smuggled or imported into the country from another country. The mere non production of evidence to prove that the goods are smuggled goods, the burden of proving that they are not smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession the goods were seized.

The appellants were the President of the said Association from January 1946 to June 26, 1946. The appellants filed a suit for accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1946 to June 25, 1946. In the suit the appellants contended that the suit was not maintainable by reason of the provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and the suit for accounts must fail. The trial court held that the other members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of 284 bales of Gwalior cloth and that the suit for accounting must fail. On appeal to the High Court, the appellants contended (i) that the suit before the trial court was not maintainable because the other members were not entitled under section 4(1)(a) of the Vindhya State Companies Act 1935, and (ii) that the other member of the Association was not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect of contracts which the law declares to be illegal. HELD: (1) The suit before the High Court was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked. [776 H] (2) The suit was not one in respect of a dissolved partnership business, but for accounts relating to an illegal association. [778 A] (3) The suit filed before the trial Court was not a suit for accounting of a dissolved Firm, but for account of an illegal Association which was in operation at the relevant time for which accounts had been asked. [77 D] (4) The suit for accounts was not one under the Rewa State companies Act, 1935. [77 E] (5) The suit in the present case was not one of the suits for accounts of any dissolved firm, but for the accounts of an unlawful association which was formed in pursuance of a Charter from the Durbar. [77 G] (6) The suit instituted before the trial Judge was not one by the members of the association. [77 F] (7) The suit, therefore, was not one, for accounts of unlawful association which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not formed in pursuance to a Charter from Durbar. The suit was therefore not one for accounting of an illegal transaction. [77 H] (8) The suit of accounts must fail because it was formed in contravention of section 4 of the RewaState Companies Act, 1934. [77 A C] (9) The suit by analogy does not really apply. [77 B] (10) The analogy does not directly apply. [78 E] (11) The analogy did not really apply because the suit was instituted by one member of an illegal partnership against another in respect of the partnership dealings and transactions. It was enough to point out that under the , an unregistered firm was not illegal. [77 C] (12) The analogy also does not really applicable. [77D] (13) The analogy is of no help to the appellants. [77E] (14) The analogy of section 69(3)(a) does not really applies. [77G] (15) The analogy do not really apply to the appellants; in our opinion, the analogy does not completely apply. [76F] (16) The analogy cannot be of any help to the appellant. [77F] (17) The analogy applies. [78G] (18) The analogy would not apply. [79G] (19) The analogy makes no difference to the appellants because the suit before us was not one relating to the partnership dealings, it was not necessary to point out any difficulty in the matter.

The words are intended to cover offences of other description for which punishment has been provided for in the Indian Penal code. [914D] 1.4. The petitioner was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The Sessions Judge ordered that a surety hl a sum of Rs. 50,000 be released on bail with sureties, and release on his own recognizance. The order of the Sessions Judge was confirmed by the High Court. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. The petitioner contended that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to release the petitioner on bail because he had not been arrested in the case and that the Magistrate ordered that a bond hl a fine of Rs. 25,000 be imposed on him. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The petitioner then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. The High court dismissed the petition. The High, Court held that the Magistrate was not competent to release the accused on bail because the Magistrate had not been released on bail and that the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction in granting bail. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Magistrate must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the Criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [885F] 2. The language of the section is clear and unambiguous. It is not a mere formality. It is a procedural provision. It is only a procedural provision which is procedural in nature. It is procedural in character. It is an procedural provision which has to be strictly construed. It is, therefore, a procedural provision and not a substantive provision. It has to be construed strictly. [886F] 3. The language used in the section is plain and unambiguous. The language employed in the section does not require any particular interpretation. It is merely a procedural provision to be construed in the context of the substantive provision. [887F] 4. The language in the section has to be given its plain and unambiguous meaning. It is the duty of the court to interpret the substantive provision in the manner in which it is intended to be used. [888F] 5. The language is plain and clear. It is meant to be used in the sense of the substantive enactment. It is intended to convey the intention of the legislature. [890F] 6. The language must be given its full meaning. It must be given a plain and unambiguous interpretation. It must not be given a restricted meaning. It should be given a wide and ordinary meaning. [891F] 7. The language should be given its natural and grammatical meaning. It has been used in the context in which it appears to have been used in section. [892F] 8. The language has to be interpreted in the context and in which it has been used. It is to be interpreted as to give a restricted meaning to the substantive enactment and not to give a narrow meaning to the language. [893F] 9. The language cannot be given a narrow meaning. It can be used to give a wide meaning to the words used in the substantive enactment so as to give the meaning to the term. [894F] 10. The language does not mean that the words used should be given the same meaning. It may be used to convey the meaning of the words used. It may also be used to indicate the intention of Parliament. [895F] 11. The language may be used in a wide sense. It may not be used to describe the words used but it may be used for the purpose of interpreting the substantive enactment in the context.

The assessee was a branch of the assessee. The assessee was a registered firm. The assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that the assessee had not been computed and included in the computation. The Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to ' Castle ' in the computation for the purpose of 429 section 15C. The High Court held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on some evidence ignoring other essential matters, and that the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was a relevant factor. The High court held that the decision of the Appellate Assistant Tribunal was one which was based on no evidence ignoring other relevant matters on which the Appellate Assistant commissioner had relied in support of his conclusion. The High ' Court, however, dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Appellate Assistant commissioner has the power to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the Tribunal. The refusal of the Tribunal to state the case is not conclusive. The refusal by the Tribunal to disclose the case is a relevant circumstance, but its effect has to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the appellate Assistant Commissioner had relied. [419D] 1.2 The Appellate Assistant Commissioners have failed to state the facts before arriving at its finding. The Appellate Asstt. Commissioner have failed to give rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. [420B] 1.3 The Appellate Assistant Commission has erred in law in arriving at its conclusion. The Appellate Asst. Commissioner has failed to appreciate the evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at the conclusion. [421C] 1.4 The Appellate Assistant ' Commissioner has erred in arriving at the finding of fact, if on a review of the evidence the Court might have arrived at a different conclusion. [427B] 1:5 The Appellate Assistant Officer has failed to consider the other relevant matters before arriving At its finding. [422D] 1:6 The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner has erred in not giving rise to a questions liable to be refered to the Court, and in refusing to require the Tribunal to specify the case and refer it, the High Court was, in error. The Appellate Officer has failed in law in reaching its finding. It has also misdirected itself in law in arrived at a conclusion. The conclusion of the Appellate Tribunal therefore suffers from a double infirmity: it assumes the only fact on which the Tribunal had arrived at a particular conclusion. [441C] 1:7 The Appellate Assistant Judge has erred in applying the single circumstance on which its decision was founded. The Appellate Income tax Officer has failed and failed to appreciate other relevant matters. [423B] 1.:8 The Appellate Assistant Tribunal has erred in holding that in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52, 'Castles ' had carried on business and had earned income. The Appellate Assistants ' Commissioner have failed in law. [424C] 1.:9 The Appellate Assistant Collector has erred in relying upon the single circumstance that in the earlier year to the assessment for the year 1951 52, the income from 'Castley ' had not been correctly computed and included. The Appellate Collector has erred by applying the single factor on which its conclusion was founded and ignores other relevant matters ignoring other relevant factors.

The order of the High Court is set aside. The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government was that the Minister in charge, of Irrigation Department was called upon to file his personal affidavit. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The Minister, however, directed that the Minister should file his personal affidavits. The Minister also directed that the Secretary of the Department should file his affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the petition. The Minister thereafter heard the party and made a detailed speaking order on March 18, 1975 confirming the earlier seniority lists. The Minister accordingly, directed that in the light of the allegations made by the Minister, the Minister should be impleaded as a party in the petition, as in the view of the learned Judge, allegation had been made against the Minister. The Minister was also directed to file his affidavit. The High Court was, however, in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded as party in the writ petition. The other part of the order whereby the Minister concerned was directed to file their personal affidavit was set aside. It seems to us that the direction for the impleading of the Minister as a party was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations contained in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, we do not feel persuaded to interfere with the order made by the High court insofar as it has directed that the Ministry should file his Personal affidavit. The other portion of the order which has directed the impleading of Minister as a Party was given by him with a view t to apprise the Secretary of his allegations made in his petition and thus, to afford him a personal opportunity of controuting those allegations, is set aside and the order of the Minister concerned is set aside, and 97 in the amended petition, Duggal respondent also prayed for an opportunity of rebuttal controverting those allegation, if he was so deemed proper, and to afford him opportunity of controeding them. The other remaining part of the judgment which has directed that in view of the findings of the High court, the Minister concerned should file his own personal affidavit.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent was a lessee of the appellant and the appellant was a tenant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent. The appellant contended that the amount had been due as arrears. The magistrate held that the arrears of rent due under a lease in favour of the respondent were due as arrears and that the amount could be recovered under section 259 of the Act. The magistrate also held that the amount due under a tenancy in favour of a tenant could not be recovered under the Act. On appeal, the magistrate held that arrears of rent were recoverable by the Board under the provisions of the Act and that the respondent was entitled to recover the same under section 259. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of section 259 of The Act were not applicable to the case. The High court held that the rent in this case was not claimable by the Board. The High ' Court held that arrears due under a contract between the landlord and the tenant could not, therefore, be recovered under s. 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : The section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent of land and buildings only if such rent is recoverable by a Board under the Act or the Rules. [347G H] The words "claimable by a Board" and "other money" must equally be governed by the words "claim recoverable by a board etc." must equally be applied by the words 'claimable by the board". [347C] The words 'claim recoverable by the board under the Act and 'the Rules" must equally apply. [347D] The words used in section 259 of Act cannot be used for realisation of arrears of rents on land and buildings. [347E] The words of section 259 are not intended to be used for recovery of rent on land and building only if such rents are recoverable by a court under the Act, and the Rules which empower the Board to let out the land or buildings upon the ground that it cannot be said to be claimable under any express provision of the Act or Rules.

The appellant was employed as a section salesman in the respondent company. The appellant was appointed as a section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The appellant, however, was employed for canvassing and promote the sales of the company in the four districts allotted to him. The appellant had been in the service of the respondent company as a section saleman and his service was controlled by the Head office through its territories office situated in New Delhi. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had been employed for canvassing, and therefore, the Reference was incompetent. HELD: (1) The appellant was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study ofthe market condition. The supervising work of the other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. [475G H] (2) The supervising work o the other local salemen was part o his work consideredby the Tribunal as incidental to his primary work of canvassing, and promotion in this area. The supervising duties of other local salesman were part of his main work considered by it as only incidental t o his main work. The supervising works of other local sale men were part of their work considered by t he Tribunal as only ancillary to his main function of canvassing and promoting the sale of the product of the company. [425B] (3) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant is not a workman employed for manual, skilled, unskilled and/or clerical in nature. [426C] (4) The Tribunal had not interfered with that finding on the question whether the appellant is a workman employed under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the Section i.e. manual, skilled and/or manual in nature. The finding of the Tribunal on the question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour Court. [422D] (5) The finding of fact on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact. It is also borne Out by the document placed before the Labour court. It is seen from the facts found that the appellant has been employed to do the business of canvassing and promote sales of the Company in the four district allotted to him by the company in Delhi. Neither the section salesmen nor the local salesmen were employed by the company. Therefore, the Labour Court was right in dismissing the application only on the ground that the appellant cannot be held to be a workman employed by the respondent company and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [423D] (6) The Labour Court had given findings in favour of the appelant on the question as to whether the appellant was a workman employed in the shop of the wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell the product of his company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company. It was only incidental to the main function of the other Local salesmen and local trav elling salesmen and the local salesman appointed in the area. [424E] (7) The Labour C ourt had given findings on the question Whether the appellant is an "workman" or not.

The Company was a Government lessee under section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007. The Company was not a Government lessee within the meaning of section 181 of that Code. The Company had not become a `pakka ' tenant under section 185 of the Code. The High Court held that the Company was not an occupancy tenant under section 54(vii) of Part II of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Land Reforms Act, Sampat 2007 (Act No. 66 of 1950) as it had not become an ordinary tenant. The High court held that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. The Company filed an appeal against the order of the High Court dated 20.9.1980 in First Appeal No. 1 of 1961. The High Curt held that the company was not a `pukka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. The Company, however, held that the High Court had found in the earlier proceeding that the land measuring 495.05 acre was held by a Company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The Company 's appeal was dismissed by the High Court. The Company preferred a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of this Court dated 20,9.1980. The High, Court held that since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the lease, proceedings were initiated by the 178 Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977. The Company challenged the order of High Court dated 1. 10.1977 in First Appeal Nos. 1 of 1962 and 1 of 1961 whereby the High Court dismissed the Company 's Appeal, holding that the Company had not been holding the land as a `phakka ' tenant. The State of Madhya Pradesh filed a Special Leave Petition in this Court. The High ' Court held that in terms of sub section (1) of section 182 of the Code, the Company was entitled to remain in possession of the land as an ordinary tenant and that it had never been an ordinary tenant under section 55(vii) and was, therefore not liable to proceed against in terms Of section 182. In the circumstances, the High Court held in the earlier proceedings that the Company did not enjoy status of a Gair Mauriusi tenant and that the Company could not be evicted by the summary proceeding provided for under that section. The High "Court further held that the Tribunal had not committed any error in holding that the land in question was not a 'pakka' tenant under section 181(2)(i) of the Code as it had never become an ordinary tenancy. The High Judge held that the order of Additional Collector dated 1.11.1977 in Misc. Petition No.84 of 1978 was not a pakka ' tenancy under section 185. The Company appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court had not committed an error in holding the Company to the contrary. [419D] 1.2 The High Court has found in the previous proceeding that the Company has been holding the lands in question. The finding of the High court to the contrary was, in our view, totally unjustified and opposed to law.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands in the State of Orissa. They were cultivating the lands in the year 1949. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court held that the Act was not law in force until a notification was issued bringing into force the provisions of the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) into force, and that the notification issued in exercise of the power under section 1(3) was ineffective. The petitioners contended that the Act did not apply to the petitioners because the Act was repealed by Act 15 of 1965, and that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 was not law. Held, that the Act in force when the Act was brought into force was ineffective. Section 1(3), of the principal Act was not a law in force when it was repealed by the Act. Section 1 (3) of the Act was a law in operation, but until the power is exercised by the State Government to issue an appropriate notification, the provisions of Ch. IV could not be deemed to be law in force, and since no notification was issued before Ch. IV of the principal act was repealed, there was no ceiling limit applicable to the landholders under any law for the time being in force. The right to compensation which is not less than the market value under any law providing for the acquisition by the State of any land in an estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the ceiling limit applicable under the principal Act. The right of compensation which is guaranteed by a second proviso only when the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus land which is within the Ceiling limit applicable to him under any law relating to the acquisition of such land, building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to acquisition of such property, provide for payment to him for extinction of the interest, the Market value of that portion of the surplus lands which is within his ceiling limit under the principal act. The right is exercisable by the State Govt. to issue an order for the compulsory acquisition of the land which may be laid only if the law provides that payment to the owner for extinction of interest, the land is not lessthan the market value thereof if such land be within the ceiling limits applicable to him. The right under article 31(2) read with article 31(3) of Constitution was not exercisable by the successor State. The right was exercisable by the Government to issue a notification, and was repealed by section 1(4) on the date appointed by the State. The power to bring into force the provision of the Travancore act 14 of 1125 (M. E.) was exercisable by a notification, but until a notification is issued before Ch IV of the Principal Act was repealed, the provisions Of Ch. IV were not applicable to the petitioners. The right conferred by section 1 (3), of Act 16 of 1960 was not in force until the power was exercised by the Government. The right could not be questioned because section 1(2) was existing law on July 1, 1949, but until it was repealed, no notification was made before Ch. V of the principal enactment was repealed. The right which was not less than that the market value was guaranteed by the first proviso only where, the land was within the ceiling area applicable to him, under any law, for the timebeing in force, or any building or structure or appurtenant thereto. The right, under article 31 (2) readwith article 31(1) of the Constitution was exercisable by an successor State.

The widow 's estate was in the hands of the widow and her husband. The widow 's property was in the possession of the widow. The widow was the absolute owner of the property. The widow, however, made a surrender of her estate to the widow. On the death of the widow, the widow became the absolute owner. The widow filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that the widow was in possession of the properties during the period of her widow 's natural life. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the widow 's right to recover possession of the estate during the period from the widow ' 's estate had been extinguished by adverse possession exercised by the defendants, and that the widow had no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversions. The High court, however, held that the reversionary right to recover the possession of property during the period between the widow ' and her husband 's estate could not be surrendered to the reversioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the widow herself was in possession and that the reversion was not for legal necessity, so long as the widow remained alive and her expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the part of the widow 'Sreeramu. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The widow herself is in capable of disputing the title of the alienee or of the person who has acquired interest by adverse possession against her, a like disability attaches to the reversioner also who could not have obtained the properties but for the surrender made by the widow. [356 G] 2. The widow is under no legal obligation to surrender her estate. [356 A B] 3. The widow becomes the absolute owner and the property is the property of the widow after the death of her husband. [356 C] 4. The widow has been given a right to make a surrender, but as the widow has paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on the expectation of enjoying it so long as she suffered physical or civil death, there is no justification why the reversioner should not, subject to any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession by the widow, even though the alienation was not for valid necessity, so far as the reversions are concerned, long as the husband remains alive and his expectations have been fully cut short by the widow and she is under no Legal or moral obligation to surrender his estate. [358 D] 5. The widow's right to recover property during the widow ''s lifetime was treated to be the same as that of an alienee from her and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow she would remain alive and his demands have been cut off by a surrender made by her. [356 E] 6. The widow also becomes entitled to challenge the right of the alienor to recover possession from the widow. If a surrender is given by the widow to the widow, it is for legal necessity. [356 F] 7. The widow gets the inheritance even during the widow lifetime, if she suffered physical and civil death, and if a surrenders is made subsequently, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. [356 D] 8. The widow cannot challenge the right to recover ownership of the property during the life time of the widow's lifetime on grounds of equity, justice and good conscience in proper cases, it is clear that in the case before us no equitable considerations at all arise at all arise. [356 H] 9.

The appellants, who were the Directors of the Polytex Company, were the Directors and were the Directors. The appellants were the Directors in respect of the shares of the Polytechnic Company. The appellants filed a suit for a declaration that the order of the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares of it and that the meeting was not validly called since the Cotton Mills Company had ceased to have the rights of a member under section 169 of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order passed by the Collector being a charging order, the Receiver had no right to vote at the meeting or to issue a notice under section 169 Of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of the High Court being an orderin the nature of an charging order the receiver had obtained an enforceable right in the share in question and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton Mills Co. had lost its right to the shares. The order of Collector being an Order in the nature o.i.e. a charging order under the English Law is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of a Receiver under the Land Revenue Act. [501 B] 1.2 The order of a Collector being an administrative order, the receiver had no right in the rights of the members of the Polyital Company. The order passed by him in respect of certain shares of the polytex Company held by the Cotton Mills company could not be treated as the holder of the shares pledged in its favour. [502 C] 1.3 The order of an Collector being an executive order, the High Court was not justified in holding that the order was an order in nature of a charge order. [503 D] 1.4 The order of attachment of the shares in question was an order passed in the nature, of a charging Order. The order was passed under section 169 read with section 190 of the Act and there being any other legal or legal equitable right which could be exercised by the Collector, that a part of it had also been pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh also would not make any difference Sections 172 to 178 A of the deal with the contract of pledge. [505 E] 1.5 The order of confiscation passed by the Magistrate was an order under the Indian Companies Act. The order could not be said to be an order in a nature of a charged order. [605 F] 1.6 The order of seizure passed by the magistrate was an order of a charging section order. The High court was not justified by the fact that the order had obtained an effective equitable right in favour of a member of the Polyester Company who what that a Receiver had been attached by the Collector. The order had been passed under section 17AA of the Act by the Collector and that orders had been passed in accordance with the order of his Collector. [606 A B] 1:7 The order of detention passed by the High Court in the instant case was an order made under section 17A of the Act in the nature as a charge order and the Receiver had been appointed in respect of these shares. The High 'Court was not justified to hold that the order dated February 1, 1985 was an order which was an orderin- the nature of charging order. [706 C] 1:8 The order of suspension passed by the Board of Directors was an order by the Collector under the Indian Societies Act. The High "Court was not right in holding that an order in an administrative order could not deprive the holder of a right which would otherwise prevail over it.

The plaintiffs were the owners in posses 833 sion of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat in the course of its written statement inter alia pleaded that the land in question belonged to the Panchayat and that the suit land was shamlat deh. The plaintiffs had, however, questioned the correctness of the entries in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit land. The trial court held that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the question involved in the suit was merely one of title to the suit property and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit land belonged to the Gram Panchayat, the question involved was not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Act and consequently the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The civil court had no jurisdiction to try such suits. [833B] 2. The civil courts had jurisdiction to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any property or is not shamlat deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or in any other original suit, application or execution proceedings. No civil court could have jurisdiction to entertain any suit application or execution proceeding. No civil suit could have been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the suit property belonged to the village. The civil Court had jurisdiction to decide such claim in such manner as may be prescribed. [834C] 3. The civil suit had been filed against a Panchayat and the Gram Panchayat had expressly admitted that the land belonged to it as shamlat deh and it had been vested in it. The civil suits had been filed by the plaintiffs and the Panchayat was, therefore, competent to decide such question. [835D] 4. The civil Courts had jurisdiction to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question belonged or not. The civil jurisdiction had not been taken away by virtue of the provisions of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act. [836F] 5. The civil proceedings had been filed in the civil court and the Panchayat has expressly claimed that it belonged to the gram Panchayat. The civil authorities had jurisdiction to determine such claim in the manner prescribed. [ 836F] 6. The civil disputes had been filed before the trial court and the civil court was competent to decide the same. [837G] 7. The civil dispute had been filed on the basis of the entries made in the revenue record which showed that there was no sort of right or title in it. [838F] 8. The civil litigation had been filed only against the Panchayat. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration that the suit lands belonged to the panchayat or not. [839F] 9. The civil proceeding had been filed for the civil court to make a claim in writing and signed and verified in the prescribed manner and that the Collector had jurisdiction to adjudicate such claim in respect of any matter which the Commissioner or the Collector was empowered by or under the Act to determine.

The petitioners were appointed as Deputy Directors in the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Telecommunications Research Centre in a Telecommunications Department. The petitioners were appointed to the Telecommuni cation Research Centre in an Telecommuni ce Research Centre in which the petitioners were working as officers in the Tele Communication Research Centre. The petitioners, who were working in the TeleCommunications Research Centre, were given Special Pay of Rs. 150 per month in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.1.1973. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners challenged the validity of rules of promotion on the ground that the rules of recruitment contained in the recruitment rules were not applicable to the petitioners. The petitioners contended that the rules were not discriminatory and violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. The petitioners have filed these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The rules of promotion contain a clear distinction between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transferred officials have to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition to the pay scale of direct recruits because the transferred officials had to perform in the Tele Communications Research Centre duties which are not in their general line. [1309713] 1.2 The petitioners are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Tele communication Research Centre duties. They are graduates engineers and have to be given Special Pay in lieu of their pay scales which is the same as the scale of pay of direct recruits. [13109H] 1.3 The petitioners are graduates engineers. They are graduate engineers. They have been working in the telecommunications Research Center duties which are also not in their special line. [1010B] 1.4 The petitioners are Graduate engineers and have also been working throughout the Telecommunication Technology Centre. [1020C] 1.5 The petitioners are diploma engineers and have got Special Pay in the Tele communicate Research Centre duties in the Telecomunications Research Centre. [1120D] 1.6 The petitioners are not competent and are not able to discharge their duties. All the direct recruits are graduate engineers, having been working throughout, in the Tele communications Research Centre. They are also graduate engineers and having been working in that centre with effect from the date from which the transferred officers have been drawing the Special Pay upto date and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred officers continue to get it. [1021B] 1:7 The petitioners are entitled to the Special Pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in that center with effect from th date on which the transferred officials commenced to draw the Special Pay up upto date and the continuing to pay it. [1121C] 1:8 The petitioners are also graduate Engineers and have been in working throughout the telecommi cation Research Center. [1022D] 1:9 The petitioners aregraduate engineers and have become working throughout in Telecommunication Research Center. They are working throughout in their general lines. [1023D] 1.:10 The petitioners are postgraduate engineers and have be en working throughout in t he Telecommunication Research centre. [1024E] 1.11 The petitioners are Graduates engineers and have completed their duties in the telecommunication Research Centre duties on the same posts and discharging the same functions as the petitioners. [1025E] 1:10 The petitioners have been working continuously in the Tele Telecommunication Research Centr ed Research Centre.

The appellant was an employee of an industry governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The appellant was dismissed from service on account of any dispute relating to change in respect of an industrial matter specified in Schedule 11 of the Act. The appellant filed an application under section 42(4) of the Act before the Labour Court claiming relief under section 7 8(1) of the said Act. The Labour Court rejected the application on the ground that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(1) or an employee desiring a change in respect thereof. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under Section 42(4). The State Industrial Court held that it was necessary for an employer to give notice of such intention in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees. The State Industrial Tribunal held that it had jurisdiction under the Act and the Labour Court had jurisdiction under section 78(1)D of the Act to decide all the disputes covered by section 42(3) of the. The State Government preferred an appeal under section 78 (1)D. The State of Bombay preferred an appeal before the High Court contending inter alia that it was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed that the order of the Labour Court should be set aside on that ground alone. The High Court held that the third Respondent had failed to complied with the provisions Of law in that the thirdRespondent had failed to do so. The appellant has preferred this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Labour Courts are to have power to decide all disputes covered by paragraph A of sub section (1) of section 78. [723C] 2. The scheme of section 7 8 (1) seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour Court. [724D] 3. The scheme does not stand on reason that an employees should be able lo step all this. [725E] 4. The scheme is that disputes should not be settled as long as possible and basically through conciliation and agreed agreement, it do not stand to ground that an employee could be able to effectively step all this By a direct reference, to the Labour court. [726B] 5. The scheme envisages that disputes should arise if within the period prescribed under the proviso to sub section (4) of section 42, no agreement is arrived at in respect of any order passed by the employer under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of dismissal, to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to the Labour Judge. [727C] 6. The scheme contemplates that disputes should have first arisen if within the prescribed period under the proviso, no agreement was arrived at. [728B] 7. The scheme also contemplates that disputes must be settled as expeditiously as possible and ordinarily through conciliation and negotiations and agreement, the same does not stand the reason that an employer intending to effect any change in respect Of matters covered by section 4 of the Act, which would of need include an order to see whether the same was possible to be brought to any agreement. [729C] 8. The scheme further contemplates that disputes shall be settled as soon as possible and whenever any dispute arises, the employer intending to make any change in regard of any order, matter or change referred to in the said proviso. [730C] 9.

The respondents, who were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years, filed a suit for eviction under section 12 of the Act before the Munsif, Ranchi, claiming that the appellants ' application under section 12 was not maintainable before the Munsif. The Munsif, Ranchi held that the appellants were not entitled to move the Court by an application under section12 of the Act because the landlord had no other good and sufficient cause for terminating the lease on the expiry of the period of a fixed term tenancy. The appellants ' application was allowed and an appeal therefrom was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi. The respondents then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, inter alia, contending that the appellants' application under section 13 of the Act was not maintainable because the landlord was not entitled to file an application under Section 12 of the act. The High Court dismissed the revision application. The appellants then moved the High Court in revision. The High court held that the application under section 11 of the Act filed by the appellants was not maintainable and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The High Curt held that the appellant 's application under section 10 of the Act had not been maintainable before the court. The appellants filed a revision application before the High Court. The High, Court held that the order passed by the Munsif was not one under section 47 of the Act and the entire proceedings was mis conceived and therefore the entire proceeding is mis conceived. It was held that the landlord had any other good and reasonable cause for terminating his lease on the termination of the lease on 31.7.1971 as tenants from month to month. The High curt also held that the tenant had no other sufficient cause for termination of the tenancy. The High ' Court held that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was maintainable before the civil court. The High Courts held that the suit was not maintainable. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question is whether the petition filed by the respondents as an application under [section 12 of the] Act before the civil Court was maintainable. [912D] 2. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of period of a lease is entitled to move a Court by an order under section 47, and the order passed under section 47 would have the effect of a final order under section47, and the present case is a most appropriate one for exercise of such power. [913E] 3. The question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy is concluded by the first appellate court in favour of the appellants. The occasion for filing an applica tion under section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [914F] 4. The occasion of filing an applicat tion under section 11 is wholly inapplicable In the present case, the appellants by their notice, did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. The occasion For filing an applic ation under section 12, and an application under sections 12 and 13 are to be filed. [915F] 5. The question of whether a landlord before the expiry of a period of a specified term lease is entitled, to move the court by an application Under section 12 of The Act, is whether the application under Section 11 of the act is not maintainable in the facts of the case as the appellants were entitled to move this Court by an appeal and a second appeal. [916G] 6. The question also does not affect any substantive right of th appellants as the controversy was concluded by the second appellate court in favor of the respondents. [917G] 7.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that the election of the Secretary of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary of a Society. The trial court held that the appellant ' Society was not the Secretary of that Society and was, therefore, not entitled to prosecute or withdraw the suit. The trial Court held that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable and the High Court was in error in dismissing the appellant ' s application. The appellant filed a revision application before the High Court which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. The appellant challenged the correctness of the trial court 's finding in favour of the respondent. The High Court dismissed the revision application. The High court held that in the exercise of inherent power under section 15 I of the Code, a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. The High ' Court, while confirming the order, said that in the exercising of inherent power, a court cannot vacate an order passed by it. The appellant 's revision application was also dismissed. The appellant Society challenged the correctness and legality of the trial Court 's finding on the merits of the case. The High, Court, while affirming the order, observed that the trial court had jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power. The High Curt, while confirming that it had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting the withdraw of the suit, held that the only remedy of the appellant is to institute a suit. The High Courts, while confirming this order, said, that in the exercised of inherent power the court had the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the decree if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. The trial Curt, however, did not exercise a jurisdiction vested in it by law. The High courts were, therefore, right in holding that the trial Court had no jurisdiction, and the High court should have inter ved in its revisional power on the ground that the trial cour ted in its inherent power was not the President of the appellant Society. The High cour ting the matter to the trial court for reconsideration of the case on merits, the High Court should have inter pened in its revisional jurisdiction on the assumption that it had jurisdiction to recall the order permitting withdrawal of the suits under its inherent powers. The High High Court, while upholding the correctness of this finding, said that the trial Curt had no jurisdiction in holding that it had not jurisdiction to recall Its order permitting the withdrawn of the suit. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that it had power to recall its orders permitting the withdrawal o f the suit under Its inherent power. [515E] 1.2 The High Court, in the exercise o its inherent power under Section 15 1 of t he Code of Civil procedure, had the power to do so. [516B] 1.3 The High Court while confirming the impugned judgment, said that it had powers vested in it under section 151 of the Code. The only remedy to the party is to institute an suit. The only right to institute a fresh suit is to institute the suit. [517C] 1.4 The High Court was, therefore not right in holding the application of the appellant invoking the inherent jurisdiction of the court. [518E] 1:5 The High Court had rightly held that the trial courts were, thus, wrong in dismissing the appellants ' application as not maintainable.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and was appointed as a member of a Civil Service. He was appointed as an officer of the Indian Revenue Service. He had been in the service of the Government of Jammu and Kashmir. He was promoted as an officer in the Indian Revenue Services. He was confirmed in the Indian Civil Services and was confirmed in that post. He was also confirmed in that service. On April 1, 1946, the appellant was appointed as the Secretary of the Indian Administrative Service. On April 2, 1946, he was confirmed in his substantive post of the Indian Police Service. On May 1, 1946 the appellant was promoted as a member. On April 3, 1946, a notification was issued by the Government of India under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government India Act, 1935, declaring the period of emergency referred to in section 3 of the India and Burma (Termination of Emergency) Order, 1946, as the period of Emergency referred to in that section. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the said period had expired on April 1, 1947, and that the Ordinance had been promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 Of the 9th Schedule of the Government. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Ordinance promulgated by the Governor General on April 1. 1946, was not in operation on July 11, 1953, and that as soon as the declaration of the emergency had come to an end, the original position was restored and the Ordinance in question which had been promulgated was in operation. Held, that the Ordinance was promulgated in exercise Of the emergency powers conferred by section 72 of that Act without any limitation on its duration and was therefore not limited to the space of not more than six months from its promulgation. The Ordinance was promulgated by the Government in exercise of its emergency powers ipso facto and did not cease to be in operation after it was repealed. The Ordinance having continued in operation even after the declaration of emergency having come to an expiry was made on April 1., 1946, the said notes continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India, though the position in Jammu and Kashmir in regard to the same could not be affected by reason of the , not having been made applicable to the State of Jammu and Jammu and Kashmir as stated above. The Ordinance had continued in operation on April 1,. 1946, and the Ordinance having continued to be in force until it was repealed, the said note continued to be effective until it was superseded.
