The appellant was a partner in a firm called Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in 1939, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The appellant was charged with having entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart. The appellant pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949, by Shri A. Inspecting Commissioner, and that the appellant had been exonerated of the allegations and imputations made against him on each occasion. The appellant also pleaded that there was an enquiry in 1952 by Shri A, Inspecting Commissioner, who was appointed by the Commissioner of Income tax as Inquiring Officer. The appellant contended that there had not been an enquiry at all, and that there had also been an enquiry into certain matters by Shri A., Inspecting Commissioner, in respect of which charges were actually framed and fully enquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice was not challenged. The High Court dismissed the appellant 's appeal. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently, been forgotten. The question whether the departmental proceedings were null and void could vitiate the whole departmental trial. Unless such a point could be raised, there could be no declaration that the departmental proceedings had been null and void. [696B] 1.2 The question whether a departmental proceedings were valid and void could not be raised, it was not enough to merit cancellation of the special leave. [697C] 1.3 The question whether an opportunity denied is of a kind which amounts to a denial of natural justice or would have affected the final decision it could not be material. Unless such an issue could be raised at any time subsequent to 1939 also. [698C] 1:4 The question whether any charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry, overlooks that no charge was framed. The question which could affect the final decision of the departmental authorities was whether the departmental proceeding was null and void, and did not affect the final result. [699D] 1.5 The question whether there was an order of suspension of the appellant was of such a nature that the departmental proceeding could vitiate the entire departmental trial. [695B] 1:6 The question whether certain material 586 facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave, could not be of such nature that the denial could affect the ultimate decision. [694C] 1.:7 The question whether some material 586 facts are suppressed or misrepresent for the purpose for obtaining special leave could not be decided at this stage after hearing arguments. [692D] 1:8 The question whether it goes to the root of the jurisdiction and the conduct of the department trial and vitiates the result. [600E] 1.9 The question whether, in the case before us, the appellant could be subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no other charge was found established. [693A] 1.10 The question whether in the case of a departmental proceedings, the appellant should have been given a reasonable opportunity to meet a new case. [691B] 1.:9 The question of fact which could affect a final decision it was not necessary for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities, which had looked into the case upto its final stage, that he had suffered some injustice which to be set right. [690C] 1 :10 The question of law whether the departmental enquiry was null and invalid could not be considered at this stage when the first appeal was heard by the High Court. [602B] 1 :11 The question whether departmental proceedings were invalid could not have been raised at the time of hearing of the appeal.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants were the purchasers of manganese ores within the State. The appellants contended that they were not the last purchasers but the M.M.T.C. was the only purchaser within the State and therefore the M.T. C. was liable to pay the tax. The High Court held that the contracts between the appellants and the M. M.T.,C. were integrated contracts in the course of export. The appellants challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Court in the appeals by special leave. The principal question in these appeals is whether the contracts between them were integrated activities in the course o export. The contracts between the M.S.T. and the foreign buyers were inter separate and independent contracts with their foreign buyers on F.O.B. and the S.T.Cs. and the appellants were liable to pay tax. The contracts were inter separate. The contracts of sale were entered into by the appellants with the foreign buyers on the basis of the contracts of sale entered into by them with the foreign buyer on F. O.B. The contracts entered into by their foreign buyers with the foreign sellers on F.A. and the Indian buyers were inter independent and con tracts of sale. The contracts with the foreign purchasers were inter separate in the course Of export. The buyers were the importers and shipper of the goods. The appellants also contended that the contracts of the appellants with foreign buyers were integrated contracts with their Foreign buyers on F,O.B., and that the contracts were inter independent. The High court held that the contract of sale was integrally connected with the contract entered into by M.M.,T.C., and that there existed a bond between the appellants with their foreign buyer and the foreign buyer. The High ' Court held that there existed no bond between the parties and that the contract between the appellants was integrally related with the contract entering into independent contracts with the Foreign buyers. The High " Court further held that the agreements between the appellants were integrated contracts and it was the S. T.C. which entered into direct contract with their foreign customers on F.F.O. B. and the Foreign buyers were the contracts of sales entered into by both the appellants with Foreign buyers on the F.O.,B. and F.O,B. and that the agreement of the appellants was inter independent and inter independent con tracts of contract with their Foreign buyer. The appellants ' contract of sale between the appellants on F.I.B. was the contract of the sale of manganese ores and that the appellants were not the first purchasers within the State, and therefore, the M.O.C. could not be said to be the last purchaser of goods within the State as they were not in the course. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The contracts executed by the appellants were inter independent contracts with foreign buyers onF.O., B. and FO.B, and therefore the contracts between M.M..T.C and the foreign sellers were integrated in the course in export. [412C D] 2. The contracts in the instant case were inter independent in the courseof export. The contract of sale entered by the appellants on the F,O.,B and F.F.,O.B was the contract between them. The contracts are inter independent and the contract between M.S..T. C and the foreign customers are distinct. The contracts inter independent and in the course thereof are distinct. [413E F] 3. The contracts which were inter independent were contracts between the S.S. T. C. and the appellant.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Officer, Bhatinda. The appellant was served with a "charge sheet" by the Settlement Officer. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. The Enquiry Officer held that the order of termination of employment was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution and no penalty was imposed upon the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The appellant contended that the order dated March 17, 1955, was not the order pursuant to which employment of the appellant was terminated, and that the provisions of article 311(2) had not been complied with by the Enquiry Officer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order dated March 18, 1955, is not of that nature. The appellant is entitled to the protection or article 311 (2) of the Constitution. [776D] The order dated April 17, 1955 is not of a nature as to impose punishment and not to an enquiry whether a probationer should be confirmed. [775G] The order of termination passed by the Settlement officer is not of the nature of an order of punishment and therefore, there was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order terminating his employment for unsatisfactory work and conduct. [778G] The appellant was given an opportunity to make his defence and it appears that witnesses in support of the charge and in defence were examined before the Settlement Officer and the appellant was not liable to be dismissed or removed from service. [782G] The third proposition in the latter (Gopi Kishore Prasad 's) case refers to an enquiry into allegations of misconduct or inefficiency with a view, if they were found established to impose punishment, because it puts a stigma on his competence and thereby affects his future career. The appellant, was a temporary employee, but, in principle, it will make no difference whether the appellant was a probationer or a temporary employee. The appellant had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the order of terminating his employment.

The appellant was promoted as Professor in the Department of Science and Technology, Government of Jammu and Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission. The appellant was promoted to the post of Professor in the department of Science and technology, Government of India. The appellant challenged the promotion of respondents Nos. 1 to 4 on the ground that the Commission was consulted in accordance with its requirement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the Commission had not consulted the Commission in regard to the principles to be followed in making the promotions in question, or on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the selection made by the Commission. It was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the Commission did not consult the Commission in the manner required by section 133 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred while holding that the selection made was vitiated for that reason. [873H] 1.2 The High Court was not justified in holding that section 133(2) (b) was not correctly interpreted and that the Public Service Commission for the State of Jammu and Srinagar and Kashmir,hereinafter referred to as 'the Commission ', had been consulted in accordance With its requirement. [874C] 1.3 The High Court had erred in holding, on the facts of the case, that the Commission, was consulted in regard to all the relevant matters, and that the selection was made by the Selection Committee which was "formed" by the Commission, and a member of the Commission was appointed its Chairman. [875F] 1.4 The High Court, erred in holding the Commission was not consulted in the manner prescribed by section 133(1)(b) of the Constitution and that the Selection Committee was not consulted on the suitability or suitability of the candidates for promotion. [878F] 1:5 The High Court failed to appreciate that the Commission is not consulted in regard, to the principles for be followed in the making promotions in question or on the basis of the suitability of the candidate for such appointments. [879B] 1.6 The High Court also erred in holding on the facts that the Commission has not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, and that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [880C] 1:6 The High court erred in holding in holding that it was applicable only to 'making promotions and transfers from one service to another, and on the suitability and suitability of candidates to such appointments, promotion or transfers. [882F] 1.:6 The High ' Court erred in observing that the Commission could not be consulted in the matter of making promotions and transfers. [888A] 1.7 The High Court has erred in holding so. [884B] 1:8 The State Government has in fact placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969, which makes it quite clear that the State Government consulted the Commission under section 133 of Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured themselves to take a stand to the contrary. [885C] 1.:9 The State Government at first framed rules on November 15, 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. "at its direction" and "at its directions" were complied with.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Bihar Legislative Council. He was declared elected to the Legislative Council. The petitioner challenged the validity of the election of the petitioner on the ground that the Committee had no power to make the declaration of the petitioner as a member of that House. The petitioner contended that the Committee was not competent to make the said declaration. The High Court held that the Committee could not be said to be competent to make a declaration of the Petitioner as a member. The petitioner 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. The petitioner then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of his election. The High court held that the petitioner was entitled to succeed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred on a citizen under article 19(1) of the Constitution. [696G H] (2) The privilege of preventing the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect of the proceedings directed by the Speaker to be expunged by the Chairman to be expunged must be such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature by law. [697C] (3) The privilege imposed on the Legislature by the latter part of article 194(3) on a House of Commons of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, at the commencement of the Constitution, i.e., January 26, 1950, is preserved despite the provisions of article 194 (3) on the said date.

The private college in the town of Behram pur, Ganjam District, Orissa was established by the name of Khallikote College. The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971, and a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the College and the Governor of the State. The College after the take over was administered as a Government College. The College was administered as an approved Reader by a Circular of that date addressed to the Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa, which appears to supersede the earlier circulars on the subject. The Government revised the pay scale of the Respondents as Reader on the basis of the recommendation of the Public Service Commission for consideration of their suitability for appointment as Readers in the Government College. In the meantime, the Government of Orissa issued a circular dated March 23, 1971, which was subsequently superseded by another circular dated April 23, 1971. The Respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said circular. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the said circular and directed the Gov ernment to take into account the experience of the Readers in the private college since, according to them, the necessary qualification was eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.S.). The High Court held that the condition of draw ing of Rs.600/ or more on the date of take over was arbitrary and discriminatory. The High court also directed the Gov arnment to consider the cases of the Respondents for appointment as Reader in the Government Colleges. The State Government filed a Special Leave Petition in this Court. The State of Orissa challenged the validity of this circular and the High Court allowed it. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in directing the Gov ernalment to take in account as experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the private College since, according t o him, the necessary qualifications were eight years experience of Class II,Orissa Education Serv ice(O.E.) and that since under the said terms of the take over they were drawing a salary of less than Rs.600/- on the date o take over, their names were not referred to the Public 778 Service Commission for considering their suitability for the post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The condition of draw of Rs.610/ or more, on the date on which the take over of the management of t he College was administered, is arbitrary and discriminatory and is violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [675G H] 1.2 The condition of drawing of Rs.60/ and Rs.600 / respectively on the date the take over were not applicable to the private college. [676G H] 2.1 The Government circular of March 23,1971, alone, was in controversy in the High court, as well as before us. The only differentia was, therefore, the salary drawn by the Readers on the date Of take over was a seriously grim issue. [696A] 2.2 The teaching experience of the Reader in Government service, for consideration for appointment as Professor is a seriously giri tions make a person eligible for appointment. [697B] 3.1 The teaching experience in a college and the fulfilment of other ' requisite qualifica tions make an person eligible for appoint ment as Reader. [698C] 3.2 The Government circular dated March 24, 1971, alone, is arbitrary, discriminatory and is discriminatory. [699D] 3.3 The Government circular was issued by the Government on March 23, 1972, which was later superseded by another Circular dated April 23. 1971.

The appellant was the son of Sarup, respondent 10. The appellant was the daughter of Sarup, who delivered the principal judgment of the Board, explained the earlier decision of the Privy Council in Narotam Chand 's case (1) and observed that the ancestral estate in which, under the Hindu law, a son acquires jointly with his father an interest by birth, must be confined to the property descending to the father from his male ancestor in the male line. Sir Shadi Lal, who delivered his principal judgment of this Court, explained the previous decision of the Full Bench in Narotham Chand 's Case (1) that the ancestral property in suit was ancestral property qua the appellant and so it allowed the appeal preferred by respondents 1 to 9 and dismissed the appellant 's suit. The appellant contended that the property inherited by him was ancestral property and so it dismissed the appellant suit. Held, that the property in suit is not ancestral property but that the appellant has no right to bring the present suit. The property inherited by a Hindu from his maternal grandfather is not ancestral qua his descendants under the customary law of the Punjab. It is only the ancestral property which comes from a maternal grandfather and it is governed by the custom of the Punjab that a son acquires a share by birth an interest jointly with him. The law of the customary law is that if the land comes to a person by descent from a lineal male ancestor in a male line, it should not be treated as ancestral property. The law is that the property which comes to a female by descent from an lineal male ancestor is ancestral property and that such property in the hands of a daughter can be given that description. The law does not say that the property acquired by a Hindu by descent from his maternal father is not ancestral. The law has to be interpreted in the light of the facts and circumstances of each case. The law in this regard is well settled. The law laid down by the Privy Council is that the law of the land in suit is the property in his hands ancestral property and the law has to apply. The law which has been followed by the community since 1895 is the law of succession is the property of the deceased. The law, therefore, does not apply and should present no obstacle in holding that the property held by a Hindu is ancestral property.

The appellants were charged under section 449 and section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted them under section 449 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 307 read read with section 149 of the Indian Indian Penal Code and for two years each under section 449. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the conviction of the appellants under section 449 read with section 109 of the Indian Evidence Act was not sustainable in law. Held, that the conviction under section 449 was not sustainable. The words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of Indian Penal Code but in section 457 of the Indian Code. The words used in section 449 are not intended to be used by the Legislature but also by the Legislature. The words 'in order to have committed the house trespass or house breaking by night are prescribed quite inde pendent of the question whether the offence "in orderto" has been actually committed or not. The words are not intended merely to be used in section 448 of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code but also in section 457. The words have to be used with the knowledge or knowledge of the person who caused the death. The words must be used with such knowledge or knowledge and under such circumstances that if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder. The words cannot be used with knowledge or knowledge. The words should be used with reference to the section and so, where the act is done by a number of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed an offence punishable under section 307 of the Indian. The words may be used with respect to the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment. The words of section 449 are intended to be utilised with the knowledge of the persons who do not use the dagger must in law be considered to have committed this offence of murder. It is quite clear that the words used in the section are intended to cover the commission of a offence punishable with death. The word 'in order' has to be used for the purpose of committing an offence punishable as if the act had been done by a person who had a particular intention or knowledge. If the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of offence punishable under Section 449 of the Code, the legal status that results is the commission. The words can be used with a knowledge or knowledge, and under such circumstance, each of them becomes punishable under section 452 of the Indian Police Penal Code.

Held, that the appellant 's right to succeed to the self acquired property of her father was not a mere declaration but was merely a declaration of the intention of the parties to the suit. The appellant 's claim to have discharged this initial onus in two ways, namely (1) by producing the Riwaj i am of the Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and (2) by adducing evidence showing that the collaterals were beyond the fourth degree and (v). that the appellant did not file any document to show that the collateral of one Harnam Singh was not a genuine or trustworthy document. The appellant was not entitled to succeed to her father 's ancestral propertie 'section The appellant was entitled to succeed in her father ' s ancestral propertiee 's self acquired property in preference to collaterals even though he was not within the fourth degree.

The appellant was the Managing Director of Messrs Bird and Co. Ltd., and of Messrs F. W. Heilgers and Co., Ltd., who were acting as Managing Agents of several Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. Das Gupta, J. was of the opinion that the different capacities of the executant were distinct matters for the purposes of section 5 and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. The appellant contended that the instrument in question was a power of attorney and that the document was a power to attorney and that therefore the instrument was liable to be taxed under the Act. Held, that the instrument is executed by one person, if he fills several capacities and the authority conferred is general, there would be distinct delegations in respect of every transaction entered into by him in his personal capacity. The fact that the donor of the power of attorney executes it in different capacities is not sufficient in my opinion to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be 855 stamped with the aggregate of stamp duty payable in respect of the transactions entered into by the donor in his personal capacities. The fact, however, that the donor is capable of performing whether in his individual capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executor or administrator is also comprised within the instrument and are not distinct matters to be dealt with as such so as to attract the operation of section 5. The fact of the case that the donor was capable of performing either of the two capacities is not enough to constitute the document one comprising distinct matter. The fact however, that he, as trustee, executor and so forth, is entitled to exercise all these powers in relation thereto. The fact is that the donor, of the power attorney, executed it in different capacity is not entitled to exercise any of these powers, the trust property having vested in him and in respect of all the matters in which he could act, the trust properties having vested in them and if that is the position, it is but logical that whatever acts the donor is incapable of performing whether the instrument is capable of performance whether in his representative or in his representatives capacity as trustee, administrator or administrator are also comprised within his instrument and are also comprised in the instrument and is not distinct matters. The fact therefore, that the document in question does not comprise distinct matters and therefore requires to be 854 stamped with the total stamp duty payable if Separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act within the meaning of section 5, and as, in the present case, the instrument in dispute is a power of Attorney, it would fall under article 48 (a) in whatever capacity it was executed, and there being only one category, there would not be any distinct matters within section 5.

The assessee was a Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two appeals, and the assessee was the Mahalaxmi Mill Ltd., in which the assessee had filed the appeals in the other three appeals. The Income tax Officer, in ascertaining the written down value, deducted depreciation which would have been allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and allowed the deduction of depreciation which would had been allowed if the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 had been in force in the past. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Income tax Tribunal, however, took a different view and held that the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was a deductible amount in computing the written down valuation. The High Court, however, allowed the appeals of the assessee. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the depreciation was allowable under the Bhavagar War Profits Act, 1949, and that the depreciation had been allowed to the assessee if it had been in existence and a claim had been made supported by prescribed particulars. Held, that the depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State before it became included in the Part B State was within the first portion of section 13(5) (b) of the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, the written down Value had to be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance allowed under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 irrespective of whether any difficulty had or has not arisen in a particular case in giving effect to the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, 1949, which require "all depreciation actually allowed" under any laws relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating to income Tax on profits of the business, to be taken into account in computing the income tax and the written down values under section 10(5) of the Indian Incometax tax Ordinance, 1948, were sufficient to express the intention that if the Income tax Act had in fact been in force, the depreciation that would have been allowed if proper claim had been making should be deducted in ascertaining the actual cost thereof under any laws, or rules of law relating to Income tax and supertax or any law related to tax on profit of business which was law of a Part A State. The words actually used are not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. The words 'any law relating To tax on profits or of business which is law of aPart B State, would also have been omitted and this part of the paragraph would have read as "all depreciation already allowed under any law or rules of any Part B State relating to income taxation and super tax on profits and of business." The words "or which would havebeen allowed if proper application had been made" in paragraph 3 of the Removal Order, 1949 were sufficient to indicate the intention that the depreciation should be allowed if proper claims had been made and substantiated, assuming the Indian Income taxes Act, 1922,. was in force in that past. The words used in paragraph 2 were apt and sufficient to express that if the income tax Act, 1961, which was not in force in any particular case in give effect to the provision of the Indian income tax Act,. 1922, would also be entitled to deduct the depreciation actually granted under any laws and rules of aPart A State relating to Income Tax and super tax and any law relating thereto, tax on profits tax and super Tax on profits or business.

The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground of delay. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the appellant did not strictly comply with the requirements of paras III, V and VI of the N.I. T. and the other documents referred to in para V. [623C] 1.2 The preconditions for eligibility to submit a tender for the contract are only the three conditions set out in para I of the N,I.T. and other details called for vide para 5(c) of N.I.,T. and that the documents referred to therein can be supplied at any time before the final award of the contract. [624C] 1:3. The preconditions are only the two conditions set out therein. They are those: (i) the pre conditions and (ii) the documents referred in the other paras can be supplied only at any time after the final award. The pre conditions are only for information and are such they could be met before consideration of the tenders. The more harmonious and practical way of construing the N. I.T. is by saying that before the tender books can be supplied, an intending ten der should satisfy the K.P.C. by supplying such of the documents called for in para V as are material in assessing the capabilities of the tenderers as well as their eligibility and simply because Mr. In this particular case, the lacuna in furnish ing the information has been set right subsequently by the tenderer before opening of the price documents, the Chief Engineer had 240 come to the conclusion that the firm had fulfilled all the prequalifying requirements and as such the tender of M.C.C. was found to be in order. [626D] 1.4 The preconditions and that all the documents referred t o in the other paragraphs can be supplied before the final Award of the contract can be supplied. [627E] 1.5 The preconditions of eligibility to submit tender forms are only the four conditions set out under para I. The pre condition and that all documents referred to under para I have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply of tender forms. [628G] 1.6 The preconditions in para I are not intended to verify the fulfilment of the three prequalifying conditions as well as that all the document referred to in the other para can be supplied by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. The only thing that is required is that the pre conditions are not intended for verifying the fulfilment of three prequalification requirements of para I. [629F] 1.7 The pre conditions and that all other documents referred ta para can be supply at any time during the final award and if a party comes to Court say that the rule is likely to be relax, the Court will decline relief. The appellant was a displaced person. He was a displaced and displaced person. The Custodian General of Evacuee Property issued a notice to the appellant under section 38(1) of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947, on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of the Ordinance. The appellant filed a revision petition before the Custodian General of East Punjab, Delhi, which was dismissed by the Additional Custodian General ofEast Punjab, Delhi. The appellant challenged the order of confirmation passed by the Additional Deputy Custodian General of the EastPunjab, Delhi, on the grounds that the order of confirmed against him was not a quasi judicial order and that the order was not a final and conclusive order. The appellant contended that the order passed by the Custodian General in such a pending application was not open to appeal or revision and it was specifically declared to be final and conclusive. The Custodian of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949 (XXVII of 1949) was replaced by the Central Ordinance No. (3) Notwithstanding the repeal by this Ordinance of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1949, or of any corresponding law, anything done or any action taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under the Ordinance shall be deemed to have been done or taken in the exercise of the powers conferred by or in the exercise Of the powers conferred under or under this Act as if this Ordinance were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action was taken. The appellant also contended that the application for confirmation pending on the date when the Central Act XXXI of 1950 came into force and superseded the earlier legislation in this behalf had to be disposed of in accordance with sections 5 A and 5 B of the East East Punjab Act XXXI of 1947, as amended in 1948; that the order dated 20th March, 1952, was not open for appeal or revision; that the application of the appellant for confirmation pending in the High Court was not open, and was thus not competent to appeal or revisions and it was not open under the provisions of section 27 of the Act. Held, that the application made by the appellant in 1948 and which remained pending until Act XXXI of 1949 came into force, had to be dealt with and disposed of under the Act and the order of the Additional Custodian in such a case was not open. The application for confirmation of the order of confirm passed in 1952 was not open as it was not specifically declared to have been passed in 1952. The application of the respondent for confirmation pending at the date when Central Act XXXIof 1950 came into operation had to be dismissed in accordance with section 40(4) of the Act and it was clearly declared to be a final and binding order. The application was one made long prior to the time when the office of the Custodian General was set up and he was clothed with powers of revision vested in the Custodian General under section 27 of that Act. The application under section 27 was not open and became final and conclusive and was therefore, not competent to file an appeal or revision. The application filed by the appellant for confirming the order of confirming was not open by appeal or revision but became final and binding.

The appellant company was a registered company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and its employees were employed in the establishment of the respondent company. The respondent company claimed bonus for the relevant four years. The Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act." The Tribunal held that the claim for bonus for the years 1965 and 1969 was founded on tradition or custom or 596 condition of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short chits of the workmen "s plea in the words of reference, to go into a different claim. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the claim was founded on custom or usage or custom or arrangement between the employers and employees, creating a term of employment for payment of Puja bonus or that even where no express agreement can be inferred, it may be payable as a customary bonus, and that the bonus was customary and traditional bonus, and so, the Bonus Act did not apply by reason of its provisions either as to exclusion or exemption to raise a dispute with regard to bonus based on profit bonus or does the Bonus Act speak on the topic of bonus. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The subject matter of the dispute, as referred by the Government, deals with bonus based on custom or condition of service. The object of the Act and its scheme, it is not possible to accept the construction suggested on behalf of respondent that before the Arbitration Board no case of customary or traditional bonus was urged for the year 1965 and so, this Court took the view that so long as that award stood, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be subversive of the rule of res judicata. [605 E] 1.2 The question of profit may or may not arise at all and such customary and traditional Bonus will depend on the content and terms of that custom or the tradition on which the claim for Bonus is made. The object and reasons of the Bonus Act indicate that the subject matter of dispute, as defined in the Act, is 'the question of payment of bonus based on profits to employees employed in establishments '. The object is not to retain the right to claim bonus by way of industrial adjudication for those who are either excluded or exempted from the Act, unless it finds statutory expression in the provisions of that Act ? [605 G] 1.3 The question of bonus will depend on whether the workmen are either excluded and not excluded from claiming bonus under the or such other Act is not correct. [606 F] 1.4 The question of deduction of the bonus from the flank in that manner, does not arise at any stage and such customary or traditional Bonus will decide the question of profit. [607 G] 1:5 The question of profits will depend on what the claim for the bonus is made. If, however, Parliament wanted to retain the rights to claim bonus through industrial adjudication for these employees, it would have made an express 612 saving provision to that effect as it has done for employees in Coal Mines. The object, of the Act, and its scheme is not to allow an invasion from the flend in that manner. [608 G] 1.:6 The Tribunal was called upon by the terms of reference, and so long as the award stood, it would be subversive of that rule of resjudicata. The Board enquired into one cause of action based on profit motive bonus.

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana and were confirmed in the Superior Judicial Services of Punjab andHaryana and Haryana and the petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Superior judicial services of the State. The petitioners were appointed in the Superior Administrative Service of Punjab, before December 31, 1976. The petitioners contended that the rules governing seniority of direct recruits and promotees appointed to the Higher Judicial Service of the State were bad because the Governor of Haryana amended rule 12 by the Haryana First Amendment Rules 1972 providing that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation) and that after every two promotees are confirmed one direct recruit has to be confirmed and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. The High Court rejected the contention of the petitioners and held that the rules of the Superior Judicial service were not applicable to the petitioners. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the amended rule 12. The High court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners challenged the validity of amended rule 12 and the power conferred upon the Governor by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution. The petitioners also challenged the validity and correctness of the decision of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule of rotation at the time of confirmation of the members appointed or promoted to the Superior judicial Service of Punjab is to be determined by a length of continuous Service (in a service irrespective of date of confirmation). It may be recalled that in the High Courts of Punjab and HARYANA, the quota rule prescribed by rule 8 justifies, without more, its extension at the time when every two promotees were confirmed one direct recruits has to be confirm and until that was done, promotees can be confirmed even though vacancies are available in their quota in that particular year. [422C D] 2. The High Courts of Haryana and Haryana have to decide in those cases the narrow question as to whether, on a true interpretation of rules 8 and 12 of the Superior judicial service Rules of Punjab and Chandigarh, the quota Rule prescribed by rule 9 justifies, without applying the rule or rotation and in the light of the directions given by us in the Punjab Writ Petition, in so far as it confers the power of confirmation on the Governor, to frame rules regulating the recruitment 1054 and service conditions of judicial officers of the State, without applying rule or rotation. [423C D] 3. The High courts of Punjab and Punjab have to decide whether the Governor in the exercise of power conferred by the proviso has the power to frame rules regarding seniority of judicial officers in the judicial service of the State and not in the High court. [424C D] 4. The High 'Court will re draw the inter se seniority (i) of such of the petitioners, respondents and others who were appointed to a post in service irrespective of their date of confirmation, without applying Rule or rotation and (ii) of such Of the petitioners, Respondents and others who are appointed to a posts in the service on or after December 31,1976 in accordance with the amended rule, 12. 3 therein by the application of the aforesaid principles and in accordance with law. [425E F] 5. The High "Court will re drawn the inter se Seniority (i)of such of the petitioner and respondents as were promoted or appointed to the superior Judicial Service prior to December 31, 1977, on the basis of the respective dates of confirmation, with reference to the dates of confirmation. [426C D] 6.

The Tribunal, by its order dated October 6, 1989, directed the State Government not to organise any Class or classes of posts in a civil service of, or any class or class of civil posts in the State. It was contended on behalf of the respondents Nos. 1 to 3 that the State Government had no power to organise any classes or classes of Civil posts under the state. The Tribunal held that the State had no power under proviso to paragraph 3(1) of the Order to organise any category of posts in any department, when more than one cadre in respect of such category exists in each department; and that the creation of a separate cadre in respect o f any category of post in any department is illegal, contrary to order issued in G.O.Ms. No. dated October 20, 1975. The Tribunal also held that the creation was illegal, contrary t o order issued in R.P., No. 2404 of 1987. The State Government filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed the appeal. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for Adilabad and Warangal Divisions is illegal, in contravention of order issued in GO.Ms.No. dated October 5, 1975. No. Dr. No. N.N.N. N. N. Rao, J. (as he then was) has been given power under proviso by an order to require the State Government whenever he considers it expedient so to do to have the power under paragraph 3(2) before the expiry of the period of twelve months prescribed in sub paragraph (1) of para graph 3. No. In exercise of the power under proviso, the President may require the State Govt. to so organise any class of posts in the civil services of and class or classes or classes thereof for such part of the State as may be specified by the State Government, in respect of that category in such department for such part or class or classes thereof as may be prescribed. No. The power given to the State Govt., in subparagraph (7) of paragraph 3 of the Order is only to organise a separate cadre, in respect o any category ofposts in any department when more than two cadre in respect thereof exists in each Department. [723C D] 2. The creation and maintaining separate identity of Junior Assistants for Adilpur and Warangal Division is illegal, void, contrary to the order issued in the G.O.,Ms. No, dated October 20. 1975. [724E] 3. The creation or maintaining separate identity in respect of any category of civil posts is illegal, arbitrary, contrary to law and contrary to order passed in G. O.Ms. Nos. dated October 10, 1975. [824F] 4. The creation, maintaining separate identity, in respect to any category of persons in any department cannot be said to be illegal, contrary, to order issued by the State Govt in accordance with para 3(1). [824B C] 5. The creation is only for the purpose of administrative convenience, not for the purpose o f recruitment, seniority or promotion etc., as the case may be. No.

The appellant was the auction purchaser of the mortgaged property. The appellant contended that he was subrogated to the position of the Bank, that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding on the defendants, that he was the auctionpurchaser in execution of that mortgage decree and that the Patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage thus came to an end and he was entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decree passed by the High Court dismissing the plaintiff ' s suit was binding and operative against the appellant and that the decree was binding on him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the mortgagor in possession had the power to lease the mortgaged property in the usual course of management but was not competent to grant a lease unusual terms or authorise the use of land in a manner, or for a purpose, different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage. [1192A B] (2) The High court was in error of holding that the plaintiff 'S suit was not maintainable against the appellant. [1193C] (3) The High ' Court was in wrong in holding that a mortgagor was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing took place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. Mukherjee J. had occasion to consider this very case in Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar(1) and he cited it in support of the proposition that a mortgagor is not restricted in his management by making a lease but was not entitled to disturb the graves of those who had been: buried the land while the mortgagor had continued to hold it.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in question. The appellants filed a suit for a decree for possession of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants challenged the decree on the ground that the execution was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the objection as regards the executability of the decree pleaded by the judgment debtors was barred by the principles of res judicata and further on July 23, 1960 for default of the judgment debtors. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to the executability and further the bar of section 4(c) are not applicable to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor. [916G H] 2. The words of section 4 (d) are wide enough to cover the claims made against the estates which have vested in the State and no others. [917G H] 3. The words used in section 4(e) are wide and wide enough to include the claims made by the judgment debtor. [ 917G H; 917A] 4. The words "no suit shall lie in any Civil Court for the recovery of any money due from such proprietor (proprietor whose estate has vested in the Government) or tenure holder the payment of which is secured by a mortgage of, or is a charge on, such estate or tenure and all suits and proceedings for the recovery thereof any such money which may be pending on the date of vesting shall be dropped". [917B] 5. The words 'no suit shall be instituted in any Civil court ' for the recovery or of any such money as may be pending before the date of the vesting. The words are wide enough and wide enough. They are wide enough. It is difficult to confine the application of section 4 to execution proceedings. [918G] 6. The object of the Act is to provide for the transference to the State of the interests of the proprietors and tenure holders in land and of the mortgagees and lessees of such interests. [919A] 7. The object is to provide that on and from the date of commencement of the Act all lands used for agriculture or horticultural purposes which were in khas possession of an intermediary on the date a vesting (including certain classes of land specified in that section) shall subject to the provisions of sections 7A and B be deemed to be settled by the State with such intermediary and he shall be entitled to retain possession thereof and hold them as a raiyat under the State having occupancy rights in respect of such lands, subject to the payment of such fair and equitable rent as may be determined by the Collector in the prescribed manner. [920B] 8. The object sought to achieve is to provide a transference to a State of the interest of the proprietor and tenure holders. [921B] 920A] 920B] 921A. The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) Act, 1974 by the Central Government. The grounds of detention were served on him. The appellant was arrested on the ground that he was not a friend of the detenu and because of his professional experience he liked to help the detenu. The Advisory Board rejected the appellant 's request for assistance of a friend at the hearing and for the reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit the request was turned down. The appellant challenged the order of detention before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the detaining authority was not a man of ordinary prudence and that the detaining authorities were not justified in refusing to permit the appellant to represent the case of the detenu. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority or the Government should have the facility of appearing before the Advisory Board with the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser. Regard must be had to the substance and not to the form since, particularly in matters like the proceedings of Advisory Boards, whosoever assist or advises on facts of law must be deemed to be in the position of a legal advisers. Regard must also be had to facts of law. Regard must, be had to a substance and not the form since. especially in matters like those proceedings like the proceedings in Advisory Boards, whatever assist or adv advise on facts of the case must be deemed not to be in position of a Legal Practitioner. Regard must always be had to that substance and not a particular form. [792D] 2. The detaining authorities or the Government must have the facility for appearing before the Board through a legal practitioner. Regard must have to the substance or not to the forms since, especially in matters such like the proceedings like the proceeding of Advisory Boards etc., whosoever assist oradvises on facts. [793A] 3. The detaining Authority or the Government may take the aid of legal adviser in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. But that facility should be denied to the detenu. Regard must to the substance & not to the Form since, particularly, in matters like this the proceedings of the Advisory Board, whosoever assists or advises may appear before the Board with the help of a legal Practitioner or a legal practitioner, may assist or advise on facts of legal advisers on facts of laws must be deemed so to be in that position of a lawyer. Regard must therefore be had to, the substance and/or not to the substance. [794B] 4. The detaining Board has, of course, to be careful in permitting assistance of a lawyer but that facility should not be denied to detenu. [795C] 5. The refusal by the Advisory Board to permit the detenu to be represented by a legal practitioner is bad and continued detention of the appellant became vitiated. [796D] 6. The refusal of such assistance to the detenu was not justified. [797A] 792A] 8. The refusal to permit the petitioner to be represented through a legal Practitioner was bad and continued.

The appellants were owners of certain lands in the State of West Bengal. The appellants were the owners of certain land in the State. The appellants claimed that the lands were requisitioned and acquired by the Government of India on September 30, 1946, and that the property in the goods passed to the Government of india on September 30. 1946. The Government of India issued a notice under r. 75 A (2) of the Rules to the appellants to show cause why the lands should not be acquired. The appellants contended that the notice was not properly served and that the notice did not apply , to the case, and that as the notices were served on the appellants, they were not served on September 30; 1946, under r. 76 A (2), of the Rules, the property in them did not pass on September 30 1946, and the property in their possession was not passed on September 30,. 1946. Held, that the notice of acquisition in this case was not properly issued and that the appellants were not served with the notices of acquisition in the manner provided in r. 75A (2) and therefore there was no acquisition following on the service of the notices in this case. The notice of acquisition was not properly serving and reasonable way of service in the matter of notices of acquisition, for in substance the two services were effected exactly in the same manner on the principal officer of the mills, which 'in one case were in possession of the goods and in other were owners of the goods. The service of the notice in this case is also good service in the case of notices of acquisitions, for in the case Of notices of acquisition there was a schedule attached and that the real owners were being addressed &a managing agents of particular mills. The service on the owners of the mills was effective on the mills as owners for the purpose of r. 75 B (2) was that the notice must be brought to the knowledge of the person whose interests are being affected by it and that this was not done in this case, for neither the holders of the pucca delivery orders nor the mills were apprised of the orders of requisition on September 30., 1946, for the purposes of r. 76A (2). The service of notice in this context was also good service and reasonable way was also not in dispute. The service was also effective on the mill as owners for this purpose of rs. 75 A(2) of The Rules. The service in this case of notices in this context is also good. The service is also good for the purpose for which requisition was made. The service must be in accordance with r. 75 C (2) is that provided in 0. XXIX, r. 2 in the case o orders of requisition so in the caseof notices of acquisition the property in those cases had not passed on the same day one after the other and were substantially the same. The service should also contain that the managing agents were being addressed anda managing agents were also addressed &a Managing agents of particular Mills. The service were also effected exactly in this manner on theprincipal officer of the Mills, which 'In one case were the owners and in other was owners of the property. The service notices of acquisition were also served on the same date one after the others and were substantially identical. The service by the appellants in this case on the managing agents of the mills is effective on the basis of the service of notice on them. The service to the appellants in the case was also effective in the matter o r. 75 D (2) would apply and the property was in the goods passing to the Government. The service, of the notices of acquisitions in this case by the mills was also effective service on the mills. The appellants in this appeal were not served in the manner prescribed in r. 2 of 0. XX X, r.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The assessee was a private Limited Company. It was a Private Ltd. Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. The assessee claimed that it was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken up for hearing. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserve. The High Court held that the assessee was a reserve, and should be excluded in its capital. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the said amount being a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice was a provision and not a reserve. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The distinction between a provision and a reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a reserve and a reserve. "The distinction is between provision and a Reserve. The distinction is between a provision. The distinction must be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L. account and the balance sheet. [912D] 2. The words "the reserve" and "the balance sheet" are not conclusive. The words used in the balance sheet by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they are made are conclusive. [913E] 3. The words 'the reserve" are not exhaustive. The words are not exhaustive and are not exhaustive, but are merely illustrative. The words have to be construed in the context in which they are used in the context of the business. [914F] 4. The words in the balance sheets by way of deduction from the assets are conclusive. The word ' reserve' is not used in the sense in which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. The words cannot be construed in isolation. [915F] 5. The words must be construed in their ordinary sense. The words should be construed in its ordinary sense. [916F] 6. The words of the statute must be construed as having been used in the ordinary sense of the words used in it. [917F] 7. The words employed in the balancesheet by way ofeduction from the assets by which they are rep resented are conclusive. They are not exhaustive but are merely indicative. The words may be construed in a manner which would lead to the conclusion that the provision made by the assessee in its books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23A) was indeed a provision and cannot be construed as a reserve. [918F] 8. The words can be construed as including the words 'the reserves ' in appropriation of profits, the assets by way of deducted from the assets. [919F] 9. The words, 'the reserve ' in appropriation ' are generally shown in the balance Sheet by way of deduct from the assets, the assets and the balance sheets. [920F] 10. The words do not mean 'the reserve'. [919G] 11. The words relate to the anticipated liability. The words include the reserve. The words also relate to the contingency of the liability of tax. [921F] 12. The words refer to the contingency and reserve funds. The words indicate that the provision is a charge against the profits to be taken into consideration against gross receipts. [922F] 13. The words apply to the contingency. [923F] 14. The words mean 'the reserves' and 'the balance sheet. The words therefore refer to the contingencies and reserves. The words need not be construed in any manner. [924F] 15. The words were not exhaustive. [926G] 16.

The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts on the basis of the competitive examinations and those that were recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Service Commission and the Union Public Service Commissions, the petitioners were absorbed into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I. The petitioners were appointed as temporary Assistant Engineers on the basis that they were recruited on the basis Of the competitive examinations. The Union Public Service commission, in its meeting held on September 17, 1965, decided to the effect that the Officers so absorbed into the Iona wait by giving weightage of half of the length of continuous service as temporary Assistant Officers subject to the maximum of five years. The Union of India, in its resolution dated September 17,1965, decided to give weightage of half the length of service as temporaryAssistant Officers subject to maximum of five year. The Union Government, in its letter dated September 17. 1965, informed the petitioners that six of them would be absorbed into the services of the Indian Railway Services of Engineers Class 1, every year, and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis thereof. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said resolution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions of the petitioners. The petitioners have filed these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners were absorbed in the Indian Railway service of Engineers Class II on the basis their length of continuous services, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the Iona waiting by the Union Public Services Commission, were placed above those appointed on the basis o the results of the competitive examination. [912G H] 1.2 The petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the reservation of half the total length of continuous Service subject to a maximum of fiveyears, because of the history, origin, and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed however as to the validity of this given weightage of half in the length of the service subject to a minimum of five years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. [913C] 1.3 The petitioners were recruited by the Union of India and the Railway Board as respondents. They were aware that six of the petitioners, would be absorbed in the Iona Waheeda 's case (supra). [913E] 1.4 The petitioners were selected by the Union Government on the basis on the results of competitive examinations and were appointed to permanent posts on the Iore wait by the Union. The petitioners, therefore, were not entitled for the benefit of reservation of half of their length of service. [914F] 1.5 The petitioners were entitled to the benefits of reservation of one half of the total length in service subject to the minimum of five year, because of their being questioned elsewhere, particularly in the field of the right to equality in matters relating to employment on appointment in service. [813F] 1:6 The petitioners were also entitled to the same relief and this time by the Temporary Assistant Officers subject, to the maximum limit of five years and they were appointed to Temporary posts subject to the Maximum of five years in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. [915F] 1.:6 The petitioners, in the instant case, were appointed to the temporary posts on temporary basis on the basis the results of their competitive examinations and the various tests laid down by this Court in Katyani Dayal 's case. The petitioners are entitled to the relief of equality in the matter relating to employment in service. The petitioners cannot claim the benefit of equality in matters pertaining to employment on appointments in service.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 9 and 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, and was convicted by the Special Court under section 11 of the Ordinance. The Special Court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 11 and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that section 5 (1) of the Saurashtra Act, with which we are now concerned, imposes a duty on the State Government to classify offences or classes of offences or classes thereof, and that the delegation of such power to the executive Government was beyond the competence of a legislature and was void under article 13. The appellant contended that section 5(1) of that Act was ultra vires and void under article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that section 5 of the Saurashtra ordinance, with which the Special Courts Act, 1949, was enacted, was not ultra vires and the notification issued thereunder was not ultra est. The notification issued by the State of West Bengal under section 5(l) of the Ordinance was not ultra rites. The notification under section 5 (l) of that Ordinance was not a valid notification and was, therefore, void under article 19 of the Constitution and was void. The notification was, therefore invalid. The notification dated May 5, 1949, issued by the Government of West Bengal in that case was, therefore valid. The notification in that case did not contravene article 14 of The Constitution. The notification, therefore, was not invalid. The Notification issued by the Central Government under section 5 of that Ordinance, was, therefore not invalid. [412 E F] The notification issued under section 5 was, therefore void under article 15 of the Constitution, and was void as offending against the provisions of article 13. [413 F] The Notification issued under section 6 of the Saurashtra Special Courts Act in that case, was, however, different from the notification issued by a State Government under section 6. The notification did not contravene the provisions of the equal protection clause of the our Constitution. The Notification was, therefore illegal. The notification which was issued under section 4 of the Saurashtra Regulation, was not valid. The Notification dated May 5. 1949, issued under section 11 was, therefore bad.

The appellant Corporation was a State Road Transport Corporation created under a State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to the Transport Corporation Act of 1950 ( 'Corporation Act ' for short) is in appeal by special leave. The employer Corporation contended that the employees were probationers and the order of discharge in every case was on account of unsatisfactory service. The Labour Court held that termination of services was bad, but did not include (a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or (b) retirement of the workmen on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or (c) termination of the service of a workman on the ground of continued ill health. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that termination was bad, and the order was on account for unsatisfactory service. On appeal, the High Court held that the termination was bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour Court. The High Court held: (i) that the termination of the services of a probationer was bad and accordingly it upheld the award of the Labour court. (ii) that the order of retrenchment was bad and the award of reinstatement was upheld. (iii) that the retrenchment was bad. (iv) that the provisions of section 25F of the , were not applicable to the employees of the Corporation. (v) that the employees had been terminated on the ground that they were probationers. (vi) that the orders of discharge in each case were on account of unsuitability and it was not a case of retrenchment. (vii) that the expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of the employment of a probationer by an act of the employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking was to be treated as 'retrenchment for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. The High court, in appeal, held that the order was bad and hence it upheld the order of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'retretrenchment ' has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word; it means the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever is no more good law and in fact the decision of the full Bench of Kerala High Court in L. Sundara Money 's case was approved in the aforementioned three cases. Once the conclusion is reached that retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the covers every case of termination of service except those not expressly included in section 25F or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF, the termination of service of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [793A B] 1.2 The decision in Sundara Money, Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Bharat Electronics Ltd., was not at all inconsistent with the decision of this Court in L Sundara Money.s case. [794C] 1.3 The decision in L. Chandara Money 'S case was not at least required to be a precedent for the purpose of section 25FF of the , and not for the purpose for notice, compensation, etc. [795C] 1:4. The decision in Chandara Money, was not at any inconsistent with the decisions of the full bench of Kerala High court in L. Chandra Kumar vs Bharat Electronics, [1971] 1 SCR 591, referred to. 1.4 The decision in the Sundara Money was not at All inconsistent with the view expressed by the Bombay High Court in Hariprasad Shukla 's case.

The question raised in these two appeals is directed against the question:The assessee South Eastern Railway disposing of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assessee's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee then applied to the High Court at Calcutta for revision of the order of the Board of Revenue, West Bengal. The High Court dismissed the revision application on the basis that the disposal was a regular phenomenon of the carriage of goods by the Railway. The assessee appealed to this Court. The question for consideration in these appeals is whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Controller of Stores, Eastern Railways was a "dealer". The High Court held that the activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage. It was contended on behalf of the assessee that the activity was adjunti cial to the principal activities of the carriage o f goods by the railway. It was also contended on behalf o the assessee that unclaimed and uncon nected goods came into possession of the assessee but not as a result of any activity of purchase or of manufacture for sale. It was further contended on behalf Of the assessee that since the goods were not sold under the Act and that therefore a sale of goods took place. The High court held that the assessee was a " dealer" for the purpose of as sessment under the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1941 and that therefore he fell within the ambit of the Act and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. The High ' Court held that a sale of Goods took place. It was held that the mere sale of goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment. The High Curt held that the sale of goods was involved in the auction held by the assessee and that therefore an sale of goods taken place. The assessee was entitled to his costs in each case. The assessee filed an application before the High Court for revision of its order. The High, Court dismissed the application on merits. The assessee thereafter applied for revision of his order. The assessee applied for revision before the Board of revenue, West Bengal and simi lar contentions were raised before the High court at Calcutta. The High Judge dismissed the revision petition on the ground of delay. The assessee challenged the order of High Court in the High Court. The High. Court held that there was no sale of goods by a Railway and that therefore no sale of Goods was involved in this case. The High Courts held that the transaction did not indicate the fact that the Railway was carrying on the business as a " dealer liable to tax under the Act. It was not disputed that the activity carried on by the assessee was adjun cial to that of the carriage or of manufacture or sale for sale. The HighCourt held that the activities of the Railway were adjunctive and ancillary to its business as carrier of the goods. The High curt held that a transfer of property was involved in a auction held by a Railway. It was, therefore, not a "dealer " within the meaning of the Act, and that the assessee had not been a "dealer." The High Court also held that the sales effected by the assessee were sales under the Act, but that the assessee did not indicate any that the Railway did not carry on business as an "dealer" for the 781 purposes of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941, and that consequently the assessee was not a " dealer".
