The appellants were appointed as ministerial staff in the ministerial service of the State of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. The State of Gujarat was formed in the year 1956. The State Government of Gujarat was constituted in the year 1957. The State was constituted in 1956. The appellants were appointed in the ministerial cadre of the Secretariat of the State. The State 'regularised the service of the appellants in the Secretariat of Saurashtra and Kutch. The State made a representation to the State Government for treating their services as servants of the "Secretariat cadre" and to forbear from enforcing their order treating the persons whose names were specified in the annexure to the order as servants of that "Secret Secretariat cadre". The State Government rejected the representation and directed the State Government to treat their services as "illegal, void and of no effect" and to restrain from enforcing its order treating the appellants as servants of their "Secretaries cadre". The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States was not open to objection. HELD : (1) The State of Bombay was competent to transfer and did transfer the appellants to perform service in connection with the affairs of the former Gujarat State and that the State of Kutch was competent to do so. [446C] (2) The State Government was competent to make a final decision, it was not open for the State Government either to transfer officers from the Districts and to post and assign them duties in the Secretariat or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the Secretariat performing ministerial duties. [447C] (3) The State was competent to exercise its power under article 309 of the Constitution to transfer the appellants from the districts and to post them in the Secretariat. [448B] (4) The State had no authority to transfer the former Saurashtra or Kutch States. [449C] (5) The State could not take away the statutory right vested in the personnel of the former Kutch and Kutch State which they acquired under the , to hold posts in the 'new State which were equivalent and on terms not== Nomadica geous to those they were already entitled except with the previous approval of the Central Government. [445C] (6) The State 's right to be absorbed in equivalent posts in the Secretariat cannot be challenged, and that because they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts they will not be deprived of their statutory right under section 115(7) proviso. [456D] (7) The State is competent to transfer the appellant to perform service on account of the affairs of another State and were allotted to serve in connection with that affairs of another state. [457C] (8) The State has no authority to make a decision to transfer the employees from the districts or to fix them their pay and emoluments in the Secretariat and on terms which were not, unless the previous approval was obtained, disadvantageous. [458E] (8)(a) The State can make a final order, that is, before embarking on varying the conditions of service, the State Governments should obtain the concurrence of the Central government. [455E] (9) The State cannot take away the legal right vested in it in the personnel and the ministerial staff. 138 (b) The State, in the absence of determination of equivalent posts under the orders of the Central Govt., the State of Bombay, was competent to issue the concurrence of Central Government.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were dealers in cotton and sold them in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The petitioners in these petitions were dealers who were registered dealers in cotton. The petitioners were dealers in goods which were sold in the course for inter State trade and commerce. The goods were sold in their course for inter state trade or commerce and the tax was also levied at the same rate and therefore the tax was collected at more than one stage. The petitioners contended that the tax was levied on the purchase of goods which were purchased not later than six months after the close of the year to a registered dealer, but on sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay tax under section 5(2)(a)(vi) or a refund under section 12 of the Act. The petitioners also contended that the sales tax was levied at the rate of one rupee as the State Government had no power to levy tax on the purchase or sale inside the State of any declared goods. The petitioners further contended that the levy of tax was illegal as the tax was not levied at more than six naye paise in a rupee as the tax could be collected only at one stage and that the tax could not be said to be higher in the case of imported goods. The High Court rejected the contentions. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The tax is at the same rates and therefore the Tax cannot be said to have been levied at morethan one stage. [776C] 2. The tax can be collected only when the goods are sold in the State and the stage of sale is also the sale of such declared goods by the first dealer liable to tax. [775D] 3. The tax cannot be said either to be higher or higher in the nature of tax. [771E] 4. The tax has to be levied only at one point and that stage shall be (i) in the case where goods are sold by the last dealers liable to pay the tax, the stage of purchase is the sale of the goods by the next dealer liable to be paid the tax. [761B] 5. The tax levied is at the higher rate and therefore it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to pay sales tax, must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund, at a later stage. [772A] 6. The tax was levied, whether on sale or purchase inside the State, the stage is purchase by the last purchaser liable to pay to the tax. It is said that the tax can be levied only on the first purchaser. [773C] 7. The tax, therefore, cannot be said at more than two times. [774A] 8. The tax could be levied only when the sale or purchase outside the State is effected by the last person liable to pay it. [775B] 9. The tax may be collected only on one occasion and that stage is the sale or sale of such imported goods by the subsequent last dealer liable. [776B] 10. The tax payable under section 5 (2)(a) (vi) of the Act is also at the same higher rate and it is also levied at more times. [736C] 11. The tax must be levied at one stage. In the case of sales tax, the tax is also levied on the first purchase in the case o sale by the last assessee liable to pay Tax.

The respondent, who was defendant No. 1 in a mortgage suit, filed a suit against the present respondent for enforcement of a mortgage, against the present appellant, who was the defendant No. 2, and for enforcement of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. The High court held that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and that the mortgage was scaled down by the High Court in favour of defendants 2 to 7 only and the amended decree directs that the said defendants do pay into court the sum of Rs. 1,05,000 and odd and it is on payment of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 2 to7. The High ' Court also held that the decree contains no such clear directions but reading the decree as a whole and having regard to the actual decision in the case, this must be taken to be its plain implica tions. The High Curt also held that as no application had been made on behalf of defendant No.1, the proposal, which seems to have been accepted by the Receivers, was that the amount payable by him under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 47 and 297 Order 21, rule 2, Civil Procedure Code, praying that as the amount thus deposited together with the payments already made completely wiped off the amount due under the decree as scaled down, the decree might be scaled down in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The High, Court also held, that the decree contained no such clear direction but reading the judgment as a whole, it was not possible for the defendant No, 1 and that by defendants 2, to 7 separately and having regard t o the actual decision of the case, it is not possible for them to pay the amount directed by defendants 2 t o 7. The High Courts, however, allowed the application of defendant No, 2 to 7 and the amended plaint directing that the said respondents do pay into the court the sum directed to be deposited by them proceeds clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debts were one and indivisible. The HighCourt also held that in case they did not pay this amount, the whole of the mortgaged property including their interest would be sold for the entirety of the mortgage amount for which defendant No.2, in substance, was entitled to avail himself of the benefit of a decree which had been scaled down. The High "Court also held, on appeal, that the mortgage amount was scaled up by the High court in favour of defendant No., 2 only and the amendment directed that the said respondent do pay into Court the sum of 1,051,000 and thereafter it is on the payment of the said amount that redemption would be allowed of the mortgaged properties even on payment of certain specified amounts by defendants 2 and 7. The appellants ' appeal to this Court was dismissed by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the decree containing no such clear Direction was not only having been scaled up but reading the order as a whole. [419D] 1.2 The High Court, in our opinion, was right in setting aside the decree. [420B] 1.3 The High Court has not disturbed the view taken by the District Judge. [421B] 1:4 The High Court by allowing the application of the respondent No. 2 to 7 allowed the application. [422C] 1.5 The High Court also agreed with this view. [423D] 1:6 The High Court is right in setting the decree as it is not permissible for the defendant no. 1 and that the view taken in the case was right and should not have been disturbed.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the premises in question under the first defendant, filed a suit in the City Civil Court for a declaration that the first plaintiff was a tenant of the premises and that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful subtenants of the first plaintiff and were entitled to possession, use and occupation of the premises as subtenants thereof. The City Civil Court dismissed the suit on the ground that there bad been no lawful subletting, by the first plaintiff of the premises to the second and fourth plaintiffs as the provisions of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. ") were not applicable to the suit. The City civil Court dismissed the plaintiffs ' suit on the grounds that there bad be no lawful subletting by the first defendant to the second, and that the suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant because the defendants of this suit did not admit that the plaintiffs were the tenants in the premises in dispute. The City District Court dismissed the appeal. The High Court dismissed the appellants ' appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit in the city Civil Court was not one in between a landlord, and a tenant, because the relationship of landlord and tenant existed between the parties, and that there was no lawful subletting between the parties to that suit. Held, that the suit filed by the appellants in the City civil Court was one between a tenant and a tenant and that there had been a lawful subletting by them to the second. The City Court correctly decided that the suit could not be said to be one between a landlords and a tenant. The City Judge correctly decided that it had jurisdiction to entertain and try any suit relating to possession of the premises.

The appellant was appointed as the managing director of the Company by the will of Dadoba. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his business to the Company. On July 8, 1955, the appellant was appointed the managing director to take over the business. On July 9, 1955, a private company was incorporated under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company. The appellant was appointed a managing director of a private company. On July 10, 1955, an appointment by a director of another person as the managing Director was made by a director to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment, was not to be included within the word "assignment". The appellant was, however, appointed as the Managing director of the company by the will. On July 11, 1955, he was appointed as managing director of that company. On August 12, 1955, another director of the appellant was nominated as the managing directors. On August 13, 1955, when the appellant was in the management of the business of the company, the appellant became the managing director. On August 14, 1955, on the basis of the said appointment, the appellant took over the business of that company and appointed the appellant Govind as the managing managing director. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that the appointment of the appellant by the will was void. The appellant contended that the appointment was void, and that the appointment by a Director to the office of the managing director was void under the section. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appointment made by the appellant was void under section 312 of the new Act. On appeal to this Court, HELD: The section does not prohibit an appointment by the director of his successor by a director, but it does not prohibit the appointment of his successor. It does not prohibit a director by a director who has been appointed otherwise than by the company in a general meeting, the shareholders have nothing to do with his appointment. The rule of construction on which the High Court relied in arriving at the conclusion that the section is intended to render void a transfer of his office by a director for the purpose of section 312 of that Act, is a consolidating Act, it must be deemed to have continued the policy of the earlier Act and, therefore, for the purpose Of section 312 of new Act, an "assignment" must include an "appointment". [341C] The rule of interpretation on which the section is based is that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of the section would have included the subject matter of the proviso.

The appellants were tenants in the premises in question. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Shop. The Trial Court held that the appellants were liable to be evicted for WITHIN ful subletting under the provisions of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960 (hereinafter referred to as "the said Rent Act"). The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal. The appellants then preferred a Civil Revision Petition being C.R.P. No. 44 of 1981 in the High Court of Madras against the decision of the Appellate Authority. The High Court dismissed the said revision petition. The appellants preferred a Civil Appeal No. 44/81 in the High court of Madras against this decision. The High court dismissed the said Civil Revision Petition. The appellants thereafter preferred a Civil Review Petition being C..R.P No. 44 / 1981 in the Supreme Court against the decision in Chhotelal Pyarelal 's case. The High Curt dismissed the said petition. The High ' Court held that it was only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. The appellants filed a Civil Revision Application against the said decision. The appellants also filed a Civil Review Application No. 44. The High, Court dismissed the Civil Revision Application. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the appellants have sublet the shop to M/s M. Adeshwar glass Mart. [446C] 1.2 The High Court has rightly held that the appellant had sublet the shop premises to M/S. Adeshwar Engineering Mart. [546F] 1.3 The High Court, in our view, has rightly held the appellants had sublet the premises to M. Adaram Glass Mart. [646G] 1.4 The appellants have sublet their shop to M. M. Adeswar Glass Mart. The appellants are before the Court though in a wrong name. [647C] 1:5 The appellants have not sublet the shop. The appellants had sublet their shop. The partners of the firm are before the court though in a correct wrong name. The appellants were before the Court although in a wrong names. In these circumstances, this contention of Mr. Nayar must fail. [648C] 1.:6 The appellants have subletting the shop to the M/s S. Adeshwar Iron Mart. [643C] 1.(a) The appellants have also sublet the shop, to M/ s. Adeshwar Steel Mart. [6446D] 1.7 The appellants have no right to raise this contention at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. It is certainly open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very belated stage and thereby delays matters for a period of more than one year. [649E] 1.8 The appellants have vacated the shop to another partner. [652F] 1:9 The appellants have been given notice by the respondent to the application and this misde scription can be corrected at any stage of the proceedings. [653A] 1.10 The appellants have given notice to the respondent to amend the eviction petition and join the partners as re spondents.

The Andhra Land Reforms Act was enacted in the year 1950. The Act was enacted by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature to provide for the imposition of ceiling of land on land situate in urban agglomeration. The Andhra Area Development Authority Act, 1950 provided for the levy of ceiling on lands situate within the rural agglomeration and the Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted for the purpose of providing for imposition of the ceiling on land situated within the urban areas. The Andhra Areas Development Authority Act was enacted with the object of providing for the imposition and collection of land revenue. The Andhra area Development Authority Act provided for the imposition, collection and recovery of land revenue on lands situate in urban areas and for matters ancillary thereto. The Act provided for imposition of a ceiling on land in the urban agglomerations. The Andhra Agricultural Land (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961 was enacted in 1950. The object of the Act was to provide for levy of ceiling of lands in urban agglomeration and for matters related thereto. The object was to provide a ceiling on lands situated within the rural areas and for purposes connected therewith. Section 2(n) of the Act provided for a ceiling on the holding of land situate within such areas. The Act also provided for the determination of the ceiling. The Andhra District Land Reforms Act provided for levy of a ceiling of land revenue in the whole of Andhra Pradesh including land situate in rural agglomeration. Section 2 (n) (A) (ii) of the Andhra Pradesh Agricultural Land (Regulation of Land) Act provided for ceiling on land held by a person in excess of the ceiling area. The Andhra Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation of Land) Regulation of Land Act, 1961 provided for the payment of the land revenue and the Andhra Area Development Board Act, 1961, was enacted in 1955. The Andhra and Andhra Pradesh Act, 1950 and the Andhra State Act were enacted in 1955 to provide for a ceiling of lands. The Andhra areas Development Authority Act were enacted by the State Legislature to provide a uniform ceiling on land holdings in urban agglisable areas. The object and purpose of the Act, as stated in the Act was that the Andhra Pradesh Acts were intended to provide for imposing ceiling on land and buildings situated within the areas of the State ofAndhra Pradesh including land situated in urban agglomomeration and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 2(n)(A)(ii) of that Act was an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified to be an urban agglomeration under section 2(m) (A)(ii), the whole of the Andhra area would be liable to be determined as on 1st January 1975 under the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area Development) Act. The Andhra Acts were enacted in the years 1950 and 1951. The Andhra enactments were enacted in 1950 and 1951 respectively. The Andhra Legislature enacted the Act in order to provide for payment of land revenues and for matters relating thereto. The provisions of the Andhra Act were made applicable to the land situate in the urban areas and the Andhra Areas Development Authorities Act, 1950 also provided for imposition and collection and recovery thereof. The respondents were workmen in the appellant Company. The respondents were workmen of the appellant Company, and the appellant Company was a member of the appellant company. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices issued by the appellant Company and the notice dated August 23, 1953, and the notice of August 23,1953, respectively. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the workmen who were found guilty of misconduct were entitled to be taken back in employment without condition and of the two men who came later, one was ill of typhoid fever and blood pressure, and that the notice dated September 17, 1953, was not mala fide or amounted to victimisation. Held, that the workmen were not entitled to be given any compensation, for the period anterior to October 2, 1953, because the workmen themselves were in custody, the latest day by which they could resume work without any condition and of their two men who were in custody. The contention was that the workmen themselves had not taken complete rest as required by the notice dated October 2,1953, and that was the reason why they were not taken back by the Company. The contention of the workmen that the workmen had not taken full rest as required under the notice dated November 9, 1953, could not be accepted. The notice dated November 8, 1953, did not show that the workmen did not join on or before October 2, 1952, and that they reported for duty on October 2, 1954, or October 2, 1951, and that, therefore, they were not entitled for any compensation. The notice of November 8, 1954, did not indicate that the workmen concerned were in a position to support the view of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The notice was not mala fides or amounted to unfair labour practice. The notice did not show any reason why the workmen were taken back in service. The notice does not show that any of the workmen were in a situation to support the conclusion that the workmen could not resume work without sufficient reason. The notice merely stated that the workmen refused to join on or after October 2, 1960, and that it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the Company unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounting to victimisation. The notice also did not show the reason why the workers were not taken away by the Company, and that is the reason why their services were not taken off by the Company in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute. The notice, therefore, did not disclose that the workmen, who were found to be guilty of misconduct, were not taken to work on October 2. 1953, or October 3, 1953, or November 2, 1953. The notice only stated that the Company had declared a lock out of the Works except for some special shifts, really terminated the services of the respondents by discharging them with effect from August 24, 1953, on being satisfied that Chattoraj was guilty of such activities. The notice stated that the workers were in custody and the Company was not justified in refusing leave. The notice further stated that the employees who had turned up on or before December 2, 1953 were not entitled, to be taken in service, and that if they were taken back by them, they would be taken back as of right without any condition. The notice mentioned that the workmen would be taken to work without any reason and none of the workmen had done any actual work for the period. The notice alleged that the workmen failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and that therefore they were not in a position of right without anything more.

The petitioners also contended that the reservation and the re designation of the plots for recreation centre were in contravention of sections 4 to 16 of the Act and the reservation was illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the lands in the Development Plan originally published on December 9, 1964 were earmarked in development plan originally prepared and published on January 7, 1964 and that the reservation was in contravention to section 9 of that Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 4 and 11(3) of the Act are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with as far as they can be made applicable, as far as possible, with the result that the acquisition might be delayed for a further period of ten years. [776G H] 2. The preparation of the tentative plan and the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authority. If the provisions of sections 3 and 11(2) of the, Act are borne In mind and the Rules framed thereunder complied, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authority acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the Act, there was no reason for the local authorities acting arbitrarily under sections 13 of the, and the rules made thereunder complied with, as appears from the rules framed under section 13. The preparation, publication of the final development plans was not something what was left to be the pleasure or power of the local authorities. If the provision of sections 4, and 11(4) of the , Act are borne and the rules prescribed thereunder complied with and as appears to be having been done in those cases there was little Or no scope for them, there was nothing to indicate what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. [782A] 5. The preparation or publication of the draft of a section of the development plan was nothing which was left at the pleasure or wisdom of the local body. [882B] 6. The preparation for the development plan in all its stages, it is difficult to envisage what other authority can be entrusted with a work of appeal and revision. [878C D] 7. The preparation was not something that was left to its pleasure or discretion. If the requirements of sections 4 & 11(4), are borne in view and the rules do not complied with and the rules are borne in consideration and the rules, framed thereunder complied. [884G H] 8.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Kutch. The State of Kutch had the exclusive right to establish and administer the State of Gujarat. The State Government of Kutch had, by a notification dated March 18, 1949, granted to the appellants a lease of the lands in question. The appellants contended that the Great Rann of Kutch was part of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions, that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year, for part of the year it was water and for the remaining part it was land. The Tribunal accepted the claim and held that the Great Cann of Kutch had sovereign rights and that the Great Bann of Kutch became Indian territory. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The Great Rann was part of the Great R Ann of Kutch and was therefore entitled to exercise fundamental rights in respect of the territory in that Sector. [475C] (2) The Great Cann was part and parcel of the Great Cambular area of Sind, and the Union of India had the power to make laws, can only be exercised by the State of Saurashtra before the State merged with the Dominion of India in 1948, or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maharao of Kutch. [425C] (3) The Great Bann was part part of the territory of Sind, because the territory of the State of Gujrat merged with the Union of Pakistan. [426D] (4) The Great Sann of Kutch is a part of India. The territory in this sector is contiguous to and in fact is an extension of the mainland of Sind. [428B] (5) The area is in different state, the highly discrepant and conflicting claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch State authorities before the State merger with the Dominion Indian. [429C] (6) The area was in the exclusive occupation of the appellants and was therefore, part of the great Rann of Bhuj. [430D] (7) The Great Dann of Kutch vested in the State Government of India. [431B] (8) The Great Gann of Kutch merged with the State of Bombay. The Great Cambral area of Sind was merged with the Province of Kutch. It was a part of the North India. The Great R Ann was part of that territory. [432C] (9) The Great Aann was part, parcel of the North and South India. The area was not indefinite and by the award of the Tribunal the true boundary of India was determined. [433C] (10) The Great Map of Kutch was indefinite and by that date the Great RAnn was part of territory which was now included the Rann of Saurashtra. [434D] (11) The Great Fann of Kutch, was a part and parcel part of the South India. [534A] (12) The Great Yeshwantrao of Kutch was a part part of India, and was therefore governed by the Maha Rarao of Kutch, and the rules earlier laid down by the Tribunal. [435B] (12A) (13) The Great Zeshwantrao was part of Indian territory.

The mortgagor 's interest in Mauza Bansjora was sold on January 16, 1937, and after th sale was confirmed, possession of Mauza Bahaldih was taken by the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937, by the auction sale. The mortgagor 's right, title and interest in the mortgaged property was transferred on April 7 1937, and by the attornment made pursuant to paragraph 7 of the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922, the mortgagor 's rights in the mortgaged properties were sold on April 7. 1937, and possession of Mauza Bhaldih was also taken by the sale purchaser on April 8, 1937. The mortgagor filed a suit on July 12, 1946, in the Court of the Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad for enforcement of the mortgage dated August 27, 1922, and for enforcement of his mortgage. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit was barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage deed was partly simple and partly usufructuary and partly usufructuary. The High Court also held that the claim was within limitation both on account of part payment of principal and interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, and that the suit to enforce the mortgage was accordingly within limitation. The appellant 's appeal to this Court by special leave was dismissed by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the mortgage security or where he is not secured in his possession of the mortgaged property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the mortgagor having lost his interest in the property, part payment will not extend the period for the suit. [100 E] 2. The right of the mortgagor to sue where he is deprived of his mortgage security or, where possession is neither delivered to him nor is delivered to him, as agreed, he is not "the person liable to pay" the mortgage debt. [100 G] 3. The right, title, and interest in Mauza Bahaldhih was transferred on the mortgagor ''s interest in Mauza Bhaldhih by the attonment made pursuant thereto. The mortgagor having lost interest in Mauzas Bansjora, Simitanr and Bahaldih prior to the payment of Rs. 600 by the auction purchasers, the mortgagor had lost all his interest in Mauzi. [100 F] 4. The right was transferred on May 14, 1925, to extend the time of limitation for a suit to enforce a mortgage. [100 H] 5. The right is governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act from the date of dispossession, dispossession having taken place in 1937 the suit filed on July 12. 1946, regarded as one to enforce the claim to recover the mortgage money is governed by Article 120 of the limitation Act from thedate of dispossession. [100 D] 6. The right under the mortgage deed could not operate to extend the limitation for the suits filed within twelve years from April 14, 1925. [100 C] 7. The right accrued to the mortgagee to enforce the mortgaged property by the mortgagor ' s interest in Mauza48ldih by virtue of the sale under the money decree passed against the mortgagor, a cause of action accrued to the mortgagor to enforce the suit, but from the date when the mortgage money was repayable, the plaintiff 's claim to enforce the mortgages was within limitation. [100 B] 8. The right accrues to the mortgagor ' in respect of the mortgaged properties, part payment, will not extend to the period of Limitation for a suit for enforce the mortgage.

The appellants were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for the transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCo factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants contended that the transport facilities provided to the employees by the appellants were not liable to passenger tax. The Commissioner held that the transport vehicles provided to the appellants were covered by the expression 'public service vehicle ' and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. The appellants further contended that the tax was leviable only if the passengers were carried on a public service vehicle carrying passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers, either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. The Commissioner also held that the appellants were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. The appellants filed appeals before the Commissioner. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals of the appellants. The appellants then filed appeals before this Court. The appellants also contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the transport vehicle provided to the appellant was reserved for them only and no charges could be levied in respect thereof. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The term 'public service Vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that too does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the Act we are of the opinion that the tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried on a private service vehicle which falls squarely within the ambit of the definition of 'public service vehicles'. [360G H] 1.2 The word 'public service ' has not be defined either by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [360G] 1.3 The word 'private service vehicle ' has not also been defined either in the Act or Rules. [360A] 1.4 The word 'stage carriage ' has not not been defined by the Act. [360B] 1.5 The word 'Public service vehicle ' is not defined either by Act or by Rules but that however does not create a difficulty because having respect to the Preamble and the Act we have been of the opinion, that the tax should be levied only if the persons are carried on the said vehicle. [360C] 1.6 The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within section 2(7) of the Act. The transport service provided to the employee by the appellants could be a public service Vehicle within the meaning of the provisions of the Act and no other member of the public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the same vehicle. [361G] 1:6 The transport services in the present cases which were registered as private services vehicle fell within the ambit Of the aforesaid definition. [360D] 1.7 The transport service was not a public service vehicles within the meaning Of the provisions of section 2(8) of the Bombay , the definition of "public service vehicle" has not been included by the Act and by the Rules. [361E] 1.8 The transport service is not a public services vehicle within the meaning o the provisions of that Act. [361F] 1.9 The transport service has not been specified by the Rules and forms in order to illustrate their point that private service vehicle was beyond the ambit of that definition. [361H] 1.10 The transport service, in the instant case, was not a private service Vehicle within section 2 (7) of that Act and no charges would be realised from the employees for providing transport facilities.

The appellants were granted a licence for a quasi permanent cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor, Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under 795 Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants was dismissed in limine by the High Court. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order granting the no objection certificate to the third respondent and the order granting licence for a temporary cinema to respondent Nos. 3 to 6. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there was a mosque, and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Government was perfectly justified in granting the same and, therefore, it was not a fit case for the interference of the High Court under Article 226 of The Constitution. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have no power to grant a "no objection certificate" certificate. [696 B] 2. The licensing authority has no power to refuse a cinema licence. [697 C] 3. The licensing authorities have no power under the rules to refuse or to grant a licence. [797 E] 4. The licensing Authority has no power under rule 101 to refuse or grant a "No objection certificate" to a person who has objected to the grant of a "noobjection certificate". [697 E] 5. The licensing officer has no power or jurisdiction to refuse or refuse a grant of a licence. The licensing Officer has no power either to refuse or revoke a grant of the "no objection" certificate. The licensing and appellate authority has no jurisdiction to refuse a grant. [698 E] 6. The licensing or appellate authority has the power to refuse or cancel a grant of licence. [600 G] 7. The licensing, appellate authority and revisional authority have no power or authority to refuse or renew a licence. It is not a fit and proper case for the High Court to refuse or not to grant a cinema licence, when under section 5(3) of the Act or the rules made thereunder the licensing authority has refused to grant a no objection certificate. [600 D] 8. The High court was in error in holding that the order granting a no objection Certificate to the third respondents was without prejudice to the right of the licensing authority to refuse a licence. In the instant case the High Court was in error. [600 E] 9. The High courts have no power of judicial review. [600 A] 10. The High and the revisional authorities have no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the licensing authorities. [600 B] 11. The High High Courts have jurisdiction to interfere in the matter of grant of a no objection certificates or a licence. If the licensing authority refuses to grant a license, the appeal must fail.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In the appeal by special leave, the plaintiffs contended that the contract was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that the earlier contract was concluded in November 1957. The High court held that the contract had not been concluded in November, 1957. The main question arising in this appeal is whether there was a concluded contract between the parties. The High ' Court held that there was a contract between the plaintiff and the defendant. The High Curt held that there had been a concluded contract. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance of the offer. The letter dated September 2,1957 was not an accepted acceptance. The letter of the acceptance was not an accept. It was not usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the Court. [623 E] In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. [624 F] In the absence of a formal acceptance, the contract could not be specifically performed and on this ground the High Court dismissed the suit [624 G] In the present case, the plaintiffs had not accepted the offer either orally or by any letter sent to the defendant before hi withdrew the offer.

The appellants were the owners of sugarcane in the State of Bihar. The appellants were the purchasers of sugarcane. The appellants filed a complaint against them under section 3 of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of the sugarcane purchased by them, within the time prescribed. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued summons to them. The appellants challenged the validity of the order of the Magistrate before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the complaint made before the police did not disclose a Cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. HELD: The complaint made before a police does not disclose a cognizable offence and as defined in section 4(1)(f) of the Cr. P.C. and consequently the same is a cognizable offence as defined in the Act. [768G H] The complaint made by the police does not discloses a Cognizable Offence and as such it falls within the 2nd Sch. of the Cr P.C., and consequently the said complaint is a cognizable Offence as defined in Section 4(1) (f) of The Cr. P.,C. and hence the same is not a cognizable offence. [766G H] (b) The complaint made in the police does disclose a Cognizous offence and as a result the police could have taken up investigation of that offence. [666C] (c) The complaint does not disclose any Cognizable offence but as such the Police could not have took up the investigation. [767C] (d) The complaint discloses a Cognizous Offence and as defined under section 4(2)(c) of the Act, it is a cognizable case as defined in that section. [712B] (e) The complaint is not acognizable offence as defined under the Act. The offence complained of is punishable with three years ' imprisonment and as such there is no substance in the contention that the complaint is not disclosing a Cognizable offences and as such no cognizance could have been taken of the offence alleged is premature. [713C] (f) The complaint disclosed a Cognizable case and as such, the police could only investigate the same. [714B] (g) The complaint did not disclose any indictable offence and the police could therefore not have taken the cognizance of the offences alleged. [715C] (h) The complaint was not a cognizable case and as defined by section 4(I)(f) the same is also a cognizable offence, the same is cognizable offence as provided in section 4 (1)(f). [715A] (hh) The offence complained was punishable with three months ' imprisonment and the same is punishable with 3 years ' imprisonment. [716B] (i) The complaint relates to the contravention of the provisions of the Act. It was not acognizable case. [717C] (j) The complaint alleged was not a Cognizable one. The offence alleged was punishable with 3 months ' imprisonment. The offence was not punishable with three year ' imprisonment and therefore the same is one cognizable offence as contemplated in section 4 of the Cr, P.C.. [717B] (k) The complaint in the complaint did not discloses a cognizable offence but as a result of the investigation of the complaint, the police was entitled to investigate the same and investigate the same, and in addition to the Sugar Control Order, 1955, it was open to the police to investigate the complaint.

The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of various types of misuse and the Government of Karnataka issued a notification dated 30th June, 1969 exempting the industries from the payment of sales tax or concessions to be granted. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court of Karnataka claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June 1969 when the order dated 12th January, 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order dated 12 th January, 1977. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30th May, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The doctrine of Prom promissory Estoppel is not applicable in a case where the source of power under which it is issued is not stated in an order but can be found on the examination of the relevant Act. The exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. [415E] 1.2 The doctrine ofpromissory Estoppel is clearly there in Section 8A. [416B] 1.3 The doctrine of promissory Estoppel cannot be regarded as good law in view of the recent decision of this Court in State of Bihar and Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC, 430 where a Division Bench comprising three learned Judges of this Court upheld and applied the doctrine ofprom promissory Estoppel. [417C] 1.4 The doctrine ofPromissory Estoppel cannot, therefore, be regarded as a good law in the view of the latest decision of this court in State of Kerala and Anr. v Usha Martin Industry Ltd., [1986] 65 STC 430 where a Bench comprising three Judges of this court upheld and applied that doctrine. [419D] 1.5 The doctrine of Quissory Estoppel has been held to be good law in respect of sales tax paid to the extent provided in the Order. [418E] 1:6 The doctrine of Discissory Estoppel can be regarded as bad in law. [422F] 1.7 The doctrine of Directissory Estoppel does not apply in the present cases because it is found by the State Government that the concession granted under the order dated 30 th June, 1969 was being misused and was undue advantage being taken of that concession by way of refunds, though in a more limited manner and that is not even the case of the appellants. The exercise Of the power must, therefore, attributed to that sources. [423F] 1:8 The doctrine of Corissory Estoppel, as there is nothing on record to show that any such misuse was being made or undue advantage taken of the said concession by the newly established industries. The exercise exercise of the powers must be attributed, to that source, and not merely certain words used out of context. [424F] 1 9. The doctrine of corissory Estoppel could be regarded as having been specifically mentioned in Section 8.A. [404C] 1:9 The doctrine of estoppel cannot be regarded to be good Law in view of Section 8A and where the source is not stated on the examination. [426F] 1 10. The doctrine must be regarded as valid in view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the doctrine must be treated as good law now. [427F] 1 11. The doctrine should be regarded asgood law in view Of the recent decision in State of Punjab and Anr.

P..C. and convicting them under Sections 302 and on applying 14 of the Act, all. [807 A B] 2.6 The non applicability Or Section 141 I PC. is, however, no bar. The non absence of any evidence discloses commission o offence in furtherance o the common intention o the unlawful assembly. The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. The assessee was a partner in a firm. The assessee had a business in the firm. The firm was assessed to tax under the Gift Tax Act, 1958. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax relying on section 52 sub section (2) of the Act. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the appeal. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had received a larger consideration for the transfer and sub section (1) of section 52 sub Section (2) did not require as a condition precedent that there should be under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of the transfer exceeded the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee. The Revenue appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the sub section did not require the assessee to show that the consideration had been under stated and the assessee had actually received more than what is declared by him. The High court held that the Income tax officer was not justified in holding that the assessee was not justified by the language of sub section (3) of section 53 sub section (4) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The assessee is a Hindu undivided Hindu family. The real consideration received by the assessee is not declared or disclosed and in most of the cases, if not all, it would not be possible for the Income tax Officer to determine precisely what is actual consideration received by him and therefore, sub section (I) of section52 sub section (II) cannot be construed as bringing within the computation of capital gains taxable under the provisions of the Income tax Act, 1961, but it is very difficult, if not impossible, to determine and prove the exact quantum of the suppressed consideration, sub section(2) provides the statutory measure for determining the consideration actually received by the Income tax officers. [523D] 2. The full value of consideration received by an assessee is not to be declared or disclosed but it is also necessary that the full value has been declared or disclosed by him. If a capital asset is transferred for a consideration below its market value, the difference between the market value and the full value thereof received in respect of that transfer would amount to a gift liable to tax under section the Gift Tax act, 1958, but if the construction of sub section(1) is literally construed as applying even to cases where the full value is correctly declared or disclosed, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by him, and which from no view point can be rationally considered as capital gains or any other type of income. [524E] 3. The full amount of consideration received in respect to the transfer is under stated or in other words, shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by him. [526E] 4. The full price of the consideration is under stated and in most cases, it is very impossible, if not difficult, to determine or prove the exact amount of the suppressedconsideration, sub section 2. [527F] 5. The full values of the consideration received in the respect of the transferred is under stated. [528G] 6. The full valuation of the consideration actually receiving by the assessee, is under stated but the assessee has actually received morethan what is declared or disclosed. [529F] 7. The full Value of the consideration for the transferred is to be taken to be the full value and the assessee has accordingly been taxed on capital gains. [530F] 8.

The appellant was charged with the offence of adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption. The appellant was charged under sec. 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption, and thereby committed an offence under sec. 7(i)(f) of the Act. The trial Magistrate acquitted the appellant. The High Court, on appeal, held that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, that the appellant had only black Tils used for Pooja, was not reliable and that the appellant was not guilty of the offence under secs. 2(i)(a) and 7 (i)(f). The High Court held that the appellant could not be convicted under sec. 5(7) of the the Act. On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant could not have been convicted under secs 2(i) (f) and (i)(a). [701B] 1.2 The appellant could have been prosecuted on the ground that he sold it in an adulterated condition ? [702C] 1.3 The appellant could be prosecuted on the basis that he sold the Til seeds with which we are concerned were not meant for human use. [702D] 1.4 The appellant could, therefore, be prosecuted on his own case. [703E] 1.5 The appellant could only be prosecuted on a charge of adulterated food only if he had been charged on the basis of the evidence produced by him. [704B] 1:6 The appellant could also be prosecuted on an charge of adulterated Food Inspector if he kept adulterated food for sale for human consumption and not as human food. [705B] 1.:705B C] 1.8 The appellant could therefore be prosecuted on that charge only if he kept the adulterated food for human consumption as food. [0705B] 2.9 The appellant could still be prosecuted on any charge of adulterated adulterated food only when he sold the same to the Food Inspectors. [706C] 2.10 The appellant could continue to be prosecuted on such charge only if the Food Inspector had been duly proved. [707F] 3. The appellant could go on trial only if he was convicted on the basis on the evidence produced before the Magistrate. [708B] 3.1 The prosecution case that the appellant sold the Til plants with which we were concerned was not "food". The appellant could never be used as food. The appellant had no knowledge that the Food Inspector could prosecute him if he kept it adulterated food. [808B] 4.2 The prosecution case was that the appellant did not sell the Til seeds for human consumption but only meant for human food. The prosecution case is that the Til plants were kept for the purpose of being sold only for pooja and not for human consumption nor as human food and that the price of the Til seeds was not fixed. The appellant did not know that the price was fixed at Rs. 1,000/ per quintal. The appellant, therefore, could not be prosecuted on this charge. [709F] 4.3 The prosecution case, that the Til plant was meant for human purpose, was not established. [710C] 4.4 The prosecution case could not be implicitly relied upon in this case. [810B] 5.5 The prosecution case as to the actual purpose for which the Til seeds sold were unfit for pooja, and not as a human food meant for human Consumption.

The plaintiff was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. The plaintiff 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. The plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that he was entitled to be treated as a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh. The suit was one for a declaration of the order of the Collector and for a declaration to the effect that the order was bad and illegal. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit was one filed within time. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit had been filed within time and that the suit could not be said to be within time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is within time. [419D] 2. The suit has been filed within six months from the date of the accrual of the cause of action. [418E] 3. The suit having been filed within the time, the right to sue accrues and where no such order is made, the right of sue shall first accrue. [421B] 4. The suit being within time, the suit was within time. It was not disputed that in the first two cases where the order of termination was passed before the Constitution came into force, cause of action shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from date when the appeal was filed or representation was made, the rights to sue shall first accrued. [422C] 5. The suit had been dismissed on the ground of limitation and our conclusion is that the suit is within limitation. [423D] 6. The suit could not therefore be said to have been within time. Reliance was placed on the observations of this Court in State Uttar Pradesh vs Mohammad Nooh, ; , where it has been held that the cause of actions shall first accrue but on the date when the order of reinstatement was made, it shall first accrue; where such order was not made, the Right to sue shall First accrue. [413G] 7. The suit, therefore, as far as Government serv ants are concerned, was within time, and the right to sued shall first accrue, and where such orders are not made, upon the expiry of 6 months from thedate of filing of the suit or representation, the right, to sue shall second accrue. [414G] 8. The suit as well as the appeal are remitted to the trial Court for disposal in accordance with law. [424A] 9. The suit shall be disposed of in accordance with the law. [413B] 10. The trial court shall dispose of the suit in accordance with its own merits.

The appellant was a tenant of a building in which a building was constructed. The appellant was a sub tenant of a portion of the building. The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the tenant had committed default in payment of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellate decree in favour of the intending appellant was not a decree of affirmance but variation in the decision of the trial Court was not a judgment of affirmance and that the appellate court was not a court of affirmance. Held, that the word "decision" in article 133(1) of the Constitution meant the decision of a suit by the trial court and not the grounds stated in support of the said decision. The word "decision " meant the decision or the grounds stated therein. The word 'decision" in the context of the present case was not intended to mean the whole of the decision or grounds given for it but the decision of that case construed the relevant provisions of section 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The word "'decision" in section 110 of CPC was not intended by the legislature to mean the entire of the decision of an appeal court. The word `decision" in that context means the entire of a decision or the ground given for it. The decision of the Privy Council in that case construed that the appellate judgment which confirmed the decision of trial court was not one of affirmance or not. The decision thus (i) If an appellate decree confirms the decision of one of the parties, then there is a right of appeal not only to the person against whom the variation has been made, but even to the party in whose favour the variation has not been obtained by parties by consent or a part of the subject matter covered by the decree has been withdrawn such variation cannot affect the character of the appellate decree.

The petitioners, who were the respondents in the two revision petitions, filed two applications under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, for revision of the order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1976, on the ground that they are not maintainable. The District Court dismissed the applications on the ground of limitation. The revision petitions were dismissed by the High Court. The High Court held that the revisional order of the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil procedure was not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High court under section 115. The High court also held that the High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in a revision petition. The High ' Court also held that an order passed under section 25 was not amenable under the revisional jurisdiction. The High " Court also held, that the High court was not vested with revisional jurisdiction under section115 of the Code. The High, Court also held the revision petitions to be not maintainable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High ' Court had exclusive Jurisdiction under section 115 and the District Court had jurisdiction under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause courts Act in respect of cases arising out of original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above, and that the High " Court had exclusive power under section 115 to the District Court in other cases. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have concurrent jurisdiction under section 5 of the Provincial Courts Act in respect to cases decided by a District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes the power of revision under section 115 is vested in the High Court in cases arising out Of original suits of a value of Rs 20,000 and above. [775G H] 2. The High courts have concurrent jurisdiction in respect of an order of the district court under section 25. The High High Court has jurisdiction under section 116 of the Code to make a clear cut division of jurisdiction between the High Court and the District Judge exercising jurisdiction of a District Court under that section. [776G H] 3. The High Curt has jurisdiction under sections 115 and 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to make an order under section 25 to the State of Uttar Pradesh. [778G H] 4. The High curt has jurisdiction to entertain a revision petition under section 115 against an order of a District Judge under section 25 or section 115 of that Code. [782A] 5. The High Judge has jurisdiction under Section 115 to entertain a petition under section115. [785B] 6. The High revision petition under Section 115 is not maintainable against a revisional order under section 115 or section 115. [786C] 7. The High Revision Petition under section 115 has been filed against a revisional application under section 115 by a District Court. [787D] 8.
