The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands belonging to the respondents, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 52 (1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 (Act for short) served on them at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road , Calcutta by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department , Jaipur. The respondents filed a petition for quashing the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of Act for the acquisition of their lands situated at Jaipur and wanted to challenge the validity of a notification issued under Section 52 (1). The Special Officer by his order dated March 13, 1984 rejected the prayer of the respondents for release of the land and recommended that the entire land be acquired by the State of Rajasthan under section 52 of the Act for the public purpose, namely, for implementation of a development scheme viz. for implementation of the development scheme viz., for implementation of development scheme viz, for implementation a development scheme at public expense viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, Jaipur for a public purpose, viz. for implementing a development scheme etc. The respondents challenged the validity of notification issued by State Government under Section 52(1). The High Court by its order dated March 12, 1984 quashed the notification issued on February 8, 1984 and directed the respondents to surrender or deliver possession of the lands acquired forthwith or upon their failure to do so to take immediate steps under sub section (6) thereof to secure such possession. The respondents preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the service of notice under sub section(2) of section 52 of Act for quashing the acquisition of the land under section 52 was an integral part of the cause of action and was sufficient to invest the Calcutta High Court with jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 226 of the constitution. [605F] 1.2 The High Court erred in holding that in the instant case the service of notices under sub section 2 of section 52 was sufficient to invested the Calcutta High court with jurisdiction to try a petition under articles 226 of the , Constitution. [606F] 1:3 The High Court failed to appreciate that the respondents did not raise any objection as to the power and authority of the State Government to acquire the notified land under section52 (1) or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section 52A of the Act. [607B] 1.4 The respondents did not file any objection as regards the power and jurisdiction of the State government to acquire the land under Section 52A of Act for implementation of any development scheme. [608C] 1.5 The respondents did neither raise any objection nor as to the jurisdiction of the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 52C of the Act or the legality and propriety of the notice issued by the Special officer under section 52B of the Act nor did raise any objection. [609F] 1.:6 The respondents did file their reply to the petition before the Rajasthan High Court, Jaipur Bench, where the cause of actions wholly or in part arose. [610C] 1:6 The respondents were not aware of the fact that the land was actually needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. with these observations they rejected the prayer for release of land and recommended for issue of the requisite notification under section 52 C of the Act, for the grant of an appropriate writ, direction or order under article 226.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the premises in suit. The appellant landlord filed an application under s.25 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of his tenant from the premises. The appellant contended that the building was constructed in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court rejected the application holding that the building had been constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to s.2(2) of the new RentAct. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the building in question had been constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the new Rent Acts had no application to the building in suit and the appellant could get any protection of the new rent Act. HELD: The new Rent Act will not apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit of s.39 of the new Act there is a change in the cause of action. [435C D] The new Rent Acts will not apply in the case of a building subject to assessment the date on Which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and where the said dates are different, the earliest of the said dates, and in the absence of any such report, record or assessment, the date, on which it is actually occupied (not including occupation merely for the purposes of supervising the construction or guarding, the building under construction) for the first time. [436E] The question in this case is whether the building in dispute was constructed substantially out Of funds obtained from sources mentioned in sub section (2) of s.2 of the new tenancy Act. [437F] The question is whether by obtaining the benefit of the new landlord the building had not become ten years old on the date of the first assessment of the house which has been accepted by the High Court and, therefore the appellant would be entitled to the benefit of section 39 as the building had never become ten years' old on the said date. [438F] The new rent Act will not be applicable to a building after the first hearing of the suit. [439G] The new Act will not, therefore, apply to a case where the building has not become ten year old on the day on which the first assessment comes into effect. [434A] The new tenancy Act will not therefore apply to a new building during a periods of ten years. [433B] The new landlord will be entitled to claim the benefit of sub section (1) of s 39 as the house has not become more than ten years old. [428C] The new tenant will be entitled only to the benefit under s.39 as the house had not become morethan ten years old and the landlord 's cost of the suit in respect thereof after deducting therefrom the there from any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section (I) of s 2 of s.30, the court may in lieu of passing a decree for eviction on that ground pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction on the said ground. [429A] The question whether the benefit of a new landlord be not given to the appellant is not a question of giving the benefit of S.39 as it relates to eviction but the question is whether the benefit under the new Rent legislation be given to the tenant.

The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings, stores and other works at Ranchi, the first of them being contract No. 21 of 1942 dated November 5, 1942, and the other two contracts Nos. 21 of 1943 dated November 5. 1942, and 21 of 1942, respectively. The appellant contended that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and that no decree should be passed in terms thereof. The respondents contended that the contract for reference to the arbitration was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that therefore the award passed therein was a nullity. Held, that the award was not one in respect of execution of works, and that it fell within item 2 and that the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not be said that the award had been drawn up accordingly and steps were being taken to execute it, as quickly as possible. The award was not a copy of the award. The award could not be validated: That was a case where the copy of an instrument cannot be validated and "acted upon" and that the law did not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents. The law does not provide for a levy of any penal penalty on lost document. The law did not, in our opinion, provide for the levying of any penalty, and that law does not providing for the levy, of any penalty thereon. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of the instrument cannot be validation: That was held in The Rajah of Bobbili vs Inuganti China Sitaramasani Garu (1), where it was observed: 835 "The original and not a copy thereof. What the arbitrator did was to prepare the award in triplicate, sign all of them and send one each to the party and the third to the court. The arbitrator did not, therefore, form an opinion, and that was sufficient for the purpose of section 175 (3) of Act, 1935. The award, therefore, secondary evidence of its contents cannot be given. Payment of penalty will not render secondary evidence admissible, for under the stamp law penalty, is leviable only on an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document actually produced in Court and that law did not providing for any levy of any penalties on lost documents".

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He was prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of a cause of action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution. The trial court acquitted the respondent on the ground that the prosecution was rightly quashed. The High Court quashed the prosecution on the ground of delay in filing the challan. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court committed an error of law in taking the view that the third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules has been misinterpreted by the High Court in taking the said view. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The third proviso to Rule 2.3 of the Punjab civil Service Rules has not been framed for a different purpose namely to provide an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing etc. of pension of a retired government servant contained in clause (b). [419D] 1.2 The third proviso is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule has been framed. [419E] 1.3 The third proviso cannot be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecution of a government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. [421F] 1.4 The third proviso has not been issued for a different object namely to provide a exception to the powers of the government. [422F] 1:5 The third proviso can be interpreted as laid down by the High court. [423C] 1.6 The third proviso, to clause (a) of Rule 3.2, is in the form of a beneficient legislation and in the third proviso, it is not necessary for the purpose of Rule making power under Article 309 of the Constitution to provide an exceptions to the power conferred on the government in respect of pension of such a government servant contained therein. [424F] 1.:6 The third Proviso to clause (c) of Rule 4.2 is in the manner of laying down an abstract rule for the benefit of a government employee contained in clause(b) with regard to pension of such retired government servant. The third proviso also cannot be interpreted to mean that even if a government servant is prosecuted and punished, in judicial proceedings initiated in respect of cause of action, which arose or a event which tookplace more than four year before such institution the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause 2.2. [426F] 1 :7 The third proviso does not mean that even when a government servant was prosecuted and convicted in judicial proceedings, instituted in respect thereof, the government will be entitled to take the benefit of the Rule. [425F] 1 8. The fourth proviso to clause(b), of Rule 2, is in nature of a beneficial legislation and in cases of doubt has also to be interpreted as to mean that only if a government employee is prosecuted and convicted, the government would not be entitled for exercise the right of withholding or withdraw etc. of the pension of such an employee contained in clauses (b) with respect to pension of the retired government servant provided in clause (a). [426G] 1.8 The third proviso of clause (b), of rule 2.2, does not mean the third proviso. [427A] 1.9 The third proviso in the third Proviso to Rule 2, which is in the shape of a beneficative legislation and in which the object of Rule 2 is not to place an embargo on prosecution.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares, with no right in the balance of the profits. The respondent company was a public limited Company under the Indian companies Act, 1913. The authorised capital was 7,500 ordinary shares and three preference shares of the value of the share, with no rights in the balance. The preference shareholder was under the Articles entitled to a specified dividend of 71. The respondent was a shareholder of the company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power. The company was a private limited company under section 3 of the Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1955, to acquire shares of Rs, 1,375, and 3 preference shares of rupees. The respondent Company was a public company under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent 's share was declared by the Income tax Officer to be distributed amongst the shareholders as at the date of the general meeting. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Income tax officer. The High Court held that the provisions of section 23 A were correctly applied for the three relevant years. The High court held that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which the public are substantially interested, is. (2) Where a shareholder holding or a group of shareholders acting in concert hold fifty one per cent or more of the voting powers are held by the public, shares entitled to a fix rate of dividend have to be excluded. The High ' Court held that in assessing whether the twenty five per% of the shares are vested in persons other than the controlling group, the shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend were not held by the shareholders as At the date of general meeting, the shares yield a fixed rate which was Rs. 1,375. The High, Court held that section 23A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 before it was amended by the Finance Act, 1955 stood as follows: "Whether in fact there exists such a control ling interest inthe hands of one shareholder or a group o f shareholders as would render the company one in which thepublic are substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company is held by the parent company or by the nominees thereof. If the controlling, interest i.e. a minimum of fifty one per% or more is utilised, the company would be regarded as one in which such public are substantially interest. If the shareholder holding or the group of shareholders is not substantially interested, the question is one of fact to be determined in each case whether it is a company in which the Public are substantially interested. If the control, interest i s allotted unconditionally to or acquired unconditionally by or is beneficially held by the company, it shall be presumed that the company is one in which it the public are not substantially interested. But in considering whether shares not entitled to a fixation of dividend carrying not lessthan twenty five per % of the voting right are not directly interested in such accumulation: it matters little to them whether the dividend is immediately distributed to the ordi nary shareholders or is accumulated, and therefore in assessing whether that share is immediately distributed amongst the shareholder, the shares owning a fixed rate have to be ignored.

The appellant was a del credere agent of the first appellant. The goods were delivered to the same Dwarkadas Khetan on behalf of another quota holder Beharilal Bajirathi. The case for the prosecution is that the bales remained in the physical possession of the first respondent at all material times and were not physically delivered to Messrs. Dwarkadas Daga & Company on behalf of the first two appellants. The case of the prosecution is as follows: (1) that the bales were delivered to Dwarkadaspatti Khetan & Company on the account of the purchaser Shree Kishan & Company; (2) that the goods had actually left the Mills ' premises, and (3) that the property in the goods had passed and when Dharsi Moolji refused to receive them they were handed over to Dwarkadash Khetan. The case is that the goods were delivered at all material time and were not actually delivered to the Mills. The case was that the bales had been delivered to the first appellant at all material places and were not personally delivered to the mills. The case further is that the sale agent had paid the first appellant for the goods and the Mills sent them to Dharsi Moolchand on account of the 13 bales. The case set up by the prosecution is based on the statement of the first accused. The first accused was the agent of the Mills. It was contended on behalf of accused that the goods remained in the possession of the second accused at all material moment and were not delivered to the Mill. Held, that the evidence of the first and the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is not reliable and that the evidence is not reliable. The evidence of PWs 2 and 3 is not reliable, and that the first accused was not an agent of the Mill. The evidence is not credible and that the statement is untrue. The statement is untrue and misleading. The statement of the second and the evidence is untrue. It is not a statement which called for the severe strictures which are to be found in the trial court 's judgment and certainly not for the savage sentences which the learned Magistrate imposed. In the column headed Full name and address of person to whom delivered the name of Dwarkadas Hassan was entered. II on the back directs that the names of "any other person" must be entered in column 3 and that the number and date of the General or Special Permission must be set out in column 2, Whether this means that goods allotted to quota holders can be pledged without permission or that only goods allotted to quotas can be pledged we do not know, but whatever it means, it is clear that the entry in column 3 is not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but means what it says, namely the person to whom physical delivery of the goods has been made whoever he may be. The record amply bears it out, that this godown belonged to Dwarkadalas Khetan & Company.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, keeping in view the capacity in which and the nature of the duties which he was performing. The appellant was charged with having committed offences under section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court held that the appellant was a "public servant" within the meaning Of the Ninth clause and that the appellant had been guilty of the offence under section 5(1) (c) of the Act. The High court also held that the ninth clause, as it stood at the material time, was wider when it came to the case of an officer who was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of a public duty and it was not necessary that the remuneration by any of fee or commission should be paid by the Government as is now necessary under subclause (a) of the ' Twelfth clause after the amendment. The High ' Court also held that since the work of an Investigator was of a nature which could well be regarded as public duty and the remuneration which was to be paid to him was by the Government. The High, Court also held, that the ninth Clause, as it stands, when the offences are alleged to have been committed would cover the case of Dwivedi as he, was an officer in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated by fees or commission for performance of any public duty by the Government who would fall within the definition of "public servant". The High Court also held the appellant guilty of the offences under section 161 of the Indian penal Code. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (1) The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not include the word "obtaining" on the part of the receivers one may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public servant; in each cases, lie obtains an pecuniary advantage by using his position as public servant; and it is wholly immaterial in what capacity he has committed the offence under sub clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. The abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1) case. [775 E] (2) The word 'obtains" in clause (d), a construction which was consistent with the others clauses of the subsection. The abuse of the position would be the necessary ingredient of the offence. [776 H] (3) The abuse being neither by corrupt or unlawful means nor by other means, the abuse being either By corrupt or illegal methods or by other words. The abuse was either by corrupt, illegal means or otherwise. [778 E] (4) The abuse of position as a Public servant is clearly implied. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (d). a construction which would be consistent with the main clauses of the section. The use of the word " Obtaining" on which considerable stress was laid is the abuse of position which is either by corrupt and illegal means orby other means of a nature mentioned in the Narayanan Nambiar ''s(1) Case. [782 F] (5) The abuse was neither by corrupt nor illegal means or any other means of his nature mentioned in gran ting the bribe by threats or coercion. [785 C] (6) The abuse is either by ill motive or by other mode of the nature described in Narayanan Nambiar "s(1).

The petitioners were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal and Telecom Construction Department of Northern Railway. All the petitioners were engaged as casual labour for the periods varying between 20 140 and 16 1 1/2 years in the construction Department of the signal Unit in the Northern Railway. The petitioners were engaged in the Construction Division in the Northern Railways. All the writ petitions having disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein are similar. The petitioners contended that the Railway Administration was not justified in treating them as temporary servants and had applied discriminatory rates of wages. The Railway Administration, respondent herein, had not treated them as temporary employees and had applied discrimination discriminatory rates of Wages. The Railway Board 's order of 1st of June, 1984, had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. The petitioners had asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The respondents had refused to go to the open line for permanent absorption. The petitioners, therefore, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Railway Board ' s order of 1 st June, 1984. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Administration that the Railway Board had not treated the petitioners as temporary servants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Railway administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. There is perhaps s blackness in enforcing the same. Even though there is break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. [144G H] 2. The Railway, Board 's orders of 1st June, 1984 had not been furnished but with those instructions now holding the post, the ambit and scope of grievances has also been reduced. Several instructions issued by the Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the Administration was anxious to take prompt steps to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. [144H; 145A] 3. The Railway Headquarters were directed to take appropriate action to remove the difficulty faced by the Casual labour but there was perhaps slack appreciation in enforcing them and, therefore, there is perhaps Slackness in enforce them. [145B] 4. The Railway Establishment Manual provides: (a) "Casual labour treated as temporary are entitled to all the rights and privileges admissible to temporary railway servants as laid down in Chapter XXIII of the Indian Railway Establishment Manual. (b) Such casual labour who acquire temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. will not, however, be brought on to the permanent establishment unless they are selected through regular Selection Boards for Class IV staff. [145C] 5. The Railway Administrations should take prompt steps for screen such of those petitioners who have been denied to join and seventeen are still continuing with temporary status. [145D] 6. The Railway Administrative Tribunal 's order dated 1st of July, 1984 had been given. It is not disputed that the petitioners should be entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. About three years back, this Court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour is combined for the purpose. Casual labour in open line as well as willing project casual labour are combined for the purposes of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in.

The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of the power conferred on it under section 12 of the Act, framed bye laws 52AA and 52AA. The Forward Markets Commission framed bye laws under section 11 of the Act. The appellant, a member of the Forward Markets Commission under section 12(1) of the Act framed bye laws 53AA and 52A. The appellant was a member of a Forward Markets Commission. The Forward Market Commission framed bye bye laws 53A and 52AA respectively. The appellant contended that the Forward Markets Act, 1951, was not competent to confer the power on the Forward Markets Commissioner under section 12 and that the power of the Central Government under section 12 was not competent. Held, that the power conferred by section 12 of Act to make bye laws under sections 11 and 12 of the , was not a co extensive with the power of Parliament to make a bye law with retrospective effect. The power of the Government to make bye law with retropective effect was not a power delegated to it by the Central Government by section 12. The power conferred by the Act was not a legislative power. The power to make bye legislation was not a delegated power. The powers of the Central Board under section 12 were not delegated to it. The power was not a delegate of the Central Govt. by section 12 and the power of its Board was not a delegation of the power to the Board. The power under section 12 is a delegated power and the power conferred is a delegated one. The power is a delegated legislation. The power can be exercised by the Board by a resolution. The power cannot be delegated to the Board by the Central Govt., by a resolution, (1875) L.R. 9 I.A. 964)

The assessee, a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. was a shareholder of the assessee company. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357 B.S., and Rs. 21,822/ for the years 1358 B.S. were taxable as dividend, and the remaining amounts were not taxable, since they were declared out of capital gains of the Company which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term mining and other leases and as compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court held that the whole amount for each of these three years was income in assessee from "other sources" and that the entire amounts for each year were income in the assessee from " other sources". The High Court also held that the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to salami was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assessee from other sources. The High court also held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salamis realized by the Ukhari Estate Zamindaries (P) Ltd. for grant of lease was not taxable, because it was not capital gain, and that the distribution of dividend out of capital gain was taxable as dividend. The High ' Court also held, that the entire sum for each year, was income in hands of the appellant, but only part of it was dividend, within meaning of section 12 as dividend income liable to tax. The High " Court further held that the amount distributed was not capital gains, and that it was not income liable to taxation under section 12 as it was not earned, and that, therefore, the distribution to assessee of the amounts attributable to salamy was not taxable. The High Judge also held that there was no evidence to show that any amount of salami was capital gain, but only the part of it having been received by the assessee, receipt of dividend within the meaning Of section 2(7A) of Income tax Act was not capital asset. The High Curt also held that it was agreed between the parties that the distribution out of the capital gains must be deemed exempt from liability to tax under section 12, as dividend income chargeable to tax under Section 12 as dividend was liable to tax under the Act, 1922, and as income of that assessee from other source was not liable to tax, the entire amount was liable to be grossedup. The High Bench also held that in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in holding that part of amount distributed which is statutorily payable on compensation is income and was not capital profit. The High Courts also held that no part of the compensation received for compulsory acquisition was still income liable to be tax from "other source" (not being dividend) under section 12 of the Indian income tax Act, 1961, and that there was nothing to show that the receipt from the capital gains was still income chargeable to income tax from " other source". The High 'Court also held that even if dividend be distributed to the shareholders of the company out of those capital gains, to "the extent of the distribution out Of the capital gains, the dividend must be deemed to be exempt from liability liability to tax.

The appellant, who was the owner of the land in question, purchased the land in dispute from one M/s. Sandalwool Oil, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The appellant was the owner and possessor of the land. The land was purchased by M/s Sandalwoo Oil, a Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The appellant purchased the land from M/s M.G.Gimba Vasava and others. The land purchased was a forest produce. The appellant filed a complaint alleging that Sandalwood Oil is not a wood oil as defined in section 2(f) (i) of the Act. The complaint was dismissed by the Magistrate holding that Sandal Wood Oil is not wood oil as contemplated under section 2(i) of The Act. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Sessions Judge. The Sessions Judge held that Sandal wood Oil is not an wood oil as envisaged under section 2 (f) (1) of the The Act. In appeal, the High Court held that Sandals Wood Oil is a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudation from living trees in the forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees while sandal wood oil is a bye product derived commercially manufacturing process. The High Court held against the appellant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'wood oil ' used in the Act is not static vehicle of ideas and concepts change, as they are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the statutory provision undergo a change. [164F] 2. The expression 'wood oil' in section 2 (k) (1), means a natural produce which includes, that is to say, the 'enumerated items in Clauses 1 and 11 'wood oil'. [164F H] 3. The word "wood oil" used in the inclusive definition of forest produce, means a natural product of the forest, directly derived as a forest produce, the oil extracted therefrom would also be within the meaning of the word 'wood Oil'. [164G] 4. The word `wood oil used in the definition of forest produces, is not static word but in an exhaustive manner, it cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the principle object and purpose of the Act, when there is nothing in the context or the subject matter to the contrary, to be applied to some things to which it would not ordinarily be applicable. [164H] 5. The expression being technical and being part of an inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense but in an inclusive manner, it can be restricted in the sense in which it is being understood in trade, business or transaction known to the trade is also inapplicable to the factual context. [164G H] 6. The word wood oil used in section 2 of the Act is also not static vehicle. [164E] 7. The expression "wood oil", in section 2, means a forest produce which includes wood oil. [164B] 8. The word Wood oil used in Section 2(k) of the Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu, like the Act, does not mean wood oil. The word is to be construed as in the context and the purpose the Act seeks to serve and the family to which sandal wool oil belongs being an essential oil would include wood oil. It must be construed in the context in which it has been used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [164C] 9.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court set aside the judgment of acquittal and convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. The High court set aside the order of acquittal. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons justifying such interference. [858 A B] The High Court has not set aside the acquittal unless there is " substantial and exceptional reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial Court. [859 C] The High court should not setaside an acquittal unless it is satisfied that there are " compelling reasons justifying interference" with the findings. [860 C] The judgment of the High Court does not disclose any such reasons justifying interference. [ 861 D] The High Courts have not set aside any acquittal unless there were " substantial and sufficient reasons justifying interference." [860 E] The High courts have not setaside the acquittal unless the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused is guilty this court would set aside the conviction. [861 E] The judgment does not disclose a such reasons justifying interfering with the findings on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused. [862 E] The evidence in the present case is of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the accused could properly be drawn. The second point on which the judgment of the trial court is set aside is the lack of compelling reasons for setting aside the judgment. [866 E] The third point on which this Court has held that the High Court should set aside an order of acquittal unless there was " substantial and cogent reasons justifying interference, as it must be disregarded in this case.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of various articles of furniture and other articles of furniture. The company was a private limited company. The appellant was a private company. The company had its factory at Jamshedpur. The company at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. The appellant Company was a private Limited Company. The company, however, was a private Company. The appellant, a private limited Company, was a company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of furniture and equipment. The appellant 's factory at Jamshedpur was a private one. The company claimed that it had amended its constitution on January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963, i.e., after the said purported amendment, the reference extended to them also and that as they were actually referred to and were actually referred, the reference was made by the Tribunal in October 1963. The appellant contended that the reference was in respect of the employees of the company wherever they may be stationed, the reference should be confined to the disputes referred to it, the parties to those disputes 'and the parties to the disputes 'and that consequently it made no difference that the name of Indoxco Labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian Oxygen Workers Union was erroneous and cannot be sustained. The Tribunal held that the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6,1963 and that as there was no dispute between the management and the workmen of the appellant company, the reference extending to them also was not justified. The appellant challenged the award on the ground that the reference in the said agreement was made in November 1963, i,e., after a period of more than 48 hours per week, 48 hours of work being the maximum provided by the Bihar Shops & Establishments Act, the company would be liable to pay at double the ordinary rate of wages as provided in that Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the reference extended beyond the period of 48 hours per day and that the reference should cover the disputes referred for adjudication. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The appellant also contended that the Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant company to grant special leave to attend the meetings of the federation and the conventions of the I.N.T.U.C. over and above the various types of leave available to the company 's workmen. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was not right in obliging it to grant special Leave to attend the meeting of the federations and the conventions. [520E] 2. The Tribunal 's award set aside. The rest of the appeal has to be allowed and the Tribunal 's order set aside. [521B] 3. The Tribunal has to be held that the Union 's constitution came to be amended as from January 6, 1964 and that consequently it making no difference that of the name of the Indian oxygen Workers Union as representing workmen concerned was included in the said contract and the said statements and not that the name was mentioned in that agreement and the statement and not the Indian Oxygen Workmen Union was erroneous. [522C] 4. The Tribunal had jurisdiction to extend the award to workmen of the company ''s factory at Jamshedpur and not to the workmen of its other establishments. [523D] 5. The Tribunal is not justified in directing the appellant company 's factory to grant special permission to attend the meet of the executive committee of the union. The Tribunal should have directed the appellant company not to grant special relief to attend the Meetings of the federating Union and the conventions and the conventions in the company ' 's factory. [524E] 6.

The assessee firm was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, in respect of income from business, inter alia, in timber at Abdullapur Depot, Simla. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939, before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 came into force. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Act. The Income tax Officer held that the firm was dissolved and on that account the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was carrying on business at the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Ordinance 7 of 1939, and that the firm alone was entitled to the benefit under section 25 (4) of that Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the business was carried on by the undivided family and that it succeeded to the business on April 1, 1939, and the business at Abdullpur in the name of R. B. Hakam Mal was settled on March 31. 1939, and on that view the assessee was not entitled to the relief under section 24(4) and to the second succession which took place on April 1. 1939. The High Court held that the partnership was dissolved on April 1 1939, and since the firm was not carrying on business, the assessee was liable to be assessed under section 25 of the Indian income tax Act, 1922, and that it was entitled to claim relief under section 26(4) read with section 25(3) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the firm Messrs Hakam Mal Tani Mal was dissolved on May 31, 1939 and on that date the business of Messrs Hakam Tani Mal became effective. Held, that the assessee had commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution of the firm Messrs bear on March 31 1939, and immediately thereafter the business of the assessee commenced. The assessee had commenced business immediately after it was brought into force and it could not be said that the business at the date of dissolution was carried on. The assessee could not be held to be carrying on business after March 31, 1988, and the firm of Messrs Hakham Mal Tani was dissolved. The assessee, therefore, was not entitled on the dissolution of that firm in March 1943 to the benefit of section 25(5) of the Income tax Act. The High court was right in holding that the assessee is entitled on the dissolved firm in March 1942 to the benefit provided in section 25(1) of the income tax Act.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Act, 1963. The appellant was a stage carriage operator. He was granted a permit under section 49 of the Act for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimoga, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal. The appeals of the respondents were allowed by the State Transport Tribunal by majority on January 29, 1969. The State Transport Appellate Tribunals had been constituted under section 64 of the Act. The appellant filed further appeals to the Mysore Revenue Tribunal against the order granting the permit. The State Government filed appeals to the State Transport appellate Tribunal against the orders of the State Government. The State of Mysore filed appeals to this Court against the order dated January 29,1969. The State Legislature passed the Mysore Motor Vehicle Rules, 1945 (old Rules) after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit. It was contended by the appellant before the appellate authorities that the Secretary to the Regional Transport authority, Shimandhar, had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the grant of permit which had already been affirmed in appeal by the State Government and further in second appeal by the Mysore Revenue appellate Tribunal against that order, the State Transport Appeal was dismissed. The State 's appeal against the order was dismissed by the Mysore High Court. The State appealed to this Court. The question that arises for consideration is whether any appeal lay under section 64(1) (a) of the Act to the State transport Appellate Tribunal constituted under section64 of the Act after a lapse period of such a short time from the commencement of the Act, to the date of grant of the permits. The question is whether any such appeal lay under Section 64(1)(a) of Act to the High Court against the issue of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Transport Committee granting the permit which had been affirmed in appeals by the State transport Tribunal and further in appeal by it. The appellant contended that the issue of the permit was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 119 of the MysoreMotor Vehicles Rules, 1945, after a lapseof such a long period from the date on which the grant of a permit was made. The appellant also contended that the question of the validity of the permit had not been raised before the appellate authority and the High Court was not right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed. The State, however, contended that the point of time for the issue of permit was made within the prescribed period under rule 119. The appellant submitted that the issue was made beyond a period of limitation prescribed under rule 119 and that the issue had been made beyond the period of limitation. The State contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction in dismissing the appeal of the respondents which ought to be allowed. The appellant further contended that the appeal of respondents was not competent under section 64 (1) (briefly the Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to the various authorities Appeal is a creature of the statute. There was, therefore, a clear error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunals in interfering with the grant granting of the permit which has already been affirmed by the State. The High Court was, therefore not right in rejecting the writ application. The appeal is allowed. The order of the High Court is set aside and necessarily the order of State Transport Appellate. Tribunal of January 29, 1968 and the order of this Court dated January 29. 1969 and the order dated February 27, 1967, also fall. The order granting the permits to the appellant stands restored.

The appellant, who was the auction purchaser for delivery of possession of the property auctioned by him was resisted by the respondents. The respondents filed a suit for delivery of the property sold by him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that in view of Article 136 of the . the provisions of the Limitation Act, the application for delivery of posses sion having been made within one year of the dismissal of the second application for setting aside the sale on the ground of fraud was not maintainable and not barred by limitation. The respondents preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and held that in view o Article 136 of . the Limitation Act the application for settingaside the sale on grounds of fraud was maintainable and not from the date of the first confirmation. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sale became absolute after the sale was confirmed, and the decree holder auction purchaser for possession of the land auctioned purchased by him was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sale becomes absolute only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 92, and that apart from the provisions of Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the Code, an application for setting setting aside the auction sale can also be made within a period of 12 years from the date o f the decree irrespective of the date of sale, which is absurd on the face of it. [620G H] 2. The sale become absolute after the disposal of the application on July 21, 1979, it should be held that the application was quite within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 136 of t he Limitation Act. [621B] 3. The sale became absolute on the dis missal of the application of the judgment debtor 's claim for setting aside sale on the dismissal of the second applications for setting aside t he sale on the grounds of fraud. [622C] 4. The application for setting set aside the sale was within the period prescribed by Article 134 of the Limitation Ac ture by Article 134. [623D] 5. The application was not one as contemplated by Rules 89,90 or 91 of the Code. [624B] 6. The application of the 4th judgment debtor for setting aside auction sale on the basis of fraud was made after the sale became complete on the dis tsal of the applications of the 4 th judgment debtor ' s claim for settingaside sale on the plea of fraud was raised after the sale being confirmed. [626E] 7. The application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable, and the period of Limitation as prescribed by article 136 of the LimitationAct cannot be computed from the date when the application for set aside the auction purchaser was confirmed. [726F] 8. The application filed by the appellant for setting aside a sale on the su ch question of fraud was within the limitation as prescribed under Article 136 of , the application for taking possession of the properties sold in execution of a decree was not maintainable; and the period for setting aside such sale was within one year from the date on which the sale was made. [627G] 9. The application seeking delivery of possession was within the time prescribed by Article 137 of the Limitation C ourt. [628G] 10. The application is not one as envisaged by Rule 92, but was within the prescribed period of limitation. [629G] 11. The application made by the appellant was within the statutory period of limitation prescribed by Article 138 of the Limitation c ourt.

The appellant 's election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14 was declared void on the ground that the said wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant 's Election agent. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari to quash the election of the appellant to the Kerala Assembly from Mulamcherry Constituency No P 14 and P 15, the High Court held that the said poster was pasted in a wall at Mattancherry constituency No. P. 14 and P. 15, the appellant ' s election agent. The High Court held on the basis of the evidence of the witnesses that the appellant had taken the photographs in question on 25th and 26th March, 1987, that the wall poster was affixed on a wall near the wall poster and that it did so. The High court also held that the publication was intended to create an impression and did create an impression that the incident of murders had taken place a day prior to the election. The appellant challenged the election of his election agent on the ground of corrupt practice under section 123(4) of the Act on the ground, that the said posters were affixed on a walls at the instance of the appellant with his knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition, and that it was not possible to prove that the incident had taken place the previous day. The High 'Court held that the appellant ' 's case was that the publication of the poster in question was intended to creating an impression and had created an impression and do create an impression which the appellant had stated in his examina tion. The HighCourt also held that in a libel action it may not be necessary to prove that those with special knowledge of the extrinsic facts were likely to interpret or understand the words complained of in a defama tory sense in an election action, it may not, be necessary to do so and all that is necessary is to prove that such words were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's election. The High "Court further held that the publications were intended to create a impression and did creating an impression that it did not believe to be true in relation to the personal character or conduct of any candidate or in relation to his candidature or with drawal, of any candidate, being a statement reasonably calculated to prejudiced the prospectus of that candidate 's Election. The appellant was also held to be guilty of the corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The contents of this wall poster directly named the first respondent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the said newspaper was affixed prior to the Election, it is difficult to understand as to how this witness had taken the photograph in question on the said days, that is necessary to prove the fact that the said pamphlet was intended to created an impression or understanding that the incident was likely to interpret the words complained in a defma tory sense, in an election actions, it may be necessary to produce evidence to prove that it did something more. [775F] 2. The contents in this wall poster along with exhibit P 1 being pasted near the wall posters together with exhibit P1 being pasted one week prior to the filing of the present election petition. The appellant had also in his examinatiOn in chief gone to the extent of saying that it was the appellant himself who along with his election agent and other workers had gone to his residence to deliver the said copy. The appellant has also in his examination in chief had stated that he had not seen the wall poster together with exhibit p 1.

The appellant union was a registered trade union. The appellant union was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of goods and allied products. The appellant was a registered Trade Union. The appellant company was a registered union. The workmen were employed in the appellant company. The appellant raised an industrial dispute. The Industrial Court held that the appellant was guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out and had thus committed unfair labour practice. The appellant contended that the employer had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continuing lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Act. The Industrial Judge held that the employer was not guilty of imposing or continuing a lockout or has closed down the business. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the award on the ground that the Industrial Court had not properly considered the evidence produced before it and that the Industrial Judge had not properly appreciated the evidence produced by the employer. The High court dismissed the writ Petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Industrial Court while rejecting the complaints filed by the appellant union which does not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, must consider all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practice and must ascertain on evidence produced before them whether the closure was a device or pretence to determine 69 the services of the workmen. [671G H] 1.2 The true test is that when it is claimed that the employer is not guilty of imposes a lockout but has closed down his business, the industrial court before which the action of the employer is questioned must keep in view all the relevant facts at the time when closure is a bonafide one or was a device to a pretence to determine whether the closure is a device or a pretence to decide whether the employer has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device or pretext to determine69 the services of workmen. [681A] 1.3 The true test would be that when it was claimed that the employee has resorted to lock out or has closed the industrial activity, the industrial Court before which the actions of the employer are questioned must keep In view all the facts at the relevant time, the Industrial Court before which an action of the employee is questioned must keeping in view all relevant circumstances at that time of closure. [682A B] 1.4 The true test should be that when the employer is claiming that the employer has resort to closure, fide bonafide wants to retocate the industrial activity and that as resumption of production is gradually expanded and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer at the time the closure but is not decisive of the matter. To accept the view taken by the Industrial Court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closing down the industrial activity will be re inducted in service. [683F] 1.5 The true test was that when it has been claimed that the workmen employed by him had not been in previous employment with them without giving first preference to the workmen who were in service of the two concerns on April 8, 1980, will be a significant circumstance to determine the true intention and bonability of the employer.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company, the objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cl. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The assessee company was a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties. The assessee Company was incorporated on June 29, 1924, as an investment undertaking, the objects set out in the memorandum of Association and more particularly the three items of that clause were set out in cl. 2, 15, and 16 of the memorandum. The assessee claimed to be a dealer in investments and properties. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee company on the ground that the assessee company was not a dealer in investment and securities and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities, immovable properties and immovable properties of the assessee Company could be taxed as business profits. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was a dealer and not an investor according as it incurred losses or made profits and that the income arising from the sales of shares, security and immovable properties could be taxed only as business profits and not as business profits, and that the assessee Company was a dealer. The High Court held that the question as to whether the profits and gains arising from the selling of shares, bonds and immovable properties were business profits was a mixed question of fact and law and that the question was a mixed one of fact and fact and was a mixed questions of fact and Law. The High court also held that the Appellate Tribunal was not competent on the questions as framed at the time of the hearing of the reference. The assessee appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business of dealing in shares and investments and properties and whether as a result thereof the assessee could be termed a dealer or an investor was itself a question of pure fact. [520 E] (2) The question whether the profits or losses arising from sale of shares are business profits or not is a mixed question between fact and law. [521 B] (3) The question is whether the profits arising from the transfer of shares, shares, securities or immovable properties of E.D. It is because the question involved in this case was not a question of mixed question of law and that this Court allowed the appeal on the last occasion and set aside the judgment of the High Court. [522 C] (4) The question of whether the profits & losses arising from sales of shares and securities and immovable property of the assessee companies can be taxed as income profits is a mixed questions between fact and laws and that this question was a question of fact.

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On June 19, 1951, the appellant was posted as District Munsif, and on July 19, 1951 he was posted in the office of the Subordinate Judge, Masulipatam, Krishna District, and on August 12, 1954, he was transferred to the office. On August 12, 1951, he was promoted to that post. On August 13, 1954, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds, firstly that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953, with effect from October 1, 1953, the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same and that the proceedings of the High Court were without jurisdiction, and secondly, that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the High court dated January 28 1954, was in contravention to article 311 of Constitution and was in contravention o article 311 of that Constitution. HELD: (1) The order passed by the High Court on January 28, 1953, by the High court on January 28 1954 was merely one of suspension pending enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e) against the Members of the State Judicial Service. [475 C] (2) The order of suspension made by the High Curt on January 28. 1954, was merely one one of suspension Pending enquiry into grave charge under rule 17 (e) against a Member of the State Legislature. [476 D] (3) The order was merely one and not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of, the Constitution. [478 E] (4) The order dated January 28. 1953, by which the enquiry against the appellant was started, runs as follows: " The Government shall subject to the provisions of rule 5, refer the cases of all. disciplinary cases in which the Government propose to pass orders rejecting such appeal or petition. " The order passed on January 28; 1954, is merely one of dismissal and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service. [466 F] (5) The order made by the Government on January 28,. 1954, is only one of suspension, pending enquiry into serious charges under rule 16(e) and such an action is neither one or dismissal nor removal of the appellant from service within Article 311 of the constitution. [412 E] (6) The order in question is merely one one. It is merely one. It does not mean that the order was one of dismissal. [413 E] (7) The order is merely one and it does not mean dismissal or removal of the Government servant within article 311. [415 F] (8) The order does not mean removal or dismissal from service within the meaning of article 311. The order does mean dismissal or termination of service within the ambit of article 311, and it does mean dismissal. [404 C] (8)(a) The order merely gives an indication that the order is one of dismissal, and does not mean termination of service. [404 D] (9) The order, therefore, does not mean the termination of service of the appellant.

The appellant company was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company a private Limited Company with its registered office in Bombay died on May 13, 1945, having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The obligation to pay the tax on the dividend so deemed to be distributed is of the shareholder, and the general provision in section 24B for enforcement of liability against the legal representative of a deceased person to pay tax which would have been payable if such person had not died, has a limited application. The legal personality of Gannon as held in Amarchand Shroff 's case(1) came to an end for the purpose of section 24B at the end of the account year in which the income was to be deemed to have been received by the legal representatives of the deceased person. The legal representative of the deceased was, therefore, liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased, Amarchand Shroff. The appellant company was assessed to income tax in the relevant assessment year, and the tax on dividend so deemed was paid by the legal representative after his death in that previous year became assessable to income tax. The appellant contended that the tax on dividends deemed to be payable by the legal heirs and legal representatives of a deceased shareholder in the hands of his legal representative when the order of the Income tax Officer pursuant to which the income is to be deemed as distributed is of a capital nature and that the tax was payable by the deceased person for the purpose for assessment in regard to those years. Held, that the tax assessed on dividend was not a capital receipt and the tax was not payable by the assessee in the hands it was not payable. The tax was payable on the income received by a legal representative which would have be deemed to be the income of the deceased. The legal status of Gannon Dunkerley as held in [ Amarchand Shroff]'s case(2) was not extended to the end of that year, but was only in respect of those years. The legal fiction created by the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953, with effect from April 1, 1952, was not extended by the Income Tax Act, 1922, with effectfrom April 1,1952, and the Legislature had not provided that the income received before his death and received by the deceased assessee before his death in the course of which such notional income must be deemed to had been received by him or his legal representatives after the expiry of the year in which such notional Income must be deemed. The Legislature has not provided that in the absence of appropriate provisions, for collecting tax from the estate after the expiry, of the year, the expression "any tax which would having been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" cannot be deemed to include the income received after the expiry date of the account in which such person died. The Legislature had not made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the legal Representatives of the deceased assessee. The Legislature was not having made any provision either generally for assessment or levy of tax in respect of such deemed income from the estate of a deceased. The Legislature did not have made any provision in the Act in support of the contention, and merely asserted that the Act seeks to tax all assessable incomes, and income received by the assessee before his lifetime, was to be regarded as extended to the rest of the year. The Legislature cannot supply it. The Legislature having not provided that it would not be deemed to has supplied the machinery for taxation of income received by legal representative to the estate after its expiry, the Legislature has not made any provisions generally for assessment and levy of tax on the dividends deemed to have be regarded for the purpose.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant was the Ruler of the Madhya Pradesh. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 and 227 on the ground that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owners of the villages mentioned in Schedules A, B and C of his petition. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground of limitation. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the villages mentioned therein were not assessed to land revenue but no evidence had been led to this effect. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler and as he was also a maufidar he fell within the definition of the word 'proprietor ' in the Act. The appellant had given no evidence to establish that the villages in question were not assessed, that he had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in his villages. The High court rightly held that the appellant had given any evidence to establish the fact whether the villages had been assessed to land Revenue but no evidence was led to this. The question whether the villages mentioned were not assessed was one by which the appellant was treated as an ex Ruler. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant could not conceivably be a mauffidar. The question is whether the appellant was a mauafidar and as he had given no proof to establish that he had any right to recover rents or revenue from person holding land in such villages. The question of fact whether the village was held by him as a maufaidar or as a mahafidar was not a question of fact, whether the villages in dispute were not assessed or land revenue but only a question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution and for the purposes of the privy purse guaranteed, the appellant was not a maufi village.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. The respondent submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. tie complained that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong for a longer period, have been allowed to continue at Shillong. The Tribunal quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: (i) The respondent is liable to transfer anywhere in India; (ii) The order of transfer is an incident of Government Service. Fundamental Rule 11 says that "the whole time of a Government servant is at the disposal of the Government which pays him and he may be employed in any manner required by proper authority". The only thing required is that the departmental authorities should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any place in India, subordinating the need of the couple living together at one place without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employees, the Court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued by the Central Government on the subject. The only thing necessary is that the Departmental authorities should consider the same having regard to the exigencies of the administration. The only reason required is that they should consider this factor along with the urgency of administration and allow the posting of both at one place. If such an order is questioned in a Court or the Tribunal, the authority is obliged to justify the transfer by adducing the reasons therefor. The only difficulty required is that if such an order was questioned in a court or the Tribunal itself, the authority should consider the matter having regard to its exigencies and transfer policy do not permit the posting of either at one place nor without sacrifice of any of the requirements. After giving preferences to the career prospect by accepting such an promotion or any appointments in an all Indian service, subordinatingthe need of the other employees, it subordinating the necessity of the posting of two spouses to reside together at one Station, if it is feasible. After giving weightage to the career advancement by accepting such promotion or any employment in an all country service, subordinated the need of each of the couple lived together at one point, without sacrifice of their requirements and the claim for such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. After having said so the learned Member recorded the following finding: "In view of the above facts and circumstances and findings it is held unhesitatingly that the transfer order No. An order of transfer made by the Senior administrative Officer (competent authority) is vitiated by malafides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions. The only question required is that whether the Court or the Administrative Tribunal can quash the order of the transfer, if any of the administrative instructions/guidelines are not followed, much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. The only answer to this question is that the Court or Tribunal can quash it.
