The Banking Companies Act, 1949, was enacted by the British Parliament. The Banking Companies Act was a special law enacted by the Indian Legislature. The Banking companies Act was a general law enacted by Parliament for India. The Banking Corporations Act was a `special Indian law '. The Banking Corporation Act was a Special Indian law. The Banking Company Act was a 'special Indian law' and the Banking Companies Act is a special Indian law. It was, therefore, a special Indian Act. The Banking company Act was a "special Indian law " and not as a piece of special legislation applicable to India. The appellant Bank was constituted by or under a special Indian Law. The Banking Bank Act was a law made by the British Legislature. The banking companies Act was enacted by Parliament of the United Kingdom. The Banking Banks Act was a selfcontained Code. The Banking Banking Companies Act which was a special Indian statute was a special Act. The appellant bank was constituted by the British Government. The Banking Tribunal was constituted under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 and not under the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1969. The Banking Tribunals Act was a new Act. The banking Companies Act was an Act to protect the British economic interests and although such a law could permissibly be enacted under the Constitutional Scheme of the 1953 Government of India Act, that law after the inauguration of our Sovereign Democratic Republic cannot but be held in view of the setting that the expression `special Indian Law ' refers or relates to a law made under the Constitution. The Banking Courts Act was a piece of Special Indian law and the provisions of section 4(e) of the Act were applicable to the appellant Bank. The Banking corporations Act was a comprehensive Act. The Act was a consolidating and consolidating Act. The provisions of the Act, as it stood on the day the Act was passed, were not applicable to the appellants Bank and, therefore, there was no question of scaling down the debt due to the Bank by the respondents. The Banking tribunals Act was a complete Code. The appellant Banks were constituted by the Central Government under section 4(1) of the Banking Companies Acts Act, 1949. The Banking Disputes Act was a central Act. The Reserve Bank of India Act was a Central Act. The Central Government was empowered to make regulations for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the said Act. The regulations were made by the Central Board of Directors of the Banking companies. The Banking Regulations Act, 1949 was a special enactment. The Banking Regulation Act was a part of the Act. The Indian Parliament was a special statute. The Banking Act was a separate and comprehensive Act. It was a special one. The Banking Universities Act was a composite one. The Act of 1949 was a general Act. The Parliament of the State of West Bengal was a special legislation. The Banking Laws Act was a specific Act. The State Legislature was a special code. The Banking Institutions Act was a code. The Act did not apply to a corporation which was created under a special law. The Act, therefore, did not apply. The Banking Acts Act was a different and comprehensive one. The appellant banks were constituted by or on behalf of the Bank under the Ordinance XII of 1969 and were not under the banking Companies Act. The Bank was formed by or under and not under a specialIndian law. The Bank, therefore, was not a corporation within the meaning of section 4 of the Act and, therefore there was no occasion for laying down that the expression 'special Indian Law' in section 4(a) of the said act shall apply to corporations formed or created by any special Indian law which, in the instant case, is the Banking Companies.

The petitioners were manufacturing sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioners were manufacturing the sugar in the country. The petitioners contended that the impugned notification was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners also contended that the fixation of ex factory prices was arbitrary and did not take into account the cost of production of a large number of units in the country and did not provide for a fair price for the ultimate consumer which must be done under the Act. The petitioners alleged that the impugned notifications were violative of article 19 (1) (g) inasmuch as the impugned notification did not fix ex factory prices and was not issued under the Act and clause 5 of the Order, and that the impugned Notification was still bad as it failed to fix ex factory price. The petitioners further contended that the notification was not issued by the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and that the Government was not competent to fix exfactory prices of sugar in the areas in which the factories were compelled to sell their products. The petitioners submitted that the impugned Act was violative of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution and that the notification did not authorise the Central Government to fix ex-factory prices of the factories in the other areas. The petitioners, however, contended that the Act and the Order do not authorise the Government to fix the ex factory prices of sugar under the Act, and that even if ex factory prices can be fixed, the impugned notification is still bad as the Government had no power to fix ex factories prices. The petitioners relied on the decision of this Court in the case of [The State of Uttar Bharat vs The State of Uttar Prades, ; , and contended that the Government had power to fix the price of sugar in any way related to the price at which the factories in other areas were compelled to buy their products. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification merely fixes ex factory prices, and is bad as it fails to fix wholesale and retail prices. [135 E] 2. The object of the Act is to secure equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair price. The object is to secure fair price for all the consumer. It does not follow from this that the object of the impugned Act is to ensure a fair price to the consumer. There is, therefore, in our opinion no discrimination between the fixation of prices in these three regions and the contention that the factories in these three areas are left uncontrolled with the result that there is discrimination after the control of sugar 136 prices in these two regions is specious and does not merit a moment 's consideration. [135 F] 3. The object sought to be achieved by fixing the wholesale or retail price is specious. It does no follow from this, that if fair price for a factory is fixed, the price all over India is practicalLy fixed, and it is not necessary to fix wholesale or retail prices. It does neither follow from this it nor is there anything in the press note that the object can only be achieved if retail prices are fixed at what they were either in the week before June 27, 1958 or in the last week of May, 1958, or in the Last week of May. [135 G] 4. The object for the Act is not to secure fair prices for the consumer, there is no reason why the Government should go on further to fix wholesale, or retail prices, and if fair prices for them would not even meet the cost of Production. [135 C] 5. The impugned Notification merely fixes exfactory prices and is bad, firstly on the ground that there is no reasonable basis for such clasSification ; factories in other parts of India are left uncontrolled without the result that the prices fixed by the Government by the impugned notification cannot be said to have been proved to be below the cost of producing.

The Company was a registered trade union. The workmen of the Company were employed in the Company. The Company was a private limited company. The workmen were employed in a private limited Company. The workmen raised an industrial dispute. The Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index stood at 344.1 and that the working classes cost of living Index stood at 400.6. The Tribunal also held that the said award was binding between the parties and that the Tribunal was wrong in law. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, for ascertaining the working class costs of living index since August 1954 up to March 1957. [696 H; 696 A] (2) The Tribunal rightly relied upon Exhibit 4, corrected on that basis. The Tribunal wrongly relying upon Exhibit 3 and corrected on the ground that there was a fall in the rate of working class cost. [697 B] (3) The Tribunal erroneously relied upon Exhibit 2, corrected on a basis of the data given by the Government Statistical Bureau,West Bengal, for determining the working class of the workmen. The Tribunal rightly held that the work class cost of working index stood at 343.1. and it rose to 400.6 in May 1957. [600 C] (4) The Tribunal erred in law in holding that the working of the Company was at 344. 1. [698 C] (5) The Tribunal was wrong, in law, in holding that there was no fall in the cost of living between dearness allowance and the corresponding entries in regard to the working class expenses of living index. [699 D] (6) The Tribunal failed to appreciate that the working staff cost of living was at 344 and the corresponding entry in regard to that work was the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial increase in the working classcost of living index by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis that the rise in the cost index by dearness allowances could not be allowed and therefore allowed they only 75 per% of the increase of dearness allowance towhich they would have had otherwise been entitled. [695 E] (7) The Tribunal had wrongly relied upon the document Exhibit 3, which showed that the working day of the agreement was the crucial date for ascertaining whether the working class was the crucial part of the working class. [692 E] (8) The Tribunal correctly relied upon Exhibit 5, corrected on June 21, 1951, with the result that there was an increase of 56 points, a substantial rise in the price index by dearness Allowance could not be granted and therefore allowed the workmen only 75 per percentage. [693 B] (9) The Tribunal also erred in law by holding that the Tribunal wrongly relied on Exhibit 3, and corrected on that ground. [694 C] (10) The Tribunal has erred in law, by holding that there were no substantial increase in working class cost by dearness allowance. [690 C] (11) The Tribunal, in law has erred in holding that in regard to matters covered by it, the Tribunal wrongly relying on Exhibit 3 and the corrected on the footing that there was substantial change in the working classes of the menial class. [600 D] (12) The Tribunal should have taken into account the fact that the working capital index was at 344,1, and not at the same rate as the working class in the company.

The appellant was a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The appellant was appointed under the scheme framed under the Madras Act 11 of 1927 (hereinafter called 'the Act '). The appellant challenged the validity of the scheme on the ground that it deprives him of his fundamental right under article 19(1)(f) and as such, invalid. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the scheme having been framed as early as 1939 under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act, could not be challenged on the ground of violation of fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens of this country under article 19. Held, that the scheme was framed as early in 1939 and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1940. The scheme was framed under the provisions of the Act and re frame them so as to make them consistent with the said provisions. The scheme having been made as early as 1948, it was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity of its scheme on the grounds that it deprives the appellant of his fundamental rights under article 19 (1)(f). The scheme was not in accordance with the provisions of this latter Act. The scheme had been framed as soon as it was framed and the Executive officer was appointed as soon as the scheme was made. The scheme could not be questioned on the ground, that it deprives a citizen of his property rights. The scheme, therefore, was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the earlier Act. The appellant 's writ petition should not be entertained because he had a definite adequate alternative remedy under the latter Act, and that the plea was rejected by the High Court with the observation that the scheme had been validly framed. The scheme framed under section 63 of the Act was not in consonance with the provisions in the latter Act.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in the school on July 12, 1982. The appellant was appointed on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. The appellant continued to serve as Hindi Teacher but no action was taken by the said authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teacher with effect from July 12,1982. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act. The appellant preferred an appeal before this Court. The only argument raised before the High Court was that the appellant is still continuing to serve as a Hindi teacher in the school with effect from January 1, 1986. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant continues to serve as the Hindi teacher in a substantive vacancy because of the Validation act. The High court rejected the prayer of the appellant for regularisation and directed the respondents to treat the appellant as regularly appointed Hindi Teacher. The appellant challenged the judgment of the High Court before this Court in a writ petition. The appellant contended that the appellant had been appointed regularly and he continued to serve till the 31st December, 1984 save for misconduct or. The High ' Court rejected the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred in denying the benefit of retrospective appointment to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [319D] 1.2 The High Court was right in denying the benefits of the Validation Acts to the appellant. [321B] 1.3 The number of teachers in the State of Orissa who are thus appointed regularly, they would have been entitled to the benefits of summer vacation along with the salary and allowances payable in respect of that period and to all other privileges such as casual leave, medical leave, maternity leave etc. available to all the Government servants. The policy of `ad hocism ' followed by the State Government for a long period has led to the breach of Article 14 of the Constitution. [322C] 1.4 The number of teacher in the State Of Orissa who are now appointed regularly, are very large indeed. If the teachers had been appointed continuously, they would, have been entitled, to the benefits Of summer vacation alongwith the salary and allowance payable in respect thereof. [323D] 1:5 The number of Teachers in the State is very large indeed,. If the teacher had been appointed validly, he would have been eligible to the benefits. [324E] 1.6 The number of posts in the State Government of Orissa who were thus appointed regularly and they would have continued until replaced by the candidate from the selected list. [424F] 1.7 The number of teaching community who are thus employed on such ad hoc basis is very large. If the Teachers had been appointed temporarily, they would be entitled to the privileges of summer vacation as long as they hold the office under the orders of the managing Committee. [425F] 1:8 The number of post in the State and the number of teachers therein are denied the salary and other allowances payable in regard to that period and the period of the summer vacation. [426G] 1.9 The number of employees in the State are large indeed. The number of vacancies in the State, who are thus selected, is very large large indeed. [428G] 1:10 The number of appointments in the State have led to the violation of Article 14. The number is very large enough indeed.

The appellant was elected as a member of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The respondent was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samitis and the ground of disqualification was based on rules 3 to 7. The appellant was the Chairman and Member of a Panchayat Parishad and the ground was based on Rule 3 to 7, which are as follows : "3. The Chairman, Vice Chairman and Members shall not be entitled to mileage allowance under clause (b) unless the journey for such work or supervision has been approved by the Panchayat Samiti or Zila Parishad, as the case may be, and the number of Members deputed for supervision does not exceed five on any one day. The payment of mileage allowance to a Chairman, ViceChairman and Members for the purposes and journeys mentioned in rule 5 shall be regulated as follows : (i) Mileage allowance by rail. (ii) Mileages allowance by rail." The appellant was a member of the Panchayat Samiti and was disqualified from becoming a member of Panchayat Samiti. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the appellant 's election. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 6 of the Rules did not convert the office of Chairman of a panchayat Samiti into an office of profit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : 1. The appellant has failed to establish that out of the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman would in fact make a sense of pecuniary gain to a Chairman of a society. [723C] 2. The appellant failed to establish the fact that out of his payment received as daily allowances the Chairman will in fact make an investment in the funds of the Panchayat Samitis or Zila Parishad as the case might be, within the district, including attending of meeting, supervision of plans, projects, schemes and other works and also for 'the discharge of all lawful obligations and implementation of Government directives. [724E] 3. The appellant had failed to establish any such allegation. The appellant could not establish that out Of the amount received the Chairman would work out of the payment to him of daily allowance. [725B] 4. The appellant is not entitled to mileages allowance under r. 3 to 7 because, in our opinion, the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under rules 3 and 7 of the Rules does not convert the post of Chairman of the Panchayat Parishad into an office or profit. [726C] 5. The appellant having failed to establish, that out of Rs. 3 of the rules received by a Chairman for travelling allowance or daily allowance is in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for 'the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties, the Chairman must be making gain out of the payments to him of the daily allowance. The payment, therefore, cannot be held to be in addition to the payment of the consolidated monthly allowance under r 3 to 7 made the office an office of profits. [727D] 6. The appellant, having failed to prove that out of this amount received as monthly allowance the Chairman will, in fact, make a saying, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office an Office of profit. [827E] 7. The payment received by a member for travelling allowance and Daily allowance under rs. 3 to 6 shall be regulated in accordance with the provisions of r. 3. [828B] 8.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The respondents filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the partition wall in the hall did not constitute material alteration as the construction was likely substantially to diminish its value substantial ly, the landlord was free to file suit for eviction without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate but the tin shed marked with letters CDGH had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin sheds marked with letters ABHG had been constructed without respondents consent, which materially altered the accommodation and on that finding the trial court decreed the suit. The appellant filed an appeal before the District Judge who decreed the suit, but the High Court reversed the findings of the trial court and decreed the suit in favour of the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether the construction was sub stantial in nature and they could be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation. [77 A B] 1.2 The High Court committed error in interfering in the findings of facts recorded by the trial court on the question of 'material alteration '. The High Court in second appeal interfered with the findings recorded by the First Appellate Court on the question as to whether the constructions materially alter the accommodation or not. The High court committed error in interfere with the findings on the question regarding 'material alteration'. [77 A C] 1.3 The High Court while interfering with the finding of fact recorded on the question, whether the constructions were temporary in nature, did not consider whether the constructions had been made with the consent or of the land lord and if so whether whether those constructions are of such substantial nature which make material alterations in the accommodation. The High Curt also committed error in interference with the findings. [77 B] 1:4 The High Court has committed error in not interfering with the conclusions of the First Appellate court on the questions whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alteration in the accommodation, and on that findings the High Court committed an error in interfering therewith. [77 C] 1:5 The High Court also committed error of law in interfering with findings of fact. [77 D] 1.6 The High Court erred in interfering with those findings of fact on the question. [77 E] 1.7 The High Court failed to consider that the partition walls did not change the front or structure of the accommodation, it being temporary in nature. The nature of constructions, whether they are permanent or temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of "material alteration". The nature and character of constructions, if any, which make material alteration in a building does not affect the question as regards whether the constructions are sub stanital in nature and the character of the constructions and the extent to which they make changes in the structure of the building. [77 F] 1.8 The nature of construction, whether they be permanent or temporary is a relevant factor in determining the questions of 'material alterations '. The nature, character of the construction and the extent of construction, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out to the tenant. The nature o f construction, whether it is temporary or temporary, are relevant consideration in deciding the question of the 'material alteration'. The nature Of constructions, whether it be temporary or permanent, is a crucial consideration in determining whether the constructions have been made with due permission of the landlord and if such construction is of such nature and character as to materially alter the structure or not.

The respondent firm filed a suit against the appellant company for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Trial Court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975 about the passing of the ex parte decree on 29 8 1975. The High Court allowed the revision, set aside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of ex parte decree. The appellant company filed an appeal before this Court. The question for consideration was whether the summons in the case was duly served on a person who is entitled to be served on behalf of the company in accordance with sub clause (a) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of C.P.C. The High court held that the summons in question was not duly serving on the company. The High ' Court held that the service of summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 4 of the Code was not valid service of summons on the respondent. The High "Court further held that the appellant company had no knowledge of the exparte decree even otherwise, before 29 7 1975. The appellant had filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code for setting aside the ex parte order. The HighCourt allowed the appeal, set aside that order and restored that of the Trial court. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in holding that since Navlakha was an employee of the company sitting in its registered office in Calcutta the summons will be deemed to have been duly served on it within the meaning of the first part. [723C] 1.2 The words "Principal Officer" in clause (b), of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. The meaning of clause (a), has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons upon natural persons. [724E] 1.3 The meaning of the word "Principal Officer " in clause (a)(a) of Order 5 would include managing agent and it can be on a corporate person. [725B] 1.4 The meaning of "partly" in clause(b) of Order 2 would include Managing agents and it cannot, under this Rule, be on juristic person. [761G] 1.5 The meaning of word "Principal " in clause(a) of Section 2 would include the managing agents and the it can, by no stretch of imagination, be regarded as due service on the defendant. [726C] 1:6 The meaning of words "Principal officer" in clause 2 would include management agents and it is not necessary to refer to the definition of "Principal Officer". [726D] 1.7 The meaning of expression "Principal Officer", in clause (c) of Section 3 of the Code, would include managing agency and it can also be on a legal person. [758G] 1:8 The meaning of 'partly" would include managing agencies and it would be on a juridical person. [759E] 1:9 The meaning of phrase "partly " in clause 2 of Section 3 would include managing managing agents and also it would be deemed to be service on the company itself.

The appellant was the owner of the land in dispute. The respondents filed a suit for a declaration that the appellant was in possession of the land and that the Magistrate passed the final order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of that land. The appellant filed a written statement and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145 the Magistrate passed an order on 17 July, 1978 directing the parties to file their written statements and then after an enquiry as provided in section 145 the respondents to file their statements and then thereafter after a full inquiry as provided by Section 145 the Magistrate called upon the parties to submit their written statements. The Magistrate passed the order on 17 August, 1978 declaring that the appellant to stand in possession of land in dispute and that the respondents were in possession of it. The appellant challenged the order of the Magistrate before the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. The High court held that the final order of the magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that there was an apprehension of breach of peace existed at the time when the order was passed. The High ' Court, however, allowed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the final decision of the Magistrate was vitiated in view of the fact that there was no finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was a breach of the peace existed at that time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in holding that the final orders of the Magistrate were vitiated in absence. [723C] 1.2 The High Court erred in holding that there was breach of the law laid down by the two parties. [724D] 1.3 The High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, would not go into the question of sufficiency of material which has satisfied the Magistrate in his final order. [725E] 1.4 The enquiry under section 145 is limited to the 95 question to which the satisfaction of the Magistrate is based. The enquiry under Section 145 is limited only to the 95 questions to which the Magistrate is satisfied that at the time of passing the final order the apprehension of breach exists. [726F] 1.5 The enquiry under sub section (1) is limited to a 95 question to whom the opinion of the Magistrate has satisfied the requirements of sub section (5) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [727C] 1:6 The Magistrate has to pass a preliminary order under sub section(5) of Section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code, assume jurisdiction only if he is satisfied that there is a breach of peace. [728G] 1.7 The enquiry under s 145 is limited in the sense that he has not to record a finding again about the existence of a dispute likely to cause a breach of a peace. [828A] 1.8 The enquiry under the section is limited to that extent only. The enquiry is limited to those cases where there is no clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section(1) of section145 of the Code. [729B] 1.9 The enquiry under sections 145 is limited by the words "of the peace" and "of the dispute having ended so as to enable the Magistrate to exercise his revisional jurisdiction". [729C] 1 1.10 The enquiry under that section is limited only if he has satisfied on these two conditions the section requires him to pass a final order under sub Section (5) and thereafter to make an enquiry under sub Section It is not necessary that at the stage of passing the preliminary order the apprehension should continue or exist.

The appellant was a resident of the State of Bombay. He was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and was assessed to tax under the Act. The Income tax Officer, however, rejected the appellant 's contention that the transactions were benami for the purpose of section 14(2) (c) and that the profits could be taxed only if they were remitted to British India. The Appellate Tribunal held that the transactions did not fall within the ambit of section 14 (2) (a) and that section was not applicable to nonresidents and consequently rejected the appellant's contention. The Tribunal held that section 14(1) (c), and section 42(3) applied both to nonresident persons and consequently rejected his contention. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the transactions in question did not fall under section 14(3) (c). The High Court, however, held that the decision of the Tribunal was not correct in law. The appellant contended that the decision in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co.(1) was not correct. Held, that the decision was not correct, and that the decision did not lay down any law. The decision of the High Court in Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay vs Ahmadbhai Umarbhai & Co.(2) was not even so much as referred to in the (1) (2) 710 (3) (b) (c); and that the High Court was right in rejecting the appellant ' 's contention. The decision in Commissioner Of Income tax, Madras vs Ahmedbhai Ahmedbhai Umarubhai and Co.(2), was not even a question of law which could be referred to the court under section 66(1). The decision of this Court in Commissioner Of Incometax, Bombay v Ahmedbhai Umarabhai and Co.(3) was not a decision of the Court under section 66 (1). The only point for determination was whether the finding of the Commissioner was correct in law or whether it was perverse. The decision was not a pure question of law. The only point was whether the Tribunal had found that the intermediaries, firms and companies were benamidars for the appellant, that a question of benami was one of mixed law and fact and that therefore a finding of fact was a question of fact or of law according as the point for determination is one of pure (1) [1955] 2 S.C.R. 869. (2) [1955) 2 S. C.R. 969. (3) [1955 1 S.C R. 869, 969.

The assessee was a partner in a firm of which the assessee was a Director. The assessee was a director. The assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager of the firm. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of deduction on the ground that the amount of Rs. 70,465 paid to the assessee was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income Tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount was laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business and therefore the commission paid to Shri Vaish was not an amount laidout or expended wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of business. The Appellate Tribunal held that the commission paid was not an expenditure laid out or incurred wholly or exclusively exclusively for the purpse of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Commissioner held that in the circumstances of the case, the amount of commission paid to him was not an allowable deduction. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who by his order, dated October 31, 1949 found that Rs. 75465 was an amount laying out or expended entirely for the purboSe of business, trade or profession as required under Section 10(2) (xv) of Income Tax Act. The Appellate Appellate Tribunal held against the assessee. The High Court held that the payment was not real or that it was not laid out wholly or exclusively to the purpose of carrying on business. The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD : The principle of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively lay out for the purpose Of the business, reasonableness of the expenditure should be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not (1) (2) (2). [75 D] The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in case the amount of money laid out or spent wholly or exclusively towards the purpose of business of the assesee is entitled to consider the extent of his business, the nature of the duties to be performed and special aptitude of the employee, future prospects of extension by the business and a host of other related circumstances. [75 E] The principle that the rate of 121/2 % commission was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee within the meaning of section 10(1)(xv) is not the function of the Tribunal to determine the remuneration which in their view should be paid to an employee of the assessee. It was also pointed out in that case that an employer in fixing the remuneration of his employees is entitled to considered the extent of their business, the character of the duties which in their opinion should be paid from the point o view of the realized from the point where it was old and dilapidated and the special aptitude. The case of the assessee, however, is that a higher rate of commission was fixed for Shri J.P. Vaish because the mill was old and old and dilapidated. It never made profit of even a lakh of rupees in the past and that the rate was reasonable and it never made profit. The case is that a lower rate of commission of 25% was fixed for the purpose by the business of Shri Vaish. The case was that a higher amount of commission was laid out or expenditure was laid out exclusively for the business of that assessee and to disallow it.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On March 7, 1957, the appellant filed a fresh petition stating that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying that the agreement filed in respect of his case should not be accepted and that he and his agents should be heard before the disposal 199 of the case. The Tribunal rejected his application for separate representation. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed his petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting his application to be represented by a person of his own choice in preference to Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and that the Tribunal erred in rejecting his prayer for representation by a person who is a party to a dispute. HELD: (1) The Tribunal committed a grave error in rejecting the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his own volition in preference to the Fateh Singh, and the Secretary of Union. [966 C] (2) The Tribunal erred in refusing the appellant ''s prayer for representation. [967 E] (3) The Tribunal was in charge of the conduct of the proceedings on behalf of both the parties. [968 F] (4) The scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act, when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen. [912 E] (5) The scheme does appear to suggest that the machinery providing therein should be kept in motion to settling only disputes which involving the rights of the workmen as a Class and that a claim touching the individual right of a workman who is a member is not intended to fall within the ambit of the expression "any dispute touching the personal rights of a workmen" in section 2(k) of the Industrial disputes Act. [913 F] (6) The scheme is not unreasonable to think that section 36 of the Industrial Dispute Act recognises this position, by providing that the workman who is an employer may claim to be represented in any proceeding under the Act by (a) an officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member, (b) an officer Of a registered trade Union of which he has a member is affiliated and (c) where the workman concerned is not a member. [914 F] (7) The scheme, by providing, that the workman, who is a Party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represented through an officer of that Union.

The appellants were the tenants in the suit premises. The suit for ejectment was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent against defendant No. 1. The appellants filed an appeal against the decree in the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial Court. The appellants preferred an appeal against that decree. The High court reversed the decree of trial Court and allowed the appeal. The appellants then filed a second appeal in the High court. The High, Court held that the surviving appellants were competent to continue the appeal in view of O.XLI, r. 3 of O.XXII, r. 33 of the Code, that the surviving plaintiffs were competent to do so and that they could continue the appeal even after the death of Kedar Nath and the abatement of the appeal so far as they were concerned under O.XXI, r.33 was not intended to apply to an appeal filed by some of the plaintiffs against the whole decree in favour of all the original plaintiffs and that they were not competent to continue their appeal in view Of O.XXIII applied and the appeal of Kedar Nath was not competent. The High ' Court also held that the provisions of O. XLI, r, 33 were not intended to operate to apply to a case which was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent. The appellants thereafter filed a second revision in the High, Court. The appeal was allowed by the High Court and the appellants were directed to be impleaded as respondents. The appellants thereupon filed a second application in the High High Court. In the appeal by the appellants the High Court held that since the surviving appellants had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant No, 2 and such decree could have been on a ground common to all of them. The High Judge held that the appellants could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in the appeal and that they had abated their appeal in the view of OXLI, R. 3 of the Code and that they should have continued their appeal in accordance with O.XXIV, r. 32. The appellants appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of OX LI, r. 4 of O. XLI, r. 34 are of no greater help to the contention of the appellants that the surviving appellant could have instituted a appeal against the whole of the decree in respect of the rights and interests of Kedar Nath as well. [966 C D] 2. The provisions Of O.XI, r, 4 of O., XLI, R, 33 are of no less help to the appellants. [967 E] 3. The provisions in O.XXVII, r.4 of O.XXXII, r,33 are of no more help to the appellant. [968 C D] 4. The appeal by the surviving appellants is not competent in the circumstances of the case and, therefore, the provisions of 0. XLI, R. 4 of the Code could not have applied to an appeal which was not an appeal against a defendant under the Code. [912 E] 5. The appeal filed by all the plaintiffs as an appeal against O.XXVI, r.3 of O. XLII, r., 33 is of no greater assistance to the contention that the surviving respondents could have been dismissed. [913 F] 6. The appeal against OXLI is not competent under the circumstances of this case and, accordingly, the provisions Of 0. XLI r. 33 are of little assistance to the appellants when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated. [914 G] 7. The appeal of the surviving appellants was not competent in O.X LI, R. 33.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of the tenancy under section 111(g) of the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929, on the ground that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111 (g) of that Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the lease was determined by forfeiture, not in terms of section 111(h) of the Act but on the application of the principles of justice, equity and good conscience, that the forfeiture of the lease caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(a) of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The tenant 's termination of the tenancy in this case is not based on the principles of equity, justice and good conscience. [920 E] 1.2 The tenant ' s termination of the lease is not based upon any principle of justice, justice equity and good law. The mere institution of legal proceedings for ejectment would be tantamount to an act evidencing the intention of the lessor to avail himself of the forfeiture clause and sufficient to satisfy justice, equity, justice, equity or good conscience. The mere Institution of legal proceedings would not be tantamount to a act evidencing the intent of the lessor. [921 E] 1:3 The Supreme Court has ruled in Namdeo Lokman Lodhi vs Narmada Bai & Ors. that 'there being no requirement in English law of a written notice to the lessee of the intention of lessor to determine the lease on forfeiture, the provision of a notice would not be considered as being consistent with the rules of equity, equity and justice, equity. [922 D] 1.4 The Supreme Court had ruled in Namaji Lokman Lodhi the Supreme Court was directly concerned with the question of the requirement of a notice in writing to the lessee. The crucial question for consideration is whether the particular provision introduced in sub section (g) by the amendment of 1929 is but a statutory recognition of a principle of justice equity, justice or good conscience and would not be deemed to be consistent with the principles of law, equity and fair conscience. The crucial test is whether the person who has received notice of the intention to determine the tenancy on forfeiture, has to stand or fall by his submission that justice, equity is the alter ego of section 111 (h) of TP Act in its dual requirements of (a) the breach of a condition providing for re entry and (b) notice in writing, to the lessee, by giving notice in that behalf. The crucial aspect is whether the tenant has to stand and fall by his submissions that justice, justice, justice and fair play is the altere of section 111 of the TP act in its dual requirement of (a). [922 E] 1 2.5 The Supreme Court was not directly concerned with this part of the argument that in the High Court arguments proceeded on the footing that the tenant had terminated the tenancy under Section 111(g), but on the basis of the principles embodied in section 111(b) of the, TP Act, which was applicable, did not, ipso facto, extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the leased lease, by giving him notice in that respect. [923 E] 1 3.6 The Supreme Court in NamajiLokman Lodhi vs Ganga Bai & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Governor on the ground of conduct which led to his conviction on a criminal charge. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the satisfaction under the unamended clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution was not necessary to give the said Shri P. K. K.K. The High court held that the satisfaction was that it was not expedient to give the appellant an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : The satisfaction under the amended clause (2), therefore, that the Governor had to arrive at was that it is not expedient to hold such inquiry. [657C] The satisfaction under section 3(1) of the unamended clause was that the Governor was satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State it was not desirable to hold such enquiry. [658D] The satisfaction required under the proviso to clause (2)(a) of article 310 of the Constitution is that in the interests of the security it is not practicable to hold such an inquiry. [613B] The satisfaction of the Governor under the unamended provision, therefore, that in the Interest of the security the State is not expedient or practicable to hold the inquiry under the principal clause, that clause shall not apply. [659E] The satisfaction contemplated under the unamended section was that in the case of the appellant the Governor had arrived at a satisfaction that in the public interest it was not necessary or expedient to hold the enquiry under the principal clauses, that clause should not apply. The satisfaction under clause (2(a) of Article 311 of the constitution, therefore, was that in view of the satisfaction under section 2(1) the Governor had no jurisdiction to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank. [660F] The satisfaction was that the satisfaction required was that in public interest it is not desirable to give the government servant an opportunity of show cause against the actions proposed to be take in regard to the appellant as stated above. The satisfaction was not that in the present case the Governor had reached the satisfaction that it was expedient to hold an inquiry under the proviso, but only on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry. The satisfaction contemplated by the amended clause was that it had been expedient to hold that in the circumstances of the case it was not practicable to give the Government servant an opportunity to show cause against his action proposed to take in regard thereto.

The petitioners, who were the Shias ' community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, had filed a suit for the enforcement of which the instant Writ Petition had been filed. The petitioners, who are the Shias of the Shias, filed a suit in the Allahabad High Court for the enforcement and enforcement of which they had been impleaded as defendants. The suit was decreed by the Civil Court. The petitioners filed an appeal in the Allahabad Court. The appeal was dismissed by the Allahabad High court. The petitioners challenged the order of the Allahabad High Curt. The Allahabad High Court dismissed the appeal. The petitioners then filed a writ petition in the Allahabad Curt. In the meantime, the Shias had filed a writ Petition in the Allahabad court. The Allahabad Curt allowed the writ petition and directed the Shias to perform their religious ceremonies and functions over the plots and structures in question under the decree of the competent Civil Court for the execution of which the petitioners had been impleaded. The petitioners thereafter filed a writ appeal in the High Court. The Allahabad Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners thereupon filed a writ application in the Allahabad and the High Court dismissed their writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Shias could not be denied the customary rights of the Shia community to perform their their religious ceremonies, practices and observances over the other plots and structures thereon which had been listed as Shia Wakfs under the Notification dated 1st December, 1956, particularly when it was now common ground that the mosque on Plot No. We are not concerned with the question whether the assumption made by this Court was right or wrong, the fact remains that there was no adjudication or decision on the rights of the parties on merits as a result of the final order passed by this Court in Civil Appeal No.941 of 1976. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board on 1st of December, 1956 under Rule 5411(vii) was the Notification under section 5 (1) of U.P. In the instant case, the Shia Community of Mohalla Dosa, Varanasi had established their existing customary rights to perform their respective religious ceremonies and function over the other 8 plots and structures therein which had been included as Shia Waqfs for performance of their religious ceremonies. [523C] 1.2 The Notification dated 1 st December, 1956 issued under section5(1) was the notification under section 5 of the 1936 act by the Sunni board on 1st December of December,1956 under Rule 54 1136 (vii) was not the Notification under s.5(1). [523D] 1.3 The Notification dated 25th February,1944 issued under section 6 of the 1936 acts as a result thereof. [524E] 1.4 The Notification dated 16th January, 1944 under section 5 was the Notification issued under section 4 of the 1936. [526F] 1.5 The Notification dated 15th January, 1954 issued under section 7 of the 1936 is the Notification under Section 5(1). The Notification dated 20th February, 1945 under section 5 is the Notification issued by the Sunni Central Board on 1 st December of December of 1956 under Rule 56 of the 1936 Rules. [527G] 1.6 The Notification dated 17th February, 1943 under section 5 has been issued under section 13 of the 1936 and published in the U.P., Allahabad, and published in U.P, Allahabad, and the Sunni community of Mohalla Shia Central Wakf Board, Sunni, Varanasi. The Sunni Board had published the Notification under Rule 5436 (vii).

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58 under the 1922 Act. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that the loss was not determined as required under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of set off. The assessee 's appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Assistant commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeals by holding that there was no genuine loss. The assessee filed a revision before the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Tribunal held that the claim for setting off was admissible in the computation of the loss under Section 24 of the 1922 act. The High Court held that the assessee had filed its return show ing the loss and the Income tax officer had not computed the loss as required under section 24(3). The Revenue 's appeal to this Court was dismissed by this Court. In the appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the claim of the assessee for set off was admissible under the 1961 Act to the extent that it was a notional capital loss and the Appellate Tribunal had erred in holding that there had been no genuine loss and the claim for carry forward and set off was not admissible. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The assessee had filed a return showing the loss as computed by him for the purposes of the 1961 Act. The assessee had not filed its return showing the losses as computed by it for the purposes o f the 1961 Act and the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim was admissible in its computation of the income as computed by the Income tax Officers under Section 24. [1166G] 1.2 The assessee had also filed its return disclosing the loss as determined by the Income Tax Officer. The assessee did not file its return showing loss as computed under Section 24 (3) of 1922 Act. [1167B] 1.3 The assessee had produced its return showing losses and the Income Tax officer had not assessed the loss as claimed by it. [1168C] 1.4 The assessee had failed to file its return disclosing loss as computed in pursuance of a return filed under Section 139. [1169D] 1.5 The assessee had placed on record the return showing losses as computed under section 24 (3). The assessee had furnished the return showing the net result of the compu tation under the 1961 act. The assessee was not entitled to take advantage of his own failure and reject the assessee ' s claim of carry forward and setting off of loss on the ground that loss had not been determined as required by section 24(1)(a) of the 1961 act, and the claim of carryforward and set off of loss was admissible in accordance with the provisions of sub section (2) of Section 74A. [1170E] 1.6 The assessee had made a claim for setoff against the capital gains under the 1961 law. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage under his own failure. [1171B] 1:7 The assessee had submitted its return showing all the losses as assessed by it for more than four years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed under the 1961 order. [1172G] 1:8 The assessee had given a declaration that the loss had not taken place which he was entitled to have set off under the 1961 provisions. The assessee also did not file the return showing loss. The Income Tax Officer had not computed any loss or passed an adverse order. The Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had not computed anything more. The Appellate Commissioner had not determined the loss as assessed by the Incometax Officer. [1173D] 1:9 The assessee had no right to claim set off under section 24 of the 1961.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), briefly called DTD & P. at the relevant time, the Defence Science Services had three units under it, namely, 1) Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), 2) Director ate General of Inspection (Air) (DTD & P). The respondent was appointed as a Senior Technical Officer on October 13, 1966 in DTD &P. at the material time. He was then posted in the DTD & CP. at the time of his retirement. He was promoted as a Senior Administrative Officer on October 11, 1966 in a Defence Science Service, and was posted in DTD. at the same time. The respondent was posted in a Defence Scientific and Technical Development Organisation (DTD) and Production Organisation (Air), which was later on reconstituted into three dif ferent services as stated above. The respondent, who belonged to another unit, viz. DAQAS, was appointed as Senior Scientific Officer in the Directorate. The respondent retired from service on attaining the age of 60 years. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Union of India has preferred this appeal by special leave. The respondent contended that the Government had power to vary the service conditions from time to time. The High court, however, held that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the enhanced superannuation age to the members of one 24 unit while the same was granted to the members o f the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government had power under Rule 12 in DAQAS and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DRDS which reads as follows: "Other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of service of the members of the service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these Rules, shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect of the service, be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. (2) The conditions Of service of the member of the service shall mutatis mutandis apply to officers (civil ians)of corresponding status in identical scientific institu tion under the Government Of India. (3) The conditions relating to service of the employees in respect of matter not expressly provided in the Service Rules, shall be mutatis mutandis and Subject to any special order issued by the Govt. in respect of such service, be ted. (4) The conditions regarding service of the officers (civil) of corresponding Status in similar scientifics under the Government o f India. (5) The conditions for service of the persons working in the various units, including scales of pay, superannuation age, etc. are the same and those applicable to Officers (Civil ianans) of equivalent status in similar Scientific institu tation under the Government. (6) The conditions governing service of the personnel in respect of whom the age of superannuation of the members was increased, shall mutatis apply to officers of equivalent status under the Government, of India. [723E F] 1.2 The respondent was also entitled to the benefits of the enhanced age of 60, years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. [724A] 1.3 The Tribunal, therefore, held that in spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the age of 58 years.

The appellant was a member of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. He was elected to the Sangli City Municipality on the previous day. The election of the appellant was held under the Act. The appellant filed an application under article 226 and 227 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Judge. The trial court rejected the application on the ground that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine on the ground of corrupt practice and dismissed the writ application. The appellant then filed an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the election petition was barred by limitation and that the High Court was not right in refusing to quash the order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in refusing the writ petition. [975 E] The High Court has rightly set right by quasbing the order of trial court. [976 A] The trial Judge was right in allowing the appellant to be called as court witnesses. [978 B] The trial court was right in rejecting the evidence with regard to the distribution of the pamphlet by the appellant as alleged by the appellant. [916 C] The trial judge accepted the evidence with respect to the distribution by the appellant and found the appellant guilty of corrupt practices. [917 C] The High court was not right. [918 D] The trial Court was right. [1078 E] The trial Magistrate was right in dismissing the appellant on the ground, that there was enough material for the court to come to the conclusion that there was no fair trial of the petition to the prejudice of the appellant. The trial Judge accepted the evidence of these two witnesses with regard to distribution of the first pamphlet and distribution of it by the appellant to the detriment of the appellant materially in the eyes of the voters as a result whereof he lost the election and that the first of these two persons, the appellant, was guilty of trying to arouse religious sentiments of the voters of the particular ward a majority of whom were Muslims.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, its registered office being at Kanpur in the State of Uttar Pradesh, and it carries on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. The petitioner was assessed to sales tax in accordance with the notification dated March 31, 1956, issued on March 31, 1957, as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956, vide Adarsh Bhandar vs Sales Tax Officer (1). The petitioner challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The High Court held that the Validation Act was not ultra vires entry 55 of List II, and that the Validation was not saved by the new Act. The petitioner contended that the Validation act was not ultra within entry 54 of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution, and that it was not a law which the State legislature was competent to enact and it was therefore a nullity. Held, that the Validation acts were not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54 of list II of the Constitution. In the instant case, the Validation Act is not ultra vires, and the Validation Act has to be determined solely on the construction of entry 54 in List II in the Seventh Schedule, and any other provisions of the Constitution bearing on the question. The Validation Act is therefore not ultra vires. The Validation act is not ultra within the saving of the Validation Act. The Validation acts are not ultra vires and the Validation acts are therefore ultra vires.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court and sentenced to undergo from the appellant for the offence under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000 and in default of payment of fine, to undergo further rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant contended that the conviction was bad in law as the appellant was in his early twenties and signs of repentance were seen. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive,uttableeaty molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexually harassed. But here the offender is in his early Twenties and sign of repentation is seen. The present case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [620 E] 2. The appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. The restorative approach must be more enlightened than the blind strategy of prison severity where all that happens is sex starvation, brutalisation, criminal companionship, dehumanised cell drill under 'zoological ' conditions and emergence, at the time of release, of an embittered enemy of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully ' processed into a hardened delinquent, thanks to the penal illiteracy of the Prison System. The current efforts of Governments, Central and State, to reform jail regimen, we hope, will give a better deal to the caged community. [621 E] 3. The appellant, as a 'habitar ' and has a reasonable chance of shaping in a balanced person. In this background, we deem it desirable to superadd to the sentence of imprisonment a few directives to ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a new leaf of normal life. The emphasis is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on furlough, furlough or order, the young Appellant turns a newishing medium. The current steps of Governments, central and State, are to reform jail Regimen, we hopes, will give an better deal to this goal. [622 A] 4. The appellant 's father has a reasonable opportunity of shaping upon his cousin 's wife snatching a tricky opportunity. Even so, the incriminating company of lifers and others for long may be counter productive, and in this perspective, we blend deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment. The assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintains its accounts on the mercantile system. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.7,24,914 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator, 24 Parganas, Calcutta. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the amount of compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assessee, that the amount received by the claimant was not a receipt of a revenue nature. The High Court held that the compensation received by it related to the acquired land which was stock in trade. The High court held that the sum of Rs 7,24, 914 was income arising or accruing to the assessee on the date when possession of the land was taken by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment 1956 57. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the amount was not a receipts of revenue nature. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in the view taken by it and, therefore, this appeal must be dismissed. [723B] The High Court is right in the interpretation of section 18 of the Act. [724C] The legal position was explained in further detail by the Gujarat High Court in Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, The Gujarat High Court was called upon to decide whether the amount of Rs. 7,24,.914 payable to the appellant related to the acquiring of land which is the stock intrade of the assessee. [725D] The High court was right in holding that the amount paid by the assessee was not a deposit of revenue nature, and was therefore, a receipt of revenue nature liable to tax. [726C] The High Courts were right in the decision of the Gujarat High court in Topashandas Kundanmal & Sons. vs Commissioner of income tax, Gujarat [1962] 1 SCR 676; referred to.

The appellants filed a suit against the appellants in the Court of Second Civil Judge, Class II, Gwalior for a decree for eviction from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants filed a petition to that effect in the Trial Court which passed a decree for possession and for certain reliefs. The Trial Court decreed the suit and passed a decree in accordance with the terms of the compromise. The appellants challenged the decree before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree. The appellants preferred a revision petition to the High Court which dismissed the revision petition. The High court allowed the revision petition and set aside that order. The appellants then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. The appellants contended that the compromise was legal and was within the purview of the plaint. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The compromise was legal, that is to say, lawful and was in accordance with law. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise. the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded, and shall pass a decree in conformity therewith so far as it relates to the suit." The meaning of paragraph 1 of the compromise petition is clear and definite especially in the background of the pleadings of the parties and in our opinion it squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of Section 12(1) (f) of the Act on admission of the appellants. [782G H] The meaning of the paragraph is clear and unambiguous. It squarely makes out an case of eviction where the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for ejectment because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law. [785B] The meaning given in paragraph 1 of a compromise petition is plain and unambiguous. The meaning of paragraphs 1 of the agreement is clear and explicit especially in the context of the pleadings and other materials in the case that the tenant expressly and impliedly is agreeing, to suffer a Decree for eviction because the landlord in the circumstances was entitled to have a decree under law.

The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the loss was due to a capital loss. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had suffered a capital loss of Rs 12,00.000/ on the ground that it relates to the price paid for the shares purchased for the purpose of acquiring the managing agency of the company in the Elphin Stone Mill Ltd. and that it was due to this loss that the loss of depreciation in respect of the shares purchased was due to that loss. The High Court held that the amount of Rs.12,00, 000/ as a result of the depreciation of the value of 83 shares held by Elphin Dhar was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he, therefore, cancelled the orders of the Income tax Officer under section 23A (1) and levied additional super tax @ /4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs. Commissioner took the view that the loss suffered by the assessee on account of Depreciation in the value Of 83 shares held in Elphinsstone Mills Ltd., was a capital loss and that it related to the price payable for the shares held in the value. [690 C] (2) The assessee was entitled to claim the depreciation of that value of the stock of the shares sold by Elphinestone Mills Ltd, and the assessee was entitled only to the depreciation of those shares. [691 B] (3) The assessee has suffered a capital gain of Rs. 10,00,00,001/ on account Of depreciation in the market. The assessee has also suffered a capital expenditure of Rs. 9,00,0.000/ in the relevant accounting years. [692 C] (4) The assessee is entitled to claim depreciation of the amount of any other tax levied under any law for the time being in force on the company by the Government or by a local authority in excess of the amount, if any, referred to in clause (a), clause (b) or clause (c) and the dividends actually distributed, if any. [695 E] (7) The assessee shall be assessed to tax for the year in question in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [696 E] (8) The assessee will be entitled to claim deduction of the amount actually transferred to a reserve fund under section 17 of the Act, if any of the shares are not sold.
