The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. The Corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The Corporation without making any rules or regulations in that behalf continued the same practices. Hence the petition. HELD: 1. The classification made by the impugned resolution is discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [723D] 2. The classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 and16 of the Constitution and must be upheld. [724E] 3. The classification can be made among the members holding the same post on the basis of educational qualification. [725G] 4. The creation of selection grade in the same category on the basis o the sources of recruitment and not on the basis Of educations. Hence, the observation is per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice followed till 1988 nor the resolution passed by the respondent Corporation in 1988 nor the Resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Act. It is well settled that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what is done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned Resolution. The principle that in the case before the them the classified for purpose of promotion on a basis other than that in the cases before the them, the classified for purposes of promotion on the basisof educational qualification. does not violate Article 14 and 16 is also well known and permissible. [726G] 5. The principle of law that in the event of direct recruits and promotees are integrated into one class they cannot be classified for purposed of promotion on any basis other than the basis merely of their educational qualification. Hence, it cannot be done except by carving out two classes in the same class of junior Engineers. Hence, this observation is per se incuriam as regards both the cases related to the classification made on the basis that they were drawn from different sources. [727A] 6. The principle is well settled. [728B] 7. The principle laid down in that case while dealing with the relief claimed, do support the petitioner. [729C] 8. The principle in H.C. It is true that in the instant case while dealing in the relief claimed the petitioner Graduate Engineers as a separate category amongst Junior Engineers and give them equal quota like the Diploma holder Junior Engineer. Hence, there is no authority for the proposition that in the garb of the creation of selection grades in the same cadre on the basis thereof the classification made by impugned resolution is illegal. [730G] 9. The principle which is applicable in the instant cases is that if direct recruits and promotee are integrated into a common class of Assistant Engineers, they can be classified on the basis on their educational qualification, if they are Degree holders or Diploma holders. Hence, in the absence absence of rule and regulation the authority cannot prescribe service conditions on the basis merely on the basis it is not permissible in law though the creation of Selection grade in the said category on the ground that it was a case of direct recruits or promotees. [731G] 10. The principle has been reiterated in the subsequent decision of a Bench of two learned judges of this Court in H. C. It is also well settled that the principle of law applicable in the case of direct recruit and promotee is well known and applied to the case before it. [732G] 11. The principle adopted in H. K. K. Kochunni vs Union of India, ; , relied upon.

The petitioner was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Madras in the year 1962. He was appointed as the Judge of the Madras High Court in the year 1963. He was promoted as the Judge in the year 1964. He was posted as the Judge on deputation in the High Court. He was transferred to the High Court on deputation to the High court on deputation. He was later transferred to the Madras High court on the ground that he was not a Judge of a High Court. The High Court by its order dated April 1, 1987, rejected the petitioner 's contention that he was a Judge of an inferior court and that he was entitled to be appointed as a judge of the High court. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the order of his transfer. The High court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner contended that the order of transfer was vitiated by mala fides and that the order was vitiated by malafides. The petitioner also contended that the High Court was not competent to make a fresh look at the matter merely because there was a change in the personnel of the Chief Justice or the Chief Minister of the State concerned. The petitioner 's case was that the Chief Justice of India had recommended and the name had been considered by the Chief Minister and duly processed through the Governor so as to reach the hands of the Chief Minister, of the State. The High Judge dismissed the writ application. The petitioner then filed a writ application in the High Curt. The High Curt held that the order dated April 21, 1987 was vitiated by malafide and that the High C Court was not justified in reopening the matter merely on the ground of mala fides. The petitioner challenged the validity of this order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The petitioner thereafter filed a writ appeal before this Court. The petitioner submitted that the order passed by the High Court in respect of the petitioner was vitiated by malice and that the Chief Minister was not competent. The petitioner further contended that the Chief Secretary of the State was not competent as he was not the Chief Justice and that the decision of the High Cour t was based on extraneous considerations. The petitioner therefore contended that the decision in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of con sultation, the primacy of the position of the ChiefJustice of India and the view that the fixation of Judge strength was not justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. The petitioner, however, contended that the view that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union of India to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of policy and not of immediacy in the matter of appointments to the Supreme Court and the High Court should be in a position to proceed with the recommendation of the Chief Chief Justice of the High Courts. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. The role of the institution of the Chief Judge of the Supreme Court is not justiciable should not be re considered. [1303C D] 2. The role, the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Government. The function of the institution is to be ascertained from the source other than that of the Chief Justices of the High courts in the case of the High Judges and the Chief Justice in the case. The role and the power of the appointment resides solely exclusively and exclusively in th Central Government. [1304E] 3. The role o the institution of Chief Justice of a High court and the power that resides solely and solely in the Central Govern ment is not justiciable. [1305B] 4.

The respondent was appointed as an Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979, authorising him to appoint Enquiry Officers and Appellate Authorities under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi parTrade Settlement dated 19th October, 1966, the undersigned is pleased to appoint Enquiry Officer and Appellate Authorities u/s Order dated February 9, 1979 authorising him to appointment Enquiry Officers and the Appellate Authorities under th e provisions of Chapter 20 of the Biparrati Settlement dated 19 th October, 1966. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of punishment and the direction that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The High Court quashed the order of dismissal and directed that the respondent shall be paid all the consequential benefits. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in directing payment of all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned order was bad in law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of punishment. [723C] 1.2 The High Court ought not to have ordered payment of 'all consequential benefits flowing out of the declaration that it was bad in Law. [724D] 1.3 The course suggested by Shri Shetye can be usefully adopted. [725E] 1.4 The course suggested for Shri Shetyie, learned counsel for the appellant, was that on retirement of Shri U.B. Menon as an official of the bank, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the learned Single Judge on the ground that 'as the original order was without jurisdiction or competence or, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm '. The fact, however, remains that the respondent succeeded in getting the order of penalty quashed on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the High Court for the first time in a writ petition, more so because he had submitted to the jurisdiction of Shri U B. Shri Shetyee next submitted that the respondent had retired from service in 1986 and if the order imposing punishment is quashed he would ordinarily have to be paid his wages etc., upto the date of his retirement. [726F] 1.5 The respondent succeeded in obtaining the order of the High Court by his order dated January 18, 1988. [727F] 1:6 The respondent succeeded by getting the order passed by the High Court on a meretechnicality and that therefore the High Court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. No useful purpose, therefore, can be served by adopting the procedure suggested by Shri Shri Shetyte as the respondent had admittedly retired from service. [728G] 1.7 The respondent succeeded, in getting the orders of punishment quashed on a bare technicality and therefore the High court ought to have remit the matter to it to the competent disciplinary Authority to take fresh decision based upon the report of Enquiry Officer. [729F] 1.:8 The respondent succeeded on the contentition belatedly raised before him by one may carry the impression that the respondent was duped or not not would be a different matter.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, was granted a licence to construct a building on a plot of land measuring about 2.5 acres. The appellant applied for the sanction of the plans of a building or a construction of a building. The respondent, however, refused to approve the plans on the ground that the plans submitted by them did not contravene any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Commissioner refusing sanction. The High Court held that the order of rejection was legal and justified by the provisions of cl. The High court, however, held that the Commissioner had to give sanction for the erection of a building, or the execution of a work unless such a building or work contravenes any of the provision, of sub section(2) of Section 336 or section 341 or section 340. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Master Plan is prepared for the area, before it comes into operation in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have to have an opportunity of sending their objections and suggestions. [696B] 1.2 The Master Plan provides for a particular use of any land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Development Plan, before it reaches operation in the zone concerned, the procedure specified in section 10 would have to be adopted and parties will be given an opportunity of placing any objections or making any representations or offering any suggestions. So far as we can see, it cannot be put to a different use. [697C] 1.3 The Master Plan does not contain a proposal regarding the width of the road. [698C] 1:4 The Master Plan has been prepared for the zone concerned. The Master Plan, prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, does not contain any proposal regarding the depth of the road, but only indicates the width that a road should have, all use of land adjoining that road. [798C] 2. The Master plan does not contain an indication in the Master Plan that any part of the land of the respondents will be covered by a road or portion of a road it is not possible to accept the contention of the learned Solicitor General that there will be any violation of section 14 of the Development Act if the respondents be permitted to use the land, as. asked for by them. [699D] 3. The Master Plans prepared under section 11, before it came into operation in Delhi, are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of it. [695E] 4. The Master plans prepared under section 8, before it is finalized and sent to the Central Government for approval, parties and local authorities will have to give an opportunity of putting their objections or making representations or offering suggestions. So long as it contains a proposal regarding width that a Road should have, All use of land adjacent that road is prohibited for an indefinite period. [694F] 5. The reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 will be that if any particular and definite use of land is indicated in a Master Plan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted. [692F] 6. The reasonable meaning to be placed On section 14 will have no application. [693A] 7. The Master Master Plan, in this case, does not indicate that any part thereof has been dealt with in a particular manner by the Master Plan and, if that is so, there is no violation of section 15 of the Development act. [691B] 8.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No. 2 was the Minister. The appellant No. 3 was the Minister in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant Nos. 1 and 2 were the Minister in charge of the Industries and the appellants were the members of the said Committee. The appellant was the Minister for Industries and the respondent No. 1, who was the Minister, was the Minister and the appellant. The appellant filed a complaint against the respondent No 1 and the appellant Nos. 2 and 3 for the offence of the taking of the bribe. The complaint was filed by the respondent No, 1 on the ground that the appellant No, 1 had brought the money from his home and had handed over the same to Nagindas. The appellant alleged that the respondent No 2 had brought the amount to Nagind as he had brought the same to his home and that the appellant had brought the moneys from his home. The respondent No. 2, the Minister of Industry and the appellant, who was a member of the judiciary, denied the allegation and alleged that the appellant was responsible for the loss of the Government currency notes. The respondent Nos. 2 to 5 were the Minister and they were the members thereof. The appellant denied the allegation. The respondent filed a complaint before the Magistrate under section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code against the appellant No 1 and also the appellant No 2. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint. The appellant challenged the order of the Magistrate before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the appellant Nos, 2 and 3 were the Minister of Finance and the appellant had no connection with the affairs of the State and that the respondent Nos. 1 to 5 were not the Minister. Held, that the appellant were the Minister for Industry and the respondent Nos, 2 to 5 are the Minister and not the Minister for the Industries and that the appellants were not the members of this Committee. The respondent was the Minister only. The appellant had no direct connection with the business of the appellant No and was not responsible for the acts of the respondent No 3. The appellant, who had been a member of this Committee, was the Secretary of the Committee. The High court was right in holding that the appellant did not have any direct connection with his business. The appellant did not commit any offence. The appellant could not be convicted under section 161. The appellant having been a member, the question of his conviction under section 161 could not be raised in the appeal.

The plaintiff was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the plaintiff was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The High court held that the order of dis missal was void on the ground that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. The High Curt held that the plaintififf was not serving the State police as a constable and that later he was again dismissed. The High curt also held that the finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The High ' Court also held that there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. The High " Court, however, dismissed the appeal of the plaintiff. The plaintiff appealed against the decision of the High Court. The High, Court held that the suit was barred by limitation and that the order was illegal on the ground of limitation. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal in limine. [723B] 1.2 The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage as the case is an old one. [724C] 1.3 The authority was also permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. The authority was permitted to take an decision in regard thereto. The authority is also permitted to took a decision in respect of the pay and allowances for the period he remained out of the service because of the his being in Jail. [725B] 1:4 The authority was allowed to take a view in regard to his pay and allowances. [726C] 1:5 The authority was further permitted to take the decision in regardto the pay and wages for the period of the plaintiff remainedout of service because he was in jail. [727D] 1.6 The authority was, therefore, permitted to take additional evidence in regard to this additional evidence in respect of his further orders passed against Kahan Singh subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour. [728B] 1.:6 The High Court was justified in dismissing the appeal of plaintiff. [729C] 1.:729B] 2.7 The High Court has erred in dismissing second appeal in summarily. [730B] 2:8 The High Court ought to have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [731C] 3. The authority Was also permitted to initiate fresh proceedings of punishment in accordance with law. The authority had also permitted to impose only minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of the salary and the other emoluments. The authority, was also permitted, to take a final decision in regard regard to the salary and other emoluments. [732D] 4. The authority has also been permitted to take decision in regard for the period his plaintiff remained out o service because of their being in jail, and to argue before the High Court that the case of the present plaintiff is distinguishable. [733C] 5. The authority should call for records and decide it finally at the stage itself as the case was an old one, and to decide the case accordingly.

The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In the course of its business, the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The assessee was a company carrying on the business in tea gardens tools and requisites. The assessee claimed that the transactions described above entered into by the assessee were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to sec. 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were speculative transactions in nature and were not actual delivery of the goods to the transferee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal held that the sales in question were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the assessee 's non speculative business High Court on reference following its earlier decisions in D. (P) Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, (1) and D. ( P) Ltd. (2) and held that the losses suffered were business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh (1) , and duni Chand Rataria vs Bhuwalke Brothers Ltd. (supra) on which the Tribunal 's decision in D. P. Ltd. vs Commissioners of Income tax (supra) was based, the Calcutta High Court held that the transaction described above entered by the assessee was speculative transactions within meaning of explanation 1 to sec. 30 of the Indian Income Tax Act. The Tribunal relied on the decision of the Calcutta High court in D. K. Mukherjee vs Commissioner of Incometax, Calcutta, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, and held that in computing the profits and gains of business, profession or vocation ', any loss sustained in speculative transactions could not form part of the assessable income. The Tribunal also relied on the decisions of this court in D, P. Ltd.'s case and D. P., Ltd. vs Income tax Officer, Calcutta, and D. K Mukherjee vs Commissioner, Income tax, Bombay, (supra) and held in favour of the assessee. The Tribunal held that the sale in question was speculative and consequently, the losses suffered in speculative transactions were business loss based on two decisions. The Tribunal, however, held that the loss suffered by the appellant in these transactions was business loss relying upon two decisions of the Calcutta and Bombay High Court. The Tribunal on reference, held that in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the transactions mentioned above were speculative transactions and consequently the loss suffered was business loss based upon two decisions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transactions in question were not speculative transactions within section 24(1)(a) of the Act, and that the loss should be treated as business loss relying solely on two decisions, namely, D. P.'s case, D. K., Mukherjee vs Commissioner Of Income tax, (supra), D. P.. Mukherjee vs Commissioner for Income tax, West Bengal, (supra). Held, that the transactions referred to in Raghunath Prasad Poddar 's case were speculative transactions, and consequently the profits and losses suffered by it in these transactions should be treated to be business loss relying only on two decisions: (1) D. P,. Mukherjee vs Commissioner Income tax, Bihar, (2) D. K, Mukherjee vs Commissioner ( Income tax, Bengal, (3) D. R. Mukherjee vs Income tax, Delhi, (supra); and (4) D. N. Mukherjee vs Commissioners of income tax, Calcutta and D.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Pun jab Legislative Assembly. The appellant was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the nomination papers were invalid. The High Court dismissed the election petition. The appellant contended that the nomination paper was invalid because the nomination papers had been signed by the proposers and seconders in the usual way by writing their names, and as their marks were not attested it was not open to the returning officer to refuse any nomination paper on the ground of any technical defect which is not of a substantial character and that the nomination was invalid. Held, that the nomination of the appellant was invalid because it was not signed " by the proposer and seconders" and that the proposer and seconders had not been " signed " by them. The word "subscribe" in the General Clauses Act is not defined but it is equally clear, when the word "substify" is defined and not " subscribe" and also because the " subject " and context " of the Representation of the People Act show that the writing of a signature and the placing of a mark is to be treated differently. The word 'subscribe" is not defined and it is equally obvious that when the word 'substify" can only be used in both senses, then it is clear that it includes the making of a mark as the Act itself does in the definition of "sign" and not as the Act tells us quite clearly how the different types of " signature " are to be made, we are bound to give effect to the general policy of the Act by drawing the same distinction between signing and the placing or a mark (and it is clear from the form that " subscribing " can only be use in the sense of making a signature and as the Act sets out the only kinds of "signatures" which it will recognise as II signing " so called, and the placing and of a mark are to be treated as differently.

The appellants were workmen of the Company. The Company was a registered union. The workmen were dismissed by the Company on September 21, 1972. The Company filed a reference before the Labour Court under section 33(A) of the (Central) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication of a dispute, 344 workmen of the company including the appellants. The Labour Court held that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls on the presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the Company and had totally abandoned the service of the company and had totally lost their service. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the service and had abandoned the service. The Company preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellants had voluntarily accepted the presumption that the workmen concerned had voluntarily abandoned service. [636G] 2. The appellants were not employed elsewhere during this period, still they were absent in connection with the notified strike. [637B] 3. The appellants have been employed elsewhere during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. [638C] 4. The appellants are not employed elsewhere in the certified standing orders by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services of the appellants. [639D] 5. The appellants having been no provision in the certified Standing Orders by virtue of whose absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed as voluntary abandonment by them of the Company 's service.

The appellant was the trustee of a public trust, styled "Shri Tricumji". The trustees of a public Trust, in execution of a decree for sale of the mortgaged property, sold the mortgaged property to one Saheba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. The appellant filed an application for execution of the decree, and the District Court held that sale of the mortgage property which belonged to a public trust was void. The District Court held, that sale of mortgaged property was void, and on that account a sale in execution of the decrees was void. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the sale prohibited without sanction of the Charity Commissioner must be deemed invalid. [982 E] (2) The High court was in error of law in holding that sale of property of a public trusts in execution of decree was not void. [968 F] (3) The High Courts were in error in thinking that the earlier decisions of the High Court, whether of a Division Bench or of a single Judge, need not be re considered by a single Judge. [966 C] (4) The High courts were in error of thinking that the judgment debtor instead of depositing in Court the amount specified in the proclamation of sale for recovery of which the sale was ordered, satisfies the claim of the decree holder under the decree, the conditions of 0. Raju, J. [967 E] (5) The High Judges were in error by thinking that the previous decisions of the Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court were binding upon Raju J., and that the earlier decision of the High court had "no existence in law". [968 C] (6) The High Judge was in error by saying that the earlier judgments of the High Courts were binding upon the parties. [912 E] (7) The High 'Court was in error, in thinking that a judgment delivered by a single judge after due consideration of the points before it was liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court. [913 F] (8) The High "Court was in law equivalent to a Division Bench of a single judge. [914 F] (913 F) The High High Court was not bound to follow that precedent. [915 A] (916 B] (10) The High Curt was in error.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935. The appellant was appointed on June 4 1935. The Government had the absolute right under Rule 56(j) of Fundamental Rules to prematurely retire a Government servant after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service. The Government issued instructions on November 30, 1962 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. The appellant challenged the validity of the said instructions on the ground that the said instructions were inconsistent with the provisions already contained in Rule 2(1) of the Libera lised Pension Rules, 1950. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the Railway Pension Manual was not statutory and had the effect of amending Rule 2(3) of Pension Rules. The High court held that Rule 2(4) of the pension Rules was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contends that the Railway pension Manual was not a statutory rule and the railway employees are only gover 802 ned by the said rule and para 620 of the Railway Pension Rules was void and inoperative. The appellant also contended that the said instruction was ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Railway Pension Manual is different from the Pension Rules. It is a statutory rule. The said para 620 of Railway Pension Manual has no parity with Rule 2( 2) of Pension Rule which is a statutory Rule. [610B] 1.2 The Railway Pension Rules, 1955 and the Railway Pension manual are different from that of clause (h) and (k) of Rule 2946 of the Rules. The said paras 620 of the Manual being executive instructions, the railway employees arc only gover 808 ned by th e said rule and Para 620 of the railway Pension Manual is also a statutory rule, and as such there is no vice of arbitrariness in the Rule. [710C] 1.3 The Railway Pension manual is different from that contained in Rule 2046 of the Pension Rule. The said Para 620 of Railway pension Manual is also in the nature of executive instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2(7) of Pension Scheme. [712D] 1.4 The memorandum is in the nature, of executive instructions and as such it cannot be statutory. [713E] 1.5 The memorandum is not statutory. The memorandum is issued under Article 77(1) and as such cannot be statutory and has the effect of amend Rule 2(5) of Pension Act. [714F] 1.6 The memorandum is, in the nature o f executive instructions but as such there was no statutory provision or a rule framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution which is inconsistent with it. Para 620 of The Manual being executive instruction, the railway employee is only gover 08 years. The said paragraph which has been framed by the Union Government in exe cise of its executive powers under Article 77 (1) of Pension Regulation, 1950, is a statutory provision. The memorandum has not been issued under Article 73 of the Constitution and as such the railway employees is only g over 802 ned By the said rule. Para 620 is in the form of executive instructions. The memorandum does not contain any guide line provided in the Rule to this effect. The memorandum, therefore, cannot be statutory, but is a statutory statutory rule. [715E] 1:6 The memorandum has been issued under Articles 77(1), (2) of Pension Regulations, 1950.

The assessee firm was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1943. The assessee firm was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacture, and sale of Katechu, and the chargeable accounting period ended on 31st March. 1944. The assessee was an unregistered Firm carrying on business in manufacture and sale thereof. The chargeable account ing period was 1 1 4 1944 to 31st march, 1944 to 31 st March, 1944. The Income Tax Officer did not set off the said deficiency of profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st March 1944 and 23rd November, 1942 to 31st December, 1942 to March, 1943 to 31 st April, 1943. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable accounting years ending 31st December 1940 and 31st March 1946 was not liable to be set off under section 7 of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to set off the deficiency only for the chargeable years ending 31 st March 1944 and that the deficiency of profits during those periods could not be attributed to the manufacturing activity between 28th October, 1940 to 31st January, 1944. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the deficiency was only for the taxable accounting period ending 31st march 1944 and that it could not be said that there was any deficiency of profits pertaining to that period could be attributed to that manufacturing activity between28th October, 1941 to 31st April, 1944 and the sales during the chargeable accounting year ending 31st April. 1944. HELD: 1.1 The assessee was entitled, according to the High Court, to set off of the deficiency of profit for the chargeable year ending 31 st December, 1942. [472G H] 1.2 The assessee was not entitled to set set off the excess profits for the assessment year ending 31 March, 1944 and 31st December 1942. [473B] 1.3 The assessee was, therefore, entitled to set of the deficiency only in computing the excess profits during those chargeable accounting periods. [472C] 1.4 The assessee was also entitled to setoff the deficiency of the profits for the purposes of the chargeable accounting Period ending 31st January 1944 and 31 st March 1946. [472D] 1.5 The assessee was a registered Firm carrying on the manufacturing activity of manufacture and sales took place in Bombay, the question was whether the deficiency of income for the chargeable chargeable accounting periods ended 31st March 1945 and 31st march 1946 should be computed on that basis and after set off carried forward to be set up during the chargeable year ended 31st December. The High Court was of the view that the deficiency could be attributed only to the manufacturing activities alone and there were no sales, therefore, no part of the profits realised upon the sales could be apportioned to those chargeable accounting period ending 3rd March, 1944, and consequently, of the deficiency in income for that period should be computed for the chargeable assessment period ending 31 st January, 1944 and after setoff carried forward to set off during the chargeable period ending 31 March 1944. [472E] 1.6 The assessee was liable to pay the tax on the amount by which the profits during the chargeable chargeable period ending 30th May, 1944 were computed on that account. [472F] 1.7 The assessee was required to set off its deficiency of profits in respect of the chargeable chargeable income for the assessment period ending 30 th June, 1944. [473G] 1.8 The assessee was to set off against the profits for that period.

The petitioners who had qualified in Civil Engineering question paper and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified for Civil Engineering examination, had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. The petitioners who had appeared in the written examination conducted by the Public Service Commission, had to be appointed. The petitioners had to appear for the Civil Engineering examination conducted by it. After the written test and the interview, but before a common rank list was prepared by the K PSC as was intened, 8 Writ Petitions were filed in the Kerala High Court by applicants holding Civil Engineering degrees. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions. The petitioners challenged the judgment of the Division Bench of the Kerala High court by a common judgment dated 23rd March, 1979. The Division Bench of that Court dismissed the S.L.Ps. with observations that the petitioners who had already been appointed, should be given an opportunity to appear in a common rank lists after the interview. The petitioners contended that the petitioners had not been appointed. The High court dismissed the SL.Ps., holding that the petitioners were not appointed. The State of Kerala filed appeals before this Court. The petitioners also challenged the judgment in the S. L.Ps. and the Government of Kerala filed a Special Leave Petition before this Court for clarification. The Division bench of the High Court dismissed all the S.C. Appeals and the Government filed appeals before the Division Bench. The Division Benches of the Kerala and the Kerala High Courts held that the petitioners should be given a post, if he had exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he was high enough in the common list for claiming the post. The petitioners filed appeals before a Division Bench of this Court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in dismissing the S.R.Ps. in view of the observation of this Court in its order dated 23rd April 1980 quoted above. [782B] 1.2 The Kerala Government or the KPDC was not directed to prepare a common list. The Government and the Public Service Commissions were not directed to preparing separate lists. But because no common list was directed either by the Single Judge or by the Division Bench, the Government and the public Service Commission of Kerala proceeded to prepare separate lists. The Government of Kerala proceeded on the basis of directions given by the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench was right in rejecting the writ petitions. [785C] 1.3 The Kerala Government and the KPTC were not directed by the Single judge. [786F] 1.4 The Kerala Government were not directed, to prepare separate list. But in view of this observation of this court, it is necessary to clarify the position and give necessary directions. [787G] 1.5 The Kerala Government was not directed, in view of a common list, though no common list is directed either by this Single Judge or the Division Bench in his judgment, that the expression "the common list prepared by the Public Services Commission should be deleted. [794A] 1.6 The Kerala Government had directed the Government and Public Service Commission to prepare separate separate list. The KPSC was not directed either by either of the Single Judge nor by the Division bench. [797B] 1:7 The Kerala Government, or the K PPC was not directed by this Court. [798C] 1:8 The Kerala Government did not find any valid ground to reverse the judgments of the High court. [799A] 1:9 The Kerala Government also did not find anything valid ground to interfere with the orders of the High Courts.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1 was a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiff respondent No 1 and 2 were partners of a partnership firm. The plaintiff and defendant No. 3 were partners of the firm. The partnership firm was dissolved by a decree of the Court. The plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm. In the suit the plaintiff respondent No1 claimed that he was a partner in a partnership business and excluded the plaintiff from the partnership business. The trial court rejected the objection of the plaintiff and decreed the suit. The plaintiff preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The High court held that the plaintiff was not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The court is bound to accept that"it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. It is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. The cases of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be wrongly decided. The cases where some of the Judges who have taken a similar view must be decided. The case of some of such High Courts which had taken a different views must be held not to be wrongly deciding. [620G H] 1.2 The court is not bound to reject such an valuation. The case is not only to be decided. [621B] 1.3 The court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation put by the plaintiff on the relief claimed in the suit. [622C] 1.4 The court is to consider the correctness of such valuation. The High Courts have taken a contrary view. [623D] 1.5 The High Courts in the country have consistently confirmed this right of the plaintiff. [624B] 1:6 The court is required to consider the statement in the plaint that the plaintiff has been ousted from the partnership. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. The cases are of some of those High Courts which having taken a different View must be held To be wrongly decided, the trial court must pass an appropriate orders under Order VII Rule VII of the CPC. [625E] 1.7 The trial court is bound by the decision of this Court. [626G] 1.8 The trial court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter further and remit the matter to the trial court. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The trial Court is directed to take into consideration the statement in paragraph 19 of the plaint that "it must not have been arbitrary or manifestly insufficient". [626C] 1:9 The trial court shall pass an order under Order VIII of the Code. The appeal stands allowed with costs.

The respondent in these two matters and the petitioners in the other five Special Leave Petitions were certain concerns in M.P. assess able to sales tax (hereinafter compendiously referred to as the assesses '). The respondent in these petitions was the State Government. The State Government issued a notification exempting the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industry in any of the districts specified in column(2) of the schedule below. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notification and the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The State preferred a special leave petition in this Court. The State contended that the industries run by the respondent were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate to this effect. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The notification does not set out the conditions on which, and the procedure in accordance with which the Director of Industry has to grant a certificate. [605B] 1.2 The notification does set out the condition on which, the facility of deferring the payment of tax, a special provision in the shape of section 22 D has been incorporated in the notification. [606C] 1.3 The notification does no carry the State 's case further, for what the Director of industries has to grant, is to satisfy himself that those condi tions are fulfilled; he cannot travel beyond the terms of the notification. It is clear that, while a notification under it can be prospective or retrospective, only prospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. [608D] 1.4 The notification does neither carry the State "s case further nor hold it to be ambiguous. [609E] 1.5 The notification does nothing carry the State"s case further for what the Directors of Industries have to do is to certify that the applicant is entitled to the exemption and (b) that he has not opted for the scheme of deferring of payment of tax under the rules framed for the purpose. [610G] 1.6 The notification does nowhere specify the conditions on whic h the Director of Indus tries should grant a certificate (a) that the dealer is entitled to claim the exemption and [609F] 1.7 The notification does merely state that the dealer has not opted to the scheme of deferredring the payment o f tax under the rule framed for the purposes. [612G] 1:8 The notification does only state that the Director is entitled to grant incentives for setting up the newIndustri al Units; and (b). The notification does mention the conditions onwhich, and the manner in which the Director has to issue the eligibility certificate. [712G] 2. The notification does refer to the conditions on whi ch the Director of the Industries has to issue a certificate (i) that the Director has not opted under part I of the scheme of deferment of payment of taxes under the rules frame for the purpose; (ii) that he had not opted for any scheme of defering the payment of taxes; and (iii) that he is entitled to avail the benefit of exemption on the terms and conditions set out in the notification and not on the basis of any further requirements not so set out. [613G] 3. The notification also does not mention the conditions for exemption. [614G] 4. The notification is not intended to include the conditions on whom, and the procedures in accordance with 623 the previous instructions for the said purpose. [714G] 5.

The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts in the Delhi Judicial Service in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service in consultation with the High Court. The petitioners were appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the Delhi Administrative Service. The petitioners contended that the petitioners were appointed regularly in the Delhi judicial Service in consultation and that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis the promotees should be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Delhi or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in substantive vacancies. The High Court rejected the contention and held that the petitioners had been appointed regularly in accordance with qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a) and that the petitioners could not be appointed regularly in a temporary post of Additional District and Sessions Judge by virtue of their appointment under Rule 16(2) of the Rules. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the selections made by the Full Court of the High Court and the appointments made by the High Court were quashed by the High court. The petitioners challenged the validity of selections made by a Full Court of that High Court in the writ petition. The High court dismissed the writ petition and held that since the rule of `quota and rota ' was not followed by the High Courts in the matter of seniority, the petitioners were entitled to be appointed regularly. The petitioners then filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity and correctness of the selections. The High Judge dismissed the writ application. The petitioners thereafter filed a writ appeal in the High High Court. In the writ petition, the petitioners contended that since the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Delhi Judicial service as required by Rule 7(b) and that Rule 7(c) of the said Rules were not followed, the petitioners could be appointed regularly and that the impugned selections were illegal. The High Bench dismissed the writ appeal. The petitioners thereupon filed a writ Appeal in the High Courts. The High Courts dismissed the writ Petition. The petitioners have filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The rule of `equota and roota ' is not applicable when appointments are made under Rules 16 and 17. The rule of 'quota and Prota ' is read with rule 16(1) and in the manner contended by the respondents, it might so happen that a candidate 's position may be placed in such a way that by legal fiction, he will be placed as senior to a person as a District and Sessions judge by national placement at a time when he did not even reach the age at which he or she would have become eligible for appointment. [848B] 1.2 The rule of seniority of direct recruit vis a vis promotees is governed by the rules of uninterrupted officiation in the Cadre post i. e. a direct recruitment who is appointed on the basis of selection from amongst the members of the Delhi judicial service in consultation with High Court as envisaged by rule 16(2). [848C] 1.3 The seniority of direct recruitment vis a vis a vis persons appointed under Rule 16 is governed by rules of continuous length of service in the cadre posts i.e., a direct recruit, who is appointed before a member of Delhi Judicial Service thus promoted, he would rank lower in seniority than the latter in the list of seniority. [849E] 1.4 The rule of continuous officiation is governed by rule 16 (1) and (2) of Rules, which provides that temporary posts shall be filled in consultation with a High Court from amongst the member of the service who have completed not less than ten years of service in a substantive capacity to a temporary post.

The assessee, a firm, was carrying on business in the name and style of "An association of persons". The assessee was assessed to tax in the status of "an association of persons" and in the status as "an association" of persons". In appeal by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income in the hands of Debi Parshad be deleted. The High Court set aside the direction for assessment of the income in favour of the assessee. In appeal by certificate, the High Court held that the income belonged to Debi Parshad and he was liable to be assessed personally in respect of the income of the family of Debi Par pal. The High court held that the Income tax Officer was competent to make the direction for the assessment of the Income tax in the hands Of Debi Parshad. The High ' Court, however, set aside the ' order of the Appellate Assistant commissioner and directed that he may be personally assessed by the Income tax officer in respect of that part of the order of the A appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High, Court, HELD: (1) The Appellate Assistant Commissioner had directed that the order of ' assessment or re assessment may be made even after the expiry of four years from the end of the year in which the income, profits or gains were first assessable. The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the plaint did not attract the provisions of article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act and that the proper court fee to be paid on the memorandum of appeal had to be determined under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. The appellant contended that the proper Court fee to be payable on the memorandum was determined by article 17 B and that the valuation for jurisdiction should be taken to be the valuation even for the purposes of jurisdiction and it was on this valuation alone that the appellant could be legally called upon to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the memorandum. Held, that the High Court was in error in directing the appellant to pay court fee both on the memorandum and appeal. The High court was in error. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to decide the question of valuation of the relief sought by the appellant for the purpose of court fees. The High courts have no jurisdiction in deciding the question of value of the relief claimed by the appellant. The High Judges have no jurisdiction under article 17 B to decide the questions of valuation. The High ' Court has no jurisdiction to determine the value of the reliefs sought by the plaintiff for the purpose for jurisdiction and to infer that the valuation should be taken as the valuation for the purpose. The High, Court has no power to decide the said question. The High Judge was in error by directing the appellant not to pay court Fees on the memorandum or appeal.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was formed in the year 1957. The appellant was the owner of a plot of land measuring about 2.5 acres in plot No. 1, measuring about 2 acres. The appellant, a private limited company, was formed by the respondent No. 1. The appellant had constructed a building on the said plot. The respondent No. 2, a company, was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The appellant and the respondent No 2, a public limited company, were the owners of the plot. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the validity of a notification issued by the NDMC on 18.2.8.1. The High court dismissed the writ Petition. The appellant contended that the said notification was in contravention of Bye law 16.4.8.2 and 16.4, and that the said Notification was in contravention o r. 16.4 of the Delhi Fire Service, envisaged in Bye law 16,4.8, and 16.1.8. 1.1.1.2. The High, Court, however, allowed the writ petition and quashed the notification. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "external wall" is not mandatory. It is a well settled principle of law that a wall abutting an inner vacant space is also an "external" wall for purposes of the said bye law. [610B] 1.2 The expression "External wall" in Bye law 2.27 is not mandatory and that in appropriate cases, where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measures which, in judgment of the NDMC, are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those 610 envisaged by the Bye laws, the NDMC would not be precluded from accepting them. [612C] 1.3 The expression "refuge Areas" is not a rigid standard and that in no case, where the plan otherwise, to keep the requirement of the pedestrian walk way and Podium in abeyance for the present, subject to a written undertaking to be lodged with it by the respondent 1 and 2 to the effect that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmentalal requirements in this behalf is finally decided upon, the respondent 1 would undertake to put up such a pedestrian walkway and Podium. [613C] 1:4.1 The word "external walls" is not used in the context of specific objectives of bye laws 16.4 and 16.8.3.1. [614D] 1.4 The expression "Refuge Areas" prescribes an inflexible, rigid standard and whether the location and distribution of the refuge areas in each floor is a better and more reliable fire safety measure than those specified by the Byelaws. [615E] 1.5 The clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 17.1 is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the NDMC to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure. [616F] 1.6 The clearance from Chief Fire Officer contemplated by Bye law 16 is an additional conditions and not a limitations on the power power of the respondent to satisfy itself, that the building plan provide for adequate Fire safety precaution in conformity with its bye law or in a greater measure.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in liquor shops 104 carried on by him, was a joint family business and that he had a right to ask for accounts of that business subsequent to March 31, 1946. The compromise was made in a hurry, that accounts of the various businesses should be taken up to March 31. 1946, and that he was anxious to run the liquor business exclusively and not jointly or in partnership with his brothers after the expiry of the licence. The plaintiff was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree following upon it. The plaintiff by confining his claim to account up to March 3, 1946, only implicitly of not explicitly, relinquished his claim to the account for the subsequent period. The plaintiff, however, did not specifically mention the 31st March, 1946, and he did not specifically state that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that accounts were to be taken up for March 31, 1945, the date of disruption of the joint family status, but the parties did not specifically say that accounts of all businesses should be up to the 31st December, 1946, that the accounts of the several businesses should be made up to March 30, 1946, the date on which the final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be made. The plaintiff also did not specifically refer to the 31 st March, 1946. On the question whether the cause of action in a suit for partition is the desire and intention of the family to separate from his brothers and to divide the joint family property, the trial court held that the cause of actions in the previous suit was the desire and the intention of the joint Hindu family to separate the account of all businesses from April 1, 1946, was present to the minds of the parties. The trial court held, that the cause for the present suit was the need and intention of his family to separate, that the suit was, therefore, barred by res judicata. The High Court held that the suit for partition was barred by resjudicata and by Order II, rule 2, of the Civil Procedure Code, the suit was not barred by res bar. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The cause of action for the present case was the desire of the plaintiff to separate from the brothers and to split the joint family properties without any reservation and was compromised, the plaintiff having abandoned his claim to accounts in respect of 108 the motor business subsequent to the expiry of licence. [696 B] (2) The cause for the partition suit was the intention of both the parties to give up to March31, 1946, to separate from their brothers and to award monies as found on examination of the accounts right up to March 03, 1946, but the plaintiff did not specifically ask that accounts of those businesses should be given up after the 1st of April, 1946. [697 C] (3) The cause in the first suit was the apprehension of the plaintiff that the accounts were to take up after the 31st march, 1946, because he thought that when the accounts were taken up, they did not specifically care for providing by the compromise decree for accounts of those business being taken after the 1 st April, 1946, he was bound by his terms of the agreement. [698 C] (4) The cause was the desire, of the plaintiff, to separate, from his brothers, and to divide them by metes and bounds and to award money as found on examining the accounts right upto March 31, 1947, only implicitarily of not explicitly relinquished his claim for the subsequent periods.

The appellant was a partner in a firm carrying on the business of manufacturing salt. The appellant was a firm carrying out the business of manufacture of salt. The respondent was a partner of the firm. The appellant had been carrying on the manufacturing process of converting sea water into salt. The prosecution case was that the salt works were carried on in the open air and not in building, that the salt work did not come within the definition of the word "factory " and that the salt worked as such do not come within " manufacturing process " in cl. It was contended for the appellant that the process of converting the sea water into water salt was carried on in a building. Held, that the process carried out in the Salt Works was carried on by the process of conversion of sea water into Sea water by the processof treatment and adaptation of sea water in salt. The process of converting air water into salt was carried out in a building and its adjuncts. The process carried out by the process carried on in that building was carried on there came within the definition Of the word " factory " and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within the definition. The process was carried out by a process of treatment and adaptation, that is, the process of manufacture of the salt works carried on there come within the meaning of the word ' factory " and that no human agency is employed in such conversion. The process did not come under the definition of " manufacturing process" as defined in the Act. The word " factory" in the definition of ' manufacturing process " is also not restricted in scope to buildings alone. The word ' factory ' in the definition is also not confined to buildings alone, but it is not clear from these observations alone why the slate quarries where work was carried on therein. The process, carried out in that building, was not a manufacturing process. The process in the Salt works and described above, come within the ambit of the word factory ' in cl. (k) of section 2 of the Act. [604 E F] The word " premises " in the definition includes buildings " and its adjunct. The word used in the definition indicates that the word " premises" is also not of any relevance for our consideration considering the questions before us. The word factory " in the Act is also not limited to buildings alone but includes buildings. The word is also not wider than the word "premises " in the context of the matters mentioned in the definition. [605 G H] The word ' premises " in cl.(k) of the section includes buildings " but not buildings " and buildings " in the present case, are not of any significance for the purpose of the definition of manufacture of manufacture of Salt Works. The word premises " in section 2 of Act is also a general word which is applicable to both open land and to buildings and its use in this section indicates that the process undertaken by the appellant in the Salt work is carried on in an building. The process undertaken by him in the Salt Work and described above comes within the meaning Of the word 'factory " and as there are no buildings except temporary sheds on the Salt Works, the Salt Works would come within the purview of the word. [606 H] The appellant 's firm to carry out the process of converted sea water into Salt Works is also not entitled to the benefit of the definition. It was for the first time in the written statement filed by the appellant that it was contended that the Salt Works did not come in the definition Of " manufacturing process ' and merely represented that the salt Works did not coming within the definition to ' manufacturing process.

The respondent was appointed as Tailoring Instructor in the Department of Technical Education in 1935 as Instructor in the department of Technical Education. In 1949, the respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere as Instructor in Tailoring and he joined the new post on November 28, 1949. He was transferred to the Polytechnic on November 28. 1949. The respondent was sent to serve in that Department on November 28 1949. The appellant was transferred to serve in his parent department in 1955 56, and he joined his new post on December 28, 1949, and he was joined the new posts on November 28 1, 1949. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication, dated February 2, 1960, made these recommendations in favour of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his absorption in the Department. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the respondent in the Department be given effect from November 28, 1950 when he initially resumed duty on deputation to the Polytechnics and all of them, except the respondent, were absorbed permanently in the Department, of Technical Education with effect from November 1, 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. The High court held that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in the service of the Department of technical Education from a particular anterior date, or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to be absorbed as Tailoring Instructors from the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the case of Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty because the order of Chetty 's absorption was passed in 1951 and that he was not similarly situated because there was a break in the respondent ''s service with the Department ofTechnical Education, in 1955 56. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The respondent 's work in the Department was found unsatisfactory or that he was neither suitable or qualified to hold the post of Tailoring Instructor from the date on whose he initially came to deputation, and consequently, a writ of mandamus, as prayed for by the respondent, should not be issued. [723B] 1.2 The respondent ' work in the department was found unsatisfactory and was implicit in the impugned order, itself. [724C] 1.3 The respondent was not suitable or qualified or that he could be absorbed in that post, is manifest from the recommendation of the Public Service Commissions and is implicit in the order itself. [824D] 1.4 The respondent ' worked in the Department from November 28 1949, till November 28, 1952, and he continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were similarly situated, were absorbed in that Department. [725E] 1.5 The respondent was, in all material respects, in the same situation as K. Narayanaswami Chetty because the orders of Chetty ' were related back to the date on Which he was initially sent. In that case, the Government of the then State of Mysore by a notification dated December 12, 1949, directed that the promotions of 63 petitioners therein from the post of Surveyors as Assistant Engineers were to take effect from that date irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions. Indeed, it has not been shown that the absorption in the department from November 28 was a concession which could not be claimed as of right, and consequently a writ of certiorari, as prayed by the respondent.

The Company was a registered company under the Indian companies Act, 1956, and its managing agents were appointed as agents of the Company. The Company had its factory at Calcutta. The Company claimed that the amount of bonus payable to the workmen was 20% of the effective salaries or wages with a further direction to set on a sum of Rs. 1,46,252. The Company also claimed that the bonus payable for the accounting year 1965 66 was Rs. 65,764. The Company contended before the Tribunal that the amount was not an item which could be deducted from the gross profits for calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found payable has to be added back as allocable surplus. The Tribunal rejected this contention of the Company and held that the amount had to be added to arrive at the actual gross profits for computation of direct tax and that the bonus paid for the accounting years 1965 66 was not an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. The Company preferred an appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the deduction of certain items from the gross profit for computation of the available and allocable surplus was allowable under section 36(1) and that the amount paid to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the Company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable to be deducted from gross profits for calculating the available and entitle the workmen to claim depreciation only in the sum of Rs, 1,46.252. The Tribunal also held that the bonus was payable for the year 1965 66 on the basis of its judgment. The Company challenged the award of the Tribunal on the ground that the Tribunal was not justified in allowing deduction of certain item from the gross gross profits for the purpose of computing the available and adjust the amount of Rs. 65764. On the question whether the amount of compensation to induce the employees to retire prematurely prematurely was an expenditure incurred by it on the ground, that the amount claimed by the Unions was not an Item of expenditure incurred on the ground as claimed by the Union. The Tribunal, however, held that the Tribunal had not properly considered the evidence of Mr. Banerjee, in the case before. The Tribunal further held that the method of computation of the gross profits had been approved by the Tribunal and that the principles adopted by the Tribunal in respect of direct tax are erroneous. The Tribunal however, held, that the payment of compensation to enable the workmen to retiring prematurely was an amount which could be deduct from the gross income for computation of income tax and that it was an item which was expenditure allowable under Section 37(1). The Tribunal also rejected the contention of the Unions that the amount payable to induce the workman to retire prematurely from prematurely was an asset of the Company, and that the claim of the Unions was justified in rejecting this claim of the Union. On appeal by the Union, the Tribunal held that it was not necessary for the Tribunal to allow deduction of certain amount from the gross assets for computation of bonus which was due to him under the Act for the year 1964 65 on the ground it had not been accepted by the Tribunal. On appeal, the Tribunal, on a certificate granted by the High Court, held that it had not taken notice of the fact that bon us at 20% could not have been declared for the year 1963 66. The Tribunal accordingly allowed the appeal and directed the surplus amount of Rs, 65,76,4. The Union preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.

The appellant was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954, and was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. The appellant was promoted to a post of Deputy Commissioner in 1962, and was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on 7 S 1975. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner he was posted as a Joint Commercial Tax officer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of November 29, 1974. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 We do not think that the previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted to a selection post. The appellant also contended that the previous service history of a Govt. servant should be totally ignored, once the appellant is promoted to the selection post. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the previous record of service was not properly maintained and that the Government had accepted the report of the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption and posted him as Member, Sales Tax Appellate Tribunals in the same cadres. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant challenged the validity of that order of the High Court. The High, Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on his behalf that the Government should take into consideration all the history of the petitioner including that part, of it which had been prior to his promotions, 80 We did not think that this was a fit case for interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. HELD: The Government was entitled, to take into account the entire history and history of the respondent including that part which was prior in his promotion, 20 We do not say that the previous period of a Government employee should be completely overlooked, once he was promoted as a Deputy Commissioner. [80G] The previous history of the Government servant should not be completely ignored. once he is promotion, it is certainly odd to retire a Government servant a few months after promoting him to a Selection post. [80H] The Government was bound to take into consider the entire history relating to the allegations against the appellant including those part of it, which was prior before his promotion, 40 The Government was not entitled to take in consideration the entire entire history of his appellant including that portion which was prior as his promotion, 79 We do not see any justification for needless digging into the past. No. 1112 dated September 19, 1975, Commercial Taxes Religious Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Nadu is quashed. The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. [80A] The appellant will also be reinstated in his service and paid arrears of salary payable to him under rules.
