The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Act having its registered place of business at Calcutta. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1941, the appellant was required to furnish declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The appellant filed a return of the said sales made to it. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim. The appellant contended that under section 5(1)(a)(i) of the Act, the furnishing of the declaration forms by the purchasing dealer was a condition for claiming the exemption thereunder. Held, that the proviso to the said sub section (ii) of section 5(3)(a)(iii) of the said Act in effect exempts a specified turnover of a dealer from sales tax. The proviso to the aforesaid sub section (i) of section 6 of the Act in effect excludes a specified turnover from sales tax, and that the proviso is only directory and not mandatory. The proviso is not intended to give a guide for amending the relevant provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder, but does not provide any guide for amending them. The proviso, therefore, imposes a condition on a dealer for claiming the benefit of exemption. The proviso does not provide for a guide for amendment of the relevant provisions. The proviso merely provides for a guide to amend the relevant provisions and the rules making thereunder. The proviso cannot be strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purposes mentioned in the said sub clause. 27A which, according to the learned counsel, indicates that the proviso imposes a condition. The proviso also does not provide a guide for interpreting them. The language of the proviso is not mandatory and it is not mandatory. It is not mandatory, but only directory. The proviso has to be strictly complied. The proviso must be strictly complied, and if it is substantially compiled with. The proviso imposes a restriction on a dealer to produce a true declaration in writing by the purchasing dealers or by such responsible person as may be authorized in writing in this behalf by such dealer that the goods in question are specified in the purchasing dealer 's certificate of registration as being required for resale by him or in the execution of any contract. The proviso makes all the difference, for it is the proviso that imposes the condition. The said proviso is not meant to give a guidance for amending the provisions of the statute and the rules framed thereunder, but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned. The proviso therefore does not provide that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. The proviso only provides for the exemption in respect of certain sales to a registered dealer of goods of the class or classes specified in the certificate of registration of the dealer as being intended for the purposes specified in the section. That is the proviso which is not mandatory but only directory and does not provide an guide for amending it. The proviso provides for the guidance of amending the relevant provision of the Act. The proviso further provides that the person seeking the exemption shall produce a true copy of the declaration form in writing by such dealer and r. 27A with those of section 5 (2)(a) (ii) thereof enjoins on a dealer not to accept and on the purchasing dealer not to give a declaration except in the form prescribed. The proviso thus does not provide the guide for amending a relevant provision of section 5 of the Act but does not give any guidance for construing them. The said provision is not mandatory or directory. The language used in the proviso is clear and unambiguous.

The petitioners were convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Patna Central in connection with a case under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The Additional Sessions Judge dismissed the petitioners 's bail application and the third by the State of Bihar. The State filed an appeal against the order of the Additional Sessions judge. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The State preferred an appeal to this Court. The petitioners contended that the under trial prisoners whose names and particulars were given in the list filed by Mrs. It was only if these particulas are furnished to us that they were unable to engage a lawyer who would apprise them of their right to apply for bail and opposing remand provided that no objection is raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for bail is made, the Magistrates should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad guidelines indicated by us in our judgment dated 12th February, 1979. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. The State is also under a constitutional obligation to provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail and oppose remand provided that any application for Bail is made, The Magistrates or the Sessions Courts, as the case may be, should dispose of such of those cases as have been pending investigation for more than six months, if convicted, for the offences with which they are charged. The appellant was the landlord and the respondent a protected tenant. The appellant filed an application under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The High Court allowed the application of the appellant and held that the notice under section 34(1) of the Act was merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlord to terminate the tenancy. The appellant contended that the notice having been given before the Amending Act came into force, the further limitation put on the right of the landlord by subs. (2 A) on the right to terminate the lease was to be applied, in case of notices given before the amending Act came into operation. Held, that the right to termination of tenancy was accrued when the notice was given, the law existing on the date of notice. The right to terminate a tenancy having arisen when the notice is given, the crucial date is not the date of the notice but the date on which the right to terminating the tenancy is perfected, namely, the day on which the tenancy actually terminates in consequence of the notice given to terminate, it. The right of the tenant to terminate the contractual tenancy was extinguished by the notice will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right of landlord in the matter of the termination of tenancy. The right was extinguished by a notice to the tenant. The right, if any, was extinguished by an amendment to the present section. The right is always open to the landlord not to carry out his intention.

The petitioners also say that they were wrongly deprived of his rights in the houses by the action taken by the Custodian. The assessee company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee company was carrying on business in the business of manufacturing and selling of various items of machinery, plant and machinery. The assessee was a company carrying on business as a dealer in various items of goods and business. The assessee claimed that the accumulated profit will not include current profits for the purpose of section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the accumulated profits were for the purpose for section 2(7A)(e). The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to apply to the Appellate Tribunal for a reference of those questions of law which arose on its submission negatived the first question in the affirmative and the second question in the negative. The assessee appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2(8A)(e), means profits which have accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting year in which the loans were advanced to the assessee. [950 A B] 2. The expression 'accumulated profit' in section 2 (8A)(a) of the Income Tax Act is not confined to the question whether accumulated profits can take in current profits. [951 A B] 3. The expression used in the clause must mean profits which have accrued prior to the assessment year of which income profits were been assessed, while the current profit would include current profits. The expression must mean profits, which have accumulated subsequent to the accounting years of which the Income profits were being computed, while current profits would mean the income profits of the business. [952 A B] 4. The expression in the context of the clause must be construed as including current profits for purposes of section 2 (7A)(a). [950 B] 5. The expression is used here for convenience to ask for a reference to the High Court. [956 C] 6. The expression means profits which has accumulated prior to its accounting year of the assessee because no reference application was made by the assessee. In every case, it is open to the non applicant, in the event of the Appellate Tribunal agreeing to refer the case to the High court, to ask for the reference of those question of law also which arise on its submissions negatived in appeal by the Appellate Tribunal. [957 D] 7. The form of reference application prescribed by rule 48 of the Income tax Rules, 1962 specifically requires the applicant to state the questions of law arising on its submissions denied in appeal by it, in the case of the Appellate Authority. [960 E] 8. The form prescribed by rule 49 of the Incometax Rules, 1962 clearly requires the applicant who is entitled to specify the questions of fact which he desires to be referred to the High Courts.

The respondents were tenants of the lands in question. The respondents claimed to have been settled on the plaintiff by the Maharaja of Burdwan to the Rajgunj Asthal, and that the claim of the plaintiff was barred by limitation. The District Munsif held that the suit lands were Mal lands within the zamindari of Burdwan, and that there had been a permanent Mokarrari grant of those lands by the Maharaja to the Rajounj Asthal. The District Judge held that the defendants were not entitled to claim any compensation for the period of the years in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the documents on which the defendants claimed to have dealt with the properties as owners under assertion of an adverse title were not proved to relate to the suit lands, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent, and that, therefore, the claim of adverse possession was barred by reason of article 131 of the Limitation Act. Held, that the documents relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they held under a Lakheraj grant were not shown to relate to a grant by the owner entitled to the land, that the status of the Asthal had become extinguished by adverse possession for long over the statutory period, that the document was not proved to be a valid document, and that it was sufficient to sustain a presumption of a lost grant. The documents relied on were not shown by the defendants to relate to their suit lands. The documents on which they relied were not shown as containing assertions, that they held on a Lakheaj grant, and that they were not shown in the record of rights published during the settlement in 1931, that they were tenants of lands for over 200 years under assertion of title without challenge, that the character of the document was one of the landlord and tenant. The documents were not shown either to relate to any suit lands, or to any other suit or proceedings. The documents did not relate to the suits, and the suits were within time from that date. The documents could not be said to relate to such suit lands.

The appellant was the owner of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ out of which Rs. 5,000/ were paid as earnest money and a further amount of Rs. 5.000/ was paid as earnest amount and a further sum of Rs. 2,000/ was payable as earnest money. The trial Court held that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist and therefore ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Tenancy Act. The High Court was of the view that it being an incidental issue in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of agricultural land governed by the provisions of the Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1976, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question arising in a properly constituted civil suit cognizable by the Civil Court would alone be barred under section 85A of the Tenancy act. The High court was of the opinion that it being a incidental issue in the suit, the jurisdiction to decide or dealwith any question arising under the Tenancy Act would alone be ousted because the issue is not required to be decided or dealt with under the Tenancy law. The High ' Court was of opinion that it was an incidental issue and subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the tenancy Act that the issue is required to be settled, decided or dealt by the competent authority under the Tenancy ( Amendment) Act, 1977. The High Curt held that it being merely an incidental issue, it will have to be referred to the competent authority for deciding the issue and upon the reference being answered back, to dispose of the suit in accordance with the decision of the competent authority. The High, Court was of further view that the jurisdiction of Civil Court to decide or dispose of the suits would alone be bar and it, will have to take recourse to the provision contained in section 85A for reference of the issue to the competent authorities under the Tenancy Law. The High "Court was of the further view that if upon assertion and denial and consequent contest an issue arises in the context of the provisions of Tenancy Act and the Civil Court is under a statutory obligation to refer such issue to the appropriate authority under the Land Revenue Act, the jurisdiction would be barred and it, would have to be refer to the competent Authority under the Tenancy act and the civil Court will have to decide the issue or the Civil Court will have jurisdiction to decide the same and upon the Reference being answered back. The High Courts were of the view, that if upon submission and denial and consequential contest an issue arising in a duly constituted civil suit, the Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts to settle, decided or deal with the same would be barred. The High courts were of the opinion, that it being the an incidental issue arising in an incidental manner in a civil suit cognizable before a civil Court having jurisdiction to decide and deal with the issue would not be ousted because it arises in an incidental way in a civil case cognizable by the civil Court having Jurisdiction to entertain the same. The High High Court was also of the view. that the jurisdiction to settle, deciding or deal with a question arising in an ancillary or subsidiary issue which is required tobe settled, decided and dealt with by the competent authorities constituted under the Tenancy Acts would alone be excluded because the issue was not required tobe decided or dealt under the Tenancy laws. The High curt was of the firm view that the Civil Court was competent to settle, determine or deal with such issues under the Tenancy Laws.

The assessee company was a textile mill. The assessee company was carrying on the business of heavy engineering. The assessee was carrying on its business of heavy Engineering. The assessee claimed exemption under section 15C of the Act on the ground that the said section 15C was not formed out of the already existing business of the assessee. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the above facts held that the two industrial undertakings were formed by reconstruction of the business already in existence and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section15C. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the said two industrial undertakings are formed by reconstruction and hence the appellant was not entitled (1) 765 to exemption under Section 15C of The Income tax Act, 1922, applied. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to exemption from tax under section 15 C of the Act. The High Court held that the three industrial undertakings were constituted by reconstruction of business already in exist and hence the Income tax Officer was right in holding that the two undertakings were formed out of reconstruction of the assessee 's business already in existing and hence the Appellant was not entitled for exemption under section 14C. The High court held that the finding of the Tribunal that the two new undertakings were formed is not correct. The High ' Court, however, held that the Tribunal was right in answering the two questions in the negative and against the assessee. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD : 1. The Tribunal was not right in answering these two questions in negative and against assessee. [776D] 2. The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new industrial undertaking expands his existing business, which he certainly does, would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section 15A of the Act, if that section is otherwise applicable. [778E] 3. The fact of the assessee being carrying on a particular business to set up a new industrial unit on account of which exemption of tax under section15 C may be claimed. The fact, that an assessee has carried on a particular industry to set up new industrial undertaking on account of whose exemption of tax is claimed. The facts that an assessee is carrying on a business to setup a new industrial undertakings on account of whom exemption of tax has been claimed. The finding of the High Court that the two companies are independently producing arti cles which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business of assessee. [77E] 4. The fact whether the two undertakings are independently producing Arti cles which might be of aid, to the principalbusiness but yet the undertaking is distinct and not reconstructed out of the erstwhile business of the appellant. [77F] 5. The fact is that an assessee who by establishment of new industrial undertaking expansions his existing industrial undertaking expand his existing business. which he certainly did, would not prevent him from setting up new industrial undertakings and from claiming benefit under section15B if that section was otherwise applicable. The fact also that the assessee is carrying On the general business of heavy engineer expansion will not prevent him to set up an new industrial undertaking. [77G] 6. The fact the assessee is carried on before April 1, 1948. The fact about the existence of which there can be no dispute, as found by the Tribunal, will not weigh against holding that these are new and separate undertakings. The fact remains that the assessee has been carrying on the general business, namely, the business of Heavy engineering. The fact was that the assessee carried on the general trade of heavy engineering will not prevent the assessee from setting up a new Industrial undertaking on account Of which exemption of income tax under section 14 C would be available to the assessee. [78G] 7.

The inam lands were granted to the inamdars for the performance of services connected with the temple and were within the purview of section 44 B(2)(a)(i). The inamdars were granted to office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within their purview. The inamdars claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdars on the footing that the inamdars were entitled to the kudiwaram rights in the inam lands. The District Judge held that the inam lands were personal inams burdened with services and the order of resumption was therefore illegal and a nullity. The High Court reversed this finding and held that the inams were for performance of services related to the temple and the inamdars had no right to resume the inam lands and that the claim of adverse possession was not established. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the inamdar was entitled to the grant from the Inamdars on the ground that the inam land was not an inam inam inam inam estate and that the inamees were not entitled to the Kudiwaram right. HELD: (1) The inamdars are entitled to the right of resumption of the inam lands against the Government and thereby defeat the latter 's right to resume them. [623 E] (2) The inamdar is entitled to the benefit of the kudibaram rights in respect of the inam land. [624 F] (3) The inam lands are resumable under section 44 B (2) (a) (i). The grant is not a mere grant of a lease of it for a term exceeding five years. No. The District Collector held that the Inams were personal inams accompanied with services and that the alienation was not for performance of service connected with the Temple and were resumable. [626 G] (4) The inam land was resumable to the Government under whom the inamdars held the inam lands under the lease. [628 C] (5) The inam was resumrable under section 44B (2) of the Act. [629 E] (6) The inamees were entitled to kudiwarams and the inamdar were within the ambit of section 44B(2)(b)(i). [629 F] (7) The inamis were entitled to a kudiwarum and the melwaram rights were rightly resumed under section 44A(2)(c) of the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920. [630 E] (8) The inamars were entitled to receive the kudiram rights in the lands under the grant from inamdars. The inamdar was not entitled to resume the lands under section 44 A(2)(e) of the said Act.

The appellant Corporation was a charitable trust. The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The Indore City Municipal Corporation was governed by a Municipal Act, 1912. The Indore Municipal Corporation was constituted under the Indore City Municipalities Act, 1909, and the Indore Municipality was constituted under that Act. The appellant Corporation was governed under the Indore Municipal Corporation Act, 1909 and the Indore City Municipality was governed under that Act by the Indore Municipality. The Indore Corporation was governed in the Indore City municipal Act, 1909 by the Indore Municipal Act, 1959. The Indore municipality was governed by that Act. Under the rules made under the repealed Indore City Municipal Corporations Act, 1909 the Municipality was governed only by the Indore city Municipal Act, 1901. The Municipal tax was levied on the basis of the gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of the costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The Municipal taxes levied under the old Act and the rules framed thereunder on the basis that the valuation or the annual letting value of buildings was to be determined on the net and not the gross annual rent. The Municipal Corporation levied the house tax on the basis on the gross annual value at which the tax was levied. The Municipal Commissioner levied the house taxes at the rate of 7% of the gross monthly letting value at which it was levied. On appeal the High Court held that the Municipal taxes levied by the Indore Corporation were saved by sec. 73 of the Act and that the rate of 10% of the annual letting Value was saved by sec 2(c) and that the tax imposed on the basis was saved and secondly, that under sec. 79(1) of the 1954 Act the Corporation could not collect the tax assessed on the gross monthly rent. The High Court held in favour of the appellant Corporation. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Municipal Tax Officer was not entitled to levy the house tax at the rate applicable to the buildings or lands or both in any official year in which such list was in force. [775F] 2. The Municipal Taxes Act, 1909 was an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the basis thereof was for each such official year and that being so, the list so adopted was in force during the years in question and has to be accepted under section 76(6) as conclusive evidence of the annual let value as also for the amount of tax assessed thereon and entitled the Corporation to collect the tax assess on the gross income. [776F] 3. The Municipal Municipal taxes levied on the buildings or land or both in the official year in question made the entries in the assessment list so adopted conclusive evidence of that valuation and the amount of taxes assessed thereon and entitle the Corporation to levy the tax assessed thereon. [778G] 4. The Municipal authorities were not entitled to demand the tax assessed at the rate prescribed by sec. 2(c). [778A] 5. The Municipal Authorities were not entitled under sec. 2 (c) to levy the property tax at the rates prescribed by sec 2 (c). [771B] 6. The Municipal Act, 1915 was an annual Act and the Municipal taxes were levied on the gross gross annual letting values less 10% of such value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. [771C] 7. The Municipal Acts were not saved and were deemed to have been made under the Act and had to be adjusted in the light of the provisions of sec. 73. [772A] 8. The Municipal Rules made under the old Indore City Municipal Municipalities Act, 1920 were in force during those years in question. [773B] 9. The Municipal Cess Act, 1909 did not apply to the Municipal taxes of the valuation or annual letting value.
